en: *Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Volume One.
Recorded by the Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Zhanran at Fulong.

Regarding the general principles of the Buddhist scriptures, progress in practice is paramount; within the teaching tradition of this school, cultivation is fundamental. This is especially true for this present treatise.

I have specifically expounded upon the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna) as transmitted by my teachers and masters, merely proclaiming and describing it. Since receiving your compassionate instructions, I have never neglected what I have seen and heard;

I have bound them all within my heart and expressed them all in ink. I have repeatedly examined the origins of the Ten Chapters and the Ten Contemplations, and frequently researched the emergence and disappearance of the Ten Objects and the Ten Vehicles.
Furthermore, I have synthesized various treatises to refine and embellish them, while concurrently refuting heterodox attachments.

I have elucidated the *Abhidharmakośa* and sought out both gradual and sudden teachings to harmonize them. I have refuted the fragments of Confucianism and Daoism to expose their flaws. Yet, I kept this solely for my private records; who would dare transmit it?
Now that the maritime calamities have ravaged the east, I have escaped westward. Carrying only the original manuscript, I traveled by circuitous routes to bring it forth.

Upon withdrawing to reflect and advancing to contemplate it, I wonder: could I be ashamed of the obscurity of my words, or harbor such heterodox views that they remain unheard? I must, however, decline.

Upon returning to the *Vibhāṣā*, the original draft was revealed; however, as for the propagation of benefits for oneself and others, there are differences between the extensive and the concise versions. It is appropriate that both the self and others find peace of mind—this is precisely an example of that.

If the conditions and the characteristics of the Dharma were preserved in full, then the transmission and propagation from ancient times to the present would merely suffice to assist practice, with little more left over.

My intention is that if the extensive version is preserved, both paths will be excellent; yet if only the concise version exists, there will be things that cannot be fully reached. Since this is not [the fault of] Heaven...
A single sound from a drum reaches everywhere. For those who prefer the concise, how can they doubt that the extensive is a hindrance? He once said to me:
"There are those who value brevity and focus exclusively on the contemplation of principles; how should one constantly respond to them? To grasp [the full meaning] is difficult to achieve.

Consequently, while circumambulating the Buddha’s stūpa and sweeping the shrine hall, amidst these acts of veneration, he refined the essentials of practice, removing everything that obstructs the path of contemplation or serves merely as embellished literary flourish. All...

All the introductory causes and conditions (*nidāna*) and so forth are not written here; everything else follows the main text. At this time, the extensive has been condensed into the concise, according to the preferences of others.
As for what is omitted or retained, it is for no other reason than to hope that my fellow practitioners may benefit both themselves and others by engaging with these teachings.

Question: For what reasons and conditions was the extensive text abbreviated? Answer: There are ten reasons and conditions: for those of superior faculties; for those of inferior faculties; for those who prefer the concise; [and so on].

Therefore, it is for the sake of practicing the Dharma; for the sake of guiding those above and reaching those below; to emulate the holy transformation; for ease of investigation; to accord with those who seek;
and to universally plant the seeds [of enlightenment]. There are further other conditions that are identical to the *Guangji* (Extensive Record):

namely, this [text] possesses ten [features] which that lacks, and that possesses ten [features] which this lacks, because the former is comprehensive while the latter is concise. This text contains three versions in total from beginning to end. This...
This is the third version, the re-edited definitive text, which is what we now inherit; there is no need to say it is abbreviated.

Regarding the initial passage that speaks of "the clarity and stillness of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*)," these are the characteristics of all existing phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). As for the refutation and establishment of causes and conditions, I shall not recount them further.

I will directly demonstrate the sequence of the stages of the path of contemplation (*vipaśyanāmārga*) by opening up its joints. Although this does not reach the level of extensive propagation and exposition, it is sufficient for investigating the skeletal framework of the ritual practice.
According to the commentaries on the sūtras and śāstras, all are divided into three sections. In the present text, even the main exposition itself is not yet complete;
thus, it is evident that there is certainly no third section for circulation. Prior to the opening of the chapters, Zhiyi’s preface by Zhang’an may serve as the introductory section.

From the opening of the chapters onward constitutes the section of the main exposition. If one further divides the meaning of the main exposition into three sections, then the first six chapters may be taken as the introductory section.

Chapters seven and eight constitute the "Correct" (zheng) section; chapter nine is the "Circulation" (liutong); and chapter ten is the "Ultimate Goal" (zhiguī), which is not subsumed under the [first] three sections. In its meaning, it resembles the "Circulation" section.
Within the preface written by Zhān'ān for the first fascicle, he added details regarding the time and place where [the teachings] were heard, in relation to the first two versions of the text.

The general introduction (*sūtra-piṭaka-nidāna*) should be understood as the common preface; that which follows from the ancestral lineage constitutes the specific preface (*pratiniyata-nidāna*). Once again, I shall treat and describe my own interpretation, following the precedent of the transmission.
This is because the compilers were those capable of hearing [the teachings]. Although the subsequent text contains its own explanations of the names, they may be briefly understood [therein].
Regarding the term *mahā* in the title, there are two meanings. First, it serves to contrast with the mundane and thereby distinguish the "lesser" (*hīna*) forms of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

Second, it preserves the original Sanskrit sound, encompassing its rich connotations. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that *mahā* has three meanings: great (*bahu*), much (*prabhūta*), and superior (*viśiṣṭa*).
These three [terms] may also be interpreted according to all four teachings; here, they refer specifically to the *mahā* of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Thus, we know that from the "General Meaning" at the beginning to the "Ultimate Return" at the end, everything is *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and none is anything other than *mahā*.

Therefore, the explanation of the title constitutes the general overview, while the ten chapters constitute the specific details. Within these ten chapters, there are further internal generalities and particulars, as detailed below.

First, I shall explain the general introduction (*sūtrapūrvamgama*). Although this follows the standard format for compiling scriptures, it lacks the mention of the assembly of listeners; for even if there were those who heard it together, they would not constitute the "testimony of faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*).

Thus, while there are five meanings [in the introduction], here there are only four. The first four characters describe the substance of what was heard, while the two characters "cessation" (*śamatha*) and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) specifically indicate the substance of the text itself.
The two characters "clarity" (ming) and "stillness" (jing) praise the virtues of its essence. Stillness is the essence of cessation (shi), while clarity is the essence of contemplation (guan).

Therefore, the textual essence of this entire work is entirely characterized by clarity and stillness, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus, within this entire work, there is nothing that is not the wondrous Dharma of revelation and manifestation.

The four characters "unheard of in previous generations" mean that those who have heard [this teaching] have described it for themselves as well as for others; hence, it is said to be "unheard of in previous generations.
A generation is conventionally established as thirty years, but here the meaning refers to the continuous propagation of the Dharma through successive generations without interruption.
From the nocturnal dream of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty down to the Chen dynasty, there have been countless writings that have flourished in our own time, filling the eyes of all who see them;

those who entered the gates of Chan and received the transmission of robe and bowl fill the ears of all who hear them. How could one fail to have heard these two characters, *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation)?

Moreover, these two names pervade the entirety of the Buddhist scriptures; yet they do not match the present text, which brings both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to perfection and propagates both principle (*artha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) together.

He explored the essence of various scriptures and condensed the great purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to establish the practice of the ten vehicles and ten objects through quiescence and illumination.
He demonstrated the ritual procedures for "hearing first and realization later," taking both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings as his foundation. Therefore, Nanshan sighed in praise, saying:
Only on Mount Heng did both Chan and Prajñā (wisdom) flourish together; how could the rules of discipline have been falsely bestowed through sycophancy?
The two characters "Zhìzhě" (Wise One) follow the precedent of designating the founder of the school. His childhood name was Guāngdào, also known as Wángdào;

these names were established based on auspicious signs at his birth. His Dharma name was Zhìyǐ. "Yǐ" means tranquility; this was the title the Master established for him, a designation conferred according to his virtue.

Later, when he received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Prince of Jin, the Master said, "Your Majesty has condescended to accept the holy prohibitions; you may be titled 'King of Total Retention' (Dhāraṇī-rāja).

The King replied, "The Great Master transmits the lamp of the Buddha-dharma and is named 'The Wise One' (Zhìzhě). Therefore, let the kings and people within my realm all address him by this title. Thus, the title was adopted throughout the kingdom.
The Sui dynasty has already passed; this is a general account of the time the teaching was given. Since the various sutras are numerous, they are collectively referred to as "at one time.
Now, as this is but a single work, it specifically designates the Great Sui. The Sui received the abdication from the Zhou; its founder was originally a native of Huayin in Hongnong, surnamed Yang.

He first rose in arms against the Western Capital for Emperor Taizu of Zhou, eventually attaining the rank of Grand Minister of Works and being enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui. Thereafter, he ascended the throne.
The era was called Sui. *Kaishuang* was the reign title. *Huang* means "great" or "supreme.
Regarding "Jingzhou and so forth," these are examples of the locations where he stayed. In the eleventh year of the Kaishuang era, he returned to Jingzhou and established a monastery;
it was originally named Yiyin and later changed to Yuquan. This was because there was a spring at that site whose water was white like jade. This continued until the fourteenth year.
In that context, the two matters of merit and wisdom—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—are taught as the response to the kindness of the [Buddha] grounds.
Regarding "compassion being focused": if explained by way of the two conditions of sentient beings (*sattva*) and phenomena (*dharma*), there would be an end;

however, because it is explained through the unrestricted joy of objectless compassion (*apraṇihita-maitrī*), it is said to be inexhaustible. This is precisely the objectless compassion of contemplative practice. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* critiques the four masters of the Dharma.
The verse says: "Possessing great learning and vast wisdom, skilled in speech, he eloquently explains all dharmas and transforms the minds of others.
His practice of the Dharma is like a cloud; his compassionate conduct is like rain. The Great Master possesses these three qualities; he is, indeed, a supreme Dharma teacher."
Regarding "though one delights in [eloquence], it is not exhaustive": there are four kinds of discrimination, namely, meaning (*artha*), dharma, phrasing (*vyañjana*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

Although the first three exist, one must possess eloquence. Although these are words that do not exhaust [the subject], they are also auxiliary speech. Although one may exercise eloquence, it ceases at the end of summer.

Regarding the phrase "as soon as [it] arrives": "as soon as" (*cai*) means merely to have attained. Merely having reached the limit of the perceived realm, the remaining text ceases its chanting; this refers to the tenth [chapter].

From the first major chapter through the seventh, [the text] is opened into ten realms (*daśa-viṣaya*). Reaching the seventh, the realm of views (*darśana-viṣaya*), the others are no longer proclaimed.
The remaining three major chapters may be understood by analogy with the latter three of the five summaries (*pañca-saṃkṣepa*). The latter three realms may be inferred from the preceding ones.

Regarding the realm of overweening pride (*adhimāna-viṣaya*), as it says in the section on the realm of dhyāna: "A person who knows nothing attains the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm and claims it to be..."
The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The realm of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) refers to such as the four fruits attained by a bhikṣu of the four dhyānas;

this includes the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles of the *Kang* (Vaipulya/Āgama) and *Tong* (Sūtra) teachings. The realm of the bodhisattvas refers to the three types of bodhisattvas—those of the *Kang*, *Tong*, and *Bie* (Distinction) teachings.

These include the definitions of their essence, characteristics, and mutual inclusion, as found within the "Chapter on the Partial and the Perfect" (*Pianyuan Zhang*) and within the various realms among the "Inconceivable. "Fu" means "no."

However, drawing from the stream to seek its source, the following is a separate preface. What was previously called "general" (tong) refers to the general meaning while the text is distinct, because it employs specific terms such as *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation), *mingjing* (clarity and stillness), and so forth.
What is now called "specific" (bie) refers to the distinct intent while maintaining the general, because it specifically addresses the twenty-three masters.

Although the general and the specific differ, they concern nothing other than the teacher and disciple, the person and the Dharma; within the general [preface], there is cessation and contemplation. Only...
This refers to the Dharma that was heard and taught; next, it mentions the person who heard and taught it, as well as the time and place.
Therefore, the Dharma previously heard is now compared to fragrance and a stream, so that one may know the Great Awakened One to be like the root and the source.
Alternatively, these may be distinguished in contrast to the gradual [teachings] and other lineages he inherited. Within this, the transmission of the Dharma from the patriarchs is first clarified.
This is because, were it not for first pointing to the Great Sage Tathāgata, there would be no way to list him among the twenty-three patriarchs;
were he not listed among the twenty-three patriarchs, there would be no way to point to the thirteenth patriarch;

and were the thirteenth patriarch not brought forth, there would be no way to manifest [the teaching] at the cliffs and terraces of Mount Heng. Therefore, an analogy is raised, saying "drawing from the stream," and so forth. This is the present cessation.

To contemplate and dwell within the semblance of the final age is like [encountering] fragrance or a flowing stream. The Brahma-voice from the Golden Mouth is that which is expounded by the Perfect Sound;
it is like a root or a source. "To draw" (yi) means to measure or take. To measure its flow, one must seek its original spring; to know its fragrance, one must investigate its foundation.
If one is confused about the foundation, then the superior [delusion] will be conflated with true realization. If one loses the fragrant flow, then...
Erroneous teachings have become intermingled with the Mahāyāna; thus, the lineage of transmission within our own school is indeed worthy of trust. The *Śāstra* states:
"As for 'next, the excellent one,' this is intended to clarify the entrustment of the Dharma. It extensively cites scriptural evidence regarding whether there is a teacher or no teacher.

To speak of 'no teacher' refers to the Dharma realized [within oneself]. The second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: 'I practice without a teacher or protector. To speak of 'having a teacher'..."

"Pointing to what has been transmitted and bestowed as a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)" refers to the act of assigning or distributing [the teaching]. In lexicographical works, this term is mostly written simply as "bie" (separate/distinct).
The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (*Ruìyìng jīng*) states: "In the past, when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared, I was a bodhisattva named Zhòutóng (Jiṣṇukumāra)," and so forth.

Having thus cited sūtras and śāstras to prove both existence and non-existence, he next cites secular classics to simultaneously establish the two meanings of "innate knowledge" (*jñāna-utpatti*), such as [the knowledge] that is without a teacher.
"Because learning is accomplished in accordance with the predictions [of the Buddhas]. The *Analects* states: 'Those who know by birth are the highest;
those who learn and thereby know are next. Here, 'liang' (良) means 'good,' and it also implies 'growth. Worldly teachings do not discuss the causes and effects across different lifetimes;

what logical error is there in citing such analogous statements? A reader must take the sentence to end at the character 'liang' (good). However, whether one proceeds from existence or non-existence, what difference is there in terms of principle?"

However, one must distinguish the lineage of teachers regarding the cause; yet upon reaching the fruit, it is termed "solitary awakening. Therefore, at the ultimate fruit, one may say there is no teacher.
For this reason, one must distinguish between the relationship of teacher and disciple, as well as person and dharma.

"The Dharma-gate is vast and wondrous; it is blue because it reaches the indigo. This is a question posed by means of an analogy. The question asks: "Regarding the two aforementioned paths, where people are divided according to phenomena (śīla) and principle (li), is the Dharma likewise so?

"Hao" (浩) refers to the vast appearance of water. Since the Dharma is already great and wondrous, are phenomena also so? The question concerning the "Heavenly Truth" (Tianzhen) asks about the Dharma of no-teacher;
the question concerning the "indigo" asks about the Dharma of teacher and disciple. Because principle is not something created, it is called "Heavenly Truth. It is the perfection of realized wisdom.

Because it is luminous, it is called "solitary brilliance. Because it is dyed by the teacher, it is said to be "from the indigo plant" (*nīla*). When the study is complete and the task accomplished, it is named "bluer than blue.

As the Book says: "The blue comes from the indigo plant, yet it is bluer than the indigo plant; it is the dyeing that makes it so. Here, I am citing the meaning of "dyeing," not the aspect of its superiority.

"If a practitioner hears [the teaching] that reaches the fundamental source," is the general response. "Fundamental" (zong) means honored; "source" (yuan) means long. If one investigates the Dharma that has been transmitted, one will understand it;
only then will one believe in the person who transmits it. Now, our Master is the patriarchal successor of Nāgārjuna.

"From Great Enlightenment to the Subduing of Māra" is the specific answer. First, it responds doubly to the two questions. If Great Enlightenment is the true nature of heaven, then even when practice is perfected, one still receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

This applies equally to both person and dharma; thus, the relationship between teacher and disciple is established. "Enlightened" (*jue*) refers to great illumination. It is the full possession of the ten titles;

the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is perfectly clear, and the three delusions are suddenly exhausted. Thus, the great night becomes dawn. Furthermore, regarding "the fulfillment of enlightenment" and so forth, the four teachings do not... [text ends].

The same applies here; however, the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) also differs. For now, I shall speak briefly by way of the beginning of the gradual path. It is likewise when practice is fulfilled. Therefore, the practices elucidated in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are each distinct.

Regarding the period of six years from the "Subduing of Views" to the "Subjugation of Māra": he is said to have "subdued views" because he harmonized those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and he is said to have "subjugated Māra" because he crushed the Lord of Desire.
Thus, through six years of ascetic practice, the King of Trees manifested his majesty, as detailed in various sūtras such as the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*).
At the time of subjugating Māra, he spoke to him, saying: "It is only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of cultivation that I have attained Bodhi."

"You have performed an unobstructed offering (anāvaraṇa-dāna) and obtained this celestial retribution; yet there is such a vast gulf between our superior and inferior states. Why do you not feel shame? The deva asked, "What is the proof of this?
The Buddha pointed to the ground with his finger and said, "Know that at that time I was the Earth Deity. I informed the Sky Deity, and the message was transmitted all the way up to the Brahma world.
This is why it is said, "He raised one finger," and so forth.
Regarding the Deer Park and the others: once he had attained enlightenment, his teachings necessarily relied upon specific locations.
These three are cited briefly to manifest the reality of the Dharma. As for the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*): formerly, the King of Vārāṇasī hunted here and saw two herds of deer;

thus it is called the Deer Park. As for Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*): it is also called Vulture Mountain (*Ṛṣigiri*). It is named after the mountain because its shape resembles a vulture and because it is a place where many vultures dwell.

Regarding "from birds": it is called "ling" (spiritual/sacred) because it is the dwelling place of the multitude of sages. As for "Haelin" (Crane Forest): it is located at the Āciravatī River near the city of Kuśinagara.
At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, that forest turned white, resembling white cranes; hence the name.

Since a collection of trees is termed a "forest" (vana), and there were four pairs and eight individual trees, it was called a "forest. Among the two meanings mentioned above, [the former] is naturally not [the case].
Now, the true intention is entrusted to the Dharma. What is venerated here is precisely the matter of the transmission of the Dharma after the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa.

Within this, two meanings clarify what was bestowed by the Golden Mouth (the Buddha). Next, the lineage of the present masters is distinguished. The Golden Mouth clarifies both person and Dharma together;

the present masters, however, present them again through both general and specific aspects. This is fully contained within the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Dharmapada-śāstra*), extending beyond seventy sheets. Should one wish to seek it there...
Go and look. Within the *Lü* (Vinaya) tradition, there are also instances where names are recorded directly without further narrative.
Regarding Kāśyapa’s division of the eight portions of the *śarīra*: the details of this division of the relics are found extensively in the *Āgama* and *Vibhāṣā* texts.
As for the "eight divisions," the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that Kāśyapa emerged from the Pipphalī Cave and proceeded to the site of the cremation. The Buddha...
From within the golden coffin, he manifested his two feet. After Kāśyapa had prostrated at his feet, the cremation was performed.

Regarding the distribution of the *śarīra*, the *Dharmatrānupradāna-śāstra* first divides them into three portions: for humans, devas, and the ocean. The human portion is further divided into eight parts, of which Kuśinagara is one;
this is recorded in detail in the sūtras. Eventually, the various kingdoms all desired to mobilize their armies, but because of the Brahmin of the Gandhāra clan...

Being of even and impartial disposition, he extensively expounded parables and instructions, dividing [the relics] for that reason so that each might return to their own country to erect stupas and offer worship.

As for the compilers of the Tripiṭaka: after Kāśyapa had finished distributing the śarīra relics, he commissioned Ānanda to bring forth the Sūtras, Upāli to bring forth the Vinaya, and he himself to bring forth the Abhidharma.
Next, he entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda. Because he heard that a bhikṣu was reciting a verse of the Buddha incorrectly, he attempted to correct him, but the bhikṣu would not comply.
Thereupon, he took his leave of King Ajātaśatru; when the gatekeeper said the king was asleep, he immediately crossed the Ganges and proceeded toward the territory of the Licchavis.

When the king awoke and heard of this, he hurried to the middle of the river and finally caught up with him. He requested that [the Buddha] enter parinirvāṇa within his own kingdom, whereupon the Buddha entered the *vāyu-vega* (wind-swift) samādhi.
He divided his body into four parts; two remained above ground and two below. He entrusted the Dharma to Śāṇakavāsin, intending to go to the abode of Upagupta to entrust the Dharma there.
Consequently, he sat upon his bed. His disciples did not recognize him, so he raised his hand into the air and rained down ambrosia and five hundred Dharma-gates.
Most of them did not recognize him. Upon hearing the Dharma, the disciples all attained the state of Arhat.
Regarding Upagupta: while still a layman, he had already attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Upon seeing a courtesan being executed for her crimes, he attained the third fruit (*anāgāmin*).
At the time of his initial ordination, he immediately attained arhatship. As for the next two venerable ones, there is no account of them in the biographies.

His remaining life story consists mostly of instances where kings were subdued through debate and subsequently received the Three Refuges. There was a Brahmin skilled in calculation who treated him with contempt.
Regarding "many": he added many honeyed calculations to cause them to know the dharmas of rebirth in heaven and falling into hell, and entrusted [the teaching] to the Bhikṣu Pārśva.
[Pārśva] remained in the womb for sixty years; at birth his hair was already white, and because he vowed never to lie down in a corpse-like position (śava-śāyī), he was named Pārśva.
Whenever he was in the dark, he would take objects by the light of his hands. He entrusted the Dharma to Puṇyayaśas. Yaśas debated with Aśvaghoṣa; Aśvaghoṣa maintained [his position].

"There is a self. Nāgasena said, "It exists according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), but does not exist according to ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Aśvaghoṣa wished to cut his own throat to take his leave, so Nāgasena had him shaved and made him a disciple.

He entrusted the Dharma to Aśvaghoṣa. Aśvaghoṣa composed musical performances; through these performances, he manifested the sound of the Dharma, causing five hundred princes to grow weary of the world and renounce their homes.

Fearing that the population would dwindle, the King prohibited such performances from being enacted. He then entrusted the Dharma to Vīra. The treatises composed by Vīra—[the treatises he composed]—the treatises...

Upon reaching that place, his wrong views were extinguished. He entrusted the Dharma to Nāgārjuna. Nāgārjuna held the Buddha’s sūtras in low regard and instead composed his own treatises to demonstrate that he had no teacher.

Nāga invited him into the palace; during a single summer retreat, Nāgārjuna recited only the titles of the sūtras of the Seven Buddhas. Through this, he came to understand the Buddha-dharma and attained the Dharma through wondrous cultivation.
His body was initially born beneath a tree; at the time of his birth, a nāga bathed his body. He then entrusted the Dharma to Āryadeva. Deva...
He entered a temple of Maheśvara; the deity’s image was made of gold with eyes of lapis lazuli. Upon seeing it, Po glared with his eyes and moved his pupils.
Po said, "Why do you not instruct all things with your spiritual essence instead of moving your eyes? He then climbed the ladder and chiseled out the deity's eyes.
The deity knew his heart and felt no shame. That night he prepared a grand sacrifice and offered it to the deity the following day.

The deity appeared in bodily form, yet was missing his left eye. The deity said, "Your offerings are most abundant; why do you not grant me this eye? The old man then gouged out his own eye and gave it to him.
As soon as he emerged, he reached ten thousand [in merit]. The deity asked, "What boon do you seek? The old man replied, "I have no request for anything else; however—"
The people did not yet believe or accept it. The deity said, "It shall be as you wish. Thereupon, he extensively refuted all heterodox arguments. He entrusted the Dharma to Rāhula.
A certain non-Buddhist had composed a book of demon names that was obscure and difficult to decipher; upon hearing it, Rāhula understood it all. The non-Buddhist sighed in admiration and submission.
He then entrusted the Dharma to Saṃghanandin. Nandin, being an Arhat, spoke a verse, saying: "Of the lineage of the Wheel-Turner..."
Born in the middle [existence], he was able to enter *nirvāṇa*. He was neither a Buddha nor an Arhat, nor was he a *pratyekabuddha*.
An Arhat, not recognizing him, entered *samādhi* and questioned Maitreya. Maitreya said: "This is earthenware; once broken, it is no more.
As the various sages above emerged from *samādhi* and spoke thus, Ti-jia (Dharmatrāta) understood it. The Dharma was entrusted to Saṃghayaśas; Yaśas—
While wandering along the seashore to beg for food, he spoke a verse, saying: "Action is the foremost suffering; hunger is the foremost illness.
If one can perceive the reality of phenomena, then one shall attain the path to Nirvāṇa. The lord of the city led him inside, where he saw two ghosts bound to the feet of a bed.
The city lord refused to give him food. After the city lord had departed, Śreṇika gave him food, which he then vomited up as pus and blood;

this was due to his past stinginess and greed. The city lord vowed, "Seeing you suffer for this, I entrust the Dharma to Kumāralata. When Kumāralata was a youth, he was already capable of adjudicating legal matters;
he could grasp ten thousand cavalry at once and memorized the names of people, their clothing, and the colors of their horses. He then entrusted the Dharma to Śāṇavāsa.
He frequently sent food to his elder sister-in-law and committed a grave offense. The bhikṣu performed the fire-pit repentance (*agni-kūpa-pratikramaṇa*);
his sins were extinguished and he attained the fourth fruit of arhatship. He alone became a pure master of the Vinaya. The Dharma was entrusted to Vāśubandhu; Bandhu entrusted it to Manoratha;
and Manoratha, together with Tripiṭaka, divided the regions to convert two people from India south of the Ganges who held many heterodox views. [The Dharma] was then entrusted to Nanda.
In the region north of the River Hebei, there were three celestial beings of upright faith who were easily converted; they entrusted [the teachings] to the Tripitaka Master.
As for Sizi, he encountered an evil king who destroyed stupas and monasteries and slaughtered the assembly of monks. When Sizi was struck by the king’s sword, his blood turned into milk.

Regarding the statement that "all these masters were recorded by the golden mouth [of the Buddha]," this means that all these individuals were recorded by their bodily and verbal actions, which were themselves of a golden hue.

Since these venerable ones are all referred to as "sages" (ārya), they are for the most part persons who have attained the fourth reliance (*niśraya*); however, it may also include those who have attained the second and third reliances.

Regarding the phrase "In the past, the King did not establish [the system]," etc., this tradition cites these two cases to clarify the benefit of entrusting the Dharma. As for *kūṭa* (廐), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it means a stable for horses or a shed for elephants;
both meanings apply here. Having completed the listing of those who received the entrustment of the Dharma, the tradition states:

"By associating with the virtuous and good, one is able to hear the True Dharma, which brings great benefit to future lives. This is like the case of Xiang Xi, who, upon hearing the words of a bhikṣu regarding the Dharma, immediately refused to kill.
"I recently visited a slaughterhouse and saw that they still kill livestock as before; how much more so, then, with human beings?
As for those who trade in skulls, there was a brahmin who frequently brought many to sell. A householder examined them, and when the brahmin asked why, the householder replied:
'Kondañña once listened to the Dharma and made offerings to sustain his life in heaven. If even the bones from listening to the Dharma are like this, how much more so [those of others]!'"
Is it for those who listen personally? For this reason, the Dharma must be transmitted.
From the section on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* below, the current master has handed down [the tradition]. Within this, there is first the general and then the specific.

Regarding the phrase "one speaks within one's own mind," etc., this is the secret intention of Zhizhe (Zhang’an) as he recounted what he had received. If one transmits it but does not practice it, there will be words but no realization.
...practice. Therefore, it is called "that which is practiced. Thus, one should know that this entire section consists of the Dharma that has been transmitted and the Dharma that is to be practiced.

Consequently, in the Master’s *Beishu* (Letter to the Disciples), he states: "Regarding *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there is no need for formal transmission. When I privately recorded [the teachings] and spoke them to others face-to-face, I feared my intent might not be complete.

My private record, however, fully encompasses the essential meaning of the text"—this refers specifically to the ten fascicles of Zhiyi’s own commentary (*Chang’an ji*). While the Master was [still alive]..."
The transformation of the world according to capacities is not something that can be transmitted;

therefore, following the section on "the wise of lower grade," the persons and dharmas are explained separately. Regarding the ancestral transmission from the Golden Mouth (the Buddha), it proceeds from the past toward the present; now, the ancestral transmission of our Master is set forth.

Regarding the sequence from the end toward the beginning: this is done for the sake of convenience in citing the Master’s lineage from Nāgārjuna. First, in the introduction, the virtues of the Master are clarified.
At the time of his birth, his room was illuminated with a warmth that extended to the neighboring houses; he had double pupils (*dvitīya-tāraka*), which everyone knew. The *Yùpiān* states:
"The pupil (*tóng*) refers to the eyeball," specifically the small bead within the black portion of the eye. Having completed his studies of the Vinaya Piṭaka, he went to...
At Mount Daxian, he upheld the Lotus Sūtra; permeated by past affinities, he always delighted in the joy of dhyāna. Consequently, he traveled to Dasu and visited Master Si.
Upon seeing him, the Master smiled and said, "In the past at Vulture Peak you listened to the Lotus Sūtra; now you have come here once again."
He then showed him the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda. Upon reaching the second seven-day period, [Zhiyi] entered samādhi suddenly and clearly comprehended the Lotus Sūtra.
The Master said: "This is the *ādyāvartanī-dhāraṇī*, as detailed in the separate biography."

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma Master Daishou and others," this refers to Nanyue serving as the Dharma Master Daishou. After Nanyue had finished transcribing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in golden characters, he ordered [Huisi] to lecture upon it in his stead.
Regarding only the three samādhis and the wisdom of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), there were further points to be consulted and verified; all other matters were decided by himself.
The Master said: "It can truly be said that the Dharma has been entrusted to his minister, and the King of Dharma has nothing more to do."
Regarding the two kingdoms of Chen and Sui: these were named after their dynastic surnames. This was Emperor Wu, Xiao Baixian, who received the abdication of the Liang throne.
Subsequently, during the reign of the young sovereign Xiao Shupao, after entering the Sui dynasty, he followed the instructions of Nanyue Huisi, who ordered him to go to the kingdom of Chen.
Thereupon, together with Faxi and twenty-six others, he first entered the capital of Chen.

Regarding the passage "he passed away while in meditative absorption," this describes his state of practice at the time of death. Before the Great Stone Image at Seokcheongsa Temple, he appeared as if entering a state of *dhyāna*.
At that time, Jirang requested, saying, "I humbly pray that you will show compassion and resolve my remaining doubts.

I do not know what stage of realization you have attained, nor where you will be reborn after passing from here. He replied, "You have been lazy in planting roots of goodness; what benefit is there in asking about 'milk'? Nevertheless..."
I have also dispelled your doubts and delusions for you. I shall not lead a following; I must purify my six sense faculties, remaining merely at the level of the five ranks.
As for where I shall be reborn: my teachers and friends will all come from the presence of Avalokiteśvara to welcome me, just as described in the separate transmission.
Having said this, he sat cross-legged, chanted the names of the Triple Gem, and entered a state of meditative concentration. It was the second day of the eleventh month of that year.

On the fourteenth day, at the hour of Wei (1–3 p.m.), he sat upright and entered parinirvāṇa. Although the Great Master had always aspired to be reborn in Tuṣita during his lifetime, at the moment of death he said that Avalokiteśvara had come to welcome him.
One should know that the guiding principles adapt to circumstances; thus, all may attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "Thus the Sūtra says" below cites evidence for the five grades of the stage of practice (*pañca-avasthā*). This clarifies that although this stage is low, its merit and efficacy are no less than those of the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*).

Next, the citation from the "Dharma Master" chapter serves to certify the transformational activity of the five grades. Because they proclaim the Buddha’s intent, they are called "messengers" (*dūta*); because they recount the Buddha’s cause and effect, it is termed "the work of the Tathāgata.
Next, the citation from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* likewise certifies the stage; initially, it relies upon the stage while encompassing the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Those at the fifth stage who have not yet destroyed ignorance are said to possess afflictions (*kleśa*). The Great Master [Huike] immediately observed their practice and knew they possessed the secret treasury.
Regarding the section beginning with "Next, as for the wise": the one whom the wise received was Nanyue. Nanyue’s conduct and rank were made manifest.
His secular surname was Li; he was a native of Xiangcheng. In his childhood, upon seeing his peers reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, his heart...
Deeply delighting in it, he borrowed it from another and read it alone in an empty tomb. With no one to instruct him, he wept day and night.
In a dream, Samantabhadra stroked his head and departed; the place where he was touched appeared like a *uṣṇīṣa*.
Although he had not previously recognized the script, he was now able to understand it. For ten years, he recited it without ceasing. The tradition does not state that it took seven years.

Regarding the Vaipulya [sūtras], fearing that the accounts heard by the compilers of the transmission might differ, he completed the summer retreat and received the *posadha* (the end-of-summer ceremony). As he was about to ascend the hall, he sighed with deep emotion, saying:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, at the conclusion of the ninety-day period, many attained the Way. Now I have passed these days in vain, having received the Dharma-year in empty form.
My inner shame is profound. He leaned his body against a wall; before he had even reached it, he suddenly and clearly awakened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He attained mastery in samādhi. He fully accomplished the Mahāyāna dharma-gates and the various *pratisarga* (liberations).
Regarding his subsequent service under [Hui]wen of Mount Nanyue, this clarifies the lineage he inherited from Mount Nanyue as well as the conduct and virtue of his teacher.

His original biography has not been seen. The state was called Qi; his surname was Gao, and he was a descendant of Gaohi from Bohai. His given name was Xiang. "Next, Huan" refers to... [and so forth].
He governed Xiangzhou. Because none could rival him in his transformative influence, he was said to be "walking alone.
Since there was no one equal to him in Hebei and Huainan, and because the realization he attained was so profound, no one in the world could fathom it.

According to the record by later generations in the *Guoqing Baibai Lu*, there were nine masters: first Ming, second Zui, third Song, fourth Jiu, fifth Jian, sixth Hui, seventh Wen, eighth Si, and ninth Yi. However—

Huìwén did not state that he had received [the teachings] from Nāgārjuna; however, fearing that the compilers might not understand their source, he now declares, "These are the words of the Great Master," so that they may be deeply trusted.
One should know that although there was a lineage of transmission prior to this, with the arrival of the Master Huìwén, the transmitted version became distinct.
Therefore, he now exclaims, "This is not known by the world. As for the passage regarding "treading upon the earth" and so forth, it means that the Dharma is practiced by worldly people.
It is like not knowing the thickness of the earth; though the Dharma is revered by the world, it is like not fathoming the height of the heavens.

When the Wise One (*Jñānata*) speaks of "discarding the *Cittaviveka-śāstra*" and "testifying to what he inherited," his specific reference to the "High Ancestor" (*Gaozu*) should, according to the Wise One’s own indications, take Nanyue as father, Huiman as grandfather, and Nāgārjuna as great-grandfather. If, however, one speaks from the perspective of Zhang’an...
Thus, Nāgārjuna may be regarded as the progenitor (gaoszu). If "high" (gao) is used simply in the sense of being honored or revered, then it may be applied universally;

for instance, dynasties such as the Han, Qi, and Sui all designated their founding ancestors as "High. Here, too, Nāgārjuna is taken as the founding ancestor, not because he is the most illustrious among them.

The doubter says: "Below [the text] sets forth hypothetical questions; subsequent sections follow this pattern. Since it states that [this master] is a patriarch of Nāgārjuna, the Dharma-gates should not be different.
Yet, since the methods of 'dispelling' and 'establishing' are distinct, where does the principle of teacher and disciple reside?"
However, according to the response from a junior Indian scholar, those who initially cited and commented on the treatise numbered more than seventy schools.

Since the original treatise was composed in verse, what is called the "commentary" (*ṭīkā*) refers to the prose (*gadya*). As for the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, it is a concise outline extracted from the *Akutobhayā-śāstra*, consisting of five hundred verses.
Master Ying of Guanzhong stated that there were several dozen schools that had provided commentaries on the *Mūlamadhyamaka*.
Regarding the *Treatise* (*Śāstra*), which is considered the most inferior [of the three], Hexi states there were over seventy schools.
Yuankang states that in this region there are only four versions: first, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, annotated by Qingmu and translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin;

second, the commentary by Asaṅga titled the *Anu-madhyamaka-śāstra*, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei, though only two fascicles have been obtained; third, the commentary by Dharma Master Rāhula, which is also...
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* was translated by Paramārtha of Liang; it contains the commentary by the Bodhisattva Prajñāpradīpa, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prabhākaramitra of the Tang dynasty.

Since we now follow the tradition of Hexi, it is called "Seventy [Verses]. As Master Ying stated that this is the "lowest" version, its thorough negation (*prapañca-pratipakṣa*) cannot be followed entirely.

Furthermore, in the lower volume of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the treatise next cites the text to provide an answer. The original verses of the treatise contain both refutation (*pratikṣepa*) and establishment (*vyavasthāpana*).

Why, then, do you exclusively use the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* for refutation, yet claim that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are solely for establishment? Therefore, the first line of the treatise states: "That which is produced by causes and conditions."
This is establishment (*pratisthāpana*). The second phrase is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); this is clearing away (*vidhamana*). The third and fourth phrases are again establishment.

Thus, the treatise on the four phrases consists of three instances of establishment and one instance of clearing away. In both the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the preceding and succeeding sections, this text is extensively cited; in these two locations, they correspond perfectly.
The relationship between teacher and disciple is firmly established. As for "ji" (即), the *Guangya* states it means "to unite. Unity implies non-duality.
From the term "Tiantai" onwards, there is a separate explanation of what has been transmitted; therein, first comes a brief account, followed by a detailed one. Regarding "Tiantai":

the astrological division of that region corresponds to the Three Terrace Stars (*san tai*) of the heavens, hence it is named as such. It is a custom in the West to honor names; for example, as a child’s...

The name incorporates the titles of both father and mother; as the Buddha was destined to be born there, these rites were established in advance so that those who admire his virtue might commemorate him imperishably.
In this region, however, it is considered honorable to avoid using one's personal name, and thus people are addressed by the place where they reside.

"Next, they gradually depart," which explains the aspect of practice (*ākāra*). Regarding "like a ladder and a flight of steps": according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a "ladder" (*ti*) is a wooden staircase;

one uses a ladder for very high heights, while for heights that are less extreme, one uses steps (*deng*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "In order to transform and deliver all the worlds, various manifestations are displayed, just like those ladders and steps.
The character for "step" (*deng*) may also be written with the "foot" radical (*zú*), meaning to ascend and tread upon; the version with the "wood" radical is incorrect.

The intended meaning of the text here is precisely that one should apply the "stages" (*teng*). This is because it begins with the human and heavenly realms and culminates in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Regarding the "vajra jewel," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "If a vajra jewel is placed in the midst of the sun, its color is indeterminate.

Here, principle and practice are like the jewel, the teaching is like the sun, the mental capacities of sentient beings are like the objects, and contemplation is like the manifestation of colors. As for "perfect and sudden" (*yuantun*): "perfect" (*yuan*) means "complete" (*quan*).

"Sudden" (dun) refers to sudden culmination. It is like a practitioner who soars through the air: the space near the earth and the myriad blades are of one and the same substance. "Practitioner" is likened to the person; "soaring" is likened to cultivation;
and "space" is likened to the sudden principle. Regarding those of the three grades: although they differ according to their faculties, they all take the sudden principle as their object.
Therefore, these three practices are categorized together within the Perfect Teaching. For this reason, the gradual, the sequential, and the indeterminate are not the same. Because...
These three roots can all be cultivated within a single lifetime; thus, the *Xuánwén* states:

"For those who practice contemplation gradually, they proceed from the initial aspiration toward the ultimate perfection, and therefore cultivate *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) up to the stage of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

From this, we know that for those of the sudden type, both realization and practice are sudden; for those of the gradual type, realization is sudden while practice is gradual; as for those of the indeterminate type, their realization is also sudden, though their practice may be [either].

Regarding "Sudden and Gradual," in the subsequent detailed explanation it says: "The beginning of the gradual [approach] also knows the reality-mark (lakṣaṇa) and so forth. This is said to be "also knowing" in comparison to those of the sudden approach;

it is not the same as the distinct [sudden approach], hence it is said to "know reality. Because understanding arises based on the sudden, it is said to be "difficult to understand"; because practice arises based on that understanding...

It is called "practice. Furthermore, it is said to be "difficult practice" because practice does not occur instantaneously; therefore, it is called "easy practice. Within this, there are five stages (*pañca-krama*), while the meanings are thirteen.
Regarding the five stages: first, taking refuge and receiving the precepts; second, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); third, the untainted (*anāsrava*) state; fourth, compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*);

and fifth, the true nature of reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*). As for the thirteen meanings: within the first stage, there are three each for the wholesome and the unwholesome; in the third stage, there are four—namely, two... [text ends].

The two vehicles, together with the other three, constitute thirteen. Among these thirteen, the true aspect (*dharmatā*) is the principle that serves as the common object of focus for all three types of persons;
therefore, it cannot be considered a limit of difference. Thus, in the subsequent question-and-answer section, it says: "Within the gradual [approach], there are twelve differences.
This is pointed out here in advance so that they may be easily identified later on. As for those who do not reach the sudden [awakening] until the end:

The names of the "Indeterminate" (aniyata) are listed after the "Gradual" (anupūrva), hence it is called the "Prior Gradual. The "Perfect and Sudden" (yuan-dun) is listed after the text on the Indeterminate, hence it is called the "Subsequent Sudden.
Because it may be either gradual or sudden, it is called "Indeterminate. Thus we know that within the Indeterminate, one also knows the Perfect.

Moving from before to after [the preceding and succeeding sections] explains the characteristics of the indeterminate. Regarding "deep and shallow," this refers to the mutual relationship of depth and shallowness among the first five stages.

Regarding "phenomena (shì) and principle (lǐ)," sometimes that which is within the realm is taken as phenomena and that which is outside the realm is taken as principle; the same applies to the mutual relationship between the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), as well as the three *siddhi* and the single *siddhi*.
Although the dharmas herein are numerous, it is only the four *siddhi* and *śamatha-vipaśyanā* that are presented here. This is because, although all dharmas are many, they are essential...
There are only these two. As in the subsequent sections on "settling the mind" (*anxin*) and "pervasive refutation" (*po bian*), one also relies solely on these two.

From the passage beginning with "Alternatively, from the pointing finger," the explanation of the essence of the indeterminate (*aniyata*) also relies on the aforementioned two to demonstrate the model. First, it relies on the four *siddhāntas*.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are the world. To contemplate them as such is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, designating the world as the ultimate truth is called the "two aspects. Next, regarding the application of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*):

sometimes one should properly employ insight while allowing for stillness; sometimes one should properly employ cessation while allowing for illumination. Because illumination brings about cessation, it is called cessation.

It instead becomes contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Because it is contemplation through the breath, contemplation is conversely termed cessation (*śamatha*). Although there is no dullness or agitation, the merit of advancing on the Path is slight;

thus, one must change course in all cases. By alternating between cessation and illumination, it differs from the standard practice; therefore, it is called "unfixed. The four sections below, which analyze the unfixed, refer to these two pairs.
The doubter says: "Let us proceed. Examining the preceding text, the meaning of the initial question is: since these three are identical, why are their practices different?
From the words "Nevertheless," the answer is given, first in general and then in detail. How can difference not preclude identity? How can identity not preclude difference? Let us proceed gradually.

To answer in detail, one should employ the other two [categories] for comparative analysis. As for the fact that the text only contrasts them with the gradual and concludes with the indeterminate (*aniyata*), it is because...

In the stage of "Certainty" (*niyata*), they are subsumed under the fetters. While the two vehicles of the two teachings possess four types of untainted [roots], why does the present text mention only three?
The reason is that, when distinguished separately, they are divided into four persons; however, when taken collectively, they contain three while retaining one untainted [person].

Thus, by citing the collective inclusion and opening up the categories, the three are subsumed into the one. Therefore, this is called the "three within the collective untainted. If one were to suppress the collective for the sake of the separate, then...

There are six wholesome and unwholesome [factors], plus two others, thus totaling twelve. Regarding the statement "from the majority": when the modes of activity (*ākāra*) are contrasted with the principle, they are called by the names of the remaining two because their modes of activity are numerous.
When the majority is contrasted with the principle, the identity and difference [of the factors] are resolved; the meaning of this can be seen [therein].
Following this chapter, the interlocutor again poses questions regarding distinctions by means of three similarities. Furthermore, at the outset, he asks about differences by means of similarities;
thus it says, "They are suddenly and utterly different. Later, he asks about similarities by means of differences; thus it says, "What is called the discernment of distinctions?"
The two questions appear distinct, yet the two answers state they are the same; thus, the meaning becomes clear. Regarding the nine that are not identical:
by excluding the six wholesome and unwholesome [states] and combining the untainted (*anāsrava*), there are only nine. Together with the four indeterminate (*aniyata*) states, there are thirteen.

Next, regarding "all below," this establishes both identity and difference: the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is identical, while the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is different; yet these two are not separate, for in principle they must be mutually identical. Question:

Since the untainted (*anāsrava*) transcends the four [categories], why are compassion and mercy considered one? Answer: Their opening and closing follow what is appropriate; they cannot be standardized in a single way.
The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) also distinguishes three types of bodhisattvas. Thus we know that Nanyue transmitted only the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] to Tiantai.
This is the principle. Furthermore, two practices assist in the perfection of the Perfect [Teaching], and thus there are three.

Therefore, one should know that beginning from the discernment of the teachings through wisdom and hearing, the four types of self-cultivation correspond only to the Perfect; these three are entirely distinct from the three within the Eight Teachings.
Within the Eight Teachings, the *Avataṃsaka* is designated as Sudden and the *Samādhi* as Gradual; yet, among the Sudden teachings, the application to sentient beings is not fixed.
This is called "indeterminate.

Next, regarding "perfect and sudden," this explains the perfect and sudden [teaching]. From "first, the object" up to "the ultimate reality": although both the object and the act of creation belong to the subjective contemplation, the intent lies rather in the objective realm.

Next, one binds the object of focus and then releases the contemplation; because binding is itself mindfulness, there is stillness while constantly illuminating. Because binding is itself mindfulness, there is illumination while constantly still.

Since subject and object are already one, how much more so are cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*)? Regarding "a single form and a single fragrance," although the objects of focus and mindfulness belong to the realm of objects, these terms are used here to describe the contemplating subject in order to clarify stillness and illumination. Therefore, in this school’s elucidation of the Middle Way, it is exclusively...

There are two meanings: first, the departure from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; second, Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Within the context of Buddha-nature, the teachings are divided into provisional and ultimate, thus giving rise to the categories of Separate and Perfect [Teachings].
Now, following the meaning of the Perfect, all are the Middle Way. These forms and fragrances are universally regarded by worldly people as insentient (*nirjīva*);
yet, I now ask: are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the internal body sentient? If they are sentient, why did Vimalakīrti...

Therefore, it is said that they are like grass and trees. All phenomena are mind-only; how could they be separated from the mind by being stubborn or obstructive? Departing from one's own realm, one clarifies the Truth of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*).

The characteristics of the truths will be further distinguished below in the Four Great Vows; for now, we shall merely clarify the contemplation of non-action. Thus, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states:
"Within a single thought-moment, the ten realms are complete. Suffering is called non-action. Since suffering encompasses the ten realms, delusion is called non-action."
"Activity" refers to the accumulation of suffering, which is itself nirvāṇa; this is called "unconditioned cessation. Delusion is itself bodhi; this is called the "unconditioned path.
Following the section on the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it concludes with śamatha and vipaśyanā.

From the gradual [vehicle] down to the inferior [vehicles], one desires to extensively substantiate the Perfect [Vehicle]. First, the other two are distinguished; previously, the two modes of extensive and abbreviated explanation have already been completed.
Now, once again the Perfect is substantiated; therefore, it is said, "further clarified."

Regarding the passage beginning with "As for the thorough comprehension," at the start of the fifth chapter, the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (Bhadramukha), in the old translation of the sutra, Mañjuśrī asks the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha—also known as the Bodhisattva Subhūti of Profound Meaning—with two verses about the meaning of thorough comprehension. The Bodhisattva replies with fifteen lines of five-character verse.

The current text follows the Bodhisattva from departing within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) up to the point where it cannot be exhausted; it abbreviates two lines of text. Regarding the mention of "birth-and-death," this cites the lowest possible station.
Were it not so, how could it manifest the great efficacy of perfect function and the universal pervasiveness of the ultimate principle? Therefore, there is nothing by which it can be moved.

The term "a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) clarifies the shortest duration of time. It is profound without a precipice and vast without a boundary. A "precipice" (*yá*) refers to that which is steep and lofty.

Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgatas and so forth": because their principle is inexhaustible, they cannot be fully described; this remains true even for those at the ultimate stage, let alone other ordinary beings or sages.

From this point, where the Bodhisattva proceeds to the stage of establishing sentient beings, the aforementioned scripture contains fifteen verses immediately preceding this, to which the later Xianshou (Bodhisattva Wénshù) further replied with six hundred and ninety-two lines of verse. Within these, he fully elucidates the characteristics of perfect faith and so forth. Now...

Briefly following that [text]: what is meant by "perfect hearing" (*yuanwen*)? It refers to fully hearing the present text and attaining the perfection of cultivation and realization. Based on the text, one gives rise to faith; faith is the foundation of practice.
However, regarding the wisdom of the three contemplations (*sanguanzhi*), it is fully detailed in such texts as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*.

Question: Within "perfect hearing," the names of the three virtues (*sandeha*) are employed. Faith should therefore rely on hearing. Why, then, are names such as the "three contemplations," "obscuration and illumination" (*zheshao*), and "profound and vast" used instead? Answer:

The distinction lies only in the subject and the object. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely *prajñā*; the provisional (*upāya*) is precisely liberation (*vimukti*); the middle (*madhyama*) is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Illumination is *prajñā*; negation is liberation; the non-duality of both is the Dharma-body. The profound and the vast may be understood through analogy as explained above. Furthermore, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) proceed from the cause;

negation and illumination proceed from the function; the profound and the vast proceed from the essence (*svabhāva*). In the section on the successive and perfect practices, the term "exclusively" (*ekāntika*) is used to distinguish it from the other two.
Therefore, it is called "direct entry. Next, within the stage of the Perfect [Teaching], this refers to the first dwelling (bhūmi), wherein all merits and virtues are fully perfected;
therefore, it is called "ultimate."

Next, within the section on adornment (*vyūha*), there is the correspondence between the principle (*dharma*), the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis (*yoga*). First, regarding the meaning within the principle: the truths (*satya*) serve as that which is adorned, and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) serves as the means of adornment.

Because the subject is able to accord with the object, external activity becomes sovereign. One attains the merit of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the merit of the conventional (*prajñapti*) through emergence from it;

the remaining merits pertain to the middle [state]. This is because the Middle Way possesses both the aspect of negation (*apavāda*) and illumination (*vidarśana*). Each of these objects within the sensory fields (*viṣaya*) has its own...

Regarding the categories—such as the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), directions, and so forth—they can be understood by reflecting upon them. As for the subsequent passage on analogies: "morning" illustrates emergence; "evening" illustrates entry;

"daytime" illustrates both entry and emergence; and "night" illustrates neither entry nor emergence. When it says, "it is also like this," one should apply the aforementioned contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and so forth to establish the correspondence.
Regarding the term "blind and sightless": losing one's light is called "blind" (*andha*); having no eyes is called "sightless" (*kāṇa*). Furthermore...

It is said that one who has eyes but no pupils is called *gǔ* (blind), and one who has eyes but no pupils is called *sōu* (deaf-blind). Likewise, those who lack the conditions for receiving the light of the teaching are like the blind and so forth.

Therefore, regarding the mention of the Dragon Kings (*nāgarāja*) and others: while the definitions of dragons in secular classics and minor teachings are similar, here we rely on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which speaks of the Bhagavān Dragon King.
All that he rains down pervades the six heavens of desire as well as the four continents of humans. Six.
The six stages are likened to the [six] levels, all of which destroy ignorance. The four regions are likened to the four teachings and four gates;

while the four *siddhāntas* pertain to one's own practice, only the sixth is for the sake of others. "Pervading the four" means "penetrating" (*tong*); in the local dialect it means "to complete. As the Sūtra says:

"When the Dragon King manifests his sovereign power, he rises from the Vajra-limit up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, raising clouds that pervade the four continents. The varieties of those clouds..."

The various ornaments of color are explained in the sutra by means of lightning, rain, and so forth. However, the clouds are a metaphor for manifesting the body, the thunder for preaching the Dharma, the lightning for emitting light, and the rain for compassion;
these enable sentient beings to each perceive them differently. Question: What is the distinction between the two meanings of "ornament" (*vyūha*) and "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*)?
Answer: To accord with the principle through one's own practice is called "ornament"; to benefit others through external application is called "establishment."

"The beginner is already thus" is a statement by way of illustration. "Beginning" refers to the First Stage (Prathamā-bhūmi); "end" refers to Wondrous Enlightenment (Sugata); and "middle" refers to the stages in between.

"The Tathāgata’s earnestness," and so forth, serves to certify the essence of the Sublime Dharma (Saddharma), because he taught that people should not be treated with contempt, and because those who receive it experience great joy.
At the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, through both extensive and concise praise expressed by means of words that transcend words, all of this is the Sublime Dharma. It is complete.
As in the commentary (*śāstra*), this is the second fascicle of the first chapter of the *Varga* (Chapter). First, Śāriputra receives [the teaching], which is joy itself.
Next, various sūtras are cited to clarify the seeker; it is because their resolve is great and the Dharma they practice is sublime that this is so.
Regarding "Sadāprarudita and others," this refers to Sadāprarudita, Sudhana’s southern quest as detailed in the *Gandavyūha-parivarta*, and Bhaiṣajyarāja’s practice according to the Dharma.
Flower. [The account of] Puming (Universal Radiance) is like that of the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing); it is fully detailed in the extensive records.

From the time he first abandoned his body three times, he realized that the grace of the Dharma is difficult to repay. Using the four lines of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* as a standard for sacrificing the body, I now borrow that text to illustrate the few by means of the many.
Even over many periods—three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*—one still cannot repay it; how much less can one do so merely by bearing it upon the crown of one's head?
It is merely a matter of bearing [the burden]. Even if one carries it for many kalpas, the body remains; how, then, could one ever repay the grace of the Perfect Vehicle?
To bear upon the shoulder is called *he* (to carry), and to bear upon the back is called *fu* (to bear).

Regarding the phrase "the first scripture, etc.," this cites a brief passage to indicate the full extent of the teaching. Regarding the section beginning with "those who doubt," he requests proof for the remaining two [aspects].
In the subsequent formal response, the "Perfect" (yuan) is cited first because it is the primary intent; thus, the initial text first cites four scriptures, each proving three meanings.

In all cases, the scriptural teachings and their meanings are employed as provisional means to prove the contemplation (guan). Since the contemplation is formed by grasping the teachings, how could the meaning differ? First...

Citing the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, it says: "The Buddha-tree" is named Yuánjì (Ultimate Auspiciousness). Because he attained the Way (*bodhi*) beneath it, it was so named. When the Buddha sat beneath it, it was further called the Buddha-tree.

Realizing the principle of cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is termed the "extinction of nectar" (*amṛta-kṣaya*); this is the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), and thus the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is established.

The realization of the perfection of the Way is the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and thus the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is established. In reality, all four [truths] are complete; they are designated according to their predominance.

Regarding the "twofold" and the "three turnings" and so forth: this refers to the demonstration (*darśana*), the exhortation (*preraṇa*), and the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). From each turning, there arises respectively the eye (*cakṣus*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*);

these are called the wheel of twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāracakra*). It possesses two meanings: "turning" (*vartana*) and "crushing" (*mathana*). It turns for others and crushes their afflictions (*kleśa*).

It is like the jewel of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin-rāja*), which can both destroy and bring peace; for it destroys afflictions and establishes the principle (*naya*). As for the term "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), the *Abhidharmakośa* says: four... [text continues].
One thousand great continents, suns, moons, Mount Sumerus, heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and Brahma worlds is called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a medium chiliocosm. One thousand times this is a great trichiliocosm. All of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously.

Because there are no two Buddhas in the world at once, and because the essence of reality within the great trichiliocosm is free from delusion, it is said to be "primordially pure. Eighty thousand devas were all [present].

The five neighbors were called "heavenly men" (devaputra); they all attained the first fruit (srotāpanna), hence it is said they "attained the Way. Because their transformation was verified as not being in vain, it is said they served as "witnesses.

Next, by citing this manifest case of the indeterminate, it is proven that the indeterminate is indeed indeterminate. Regarding the term "one voice": its name applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, but in the present text, it refers to the Mahāyāna.
As in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the Buddha preached the Four Truths for the four kings; thus, we know it applies universally.
Small. Now, the full details are as found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and other texts. The Buddha has no vocal sounds, yet he reaches all beings everywhere.
As for the fact that both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* state that the Buddha possesses sixty-four tones, these are merely skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding the phrase "fearing," etc.:

Furthermore, let us clarify the characteristics of the indeterminate by way of the four *siddhāntas*: the world of fear, the person of joy, the antidote of wearying detachment, and the severance of doubt through realization of the principle.

Next, regarding those who realize the sudden, the meaning applies across the four teachings; yet, distinguishing the three and retaining the perfect (*yuan*), the four *siddhāntas* respond to the capacities of beings.

Therefore, regarding the statement "all dharmas arise" and "there is no self," this concludes the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]. "There is no self that creates or receives" concludes that [the self] does not exist;

"good and evil are not forgotten" concludes that it is not non-existent. This conclusion also distinguishes [this teaching] from the three [other vehicles]; the application of these principles can be seen accordingly.
Next, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) to prove the gradual [path]: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks, "How does a beginner bodhisattva practice?

It mentions the three categories of practice, learning, and so forth. Some say that while the words differ, the meaning is the same; others say it refers to the beginning, middle, and end. Regarding the "mani jewel," the *Śāstra* states:
"This mani treasure, if placed in water, manifests colors according to the objects [reflected]. Its true nature is like the jewel, and its cultivation is like the objects."

Regarding the passages "listening to the teaching is like water," "arousing [the mind] is like the manifestation of forms," and "arousing the mind is immediately sitting at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa):

since it speaks of both the initial arousal of the mind and the turning of the wheel of Dharma, we know that this refers to the First Stage (prathamabhūmi), which carries the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (yāna).

Next, regarding the citation from the *Lotus Sūtra*: if one has not yet gained faith in the sudden [teaching], one temporarily employs the "other" and the "profound. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is profound but not other; in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), it is profound but other;

in the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*zangtong*), they are other but not profound. Because these three are employed collectively as aids, it is called "the other and the profound. Since these all follow what was taught in the past, it is called "indeterminate.

Regarding "abandoning the provisional means," this refers to the aspect of setting aside the expedient (*quan*). Regarding the citation from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, [it is] the... [second/fifth chapter].
Thirteen states: "From milk produced from a cow, up to the finest essence (sarpis), these are used as metaphors for the five flavors into which poison is placed.

This text is found in the twenty-seventh [chapter]. As for the different ways in which practice gives rise to realization, they are like the indeterminate [teachings], such as the "grass of patience" (*kṣānti-tṛṇa*).

This text is found in the twenty-fifth [chapter]. Because it does not pass through the various flavors, it is like the sudden [teaching]. Next, the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (or *Anantārtha-sūtra*) is cited because it concerns the sequential progression of the three vehicles; therefore, it receives its name accordingly.

Gradually, they all received the rain of the wheel of Dharma of the three vehicles. Next, regarding those who individually realized the Perfect [Teaching]: for them, the Tathāgata-Dragon King rains the Perfect-Sudden Teaching;
it does not rain upon the lands of the inferior classes of the three [lower] teachings. Because they neither hear nor speak, they are like the deaf and mute.

The analogy of Vimalakīrti’s empty room represents the Constantly Quiescent Light (Saddharmaprakāśa). Therefore, those who gather there only smell the fragrance of the Buddha-dharma. Next, as for the *Śūraṅgama* [Sūtra]:
Rationality is like a pill; contemplative practice is like burning it. All dharmas arise instantaneously, as if possessing a multitude of fragrances.

Regarding the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Broad Vehicle" states: "If one wishes to attain all dharmas, one should study Prajñā. Next, regarding the citation from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the intention is to say that prior to this, [the teachings] were not yet complete.

Next, regarding the citation of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: its principle is as complete as the ocean, and the practice of contemplation is like bathing therein. Next, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited again to conclude the preceding three points.

Following this, the section "From above to below" serves as a concluding eulogy. Because this is based on the nine periods of time, the word "heavy" (repeated) is employed. (*Avataṃsaka*, Fascicle 31).
It says: "The Buddha-sons have ten kinds: the three periods, the nine periods, and equality. Because they reach the tenth, equality is added.

Next, it indicates the specific divisions of the transmission; there are three transmissions, [asking] which division one should transmit. "Since they have faith, etc. concludes the preceding and introduces what follows.
Regarding the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Sequential Gate of Dhyāna) and so forth, the catalog states: "The Great Master expounded this at Waguan Temple;
