Although things are impermanent moment by moment, even if they do not immediately become empty, they must necessarily become empty. Regarding "provisional existence based on conditions" (*yī luàn jiǎ zhě*): within each of the four teachings, there are respective instances of reliance on conditions.

The characteristics of the two provisionalities—the provisional as a skillful means (*shì quán èr jiǎ*)—are each distinct, and the same applies to emptiness. The provisional nature of relying on conditions does not [arise] from...

Implementation. The exercise of skillful means (*upāya*) is the establishment of transformation through compassion. Within the departure from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, even those of the Two Vehicles attain the fruit of Buddhahood, surpassing the disciples of the Three Vehicles;
they thus receive the name "Intermediate" in a specific sense, as explained in detail in the third fascicle under the section on "Opening and Closing."
If one were to proceed with the subsequent teaching, one must first refute the preceding errors.

For instance, in works such as the Āgamas and the Mahāvibhāṣā, the terms "emptiness," "non-emptiness," and "the Middle Way" appear everywhere; however, since their respective referents differ, it is necessary to refute [those earlier views].
Next, regarding the "Middle Way of Non-arising": the initial mention of "causes and conditions" and so forth explains that [phenomena] are empty. The phrase "yet they cannot...

refutes the absence of the wondrous provisional middle, which possesses the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). From the passage beginning "Even if one were to construct... onwards, it grants the two names of "provisional" and "middle" according to the specific teaching, yet no distinct principle is seen;
it merely establishes a state of mere emptiness. Even if one were to transform sentient beings at the eighth stage, such transformation would not be spontaneous. These are the three sections.
Below, the conclusion and critique follow.
Next, regarding the "infinite" [truths], there are actually three truths within it; however, this is merely sequential and cannot yet be called "perfect.

Although the three phrases accord with the text and their mutual identity is established, the sequence remains distinct. "Unborn emptiness" refers to the emptiness of the Truth of Reality (paramārtha-satya). "The provisional is identical to emptiness" refers to...
Because they emerge from emptiness, they are provisionally established in response to specific ailments; since both lack substantial reality, that which is "middle" is itself emptiness.
This differs from the former two, and is therefore called "boundless. It may also be termed "one empty, all empty.

Furthermore, when the three—successive, prior, and posterior—are all provisional, it is as if "one provisional, all provisional," yet the distinctions between the prior and posterior remain distinct. When the three are all the middle, it is likewise said to be "one [middle, all middle]."
Among all that is "middle," there is still a sequence. The middle that is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism is situated in the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

The middle designated according to capacity is situated in the stage of practice and progression (*prayoga-mārga*). The middle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is situated in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Because these three times are distinct, they constitute a sequential order.

Next, regarding the formation of the circle: all are inconceivable, and thus they do not differ from the individual [realms]. All three truths are provisional; they are also said to "equally possess" [names].
How does this differ from the individual names? Although both equally possess characters, they are distinguished by whether their sequence is orderly or not.

Next, one should understand the following: this concludes the intent. "Dharma" refers to the object (*viṣaya*). The object refers to the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*). Understanding arises based on the object, and the vow is established based on that understanding;

therefore, it is called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*). Worldly people often use the term "settling the mind" (*samādhi*) to mean "arousing the mind," failing to realize that only the making of a vow based on the object is truly called "arousing the mind.
The various expressions do not exceed sixteen [categories].
Following the section on that Pure Land, four [of the ten] have already been explained; the remaining six are omitted in brief, being merely indicated by analogy.
Each one is further divided into four distinct views to illustrate the arousal of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). This can be seen through reflection.

If a practitioner at the initial stage does not understand this, then even if they claim to have aroused the resolve (*cittotpāda*), it is entirely unreal. Even if their resolve is unreal, if they take the correct object as their condition, there is still merit.
It is still much. Although the mind may be true, there is no object to be perceived; yet because one's merit is meager, the Buddha told Dṛḍhamati in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*:
"In the final five hundred years, there will be many bhikṣus who resolve their minds for the sake of profit.
Even if they hear of this samādhi with a frivolous and playful mind, they shall still become seeds of bodhisattvas, let alone those who resolve with a pure mind."

Next, among the ten types [of contemplation], the three forms of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) serve as the concluding framework. Since the investigation of principles (*tarka*) occupies the first position, it is explained in detail; the remaining types follow this same pattern.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If one perceives this intent, by analogy one perceives the characteristics of hearing the Dharma, and so forth, up to the arising of faults.
Thus, each and every passage generates the sixteen aspects, all of which are concluded with the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

However, regarding the passage "the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) below," this correctly explains that within the Sudden [teaching], the nature of phenomena is not a numerical category. To insistently hold that three or four are what can give rise [to awakening] only increases delusion and inversion.
Now, the statement "down to four" refers to the gradual nature of the afflictions. As previously stated in the Dharma-exposition: "One, two, three, and four" refers simply to the three.
One merely contemplates the four teachings, accumulating them in sequence; thus, from one to four, this clarifies the reason for the gradual [teaching].

Next, the passage beginning with "explaining the dharma-nature" clarifies the characteristics of the indeterminate [teaching]; because there are two types of root-natures each for the provisional and the real, both internally and externally, the four are not the same.

From the section on those of dull faculties within the realm [of birth-and-death] below, the four reasons are clarified. Because of delusion and awakening, there are distinctions of lightness and heaviness, skill and clumsiness.

"Reality" (*zhen*) and "dharma-nature" (*faxing*) differ in name but are identical in meaning. Those within the realm are deluded regarding reality; those outside the realm are deluded regarding the middle way.

Although that which is deluded about and that which is awakened to are both the same dharma-nature, there is a distinction between the skill and clumsiness of the one who deludes and the one who awakens. It is in relation to these sharp and dull capacities that the four [categories] are established. This gives rise to delusion.

The origin of suffering is explained as the path to its cessation; the sharp is thus separated from the dull, and the skillful likewise from the unskillful. What is understood is thereby separated by virtue of the skillfulness or lack thereof of the one who understands.
Following this, an analogy is provided: both the internal and external realms are illustrated together, using the wayfarer as the father and the son.

The term "immediate" (ji) refers to father and son, while "separated" (li) refers to strangers on a road. For example, the very substance of suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*) is fundamentally the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

in meaning, this is like father and son. If one regards them merely as suffering and its accumulation, the meaning is like strangers on a road; this can be used as an analogy for the distinct treasury (*bhedagarbha*), where the principle is the same but the function differs, and the name does not denote bone or flesh, yet there is a forced intimacy toward what is otherwise different.
This is like the identity of suffering and its accumulation itself; it can be used as an analogy for the universal and perfect (*sāmānya-pariniṣpanna*).
From "from coarse to subtle" downwards, the analogy is synthesized. If one follows the intent of the analogy, there are both coarse and subtle, difficult and easy aspects within and without.

However, because what follows is indeterminate, it is now for the sake of convenience that they are explained in pairs in the text; thus, that which is within the realm is considered coarse, and that which is outside the realm is considered subtle.

All other instances of coarse and subtle should be understood according to this principle. Each employs the analogy of father and son; hence it says, "it is also like this. From "or says 'the realm'"... [text ends].
The internal [depth] reaches the ultimate depth; these two constitute the gradual [process]. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "Whether shallow or deep, etc., it is gradual.
Although the word "or" (*vā*) occurs, there is no textual cross-referencing; thus, it is not indeterminate.

Next, regarding the phrase "or says below": these are the six pairs of alternating indeterminate characteristics. Although the final pair lacks alternation, this is merely due to a textual abbreviation;

it should be stated that because the initial mind within the boundary (*sīmā*) is capable of destroying [the offense], it is considered easy, whereas because the subsequent mind outside the boundary only then destroys it, it is considered difficult.
The phrase "if one acts" is said because it proceeds from the general to the specific. Next, regarding the passage beginning with "all Mahāyāna," this is an exhortation.
This is the progression.

In the subsequent section on "Discerning the Essentials," the first question asks: "Since the four teachings differ regarding suffering, why do you speak only of 'segmented' and 'transformative' [samsara]?
Since their numbers are unequal and their causes and effects differ from one another. In the subsequent answer, there is first a direct response and then an analogy. First:

In the answer: To speak according to principle, both [the truths of] origination and cessation consist of two and four [aspects] respectively. Now, regarding the "origination" (samudaya), it is categorized into two based on the distinction between skillful and unskillful [means];

thus, the internal and external [factors] together constitute four. If one were to follow the perspective of delusion, origination would likewise consist of only two. Here, however, since the question regarding origination is posed from the standpoint of liberation (*vidyā*) while addressing delusion (*moha*), it may appear as though they are not equal;

this is precisely to refute the view that they are dissimilar, just as in the case of the Four Noble Truths where suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) both possess four aspects. How could there be [a discrepancy]?

They are not the same. The following examples illustrate this; these are provided as examples in response. For instance, within the realm (dhātu), there may be only one [type], or it may be divided according to the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the differences between views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), through delusion they likewise experience only a portion of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

The intent of the subsequent question is to ask whether, in the concluding verse of the preceding treatise, the first [category] is paired with the Four Noble Truths such that both are termed "arisen from causes and conditions" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).

It may be so for the Truths of Suffering and its Accumulation, but how can it be so for the Truths of the Path and Cessation? The meaning of the response is that the capacity to destroy arises from that which is destroyed;

or, when the knowledge of cessation arises, is this not itself a "birth" within cessation? Next, the Great Scripture is cited to illustrate the profound by way of the shallow: if even the Perfect and Distinctive [teachings] are thus, how much more so the others.

How much more so for the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings]? Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Only by extinguishing the accumulation of ignorance does one realize the Truth of the Path and attain Bodhi.

Since this is the case for the Truths of Accumulation and the Path, the same principle may be applied to Suffering and Cessation. Next, regarding the previous passage: since the Dharma-nature is one, it should not be divided into the principles of the provisional and the real;
why then are four categories established through the further distinction of identity and difference? The intent of the answer is that because they are opened and revealed, they are non-dual.
Because they employ skillful means (*upāya*), they are not uniform; even their integration and separation are expedient applications of the fundamental nature.

Next, the Four Great Vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) are explained: "Great" (*hong*) means extensive, and "Vow" (*shi*) means a restriction. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "A vow (*shi*) is a regulation.
Here, these four essential dharmas are used to regulate the beginner's mind, ensuring that upon reaching the final fruition, there is no deviation from one's original aspiration.

Furthermore, following the section on the Four Truths, we shall next distinguish their similarities and differences. The Four Truths are the objective realm; since understanding arises from this realm, they are said to be "defined by understanding.

Moreover, the Four Great Vows arise from such understanding, and thus they are said to be "defined by vows. Furthermore, the Truths possess both cause and effect and therefore span the three periods of time;
the Vows, however, look toward what is yet to come and thus belong to the future. Finally, the Four Truths are defined by principle (*li*), and this principle pervades the three periods of time.

The Four Great Vows are aspirations; they merely look toward the future. Since they all require seeking the supreme above and transforming those below, their names differ while their meaning remains the same.

Question: If that is so, why is it necessary to clarify them further? Answer: While the Truths (the Four Noble Truths) apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the Great Vows belong specifically to the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is necessary to clarify them further.
The propagation of the partial and the perfect [teachings] and the six stages of realization pertain exclusively to the Sudden [Vehicle].

Therefore, it is explained again here. In the initial explanation of the arising and ceasing [nature], the Four Truths are once more cited as the object. From the phrase "the mind does not arise in isolation" downwards, this refers to the truth of the origin (*samudaya*).

Because it is accomplished through these causes and conditions, it is said not to be solitary. From this point, starting with "the faculties and objects," the text demonstrates that these causes and conditions constitute the characteristic of arising and ceasing.

That the mind arises due to the faculties as its cause and the objects as its condition is precisely the dharma that is produced. Regarding the three characteristics, they are to be distinguished as previously explained.
As for the four minds, they are difficult to restrain; hence they are called "stealthy. Because they continue in succession without ceasing, they are said to be "ever-new.
Next, regarding the analogy: *xiǎn* (睒) means the appearance of a fleeting glance; *shuò* (爍) means brightness. This is a partial metaphor for the speed of mindfulness (*smṛti*) in this context.

"Shuan" (遄) means to go swiftly. It follows "se-pao" (色泡, form-bubble) below; it refers to the realm of suffering. As explained extensively in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāpāramitā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, bubbles and foam appear in the smaller [sections], while mirages and so forth appear in the larger.
Since these belong to the common category [of similes], they may be included together. Rain falling into water is called a bubble (*pāpa*). Water striking water forms froth (*phena*).

Viewing from afar, heat appears as a flame (*marīci*). A *śiṅśumāra* exhaling its breath creates a city (*gandharvanagara*). Medicines mixed with substances are called illusions (*māyā*). *Shu* (儵)...

It is also "sudden" (*jì*). As for the phrase "a single chest," it means that many poisons are contained within one chest; there is only suffering and no joy, and thus it is called "partial" (*piān*). This matter is found in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

Regarding the passage "the four mountains come together from all sides," this refers to the realm of the Path (*dào-jìng*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Suppose four great mountains were to come from the four directions;
what plan would you devise? The answer is: "One should only focus the mind upon the factors of the Path (*mārgāṅga*)—precept, concentration, and wisdom—and not depart [from them]."

Because of the three [categories] beginning with morality (*śīla*), "vertical" (*ūrdhva*) refers to the destruction of the lower [realms], which is the cessation of the object; it is the destruction of the origin (*samudaya*) by overturning the inversions (*viparyāsa*). "Horizontal" (*tiryak*) refers to the cutting off of death, which is the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha*).

As for the cessation of delusions (*kleśa*), because they are destroyed from the coarse to the subtle, it is vertical; as for the removal of suffering, because there is no further sequence of before and after, it is horizontal. This is stated provisionally according to the sequential abandonment [of the truths].

The "inversions" are [the views of] permanence and so forth; they gradually deepen across the realms (*dhātu*). "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence. "Flows" (*āsava*) refer to the four flows.
Because they cause one to be swept away by views and so forth, they are called "floods" (*ogha*). The views of the three realms constitute the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*).

All afflictions of the desire realm, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), constitute the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*). The afflictions of the two upper realms, excluding ignorance, constitute the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*).

The delusion of the three realms constitutes the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*). The sutra says "below," citing the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* as proof. The sutra says: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the past, I [dwelt] with you..."
The foolish lack wisdom and are unable to see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are.

In the "Burning House" section below, it is stated that because they do not see the Truths, they remain within suffering and its origination; attachment to craving is called "joy," while attachment to views is called "play."

Therefore, [the text] below clarifies the making of the vow. As for "Śākyamuni," etc., it cites the *Ruiying* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses) to show that Siddhārtha, weary of desire, traveled through the four city gates.
At the eastern gate, Śakra manifested illness; at the southern gate, he manifested old age; at the western gate, he manifested death;
and at the northern gate, he manifested a śramaṇa. Having seen them, the Prince questioned them, and Śakra answered all his questions. The Prince said: "Only one such as a śramaṇa..."

This was a source of joy. At midnight, he leaped over the city walls and went to the foot of a tree in the king’s fields. There he saw a plowman who had unearthed a worm, which a crow followed and pecked at to swallow.
Witnessing this, he made a vow; therefore, it is cited here now. Regarding those such as Maitreya and others: when he first felt world-weariness, he offered a jeweled terrace to Rāhula.
Having received it, Rāhula gave it to a brahmin, who then tore it apart. Because of this, [the Bodhisattva] realized impermanence.
Next, one contemplates only that which is below: the great vow of non-arising. While the object of contemplation does not differ, there is a distinction in the subject that contemplates it;

by examining it through the four natures, it is realized as emptiness. Therefore, the subsequent passage cites "self and other" and so forth to demonstrate its characteristics. As for the phrase "this mind," etc.:

One may understand this through the internal, the external, the common, and so forth. Nature itself is the emptiness of nature; there is only the inferior, which is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Emptiness and existence are non-dual; both affirmation and negation are quiescent.
As with the example below. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like the moon in the water; when a small person goes to take hold of it, a great person laughs at them.
Because of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is grasping and rejecting; because one knows that nature and characteristics are empty, there is neither sorrow nor joy."

Once the section on "Arising" (samudaya) has concluded, the four truths are illustrated individually, each beginning with the Dharma teaching followed by an analogy; however, for the Truth of Cessation (nirodha), the analogy is omitted. The intent of the analogy for Arising is as follows:

heat, space, and dust together produce a shimmering mirage, which those who are thirsty mistake for water. Likewise, through the causal power of craving and sensual objects, one superimposes the notion of desire and becomes deluded by it.
Regarding the analogy for Suffering (duḥkha) as being like the moon reflected in water: failing to understand its nature, one mistakes it for reality.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise thus. To call that which is unreal "real" is a misconception. As it says in the *Dharmapada* of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*): "One should not say 'I'.

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are themselves emptiness (*śūnyatā*), what is there to be singled out? If there were anything to be singled out, it would be like avoiding emptiness while seeking emptiness.
The analogy states: "As for the parable of the raft," this is fully contained within the text. The meaning is that if even the raft must be abandoned, how much more so that which is not a raft?
Thus, if even the Path (mārga) must be abandoned, how much more so Suffering (duḥkha) and its Accumulation (samudaya). Regarding the Cessation (nirodha), if one wishes to establish an analogy:

since cessation is itself emptiness, one should not seek a substantial essence within that emptiness. Since suffering and its accumulation cease of their own accord, why would one seek a reality in that cessation? One.
To designate a limit is called longevity; to maintain continuity is called life. Sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent; how then can one calculate their lifespan?

Following the passage from the Sūtra, in the section providing further corroboration, it says: "I do not wish to cause... and so forth. This refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin), which clarifies that within the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*), there are no thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*).
This is the fundamental nature of the Path. Now, regarding the absence of the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], this is the fundamental non-existence of cessation (*nirodha*). Next...
Following the precedent, the Master’s model scripture states that since cessation is originally non-existent, it should likewise be said that suffering and its origin are originally non-existent.
I do not wish for there to be form, sensation, and so forth; nor do I wish for there to be greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth. Since suffering is originally non-existent, [the others] are as well.

The collection [of commentaries] originally did not include this. The Sūtra mentions the superior while implying the inferior for the sake of those with sharp faculties; the Master (the commentator) reverses this by providing the illustration, and thus preserves it in its entirety.

From "But out of compassion" (*butian*) onwards, the text correctly clarifies the making of the vow. The passage omits the cause for the vow, which is supplied here by the phrase "out of compassion. It should be stated:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings who do not know the truth of the non-arising and illusory nature of phenomena, he therefore gives rise to the vow."
Next, by penetrating downward, one distinguishes the non-true to reveal the true. Because suffering and its origin are empty, they differ from the nine bonds.

Now, because one further penetrates emptiness, this differs from the Three Baskets (Tripitaka). Because the Path and Cessation are empty, they are not the same as the single liberation; now, being able to penetrate emptiness, this also differs from the Three Baskets.

Next, regarding the four distinct Great Vows, there is first the general and then the specific. In the initial general explanation, it is said that one illuminates and knows that while the single mind is unitary, its delusions and awakenings are immeasurable;
because the suffering and accumulation of the ten realms, as well as the four types of path and cessation, are immeasurable, they are thus called "immeasurable."

Next, below the section on the three realms, the Four Noble Truths are explained individually. First come Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), followed by the Path and Cessation (*mārga* and *nirodha*).

Within the initial section on Suffering and its Origin, there is first the general exposition and then the specific exposition. Although the specific details have not yet been explained in the initial general text, the meaning already encompasses the suffering of the three realms.

"The one mind" refers to the Origin; the analogy of the mind as a master painter illustrates the Origin, while the creation of various forms and colors illustrates Suffering. When the mind is designated [as the agent], it is the Origin.
The six realms are suffering.
The section beginning with "Next, as follows" specifically clarifies the origin (*samudaya*). The section beginning with "In this way, birth and death" specifically clarifies suffering (*duḥkha*).

Since suffering and its origin are that which are to be eliminated, the ten realms are fully explained. The Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*) are that which eliminate; they merely differ in the length of their discourse. The subsequent section begins by reversing the preceding.
This generally clarifies the cessation of the path (*mārga-nirodha*). It simply turns back toward the mind of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

The passage beginning with "Like a painter" is a general analogy. The painter is like the body; the hand is like the mind. The brush is an analogy for the mind that performs contemplation. The various colors represent the causes and effects of the six realms of existence.
"Washing away" refers to the destruction of those causes and effects. "Applying plaster and color" represents further cultivating the path and cessation.

Regarding what is called "the inferior": this separately clarifies the paths and fruits, each enumerating the Four Truths with differing characteristics. Within the first [section on] the Path, it says:
"The winding path and the direct path lead to the precious island," which refers to the stages of the Distinct and Complete [Vehicles].

"The winding path and the direct path lead to the transformation city" refers to the stages of the Tripitaka and Shared [Vehicles]. Within the direct path, it does not speak of impurity, but only of the emptiness of the body and so forth.
This is because it is not the same as the clumsy [approach]. It winds its way through to the Jewel Island; in full, one should say: "permanent, impermanent, neither permanent nor impermanent.

In the text, everything up to this point is an abbreviation that omits "permanent," which is why "impermanent" is stated again. As for "impermanence is emptiness," this is the gate for converting others.
Furthermore, it reiterates the previous metaphor of the conjured city’s winding and direct paths. As for not mentioning "impurity," it is likewise...
This is merely a brief summary. It concerns impermanence, arising, and cessation. Impermanence is itself emptiness and non-arising. This person perceives cessation and departure;

this separately clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Within the text, "cessation" is taken to mean the stage of severance (*prahāṇa*). This fully explains the stage of cessation according to the four teachings.
As for the statement "non-action," it refers only to the stage of the *bhūmi* (stages) in the distinct teaching (*bipartite teaching*). If that is so, then the Path...

Why, within this [treatise], are both the winding and the direct types also listed among the general jewels? This is because, regarding the categories of teaching (*śāsana*) and realization (*adhigama*), the teaching is preserved therein;

whereas the stages (*bhūmi*) proceed from realization. As it says in the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*: "The distinct school holds that non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is the fruit. Within this, the first is the stage of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*);

next is the stage of the cessation of the person's view (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi-nirodha*); and from the cessation of the person's view, there is the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*). From the cessation of the person's view, there is... [non-arising].
Regarding the stage of measurement (*pramāṇa*), from this person’s perspective, cessation (*nirodha*) has departed.

Regarding the stage of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), it is distinguished as being below [the previous]. To summarize, it proceeds from the mind. As for the statement "the path and cessation through sixteen gates," the four truths (*catuḥsatya*) are present in each of the four gates of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).
When it says "and all," it refers universally to all Buddha-dharmas throughout the ten directions.
Next, regarding the passage "contemplating this one mind" and below: based on the object, understanding arises.

That "one mind can penetrate unspeakable minds and dharmas" means that the subject which perceives is called "mind," while the object perceived is called "dharma. This one mind serves as the fundamental basis for both delusion and awakening.
Here, the intention is merely to point out the provisional mind and dharmas; when these penetrate through to the dharma-nature (dharmatā), they are termed "non-mind and non-dharma."
"Bound beneath the nine fetters": this distinguishes what is not [the case] to reveal what is. Within the afflictions (*kleśa*) lies the Tathāgatagarbha; thus it is said to be "seated within.
Ordinary beings are like those born blind who constantly coexist with the Garbha, yet remain within birth and death; thus it is said they are "wounded.

Those of the Two Vehicles are like those with impaired vision, suffering from the fever of partial truth, and regarding the Garbha as a demon. These four—demon, etc.—are used as metaphors for the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*). Not knowing it is a treasure, they instead...
"Abandoning and fleeing for over fifty years" refers to the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*). Because these are combined with the asuras, they are termed "the remainder.
From the phrase "arousing great compassion" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the making of the vow.

Next, we clarify the distinctions regarding the combination and separation of the Four Truths and Three Truths within the context of the unconditioned great vow (*anabhisaṃskāra-mahāpraṇidhāna*). Therefore, the Three Truths are used as a general designation for the object.

The object of contemplation remains the same as before, but the subject of contemplation is fundamentally different. Since the subject of contemplation is different, it causes the object of contemplation to be distinct:

this very single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) is itself the Three Truths. One need not further discuss the basis of delusion or awakening; the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is simply the Three [Truths].

This is an alternative name for the Truths. Because the three truths are mutually interfused, it is said that they are "all [identical]. The "Treasury" (garbha) is itself the provisional; the other two names are the same. Regarding the phrase "How so?
below, it provides a further explanation. As for "all are dependently originated": a single moment of mind is fully endowed with the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses.
These very thousand suchnesses are called the "wondrous provisional. The provisional is itself the dharma-nature; the dharma-nature is named the "Middle."
That which is not three yet appears as three is the conventional (saṃvṛti). That which is three yet is not three is the empty (śūnya).
One should further apply the double negation to establish the Middle Way; this is omitted in the text for brevity.
Combining the empty and dispersing the conventional constitutes the middle; identity and difference are likewise so.
The following passage provides an analogy. Generally speaking, all metaphors employed here are partial analogies (*pradeśopama*).

Among them, the metaphor of the mirror is somewhat more closely related to the matter at hand, because it clarifies that the image, the mirror, and the three [conditions] are inseparable; thus, the intent regarding their combination and separation is quite consistent.

Regarding the phrase "The character 'I' [forms] the Heavenly Eye; principle is likewise merged," the inclusion of "two or three" without obstruction is merely for the sake of following the flow of the phrasing, and thus one character is omitted.

Next, below the passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he cites evidence that the principles are identical, stating: "As the mind is, so too is the Buddha. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* praises the mind of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), saying: "As the mind is, so too is the Buddha..."

It is so. As it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. How could the phrase "not conjoined" (*fei he*) be easily explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan wen*)?
Next, regarding the citation of the *Sāṃkhyāvikrīḍita-sūtra*: because they do not understand these three, they are called "fools. Regarding the citation of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
liberation, bodhi, and the three virtues of nirvāṇa are not separate from sentient beings; therefore, it is cited to clarify this intention.
Furthermore. Next, regarding the citation of the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*: since this is Vairocana, what dharma would he not possess?
"If that were so," and so forth, explains the doubt: if all things are possessed [by him], why does the third section of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speak of emptiness? This is raised below.
The commentator’s words are partial, while the meaning is complete; such is the case throughout all Mahāyāna scriptures.

The statement regarding the "sūtra scroll within a great trichiliocosm made of atoms" is precisely a metaphor for the mind containing all phenomena. The admonition "do not cling to the literal words" and so forth is an exhortation.
Next, if one attains the lower [grade], it clarifies the realm of the Four Truths (catvāri āryasatyāni). The eighty-four thousand [dharmas] do not exceed a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*).

The detailed enumeration is fully provided in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra). In total, although the scriptures and treatises contain numerous accounts, the expression "eighty-four thousand" does not transcend the Four Truths.

The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is suffering (*duḥkha*). Worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are the origin (*samudaya*). The remedies (*pratipakṣa*) are the path (*mārga*). The *pāramitās* are cessation (*nirodha*).

Although their numerical categories do not differ, because the objects to be remedied and the remedies themselves are distinct, they constitute the Four Noble Truths. Regarding "the Buddha’s Dharma-realm and so forth": the Buddha’s Dharma-realm is the faculty (*indriya*);

the Dharma-realm of the world is the object (*viṣaya*); and the arising of the Dharma-realm is consciousness (*vijñāna*). These are spoken of according to their fundamental delusion; therefore, it is said that the faculties and so forth are identical in name as "Dharma."
Because their realms are identical, there is no distinction between them. Regarding "the transformation of ignorance and so forth": ignorance and clarity are merely delusion and awakening;

they are also termed the Four Truths, the Three Truths, and so on. As for what is called "transformation," it may be illustrated by the analogy of ice and water, just as a wish-fulfilling talisman establishes the meaning of ice and water.
The passage "Sentient beings [regard] this as inferior" below concludes the reprimand; it is also called the "vow. The passage "Therefore" below formally formulates the vow.

The first three passages below distinguish the differences and demonstrate their characteristics. Thus, one knows that speaking in terms of eighty thousand [kalpas] is fundamentally different in principle from the previous three teachings.
As for "wǎn" (宛): when the edges are high and the center is low, or the edges are low and the center is high, both are termed "wǎn"; this is because they are visible.

Next, regarding the summary through questions and answers: this is a summary by means of the four *siddhāntas*. The meaning of the initial question is as follows: previously, in the summary of what is not the Middle Way, it was stated that neither bondage nor liberation applies;
however, "liberation" encompassed both teachings. Now, to reveal what truly is the Middle Way, why are all four teachings called "correct"?

The meaning of the answer is as follows: because there is the intent of three *siddhāntas*, they encompass the previous two. Although they encompass the previous two, they reside only within the Bodhisattva stage. Therefore...

In the preceding section on "liberation," only the two vehicles were discussed. If one proceeds to the ultimate level below, one judges the provisional and the real; the real is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Because of the four *siddhāntas*, it is generally taught that there are four [truths].
For example, below, many metaphorical passages all use metaphors to illustrate reality; yet there are slight differences:

the secret formula (bhaiṣajya) illustrates the teaching, the gāthā illustrates wisdom, the milk gruel illustrates practice, and the wish-fulfilling gem illustrates principle. Regarding "the provisional and the real being revealed as 'this'":
when the four teachings include the provisional and are all said to be "this," it is exactly as explained above.

Furthermore, "one" refers to the inferior [vehicle], while "one" is another name for [the supreme]. In the previous analysis, all three were established as being real; therefore, these alternative names here no longer possess any provisional meaning.
Although such alternative names should be explained extensively throughout all the sutras, for the time being we shall follow the immediate context and employ these three names.

First, regarding the explanation of the "one great matter": "one" is the reality of the single truth (*ekasatyatā*); "great" is the path, wisdom, and practice; and "matter" refers to the unimpeded person and so forth.
This refers to the human vehicle (*manuṣyayāna*), which practices wisdom to accord with principle. Its meaning corresponds to its respective stage, and its intent encompasses three dharmas.

This is explained in terms of the causes and effects of one’s own practice. Next, to explain "Great" (*mahat*): this is the greatness of this particular school; thus, by means of the preceding "One," it explains the vast principle of the nature of greatness.

Wisdom, abandonment, and practice constitute the "person"; the "Great Person" is that which accords [with the truth]. Once the teaching has been accorded through explanation, the instruction is proclaimed.

Benefiting others is called the "Lion’s Roar. It not only benefits ordinary beings at the stage of broad ground, but also benefits the noble ones who have entered the stages according to the four teachings.

Therefore, the revelation and manifestation of the Great [Vehicle] are entirely the work of the Buddhas and noble ones. Regarding the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): the causes and effects of both self and others are none other than causes and conditions.
When the text mentions the Buddha, it speaks from the perspective of the ultimate fruit. Next, the "inconceivable" (*acintya*) is explained: [it refers to] the self...
Regarding all great matters, it is said that they are severed through contemplation of the Way. Next, "non-doer" is explained. First, "not acting" and below explain the name.

Next, "constant object" and below explain the essence; this refers simply to the constant object and constant wisdom. There is illumination without illuminating, and manifestation without manifesting.

Because the object manifests within wisdom, it is called "wisdom whose characteristics have no conditions. Because the object is without characteristics, it causes wisdom to be without characteristics; thus it is called "characteristics."

Because it is the wisdom of non-conditioning (*anālambana-jñāna*), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "Since the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) does not perceive characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) nor the locus of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasthāna*), the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is pure, and wisdom is likewise pure.
Characteristics are themselves wisdom, and the locus is itself the objective sphere."
Furthermore, this is a lower citation of evidence. That which is called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is termed "arousing the mind. This sutra is titled *Gayāśīrṣa*;
because it was requested by Mañjuśrī, it is called the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*. The present text merely follows the meaning of that scripture; it does not take the text in its entirety.

Nevertheless, this does not go beyond the meaning of the three truths: negation is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); affirmation is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); and the simultaneous negation of both is the middle truth (madhyama-satya).
Next, if one applies this analogy downward, it extends to all phenomena.

Furthermore, below the previous three, all dharmas are further categorized into thirteen levels in total. There are three at the beginning and one at the end; the first consists of superior, middling, and inferior grades.

In terms of the wisdom of causes and conditions, the Perfect [Teaching] is classified as the "superior-superior. Regarding the shared lands, these are categorized by stage: the first three are all shared, while only the Perfect is unshared.

The first three [vehicles] lack it; "shallow" and so forth refer to practice (*caryā*). The two [vehicles of] proximity and distinctness are crooked; "small," "great," and so forth refer to teaching (*deśanā*). The general and the distinct are small, medium, and great;
only the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) is the great-of-the-great-and-medium. The third, the fulfillment of the fruit of the teachings, is the partial-of-the-medium-and-perfect;

the Perfect fruit is indeed the perfect-of-the-perfect-and-medium. The general and the distinct are the half-of-the-medium-and-full; the Perfect is the full-of-the-full-and-medium. This refers to the path of teaching in the Distinct Vehicle.

This is the reality within the provisional. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), both are real; this is the reality within the real. When compared to the five pairs of the partial and the perfect in the lower vehicles, it lacks only the distinction between gradual and sudden.
The ultimate fruit of the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) is the sudden within the gradual; this is what Master Zhi used. Only the Perfect Teaching is the sudden within the sudden.

Regarding "Truth" (zhen) and so forth in terms of the Truths (di): the Truth and the Conventional (shisu) of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings are, even in the Separate Teaching, still the truth within the conventional.

In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one extinguishes the conventional; this is also the "truth within the conventional. Only in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is it called the "truth within the truth. Regarding terms such as "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), these refer to the principle through their meanings.

Terms such as "mysterious" (*xuan*) and so forth praise the principle through their names. These may also be distinguished according to the four teachings (*sijiao*). This can be understood through analysis.
Next, if one can descend [to the level of the provisional], this summarizes all the intended meanings. To know that the provisional is provisional is called "the provisional as essence" (*tǐquán*).
To know that the provisional is itself the real is called "cognizing the real" (*shíshí*). In summary, this is to cause one to rely upon the real and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

The following section provides analogies. Ten analogies are used to praise his virtues; these primarily extol the three virtues of generating goodness, extinguishing evil, and [the underlying] principle.

Of these, the first five concern the generation of goodness, and the latter five concern the extinction of evil. Regarding the phrase "the nature of gold arises": all *vajras* take the *vajra-cakra* as their intrinsic nature.
The medicinal herb *aśala* is not clearly identified. It is like a prince who is born already possessing the regalia of royalty.
Regarding the marks: based on the perfect arousal of the bodhicitta, one is endowed with the virtues of a Buddha.

As for Nārāyaṇa—the human athlete—there are ten times ten increments in strength compared to the small and large blue oxen, the three types of bulls, the ordinary and wild four-tusked elephants, the white, fragrant, blue, yellow, and red snow-mountain elephants, and the blue, white, and red lotuses (utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka). Among all these great human athletes, Nārāyaṇa is the most supreme.
"Summarizing the essentials" below concludes [the section]. "Essentials" refers to the praise that all Buddhas are likewise so. "If one understands" below concludes with a single *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

"The Jewel Beam Sūtra" (*Ratnarāśi-sūtra*) below clarifies the production of good and the cessation of evil through concrete matters, praising the bodhicitta. First, citing the *Jewel Beam*, it addresses the production of good;
the *Secret Treasury* (*Guhyakośa*) addresses the cessation of evil. The initial passage explains the evil to be ceased; the ten non-virtues, when directed toward persons, are termed...
It is grave. What is grave is evil. Furthermore, that which arises from a source of kindness and virtue is the most evil among evils. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To strike back at someone who has struck you is called evil; to strike another when they have not struck you is called great evil;
to strike one who has been kind to you in return is called the most evil among evils."

If one can lower [the mind], wisdom can extinguish bodhi. First the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy. Within the principle, first the enumeration, then the judgment. Regarding the initial enumeration, the Sūtra says:
"Suppose there is a person who possesses the aforementioned ten non-virtues; if they can apply their understanding and wisdom... The text of the Sūtra is somewhat extensive.
The current text is already complete. As for the passage beginning with "For what reason," the current text explains the meaning of the initial *bodhi*.
The passage beginning with "Like a hundred years" is a metaphor for the extinction of evil; it also serves merely as an illustration of initial *bodhi*.
This sutra is complete with the following sections. By correlating the sutra with its teachings, the first section on *bodhicitta* uses the shallow to illustrate the profound.

Now, those who commit evil do so because they take the "self" as their basis; yet now, having generated the *bodhicitta*, one further cultivates contemplation to destroy this self, and moreover seeks to extensively benefit others—how could one merely stop at ceasing evil?
If even the initial teaching is thus, how much more so the latter three!
This is an exhortation using the analogy of the *elā* tree beneath a dark place, employing a passage from the *Mahāsūtra* concerning King Ajātaśatru. The Buddha said:
"Great King, you should cultivate the bodhicitta. Why is this? Because by attaining the bodhicitta, immeasurable sins are extinguished."

The meaning of the subsequent question is as follows: In the preceding discussion on the Four Noble Truths, four propositions were presented through both general and specific pairs. Now, for the time being, we shall inquire according to the specific [pair] regarding the first proposition.

Why? Because the first proposition alone corresponds to the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-śāsana). In the answer, the first [teaching] is paired with the first [proposition], and the phenomena (vastu) are paired with the phenomena;
both of these meanings are convenient. The phrase "if one says" and below provides the explanation according to the specific [pair].
Next, regarding the six stages of realization (*liují*), the first point clarifies the reason for establishing these six stages. Therefore, it first asks: "Is it the initial [stage] or the final?
Is it the initial principle (*lǐ*) or the final fruit (*guǒ)? The question asks: "Does the present arousal of the mind (*citta-utpāda*) refer to the initial principle or the final fruit?

In the answer, the intention of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dà lùn) is cited. In that treatise, Subhūti asked the Buddha: "Is bodhi attained by the initial mind, or is bodhi attained by the final mind?"
One must rely on hearing that all dharmas neither increase nor decrease; therefore, this question was posed. The Buddha answered with profound causes and conditions:
it is not that there is no beginning, yet it does not depart from the beginning; it is not that there is no end, yet it does not depart from the end. The commentary explains:

If there were only a beginning, the Bodhisattva’s initial mind would immediately be the state of Buddhahood. If there were no beginning, how could there be an end? The end takes the beginning as its root, and the beginning [takes] the end.
This is the established period. In the sutras, the Buddha further uses the metaphor of a lamp; the burning away of the delusions of ignorance is likewise so.

It is not apart from initial wisdom, nor does it depart from initial wisdom; the same applies to subsequent wisdom. This treatise encompasses all three teachings, but here it pertains specifically to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

Now, even when the nature of reality (*li-xing*) is designated as "bodhi" and "śamatha-vipaśyanā," this refers to the six stages of realization (*liu-ji*); how much more so for initial and subsequent wisdom? Here, it is clarified that the very moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*fa-xin*) is itself what is termed [the practice].

[This is] a character. From this, it must necessarily penetrate to the principle (*li*), for all fruits subsequent to the arousal of the mind depend upon that principle; this can be seen through careful reflection.

Next, the section beginning with "If wisdom and faith... explains its intended meaning. Faith holds that the initial mind possesses [the principle], while [those who] do not realize it say it is non-existent; wisdom reaches its ultimate [realization] only when...

[The stage of] Fulfillment (Pūrṇa). Do not worry about having no share [in this]. Both the beginning and the end are pushed to their ultimate limit in the Buddha; ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) never possess it.

To take the principle as the fruit—both the beginning and the end would then be non-existent. Apart from the beginning and the end being non-existent, one must necessarily rely on the six stages of identity (liùjí).

This meaning of the six identities originated from our own school; it deeply accords with the Perfect Teaching (Yuanmen) and is forever free from all errors. Those who are arrogant (adhimāna) and those who push back the credit [for realization] both do so because they... [do not understand this].
One attains the meaning of "the six are precisely [the Buddha-nature].
Regarding the phrase "these six," below, the names are explained; only "six" and "precisely" (i.e., *ji*) must not be confused.

Regarding "principle-precisely" (*li-ji*), below, there is the formal explanation. First, explaining "principle-precisely": by interpreting the three truths according to the principle of the *zang* (the *śrāvaka* stage), then all...
All sentient beings possess the three truths, as fully detailed above in the section on the "Perfect Four Great Vows" under the heading "Names. Next, regarding the explanation of "names and reality":

throughout long kalpas of birth and death, one does not depart from the three truths; therefore, it is called "daily use. Not knowing that birth and death are themselves the three truths is called "not knowing.
The reality within reality is like the center of a square; the skillful means within reality are like the corners. This is what is being illustrated.

Ignorance is manifested through the presence of knowledge. Next, [the passage] from "Or from below" clarifies that one comes to know through hearing. Next, from "The practice of contemplation" below, it explains the identity of contemplative practice;
since one must practice what one hears, it cites [the scripture] saying: "It is like an insect eating wood; the insect does not know the characters. To hear without practicing is likewise so.
Next, the citation of Śāriputra serves to reprove those who preach but do not practice; it does not mean...
Since it is not permitted to speak [of this], I again cite the treatise. Regarding the four-line and three-line verses on the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the treatise states:

"Though born in a central land, if one cannot be transformed and does not recognize the principles of meaning, such a person is called a 'human-bodied ox. Therefore, only the fourth line can be accepted with faith.
If even hearing [the teaching] and not immediately [realizing it] is already contrary to the present intent, how much more so for anything else? Next, as in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*... [etc.]
Citing scriptures to encourage practice is like aiming at a target; it need not strike the bullseye immediately. Although one does not hit it right away, hitting it must begin from the first attempt.

Next, the "identity with the Middle" (zhong) in its semblance stage (*sādharmya*) is explained; since the text says "becoming increasingly clear" and so forth, it differs from the gradual stages of practice (*anupūrva-caryā*).

The citation from the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) is likewise a citation from that section concerning the semblance stage. Next, the "identity with the Middle" in its partial realization (*praveśa-tattva*) is explained, as found in the *Mūla-karma-bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and the *Ratna-śekhara-sūtra*.

The adornment with the six wheels is used as a metaphor for the stages. The copper wheel corresponds to the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*); this refers to the passage concerning the first stage within the "partial realization of truth" (*bhūtatathatā-vibhāga*).
Next, the explanation of the ultimate [stage] is based on the intent of the "Moon-Love" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Enlightenment (*bodhi*) belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*).
Nirvāṇa belongs to the category of cessation; therefore, both Great Nirvāṇa and Bodhi are fully endowed with all virtues. Bodhi arises from wisdom, while Nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction;
these names are established according to their respective functions. As for the statement that the appellations of these two virtues surpass those of the *tathāgata* and so forth:
since all stages have been finalized, there is no further verbal teaching; thus, there is nothing more that can be said.

From "In total" below, this analogy is established based on the six stages of identity (*liù jí*). This is the analogy of the poor woman from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which inherently contains the meaning of the six stages.

The treasure storehouse within the house represents the stage of principle (*lǐ jí*). The acquaintance who points it out represents the stage of name (*míng*). The weeding and removal of all impurities represents the stage of practice (*xíng*).

[This is] contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Gradually one attains proximity; [this stage is] "semblance" (*sādṛśya*). Having attained proximity, the "concealed function" (*gūḍha-vṛtti*) becomes "partial truth" (*pradeśa-satya*), exhausting its application until the ultimate.

[The text] asks below to provide a detailed analysis. Regarding the first question: since the six stages of "identity" (*ju-ji*) are named the six *bodhi*s, their principle extends even to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

for now, let us set that aside and not discuss it. As for the remaining five [stages], are they identical to or different from the meaning of the five *bodhi*s discussed in the treatise? In the answer, the intended meaning is as follows: first—

Furthermore, they are judged to be distinct; thus it is said they are "not the same. Next, they are reconciled to be made the same; the treatise does not say they are "identical," and for this reason they are called "separate.

If each is considered individually, they may also appear similar: the arousal of the mind before practice is the same as the stage of names; subduing the afflictions before severing them is the same as the stage of contemplative practice;
illumination having already removed darkness is the same as the stage of semblance; and emerging to perceive the principle is the same as the stage of partial truth. There is no... [text ends]

The preceding [explanation] regarding "no transgression" is identical to the ultimate [view]. Having examined the treatises, the logical flow of the meaning is very convenient. Regarding the subsequent question:

if, in the previous analysis of the various stages, it was established that all [defilements] are suppressed such that the former are severed and the latter are suppressed, why is it here that the former are severed and the latter are suppressed?

The intent of the answer is as follows: that which has already been severed is severed; that which is not yet exhausted is suppressed. Even Samantabhadra is still called one who must be "suppressed by the assembly."

The subsequent examples are as follows. Citing an example from the Hīnayāna constitutes a vertical synthesis (*yùnhuì*). Next, proceeding from below constitutes a horizontal synthesis (*héng huì*); because each stage (*wèi*) possesses all five [aspects], it is called "horizontal.

Thus, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) is cited to show that each stage is fully complete. Regarding the subsequent question: "Since the six [categories] are established in terms of stages, do they also encompass the distinct teachings?
The meaning of the response is that while the doctrinal principles of the preceding teachings are established, their ultimate principle must reside in the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*). As it says:

This is the stream within our teaching that holds that birth-and-death is itself nirvana. If one does not establish the six stages of realization (*liu ji*), how can one avoid the pride of overestimating one's attainment?

If it were otherwise, how could it differ from the three [other] teachings? What would be wrong with firmly establishing these three teachings? Thus, when each teaching is defined according to its stages, the meaning becomes naturally clear.
Next, the preceding section concludes by demonstrating that the ten "non-[dharmas]" excluded previously, though involving bondage and liberation in relation to suffering, are all termed "non-.
The Four Truths distinguish them by way of wisdom, while the Four Great Vows distinguish them by way of aspiration.
Thus, know that what follows concludes with an analogy; it is the Great Treatise (Mahā-śāstra). As for the phrase "nine layers" (*jiǔ chóng*):

nine is the ultimate number of the Yang. Therefore, this borrows the ultimate limit of principle as a metaphor. *Lí* refers to a black horse; here it is borrowed to name the skull at the nape of a dragon’s neck.
The treatise says: "The jewel is in the dragon’s nape; those with merit obtain it. It is like the instruments of hell; those with sin obtain them. Thus it is made manifest.
This is so. It cannot be attained by one who lacks the conditions; it is for those with aspiration and virtue. Aspiration is like the vow, and virtue is like the practice.

Only when both practice and vow are fully perfected can it be attained. Regarding the phrase "vying for and grasping equality," etc., this again cites the Great Sūtra to refute the three metaphors of cultivation.
This serves as an analogy for identity. Now, taking the three teachings as a general model for the three types of cultivation, they are all like entering a pool;
each person claims it is their own. *Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll One;
*Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll Two.

The Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Zhanran, at Fulong, has composed this sequential commentary on the first section, "The Intent of Coming," within the *Great Practice*. Regarding the statement in the heading, "entering the stages": even if one does not aspire for the ultimate fruit, it is still not considered "entering the stages.
If one does not enter the stages, then one’s efforts will be in vain. The meaning of the analogy is that yogurt requires churning.

It is accomplished. When the *sū* (butter) is churned until it is matured, the two types of *sū* having been produced, the *mārdhava* (clarified butter) can then be obtained. Abiding prior [to the first stage] is like the drilling and churning;

the name-and-characteristic contemplative practice (*nāmaviśeṣa-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is analogous to milk; the six sense faculties are like curds and raw or matured *sū*; from the first stage onward is called obtaining the *mārdhava*.
The "well-regulated samādhi" (*suvyavasthita-samādhi*) can be obtained at the first stage. Regarding the "inferior dharma of practice," the brief [teaching] subsumes the extensive.
"Comprehensively encompassing the lower [stages]" explains the general name. The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "In the language of Qin, it means 'the sphere where the mind acts with rectitude.

This mind is constantly crooked; when one attains practice, it becomes straight. "According to the *Dharmadhātu*" explains the treatise. These four practices all rely upon a single locus within the *dharmadhātu*.

Furthermore, names such as "constant sitting" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth are established based on physical postures. If categorized according to the Dharma, "constant sitting" is called "one practice," while "constant walking" is called "Buddha."

Standing; half-walking and half-sitting is termed Vaipulya (fangděng) and Saddharmapuṇḍarīka (fǎhuá). Neither walking nor sitting is termed "according to one's own intention" (suízìyì) and so forth. One always remains seated. These names for practices are established based on the teachings upon which they rely. Furthermore, the term "one practice" (yíxíng) is also derived from the abbreviated physical postures, rather than the principle that is the object of focus. If it were the principle that is the object of focus, then all four practices would be universal. Regarding the opening and closing of the body: [The text continues with the following: ...the body is opened or closed. Among these, the first three are called "opening," while the last is called "closing. This is because the former three involve movement, whereas the latter involves stillness. Furthermore, regarding the four types of conduct: the first three are termed "conduct" (*caryā*) because they involve the movement of the body. The fourth is termed "non-conduct" (*acaryā*) because it involves the cessation of bodily movement. Regarding the four types of meditation: the first three are termed "meditation" (*dhyāna*) because they involve mental application. The fourth is termed "non-meditation" (*adhyāna*) because it involves the cessation of mental application. Regarding the four types of recollection: the first three are termed "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) because they involve the movement of mindfulness. The fourth is termed "non-recollection" (*anasmṛti*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of mindfulness. Regarding the four types of contemplation: the first three are termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) because they involve the movement of insight. The fourth is termed "non-contemplation" (*avipaśyanā*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of insight. Regarding the four types of concentration: the first three are termed "concentration" (*samādhi*) because they involve the movement of the mind. The fourth is termed "non-concentration" (*asamādhi*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the mind. Regarding the four types of liberation: the first three are termed "liberation" (*vimukti*) because they involve the movement of deliverance. The fourth is termed "non-liberation" (*avimukti*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of deliverance. Regarding the four types of awakening: the first three are termed "awakening" (*bodhi*) because they involve the movement of enlightenment. The fourth is termed "non-awakening" (*abodhi*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of enlightenment. Regarding the four types of nirvana: the first three are termed "nirvana" (*nirvāṇa*) because they involve the movement toward extinction. The fourth is termed "non-nirvana" (*anirvāṇa*) because it involves the cessation of the movement toward extinction. Regarding the four types of dharma: the first three are termed "dharma" (*dharma*) because they involve the movement of phenomena. The fourth is termed "non-dharma" (*adharma*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of phenomena. Regarding the four types of truth: the first three are termed "truth" (*satya*) because they involve the movement of reality. The fourth is termed "non-truth" (*asatya*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of reality. Regarding the four types of path: the first three are termed "path" (*mārga*) because they involve the movement of the way. The fourth is termed "non-path" (*amārga*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the way. Regarding the four types of fruit: the first three are termed "fruit" (*phala*) because they involve the movement of the result. The fourth is termed "non-fruit" (*aphala*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the result. Regarding the four types of vehicle: the first three are termed "vehicle" (*yāna*) because they involve the movement of the conveyance. The fourth is termed "non-vehicle" (*ayāna*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the conveyance. Regarding the four types of realm: the first three are termed "realm" (*dhātu*) because they involve the movement of the sphere. The fourth is termed "non-realm" (*adhātu*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the sphere. Regarding the four types of element: the first three are termed "element" (*bhūta*) because they involve the movement of the constituent. The fourth is termed "non-element" (*abhūta*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the constituent. Regarding the four types of sense-field: the first three are termed "sense-field" (*āyatana*) because they involve the movement of the sphere of perception. The fourth is termed "non-sense-field" (*anāyatana*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the sphere of perception. Regarding the four types of dependent origination: the first three are termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because they involve the movement of causal arising. The fourth is termed "non-dependent origination" (*apratītyasamutpāda*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of causal arising. Regarding the four types of emptiness: the first three are termed "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) because they involve the movement of voidness. The fourth is termed "non-emptiness" (*aśūnyatā*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of voidness. Regarding the four types of signlessness: the first three are termed "signlessness" (*animitta*) because they involve the movement of the absence of signs. The fourth is termed "non-signlessness" (*ananimitta*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the absence of signs. Regarding the four types of wishlessness: the first three are termed "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*) because they involve the movement of the absence of desire. The fourth is termed "non-wishlessness" (*anapraṇihita*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of the absence of desire. Regarding the four types of non-action: the first three are termed "non-action" (*akarma*) because they involve the movement of non-doing. The fourth is termed "non-non-action" (*anakarma*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-doing. Regarding the four types of non-birth: the first three are termed "non-birth" (*ajāti*) because they involve the movement of non-arising. The fourth is termed "non-non-birth" (*anajāti*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-arising. Regarding the four types of non-existence: the first three are termed "non-existence" (*abhāva*) because they involve the movement of non-being. The fourth is termed "non-non-existence" (*anabhāva*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-being. Regarding the four types of non-duality: the first three are termed "non-duality" (*advaya*) because they involve the movement of non-dualism. The fourth is termed "non-non-duality" (*anadvaya*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-dualism. Regarding the four types of non-manifestation: the first three are termed "non-manifestation" (*anābhāsa*) because they involve the movement of non-appearance. The fourth is termed "non-non-manifestation" (*ananābhāsa*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-appearance. Regarding the four types of non-attainment: the first three are termed "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) because they involve the movement of non-acquisition. The fourth is termed "non-non-attainment" (*anaprāpti*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-acquisition. Regarding the four types of non-abiding: the first three are termed "non-abiding" (*asthiti*) because they involve the movement of non-dwelling. The fourth is termed "non-non-abiding" (*anasthiti*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of non-dwelling. Regarding the four types of non-form: the first three are termed "non-form" (*arūpa*) because they involve the movement of formlessness. The fourth is termed "non-non-form" (*anarūpa*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of formlessness. Regarding the four types of non-sound: the first three are termed "non-sound" (*aśabda*) because they involve the movement of soundlessness. The fourth is termed "non-non-sound" (*anaśabda*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of soundlessness. Regarding the four types of non-smell: the first three are termed "non-smell" (*agandha*) because they involve the movement of odorlessness. The fourth is termed "non-non-smell" (*anagandha*) because it involves the cessation of the movement of odorlessness. Regarding the four types of non-taste: the first three are termed "non-taste" (*arasa*) because they involve the movement of tastelessness. Regarding the phrase "or perhaps it may be equal": this means that when the assembly gathers in the meditation hall, staying alone is most excellent; therefore, it is said to be "even better. As for the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*):
first the left leg, then the right, with both feet aligned against the two thighs. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "There are many methods of sitting; why specifically the full-lotus?
The answer is: because it is the most stable; because it holds the hands and feet so that the mind does not scatter; and because the Demon King (*Māra*) fears it. Great.
Movement is called "moving. Slight movement is called "swaying. When [fruit] is about to ripen, it is called "withering. To lean against an object is called "reclining.

One who seeks to perceive the principle at the appointed time must not lie on their side for even a moment, much less lie like a corpse. Lying on one's back is called "corpse-lie" and is also termed the "prostitute’s lie. Lying face down is named the "asura-lie.

Regarding the phrase "excluding walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and so forth," "excluding" means to permit; for the sake of sleep or illness, the Buddha permitted walking meditation, which is walking straight ahead.

Avoiding insects, one should proceed neither too slowly nor too quickly. Regarding the three thousand modes of deportment, there are five types of secluded places: before the door, in the hall, beneath a stupa, and beneath a pavilion.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are five benefits that make one fit for long journeys: being able to reflect deeply, having little illness, digesting food well, attaining meditative concentration, and remaining there for a long time.

These allowances apply equally to eating and other matters; one must not rely on them as a pretext. As for "following whichever direction a Buddha faces," the words are general while the meaning is specific.

One should focus exclusively on the Western [Pure Land]. This is because it is convenient for the direction toward which one turns when the obstacle of mindfulness of the Buddha arises; moreover, the teachings praise it extensively, and many people practice it.

Regarding "fixed times" (*shike*) and so forth: "times" refers to brief intervals, citing a general short duration. Why must it necessarily refer to a *leu* (a specific unit of time) or one of the thirty *suzhu* (moments)?
Since one must not allow even a single *kṣaṇa* (instant) to be interrupted, it is said to be "general. [This applies to] "not deceiving the Buddha," and so on.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A Bodhisattva seeking the Way does not spare body or life, and thus is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

Those who are indolent, greedy for profit, and do not seek with single-minded diligence deceive themselves and also deceive the Buddhas. Regarding "not betraying one's heart": "to betray" means to fail to fulfill.
Failing to achieve one's initial purpose is called "failing to fulfill. Because it causes others to misunderstand, it is called "deceiving others. It also deceives...

Regarding sentient beings: when one speaks, one should act in accordance with silence; when there is a cause [to speak], one must speak. Minor exhaustion is called "fatigue," while great distress is called "extreme. As for internal and external obstacles:
afflictions, views, pride, and so forth serve as internal evil friends, while Māras and the like serve as external ones.

This is because one vows to accomplish samādhi without sparing body or life. The phrase "equal to the praise" is an explanation to dispel doubts, fearing that one might doubt that it is not appropriate to focus exclusively [on this].
To praise a single Buddha.

The reason for this is that it cites an analogy: just as when one is in extreme sorrow or great joy, singing or weeping provides relief. "Depressed" (*yù*) refers to a state of being generally dejected; "oppressed" (*fú*) refers to...

The mind does not leak [its intention]. The practitioner descends. This is a combined analogy. The *Śāstra* says: "The wind is named *udāna*; it touches the navel and ascends. This wind touches seven places:
the crown of the head, the gums, the teeth, the lips, the tongue, the throat, and the chest. From among these, speech arises.
The first five phrases refer to bodily action (*kāyakarma*), and the sixth phrase refers to vocal action (*vākkarma*). These two assist the mind, thereby forming the mechanism [of expression].

Regarding the phrase "if one does not understand the dharma-gates," since that person remains within *prajñā*, it causes them to accord with the Great [Vehicle], including the *sūtras* and all the practices and protocols of the Mahāyāna;
even such matters as reciting the scriptures would be neglected. Do not take this statement as a precedent for other samādhis.
The opening recitation applies to all others; the prohibitory discourse encompasses the four [categories].

Regarding the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), within these four modes of practice, I have provided a brief indication of the characteristics of the contemplation based generally upon the original sūtra. From beginning to end, one must rely [upon the sūtra].

Although there are here in this *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* some expressions resembling those of the "Ten Vehicles," they are again merely abbreviated and not fully complete. Throughout the text, I have relied upon those two *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.

The meaning is concise yet profound; it must not be misjudged. Therefore, these four practices for now pertain only to the ritual procedures, which will be explained in detail below, so I have no leisure to elaborate on them here.

For the time being, I shall briefly indicate the ten contemplations according to the present text. "Dharmadhātu," etc., refers to the objects of contemplation. "Transformative birth" [refers to the practitioner].

Arousing the mind is the stage of *śamatha* (calm abiding). Binding the mindfulness is *vipaśyanā* (insight). Severing afflictions is the stage of "pervasive penetration. Traversing the dharmas is the stage of "penetration and obstruction.
