Cultivating the path refers to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Contemplating karma and suffering is the stage of "aiding the path. Recognizing that contemplation does not err is the stage of "successive positions.

Within these successive positions, the meanings of the latter two stages are also included; subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. Regarding "sitting upright" and so forth, this generally applies to the physical posture established for both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

"Characteristics of the mind" (*citta-lakṣaṇa*). "Eliminating the lower" (*apakarṣa*) clarifies the method of cultivating contemplation (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*); from "from the beginning" to "cessation of distracted thoughts" (*vikalpa*), this is that which is to be remedied.

From "do not allow confusion" to "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*), this is also that which is to be remedied. From "merely by focusing" onwards, it correctly clarifies the contemplating subject (*vipaśyaka*). From "one must have faith" onwards, it exhorts one to have faith.

Because the *dharmadhātu* is not subsumed by the three [categories], it is known through internal realization (*pratyātma-vedya*) and explained for the benefit of others. Since the *dharmadhātu* is not limited, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is said to be "detached" from a superior perspective. Because the center and the extremes are mutually identical, one dwells in non-dwelling.

Because the mind is in harmony with the *dharmadhātu*, it is called "abiding securely. Regarding the passage "Upon hearing this," etc.: it refers to the dwelling place of ordinary beings, and exhorts them not to be alarmed.
Being able to descend in this manner causes one to contemplate the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This immediately raises the object [of contemplation] to exhort the conclusion:

because the preceding object, the Dharma, is endowed with the ten titles (*daśa-nāmāni*), one performs this contemplation of the ten titles. Since the contemplation of the ten titles resides in the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the Responsive Body is itself the Dharma, it is thus the title of the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, one must also explain these titles by way of the relationship between the object and wisdom; thus, the essence of the Dharma and the Responsive Body is one, and the two titles are no different. Moreover, as for the ten titles...

The various teachings differ, and thus the translators perceive them as distinct. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*) and "Tamer of Men" (*sārathi-satpuruṣa*) are combined into a single title, continuing up to "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) as the tenth.
In the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* (or *Śrī-garbha-vyūha*), however, these are separated into two titles, continuing up to "Buddha" as the tenth.
"Observing the Tathāgata" and below clarifies the non-duality of object and wisdom (*jñāna*). First, the *dharmakāya* is cited as the object;

since the knowledge of the object arises through wisdom, it is first established with the words "not [merely] called," etc. "Not [merely] called" is itself wisdom. "There is nothing... and below clarifies that the object is without marks (*animitta*).

"Nor is there... and below clarifies that wisdom is without marks. "The Tathāgata... and below clarifies the non-duality of object and wisdom: because they are one, there is no duality; because they are all-pervasive, there is no...

Movement: Because it is fundamentally existent, it does not act. Being pervasive yet without marks, its name does not reside in any direction. Being without marks yet pervasive, its name does not depart from any direction.
The world is not the world; therefore, it is said to be neither world nor non-world. The dual negation is called "non-duality. The dual illumination is called "non-non-duality.
That which is not wisdom is called "neither defilement nor purity."

"Contemplating this" and below concludes with a praise: because the object and wisdom are not shared [with ordinary beings], they are marvelous; because they universally transcend [all conceptualization], they are like space. Supreme virtues increase spontaneously.
"Contemplating the Buddha" and below refers to seeing the Buddha through the perfection of contemplation; although this was not the original aim, the power of contemplation brings it about.
This is precisely abiding in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). One perceives the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) and hears the Buddha’s teaching;

this does not contradict one’s original vow. For the sake of sentient beings, he describes his original vows: because of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he perceives the Buddha; because of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), he does not grasp [at them]. The same applies to adornment:

it consists solely of the adornments of compassion and wisdom, as well as merit and insight. Regarding the statement "the Buddha does not realize [them]," he cites the Buddha as an example. The Buddha...
Because there is nothing to be attained, I have no realization. To take the fruit as realization is to grasp at dharmas as attainment.
Next, observing that sentient beings in the three paths are identical to the three virtues of the path of suffering—because their principle is equal—they are thus like Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "equal in measure," it means that the number of sentient beings and the number of Buddhas are without difference, and are therefore equal. That all are called "inconceivable" further explains the preceding passage.

Previously it was said that "the arising is like the Buddha," and now it is said that "the Buddha is like the arising. This is also an exaltation of the principle of the mutual likeness between these characteristics.

Following the passage "The realm of sentient beings abides... and so forth, the intent is to clarify the purpose of contemplating the mutual likeness between the arising and the Buddha; the aim is to lead one to contemplate the arising as being like the Buddha.

Although it is empty, one contemplates it; therefore, it is said that one dwells within prajñā by means of the dharma of non-abiding. Neither grasping nor abandoning occurs because of suchness (tathatā).
This remains the case for all subsequent passages.
Next, regarding the contemplation of the path of afflictions, there are two sections. The first distinguishes the practices according to the three truths:

the practice of quiescent truth, the practice of unmoving conventionality, and the practice of the middle that transcends both. The second section, beginning with "not abandoning the lower," contemplates in accordance with principle:

not abandoning various views is the conventional; not abandoning the unconditioned is the true; and practicing the Buddha-way is the middle. What was previously called "not abandoning" is precisely this [middle] that is dual.
Zhao. What is now called "neither cultivation" and so forth constitutes the "double negation.

Next, regarding the observation of the paths of action (*karmapatha*): when the most grave karma is taken as the object, the lighter forms may be inferred accordingly. As for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): killing one's father, mother, or an arhat;

causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and shedding [a Buddha’s] blood. Three of these involve killing, and one involves false speech. One is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of taking life, directed toward its object.

To discern is called "awakening" (*bodhi*); to understand internally is called "knowledge. Knowledge and awakening are one in essence; that within which there is no sovereign controller is called "non-conceptualization.
All of these refer to the cultivation of contemplation based on the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).

All that is inferior. By using the light to illustrate the heavy, one does not seek it and thus does not depart from it. This clarifies that it is contrary to arising and ceasing, and because it is neither cause nor effect, it is called "without beginning or end."

Below the "Seal of the Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu-mudrā), the four māras are further explained as constituting the five heinous offenses (*ānantarya*). Because one complies with the three paths [of existence], the māras gain an opportunity;
yet because one contemplates them as the Dharma-realm, they cannot cause destruction. That the māras are themselves the seal means that suffering is itself the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The two māras of the aggregates (*skandha*) and death (*mṛtyu*) are the Seal of the Dharma-realm. Afflictions are themselves the true reality; the māra of afflictions (*kleśa*) is the Seal of the Dharma-realm. Karma is itself the true reality.
The Devaputra Māra is the Seal of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-mudrā). Therefore, this seal is indestructible.

To illustrate this, it is like the following example of a long-standing seed: suppose there is a jewel within [a casket]; to forget it is like losing the jewel, while hearing and believing [the teaching] is like regaining it.

One should know that for those who have attained the vision of the Buddha, what they heard from the Buddha in the past and now hear again is identical in meaning to seeing the Buddha in person. This is due to Mañjuśrī.
"Below. This is because the Buddha also once heard [the Dharma] from Mañjuśrī.

"Śāriputra, below. This refers to the realization and understanding of the three persons in that sutra; here, the text borrows from that to judge the practitioner, for the Bodhisattva is able to comprehend it.
One who comprehends is given the name Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. "One who sits near the Buddha's seat" is so called by way of fact.

This expresses the underlying principle. "Seat" (*āsana*) refers to that which serves as a basis. One who hears this Dharma obtains the principle that serves as a basis, which is equivalent to being near the seat.
If explained according to the literal fact, it is because one can only hear [the teaching] by being near the seat.

The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" below describes and establishes [the teaching]. If one attains the first stage (Prathamabhūmi), seeing the Buddha-dharmakāya constitutes non-retrogression in thought;
the six sense faculties appearing as such constitutes non-retrogression in practice. These three types of non-retrogression fully encompass all the pāramitās.
If this is used as an explanatory establishment, then for practitioners of future generations, the meaning will be universally understood; thus, it may be explained in a general manner.

If a person is inferior, one should correctly exhort them to practice; from the beginning until the attainment of entry, this is fully explained as in the "Chapter on Exhorting Study" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, because this samādhi is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Like obtaining a mani jewel," and so forth, introduces an analogy. That sutra says: "Just as when one obtains a mani jewel, it is treated by a master jeweler; the *Avataṃsaka* says:
'It is refined and polished until it is exquisite, and only then does it rain down treasures. As for the phrase 'the bodhisattvas are able to know,' etc.:

from the perspective of the three vehicles, the bodhisattvas are called 'slow' compared to the Perfect [Teaching]. Only upon hearing this single line do they quickly attain [realization]; it is like being called 'virtuous' only after hearing the *Lotus Sūtra*."
Regarding the phrase "the bhikṣus and so forth": these two have not yet heard [the Dharma] and thus are not even renunciants. As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says:
"Now, renunciation is for the sake of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Next, regarding the explanation of "Constant Practice," that sutra explains it by means of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, who is a lay bodhisattva.
As for the "three powers," they cannot be analyzed in isolation. That sutra states: "In whichever direction one wishes to see a Buddha, one shall see him immediately;
this is due to the three powers. For this reason, this sutra is also titled *The Sutra on the Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha Standing Before One*. It belongs to the [Vaipulya] division.

In the Vaipulya [sūtras], the capacity [of the teaching] extends to four types of individuals. For the two vehicles, it is not the primary focus; rather, it resides within the four types of bodhisattvas.

As for the term "abodes" mentioned in the verses, this is because they correspond unequally across the three periods [of time]. Alternatively, they may correspond with the three factors such as *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought);

or with the five feelings (*vedanā*) such as joy and pleasure; or with the various stages (*bhūmi*) and their constituent factors (*aṅga*); or they are explained in terms of their connection to the realms (*dhātu*).
This is the method for assisting and evoking samādhi; therefore, it is not equal [to others]. This textual explanation follows the general intent of the sūtra.

Although the names are identical to those of the fundamental [samādhis], because they involve mindfulness of the Buddha, the joy of concentration is doubly distinct. Regarding the avoidance of foolish people and the like:
this refers to associating with, frequenting, or befriending evil associates (*pāpamitra*), as such actions give rise to unwholesome roots in people. As stated in the *Ratnakūṭa*:
There are four things that should be avoided according to the sūtras: first, gain and offerings; second, evil friends; third, evil assemblies;

and fourth, dwelling together with those who laugh excessively, become angry excessively, and quarrel excessively. Even for one who does not receive special invitations, these are not permitted by the constant rules of conduct, let alone for one practicing samādhi.
There are ten benefits to begging for alms (*piṇḍapāta*). All the Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises prohibit being satisfied at a single location;

rather, one should visit up to seven households in accordance with the principle of few desires. This does not harm the donors, nor does one accept special invitations. It ensures that all live together equally.

As for those who eat within the Saṅgha, this gives rise to various conditions for outflows (*āsrava*); since this is commonly witnessed by the world, it is not subject to further admonition. *Xiáo* (餚) may also be written as *yáo* (肴). *Cài* (菜) means vegetables.

That which is not grain but is eaten is called *yáo* (dainties); these are also served on *dòu* (bowls). Regarding "washing with water" (*guǎn*) and "bathing" (*mù*), washing the hands is called *guǎn*, and washing the feet is called *xǐ* (the character *xǐ* is pronounced *xiàn*).

Regarding "left" and "right," one exits by the left and enters by the right, following the path of propriety. Regarding "outer" and "inner" discipline: restraining the body and speech is considered outer;
restraining the mental ground is considered inner. Alternatively, both the Great and Small Vehicles may be understood as providing distant restraint over the mental ground.

Furthermore, regarding the last three of the ten wholesome paths of action, the world says that these "small" [precepts] restrain body and speech, while the "great" [precepts] restrain the mental ground;

however, this is not necessarily the case. Therefore, one must be well-versed in both the Great and Small Vehicles before becoming a teacher of men. As for those who have heard of samādhis and so forth, this is also found in that sūtra.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also states: "One attains bodhi because of the teacher. How could there be any lack of reverence? The treatise asks: "A good teacher may be revered, but what of an evil teacher? [The answer follows: Just as...

Why? The answer is: Do not follow worldly conventions; rather, if one can give rise to the wisdom of the Self, all should revere them. One does not discard gold because it is contained within a foul-smelling bag.
It is like a person traveling at night who relies on a wicked man holding a torch. I seek their Dharma, not their wickedness.
How could things such as clay or wood possess merit? Yet by revering them, merit arises. Sentient beings are like Buddhas—how much more so their teachers? Teachers are to be honored.
If even major transgressions can be concealed, how much more so minor ones? Nevertheless, since teachers are not always able to be perfect, they caution practitioners:

"one should cut [the food] into equal portions," which means using the weighty case to illustrate the light one; "it must be protected externally" means eating neither too little nor too full, being both affectionate and encouraging toward oneself.

Regarding those who traverse dangerous terrain: if one person fails, all are lost; companions should act accordingly. As for those who require a fixed deadline, they must establish a limit and not violate it.

Regarding "arousing great faith" and so forth: since there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma, it must not be shaken. To initiate practice based on this is called "great diligence" (*mahāvīrya*):
being untainted is "purity" (*vī*), and being uninterrupted is "advancement" (*rya*). Because it is guided by the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is unassailable.

Regarding "always being with virtuous teachers" and so forth: one who seeks [the Dharma] must surely follow what is good, and in their conduct must surely forget oversteps. One protects oneself through samādhi; how could one focus solely on forgetting the faults of others?

Furthermore, regarding the term "virtuous," it refers to having a correct understanding. As for "lying down and emerging," the sutra simply says "sleeping. The present intention does not permit temporarily leaving without a valid reason.
If there is a reason to leave, one is not permitted to sleep even briefly.
Regarding "next, the oral recitation and silence": after the ninety days, he instructs on the application of the three karmas. Next, "or chanting," etc., he instructs on mental recitation.
Since both the prior and subsequent stages are permitted, the intention is to ensure there are no omissions. Every step is the body; every sound is the mouth;
every thought is the mind. Thus, the three karmas are fully perfected.

Next, regarding the "mind" (*manas*) within the exposition of the contemplations on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) serve as the object; therefore, one first brings the Buddha to mind.

As for the "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*), this is translated here as "field," which refers to the sovereign territory of a single Buddha. Regarding the phrase "constantly bringing [the Buddha] to mind for three months," the current text asks, "How does one bring the Buddha to mind?
and so forth; this is the passage from the sutra in which the bodhisattva, while in samādhi, sees the Buddha and questions him.
From the passage beginning with "the thirty-two marks" onwards is the text of the Buddha’s response within this samādhi.

Regarding the phrase "may I also attain these marks," at that time one should eliminate all other perceptions—such as those of mountain forests—and perceive only the physical marks of the Buddha's body.

Next, one further contemplates the lower [stages], giving rise to contemplation regarding the object. The first two phrases correctly trace back from the Buddha; "not using the lower" means that after tracing back, nothing can be found.
These four phrases are listed: regarding "not using the mind to attain the Buddha-mind," it means not using the mind of the self to attain the Buddha-mind.
"Not obtained by means of the body" means that one does not obtain the Buddha-body by means of my own body. This is a phrase of double negation;
the word "my" is merely omitted, but its meaning can be inferred by analogy.
"Why is this? [The text] below provides the explanation. That which can observe and that which is observed are without marks and without attainment.

Body and speech are form (*rūpa*); wisdom is mind (*citta*). The existence of form and mind arises precisely because of the existence of a self (*ātman*). Since the self sought cannot be found, it accords with the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent.

Because one breaks through this fundamental non-existence, it is called "destroying the root. Furthermore, because one cuts off even this destruction, it is called "cutting off the root. (First: the contemplation of emptiness. Next is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
In the middle [section], the text cites six metaphors and three dreams: one jewel, one bone, and one image. Their underlying meaning is largely the same.

If one wishes to synthesize these analogies, one should know that the first dream takes the nature of the mind as the object (*viṣaya*), contemplation as the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) based on conditions, and the perfection of contemplation as the dream itself.

This is a synthesis applied purely to the practitioner. Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* is like the object, the *saṃbhogakāya* is like the conceptualization, and the *nirmāṇakāya* is like the dream. This is a synthesis applied purely to...

The Buddha is the object; the practitioner is the mental image. Seeing the Buddha is like a dream. This is discussed in terms of the convergence of response and stimulus. All three types of dreams are thus.
Whatever is perceived through the mind’s conceptualization of phenomena is likewise so. Although the three are largely the same, there are slight differences.
In the first and last two dreams, one sees clearly yet cannot grasp it; in the middle dream, one clearly does not grasp it.
And they see [the Buddha]. This refers to the perspective of the "limit of seeing," which corresponds to the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
Next, within the middle contemplation (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*), the initial passage is the text from that sūtra concerning the bodhisattva’s reflection after attaining samādhi;

the present text follows the sūtra but is somewhat abbreviated. This constitutes the cultivation of contemplation, which I shall now briefly explain. As for the Buddhas who are seen, it accords with what was stated previously.

The text on dreams: A dream is itself the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and it should likewise be visible. However, following the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), because it is more convenient to speak from the perspective of the mind, it is said that "the mind creates.
Since the Buddha is created by the mind, seeing [the Buddha] is seeing the mind; thus, seeing one's own mind is seeing the Buddha-mind.
If one sees the Buddha-mind, this is seeing one's own mind, because that Buddha-mind is one's own mind. Therefore, seeing the Buddha-mind is precisely...
"My mind" refers to the Buddha-mind reaching the point of seeing the Buddha; because the Buddha is the mind, the mind does not know itself.

"The mind reaching the point of seeing the mind" means that the perceived object and the perceiving subject cannot be apprehended. Thus, all things are nothing other than the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
There is no need to further employ the expression of "neither-nor."
Next, regarding "the mind having perceptions" and below, the commentary states it is "unobtainable. That "the mind cannot be shown" clarifies that it is not something that can be expressed in words.
"All are [mere] thoughts" and so forth clarifies that the reality is free from thought; even if there were thoughts, one would realize they are all empty.
The following verse summarizes the preceding seven-character verse and further explains the five-character lines.

Regarding the first line: because one contemplates that the mind and the Buddha are neither two nor different, one attains Buddhahood. The second line concerns contemplating that the mind and the Buddha are free from defilement.

The third line concerns contemplating that the five destinies are fundamentally pure, using the analogy of ice and water; the meaning of this metaphor is clear. The fourth line concludes the intent. "The Seal of the Buddha" clarifies what was previously...
"Contemplation is the Seal of the True Mark.

From "There is nothing craved" below, the characteristics of contemplation are explained: one does not crave existence, does not cling to emptiness, and does not seek the middle. Because the three marks are absent, all that is desired is exhausted.

"Existence" refers to the object of contemplation; "desire" refers to the wisdom of contemplation. Since both the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped) are forgotten, there is no source [for craving].

Birth is likewise without anything to be extinguished. That which is disintegrated is called "extinction," while that which perishes of itself is called "disintegration. Since its essence is fundamentally non-existent, it is termed "without extinction.
Because extinction is fundamentally non-existent from the start, it is termed "without disintegration or decay. It is called "essential" because it is the supreme among all paths;

it is called "the root" because all practices depend upon it. Regarding the phrase "this seal, etc.": it subdues the inferior. Furthermore, to delude those of the Small Vehicle by severing their afflictions is called "breaking the seal. (2)
If even the Vehicle cannot destroy birth and death, how could it destroy the seal?

In the lower volume of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, a treatise is cited for comparative analysis; that treatise is purely Mahāyāna, yet it borrows the terminology of the Hīnayāna for its exposition.

This is like the "Lion's Roar" inquiry in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, where the Buddha provides a detailed response. The characteristics and causes are each distinct; this is also clearly elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Bao'en jing*.

The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are the objects of contemplation; therefore, they are explained first, as already stated previously. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its "Chapter on Nature" (*dharmatā-parivarta*), says:
"Thus, the Buddha-nature is inconceivable, and the thirty-two marks are likewise inconceivable. The intention behind the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s explanation of the marks is also like this.

Next, regarding the explanation of the forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), one should speak of the "retribution Buddha" (*vipākabuddha*). As for the term "Dharma Buddha," it refers to the unique qualities themselves, which are designated as "Dharma.
Only the body of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-kāya*) is then the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The names of these forty qualities are explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, the Great Treatise (Mahāvibhāṣā) enumerates forty dharmas consisting of the eighteen unique qualities, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.
This present passage, however, is from the *Vibhāṣā*.
Next, regarding the exhortation to practice: Real Wisdom is the Mother of the Buddha; Insight (*vipaśyanā*) is the Buddha’s Eye;

Skillful Means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the Father; and Unconditioned Great Compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*) is the Mother. If this is so, why are there two mothers? The answer is: Wisdom is that which gives birth, while Compassion is that which nurtures.
If one lacks both Compassion and Wisdom, a true child cannot be formed. Regarding the term "one *gau*": the time it takes for a single cow to graze is called one *gau*. *Gau*... [text ends]
The character should be written as [愨-心+牛]. Regarding the phrase "if one hears of samādhi and so forth," this overlaps with the treatise and cannot be fully detailed here;
I shall now briefly respond to it. This refers to rejoicing (anumodana). There are four instances of superior karmic fruition and four instances of rejoicing. As for the four:

the three Buddhas constitute three instances, and the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time constitute one instance. When those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were practicing the bodhisattva path, they rejoiced.

This is the samādhi. I am also like this. Regarding the fourfold fruit: first, not being startled; second, believing and accepting; third, practicing with a concentrated mind; fourth, being able to achieve accomplishment.
As for "if one does not practice," etc., this refers to the *Ratnakoṭi-samādhi*. There are practitioners who feel compassion for those who do not practice because they lose great benefit.
"Like a person with a nose" and so forth is a metaphor for those who do not practice the Dharma; the sutra scrolls are like...

Sandalwood is like encountering a sutra; to grasp it with one's hands is to possess it. To lack faith is like having a noseless person [unable to smell]. To be unwilling to practice is like not smelling it at all.
One who is like a common farmer is an analogy for one who does not know the Dharma. To practice the Dharma is like a mani jewel; to lack discernment is like a farmer.
To instead practice greed and desire is like bartering a pearl for an ox.
Next, within the section on "half-walking and half-sitting," the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras are first explained.

Those sutras apply to all four [vehicles], but here, for the sake of establishing the Perfect [Vehicle], the ritual procedures for practice based upon them are not yet sufficient; therefore, in the text below, it refers briefly to the *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters).

Regarding the "seeking dreams from the King" and so forth, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) cites five causes for dreams: doubt, discrimination, habitual practice, present circumstances, and... [the fifth cause].
"Non-humans came to speak with me regarding these five matters in a dream; this present dream is one in which non-humans have come to speak with me.
The Buddha told Puṣpa-rāśi, "Do not propagate this recklessly. You must take the divine spirits as witnesses. There are twelve dream-kings;
you may explain it only if you see one of those kings. That sūtra says: "Once Māra had been subdued, he addressed the Buddha and made a vow: 'We twelve...'"
"Great King, you should always uphold this dharani scripture. Puṣpaka asked: "What is the name of Māra? [The answer] is listed in full within the *Dvādaśa-dharmaka-sūtra*.
If one does not see [this], then even practicing will be of no benefit. Regarding the phrase "one should exert all effort," there are many in the world who practice with straightforward conduct;

such may not yet be called conforming to the teaching. Regarding the phrase "in a secluded place," this refers to monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) or forest hermitages (*araṇya*), but it may also include lay dwellings, as these are accessible to the common people.
The Sūtra says: "If permitted by one's parents, one may go forth to practice. If not permitted, one should silently contemplate within the home and recite this sūtra;
the ritual site (maṇḍala) should be conducted according to the procedures used in the midst of the Saṃgha.

If one can do so, within seven days one will see Avalokiteśvara preaching the Dharma for them. If the mind is distracted, it will instead increase the three miserable realms (trāya). The three miserable realms—"

Having emerged, one remains of lowly status. Regarding "both inside and outside the room" and so forth, one must apply incense to both. Regarding "the circular altar" and so forth, it should be made in the shape of a lotus flower.
Regarding "five-colored banners," there is no need to create various figurative images. Regarding "coastal incense," this refers simply to sandalwood. Regarding "invoking the twenty-four images":
whenever establishing a *dharmadhātu* (sacred precinct), one should first purify and adorn the site, and only then invoke the images.
It is said that while intending to eliminate obstacles, one instead incurs the calamity of arrogance; before the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) is even prepared, one first commands defiled persons to act.

To say, "Bring the image! Take it! Fetch it!"—how deeply lamentable this is. The latter section states: "After my parinirvāṇa, making offerings to the image shall be no different from when the Buddha was in the world."
Regarding sandals and footwear: place them separately inside and outside the *bodhimaṇḍa*. As for the length being "equal," this is for the sake of common understanding.
Regarding washing three times [daily]: if there is a specific occasion, one may exceed this; however, it must never be omitted. Regarding making offerings on the first day:

although one’s three karmas may be sincere, they require the support of merit; thus, it is increasingly beneficial to do so every day. If one does not prepare from the beginning, there will be no way to extinguish one's own stinginess and greed.
Regarding the striking and movement [of the ritual implements]: one must invite those who are proficient in both the internal and external Vinayas and have received the twenty-four precepts.
Because this accords with the Bodhisattva Vinaya, all twenty-four are termed "heavy" (grave). There must be a lineage of transmission from a master; they must not be conferred arbitrarily.

Furthermore, it may also be that they are not conferred. The Sūtra further states: "One should receive six heavy precepts according to the Dharma of an Upāsaka. Since it says "according to the Upāsaka," then...
The seven classes of practitioners all receive [the precepts] in common. Furthermore, in the sutra it is asked whether one may practice even if they have not received the six grave prohibitions;
the Buddha replied that it is according to one's inclination. Therefore, in current practice, many do not receive them. The Buddha stated that there are only two exceptions:

namely, slandering the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sutras and using the property of the Sangha, including the belongings of a bhikṣu. Regarding the mention of *dhāraṇī*, there are four versions in the sutra; one must [recite] them all.
Regarding the recitation and the confession of offenses before the teacher: if one is not proficient in both the internal and external [teachings], how can one undertake this?

As for the fifteenth day of the month, there are two such days in each of the two months (the waxing and waning); the white moon is primarily used here to symbolize the cultivation of goodness. In the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual, the date is taken from the calendar to coincide with the full moon.
As for the mention of "seven days," the intention is to indicate the absolute minimum; thus, it was said that after seven years at Mount Nanyue, ten people returned.
As for this, the Sūtra states that more than ten people may not pass through. Nanshan says: "I have observed those in the capital who practice the Vaipulya (fangděng) [teachings];

whether numbering a hundred or fifty, they are so noisy and chaotic that it is difficult to discuss the Dharma, further increasing their karmic burden. Now I say: if many people happen to be present, what fault is there in providing separate offerings?
As for the allowance for laypeople, this has already been explained above. However, one must possess the three robes and a sitting mat; if one goes out [of the monastery],...

[He] returned to wearing secular clothing. The Sūtra says: "If one is separated [from it] by more than two *zhang*, one incurs immeasurable demerit. Ānanda asked: "Is it necessary to shave the head? The Buddha said: "It is not necessary.
That people shave their crowns today is an error. The character for "sewing" (*fèng*) is pronounced in the level tone; there is no need to back-stitch.
In principle, these must be made separately; one may not borrow old ones. These are not garments for the enjoyment of those who have left the household life.

Regarding "speaking" and "silence": the one who chants acts as the leader, while the others follow the chant. As for the "ten Buddhas," they are listed in full in the sutra texts and the *Baibu lü* (Record of the Hundred [Rituals]).
Regarding the "parents": the Vaipulya *Dhāraṇī* possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom; thus, the sutra says: "This *dhāraṇī*..."
Only through *dhāraṇīs* can one truly act as a father and as a mother. As for the "ten princes," this refers to the various bodhisattvas.

The "one hundred records" (*bai lu*) and the *Nanshan yi* (Rituals of the Southern Mountain) list twelve bodhisattvas in full; these are precisely the assembly of bodhisattvas enumerated at the beginning of that sutra.

Regarding the "one hundred records," it is so called because the masters collectively compiled one hundred matters concerning the assembly. As for the "threefold service" (*trikarma-pūjā*), it consists of physically rising and kneeling.

Recite with the mouth and contemplate with the mind. Nanshan states that this is fully explained in the Tiantai tradition; this refers to the passage on contemplating the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) within the *Fahua chanfa* (Lotus Repentance).
Regarding "paying homage and making a request": the ritual requires one to approach with both knees forward, followed by the two elbows, and finally touch the forehead to the ground.
One should visualize the Buddha’s feet and receive them with one's hands. Regarding "presenting repentance": "presenting" (*chen*) means to arrange or to speak. Specifically:
Recall the transgressions previously committed. Generally speaking, these extend back to the beginningless past. Regarding the phrase "without delay" and so forth:
when the recitation of the mantra is completed, reflect as detailed in the fifth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Insight). The "second period" refers to the second cycle.

Within the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one first applies it according to principle and subsequently proceeds through specific objects, as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* where the head is likened to a palace and so forth, or in the case of Piṇḍola’s broom and the like.
"Mahā" (Great) refers to the correct object; it is called "Great" because it is neither partial nor inferior.
"One is all" is called "secret"; "all is one" is called "essential. To obstruct delusion and sustain wisdom, and to manifest the Middle Way, is called "correct.
Next, the passage beginning with "the sutra says below" concerns the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmas*). It differs slightly from the sutra; here we borrow that terminology.
"Seeker" refers to one who seeks samādhi. "Attachment" refers to giving rise to attachment toward samādhi. "Reality" refers to conceiving a self within practice. "Coming" refers to...
That "I am able to come and go" applies to both the questioner and the speaker; this should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the phrase "this is the same as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) and others," all [of those texts] refer to the general [classification], while the eighteen [emptinesses] refer to the specific. Therefore, it is said they are the same.
The eighteen emptinesses will be explained in the fifth fascicle. In the latter part of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the same point is cited.

From this point downward, one cultivates contemplation through successive practices. First, one employs the names of the scriptures as a skillful means; next, one attends to the physical forms of the honored ones, their ritual implements, and the ceremonial protocols.

The mind first seeks the King of Dreams; likewise, when practicing contemplation, one first establishes emptiness and the provisional by relying on these phenomena. It is said that, in principle, there is no beginning or end.
One first cultivates the provisional ritual procedures with an empty mind; by means of this, one will certainly enter the field of *dhūta* (ascetic purification).

This is because it is the basis upon which the principle of the objective realm is manifested. In the world, a "field" (*kṣetra*) is called such when used for threshing grain; here, the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*) are treated as the site. This is likewise that which is adorned.

The adornments are manifold, yet they do not transcend meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Although the ritual implements are numerous, only movement and non-movement constitute the ultimate.

The fragrance of the precepts is universally applied. Contemplating the ultimate truth, one observes that the aggregates (skandhas) are fundamentally empty, thereby escaping the children of the three delusions.

Unconditioned great compassion necessarily pervades the dharma-realm; since delusion is itself the dharma-realm, it is said that they are not separate. The fragrance of extinction universally perfumes, and the lamp of wisdom shines perfectly.

The Buddha of awakened wisdom dwells within the realm of principle; the wisdom of emptiness is established based upon that realm. Thus, as in the twenty-fourth [chapter] of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is ignorance.

From old age and death back to [birth] is the forward order (*anuloma*); from old age and death back to ignorance is the reverse order (*pratiloma*). As stated in the Āgamas, there are twenty-four factors for each of arising and ceasing.
Although the objects may be situated in the past, wisdom must necessarily rely on the complete [cycle]. This is like the salt, vinegar, and other items mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

when applied to the provisional and the actual of the present, it can be inferred by one's own mind. The robe of patience fits the body; "completely turning over" is called "new. The seven knowledges exclude...

Delusion. That which can wash it away is called "contemplation" (*guan*). Since the Master is also that upon which one relies, he is equivalent to the Truths (*satya*). Furthermore, twenty-four categories are established based on what is contemplated. These "correspondences" are established according to their meaning;
that is to say, they are posited so that the phenomena do not deviate [from their true nature]. As for the ten kinds of "garland" (*sragdāman*):

in the *Mūlaprakṛti-karma-sūtra*, one contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through ten different aspects: first, non-duality of the view of self; second, the mind as the agent; third, ignorance (*avidyā*); fourth...
1. Mutual conditionality; 2. Five factors of assistance; 3. Three types of karma; 4. Three periods of time; 5. Three types of suffering; 6. Essential emptiness; 7. Birth through bondage.

These are fully explained in that sutra, though they are divided into ten meanings according to their specific contemplations. The details of both phenomena and principle are as found in the text on the "Repentance of the Three Paths.

Regarding the word "etcetera," it serves to cite evidence for both phenomena and principle; within the sutra, the repentance methods for the seven classes of practitioners are fully contained. Although it is said that one is "reborn," [the text continues].

I am unable to employ this [argument] even slightly. If you were to allow it to be included among the categories, it would invite falsehood and bring about deceit; moreover, the sincere text of the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* does not state that these are such categories.

When distinguishing between the Great and the Small and establishing the regulations for each division, those such as the "eyes" are only designated as "similar" when they reach the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Regarding those who see the Buddha on the seventh day: that sutra describes distinct signs for each successive day. When ignorance is shattered, it is called the purification of afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the phrase "the three obstructions depart, etc.," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The two past [skandhas] are the roots; the five present [skandhas] are the substance;

the three present [skandhas] are the flowers; and the two future [skandhas] are the fruit. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also the house of the five aggregates is empty, etc.," since the various teachings differ, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) likewise...
It is appropriate to distinguish them. For now, let us set aside the others and retain only the Perfect Ultimate (yuanji).

Within the subsequent exhortation to practice, regarding the "threefold jewels," there is in principle no superiority or inferiority; they are distinguished according to one's own mind. Although the practice is termed "complete," [it is so only in name].

One must distinguish six levels of realization (*ṣaḍ-bhūmikāni*), as detailed in the sequence of the sutra. Regarding those starting from the [first] stage, the sutra provides an extensive comparison:
even those who merely perform offerings attain the merit of those in the middle level, which is immeasurable; how much more so for those in the higher levels!

Next, I shall explain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It belongs to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) and does not extend to the three provisional teachings. Its meaning regarding the "three practices" is no different from that of the preceding [teachings].

As for the terms "verbal expression" and "silence," these may also include the mental aspect. While the separate textual passages there merely investigate the four propositions, I have now further added the contemplation based on the elephant analogy;
this is because two sūtras are cited at the outset to testify to the characteristics of these two practices, thereby showing that these two practices must be perfected.
"Conveniently.

[This refers to] the section "Below the Two Sutras," which explains away difficulties. "Nanyue" [refers to] the section "Below," which proves that partiality is not permitted. "Especially" [refers to] the section "Below," which clarifies that because the two are not identical, [the former view] is not correct.

"Marvelous Realization" (Miaozheng) below [the title] judges the original intent of the text. The intent lies in realizing the Truth (zhen). Since the Truth is neither of those two [extremes], it refers to the First Stage (Prathamabhūmi).

"Now, traversing the text" below refers to traversing the matters [described therein]. For example, the "Lion’s Roar Dharma Gate" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or the "Pāri Tree" and so forth in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Among these, the "Elephant Contemplation" (xiangguan) is the most sequential. The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are explained below in the section on the Aids to the Path (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).
The eight liberations are as explained in the section on the meditative states (*dhyāna*). The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
All four must benefit others to be called "attraction. Therefore, it is said that "benefiting beings has many aspects. The phrase "many aspects" must encompass the four teachings.
"Those who turn their backs" refers to those whose bone-nature (*gotra*) is similar [to them]. This excludes those whose nature is not similar to the Buddha-vehicle.

Next, the explanation of "neither walking nor sitting. First, regarding the name: it is so called because it establishes four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). As for "in reality, it permeates all," this refers to the actual principle of the treatise;

the distinct practice of Mount Nanyue is what is termed "following one's own intention" (*svacittāśaya*). He asks: "From which sutra does this emerge? The answer is: "It emerges from the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
Therefore, in the subsequent explanation, the *Śūraṅgama* is frequently cited. The Great Master himself also possesses the three [practices] of self-awakening intention (*svasaṃvedanāśaya*).
[The text is] obscure. The contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*) is extremely refined.
Although the lower [exegesis] provides a comprehensive synthesis, while names and matters differ, there is no distinction in the method of contemplation.

Now, relying on the lower [text], I hope you will further rely upon the teachings. Regarding the various enumerations below, this is a question. In the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the mental factors (*caitta*) are not uniform.
Why is it that samādhi is called only "awakening-mind" (bodhyaṅga)?
[The text] answers by stating, "Exhausting all the lower [stages]," etc. It cannot be listed in full; one instance is cited to represent them all.

Regarding the section "In response to the object," it explains the meaning of the name: if one contemplates the nature of the mind, no samādhi is found; it exists only because of the mental constructions and calculations of the mind following its objects.
Third, the distinctions. Although the nature of the mind is one, three are established according to worldly convention.
Regarding such points as these, when wishing to contemplate their commonality, one first briefly refutes their differences. As for "the inversion of thought, mind, and view," the *Vibhāṣā* states:

To regard the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). The same applies to [regarding things as] self (*ātman*), bliss (*sukha*), and purity (*śubha*).

Now, this case is likewise: to reckon [things] as permanent and so forth is called non-awakening (*abodha*). To clearly realize that these cases are neither identical nor different in their characteristics, and to contemplate only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is what is termed awakening (*bodha*).
Below "The Awakened One," establish the contemplation. These three names, when viewed in relation to one another, form six propositions, as set forth in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*.

Thus, among these six propositions, "neither existent" refers to the nature (*svabhāva*), while "neither non-existent" refers to the name (*nāman*). Furthermore, it is not permitted to calculate that the nature is unilaterally one;
therefore, both are concluded as being neither one nor three. Other combinations and disjunctions may be understood by analogy with this principle.
If one understands that which is below "name," there are further six phrases that provide a detailed and layered re-explanation; these are all instances of double negation (*ubhayābhāva*).

Since the nature of name is impossible to rely upon, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are established by means of this detailed re-explanation: it is neither the single provisional (*prajñapti*) nor the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*). The remaining five phrases are to be understood by analogy with this double negation.
If one thoroughly realizes the nature of mind through both the single and the multiple [phrases], this is the inconceivable (*acintya*).

If one contemplates the lower [realms], the intent of establishing this contemplation is that the mind encompasses everything. By refuting the lower realms through suffering, one follows this example to refute the remaining latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).

Since this is a complete contemplation, it destroys ignorance (*avidyā*). For one who performs this contemplation, consciousness, volition, and ignorance are all overturned; if even ignorance is toppled, where can the various delusions remain?
Therefore, the passage beginning with "Thus, all... summarizes and condenses [the meaning].

The section "According to One’s Own Intent" (*svacittānuvartin*) refers to different names with the same underlying meaning. The first part, concerning various sutras, begins with the chapter on Avalokiteśvara;

here, while the phrasing is common, the meaning is distinct, as can be understood by analogy with what precedes. If one follows the subsequent text, within the twenty-five samādhis of the "cessation of thought" (*śamatha*) and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), these still encompass both the *Vaipulya* (Pratyekabuddha) and *Pāramitā* (Bodhisattva) vehicles.
The initial reception of the title "Please" (*qing*) involves three meanings of "requesting in return," as fully detailed in the sutra. First, it relies upon Upasena.

This is an invitation made for oneself. *Candracchattra* (Moon Canopy) is an invitation made for others. The four verses are an invitation made to protect the Dharma. Furthermore, there are three meanings:

inviting the body, supplicating the speech, and vowing with the mind. Moreover, there are five aspects: the body [prostrates], the four verses [express] the speech, and focused mindfulness constitutes the mind.

Since the capacity [of the practitioner] has thus opened up into three, the response may likewise be so. According to the method in the *Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, one must also examine the ten practices; this follows what was stated previously.

This should also be explained through both the literal (factual) and the symbolic (principle) interpretations. Regarding the fact that the *Śata-sūtra* contains the ritual procedures for providing willow branches and so forth:
this is because those Bodhisattvas hold them in their hands. If the literal act symbolizes the principle, the waving of the willow branch represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As for the "five limbs" (*pañca-avayava*), according to the *Bhūmi-vyavasthāna* and the *Āgama*, these are the two elbows, the two knees, and the crown of the head. If this symbolizes the principle, it is as follows: [as in that text...]

The Commentary on the Sūtra states: "If one rises, it is like the five aggregates departing from *sarvajñā* (omniscience). If one prostrates to the ground, it is like the five aggregates entering into *sarvajñā*.
Rising represents the five [aggregates]; entering represents the fivefold application of mindfulness. As for counting the breaths, according to this sūtra we proceed simply from one to ten;
the details are fully explained in that sūtra commentary. Through the breath, one gives rise to the practices of the Three Vehicles and invokes the names of the Triple Gem."

This indicates the removal of the three obstructions. The detailed explanation of the ritual practice is found in the *Baolü* (Record of One Hundred Matters), the *Zhengxing yi* (Ritual of Correct Practice), and their respective root sūtras;
therefore, it is said that one may consult these sūtras for further benefit. Since neither the *Baolü* nor the *Xingyi* records these four verses, one is directed to seek them in the sūtras.
Regarding "washing and confessing": the act of confessing is like showing the person [the fault]; the ritual procedure is like the lye; and the contemplation of principle is like the clear water.
Water: Its essential nature is like a clean garment; how could it conceal the stains of transgressions and cause one to enter the evil realms?
Regarding "before noon" and so forth, this refers to taking the first portion of both day and night. The remaining [practices] should follow the usual protocol and must certainly not be neglected.

The scripture states: "Next, one cultivates contemplation. First, one contemplates the aggregate of dust (the objective realm). Since even the term "emptiness" is still applicable here, it remains within the realm of arising and ceasing;

therefore, one further contemplates the illusory and the real. Within the initial contemplation of emptiness, regarding the lack of solidity in earth: first, one contemplates the element of earth within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

One first observes that the substantiality of matter fundamentally arises from conditions, yet through emotional attachment, one clings to its existence; this very clinging to existence is what is termed "solidity," which exists only in relation to the body.

The "roots" (indriya) are termed "substantiality" (dravya). By employing the designation "substantiality" with respect to the objects, one breaks through the substantiality of the afflictions (kleśa); hence it is said that "existence" and so forth are all substantialities.
The other three great [categories] may be understood by analogy with this. This is found in the response of Śāriputra to the question posed by Upasena.

The method for accomplishing contemplation is complete. Upasena attained the four great dhyānas through this and realized the fruit of Arhatship. Thus we know that [the path] exists even at the stage of the Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, for instance, regarding the refutation of the first proposition within the section on the "grounds" (bhūmi), one would have attained the fruit immediately; however, in order to prevent such a misconception, the matter is explained in full detail.

Therefore, within this text, both the nature (svabhāva) and the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of emptiness are fully explained; however, regarding the fire element alone, the text is abbreviated as it concerns only the emptiness of its characteristics.

Since form (rūpa) is thus [analyzed], the other aggregates (skandhas) should be understood by analogy. Question: In analyzing the first three elements, their functions were shown to be "common" (sādhāraṇa) and so forth; yet, when analyzing the function of the fire element itself, it is said to be "self-" (sva-) and so forth. What is the distinction?
What is the meaning of this? The answer is: there are two reasons. First, it is based on the sūtra. The sūtra says: "The fire element arises from causes and conditions;

one should regard it as being identical to itself, and so forth. Second, the meaning is the same while the names differ. What loss is there in this? That which exists is simply "self," and so on, up to "neither both nor neither."

This is simply because there is no cause; the scriptural text is abbreviated and does not mention the remaining aggregates (*skandha*). If one wishes to apply this analogy to fire, one should say that sensation (*vedanā*) lacks the function of experiencing, and its nature is unfindable.
If there were experiencing, it would be called "existent. This applies even to the "neither-nor" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*), which is also termed "experiencing.

Even up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is defined as discernment (*prativijñapti*), it is likewise. This should be fully elaborated according to the fifth refutation of the provisional (*prajñapti-bhaṅga*).

One who contemplates in this manner takes only the True Truth (*satya*) of the Hīnayāna as being "as it really is" (*yathābhūta*). Question: If that is so, one should speak of the Four Truths. Answer: The aggregates (*skandha*) are suffering (*duḥkha*);

grasping (*upādāna*) is the origin (*samudaya*); contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is the path (*mārga*); and reality (*tattva*) is cessation (*nirodha*). If one wishes to know the Pratyekabuddha, grasping is ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Upon attaining the realization of suchness (*tathatā*), it receives the name "True Reality. That the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) becomes the foundation for the wisdom of contemplation is as follows:

Without contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one merely accomplishes fruitless asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*); thus, we know that among the four teachings, only two involve suchness (*tathatā*). Through contemplation, this can be understood.

For now, let us proceed from the Shared Teaching down to the six characters of the three *dhāraṇīs*, and then from the Distinct and Perfect Teachings; moreover, the contemplative wisdom below employs exclusively the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).
Regarding the "elimination and subjugation" (*xiaofu*) mentioned in the subsequent three *dhāraṇīs*, it refers to the elimination and subjugation of the obstacles of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Poison. Next, regarding the section on the Vaiśyas: the *Sūtra on the Function of Destroying Obstacles* enumerates the characteristics of the six obstacles in detail. The Sūtra says: "Not far from here to the west.

The Commentary says: "The west is extremely distant. [Question: Why then does it say "not far"? [Answer: This is because the perceptions of ordinary beings and sages differ. It should be understood thus...
Approximating near and far by means of existence and non-existence, the following clarifies the *dhāraṇī* for destroying evil karma.

Regarding the passage "Destroying those who violate the pure conduct" (*po fàn xíng rén*) and below, the *Gōngdé néng jīng* states: "Those who violate the pure conduct, upon hearing this *dhāraṇī*, shall again attain purity.
Even if they possess karmic obstructions, by reciting the *dhāraṇī* and invoking the names of the Bodhisattvas, their obstructions will be destroyed and they shall behold the Buddha."

Next, I shall explain the six characters. Regarding these "six characters," the sutra contains three textual sections, yet here we employ only two. First, the six characters are used to treat the six realms of existence;
second, the purification of the six sense faculties is termed the "six characters. As for names such as "Great Compassion" and so forth, they are the interpretations of the Great Master.

The establishment of purity is divided into two parts concerning its lower functional capacity. First is the clarification of destroying the fundamental poison, which is to say, seeing the Buddha-way. Below the six characters is the main [section].
The commentary explains that these can shatter the six realms of existence. The names and meanings of the six realms are scattered throughout the sūtras and śāstras.
Here, the name "hell" (dìyù) is briefly explained: it is a prison beneath the earth. In Sanskrit, it is called *naraka*, which means "place of suffering. Regarding "hungry ghosts" (*gui*):

from ancient times, there have even been virtuous scholars who maintained treatises denying the existence of ghosts, yet they were moved by ghosts manifesting their forms before them, saying, "I am indeed a ghost. In Sanskrit, it is called *preta*, which means...

"Grandfather. Regarding "animals" (*tiryagyoni*): we shall not discuss them here in terms of the six classes; rather, they are generally referred to as "those who move horizontally" (*tiryañc*). Regarding *asura*:

this is translated as "not a deva" (*mùtiān*), also as "without end" (*mùduān*) or "without wine" (*mùjiǔ*), and so forth. As for the term "heavenly being" (*tiānrén*) used within the context of breaking through the human path, it is a name established according to its meaning—that is, one is called a "deva" from the perspective of principle.
As for the term "great man" (*zhàngfū*), it refers to one who perceives the Buddha-nature; only then is one named a "great man."
It is exactly as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. If one follows this meaning, there is also the "ultimate heaven" (*paramārtha-deva*) among the heavens;

furthermore, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) exists in all realms of existence. However, it is spoken of here as the "human path" for the sake of convenience, as the gods possess great bliss while those in the lower destinies suffer.
The "old friends" (pūrvajana) are the most easily attained. Regarding "the Lord obtains the subjects": Brahmā is the Lord, and thus the King governs his subjects.
Next, expanding upon the six lower [realms], there are twenty-five samādhis. As for the four such as the "illusory-like" (māyopama):

the south is the illusory-like, the east is the sun-light, the west is the moon-light, and the north is the heat-flame. Regarding the seventeen such as the "immovable" (aniñjya): six belong to the desire realm, seven to the form realm, and four to the formless realm.
This is explained in detail in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning), which states that it appears within the "Holy Conduct" chapter (*Śrī-bhadracaryā-prakaraṇa*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "this sūtra and others," this concludes that while the meditative contemplations differ, the present [teaching] applies universally to those of both the Separate and Perfect Vehicles. The destruction of hindrances applies to all three [vehicles].
The destruction of existence proceeds from two [causes]. "Self-disciplined" refers to a designation established based on its cause. "Of profound merit" means having cultivated for a hundred eons;

because merit assists wisdom, it causes the faculties to become sharp. If [the practitioner] is of inferior capacity, by giving rise to a compassionate mind and taking the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) as their object, they attain non-retrogression in mindfulness.

This refers to the stage of the first abode (*prathamabhūmi*). Regarding the "seven Buddhas and eight bodhisattvas," the seven Buddhas are according to the *Saptabuddha-mantra-sūtra*, wherein each of the seven Buddhas possesses the efficacy of their respective *dhāraṇī* repentance methods.
The subsequent passage clarifies the eight bodhisattvas, with their methods and efficacies fully enumerated in the *Bodhisattva Repentance Sūtra*.
Furthermore, in the following section, there is the Eight Dragon Kings Repentance and the Eight Hundred [Repentances] of Ākāśagarbha.

Regarding the phrase "the Sun and others," the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* states: "In future ages, those who are skilled in the Vinaya should teach sentient beings how to speak of the methods for treating transgressions.
One must consult the sūtra for the details. The *Nanshan Xingyi* (The Practice and Rituals of Nanshan) also shares this intent.
Nowadays, those who uphold the Vinaya do not demonstrate the ritual for repentance, but instead merely seek out the faults of others; this is not the virtue of a compassionate teacher of men.
Next, among the various virtues, one first distinguishes the four movements (*yùn*). "Movement" means motion; because the four minds arise and manifest, they are called "motion.
Because [the mind] is constantly moved by the four minds of the nine realms, it is called "movement. Now, when examining the nine types of persons, even the Buddha still observes the Buddha;
the movement does not go beyond the Buddha—this is the correct meaning of observing this movement. This section serves as a heading for the subsequent "Receiving and Practicing" (*zuòshòu*).

Therefore, I have discussed this in advance. Furthermore, regarding the two minds of "already arisen" and "not yet arisen" within the four movements of thought, I have caused the practitioner to observe them because worldly people consider these two minds to be non-arising.
Thus, I ask worldly people: when observing non-arising, do you observe that which has already arisen?

It is said that there is "non-arising. If it has not yet arisen, one speaks of non-arising; if it has already arisen, what need is there for contemplation? It is precisely because it has not yet arisen that it can be contemplated.

Thus, among the four mental states, two involve existence and two involve non-existence, all of which are with outflows (*sāsrava*). Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the "already" and the "not yet," it is like a person who guards against fire:

because they must guard against the fire currently present, they must also guard against both the already-occurred and the not-yet-occurred. How much more so for a Bodhisattva, who must still observe both the already and the not yet? Now, entering the vehicle of the Buddha, now...
This wholesome mind arises and ceases only in relation to the five sensory objects among human beings of the desire realm.

Furthermore, these four stages correspond precisely to the current text concerning "following one's own intention" (*svacittānuvartana*), which proceeds from the derivative to the fundamental. Although this is so, it does not mean that the various ritual procedures are absent within the other three samādhis;
therefore, one must examine each stage, both fundamental and derivative. Thus, the *Sūtra on the Examination of the Ground* states: "Contemplation is of two kinds."
First is Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*): all phenomena are but mind. Second is True Contemplation: contemplating only suchness (*tathatā*).
The present text concerns the sequential practice of Consciousness-Only; thus it says that one who can comprehend this enters the signless (*animitta*).

Nevertheless, one must fully understand the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) to establish the path of entry into the Way according to our own school. Thus, Master Fu Daoshi’s poem says: “I ask myself alone: the mind...”
What is there to cling to within? Upon examining the four modes of existence, they are all found to be unborn. How could a thousand ends and ten thousand threads bind one?

Thus we know that Great Beings likewise take this Dharma as their essential core. Although the Great Being does not explicitly mention the ten realms, these thousand ends and ten thousand threads are fully encompassed therein.
As for the phrase "one characteristic and no characteristic": by observing that the nine characteristics cannot be named, it is termed "one characteristic."
The absence of characteristics in the single characteristic itself is called "signlessness.
[This] poses a question to examine what follows. Having finished the question, the answer first addresses the "not yet" and then the "already," each with both a doctrinal explanation and an analogy.
Regarding the initial contemplation of the "not yet": since it is not truly non-existent, why is it not contemplated? Since it is not true cessation, subsequent arising proceeds from this; therefore—
Contemplate this so that the nine [categories] do not arise. "Zuo" (作) is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng). "Zuōzuò" (作所作) refers to performing the actions to be performed.
As for the fact that in the north it is consistently pronounced with the entering tone (rùshēng), this is merely a local dialectal pronunciation.

From "Next, having reflected" onwards, the answer states that [the state] exists while it is being performed; it is by no means eternally non-existent. All points are the same as before. Regarding the next question:

"If the three times do not exist, how can one observe the 'already done' and the 'not yet done'? Even the present does not abide; what, then, are the three times? In the subsequent answer, first there is a general refutation.
From "If the past... onwards is the specific answer. First, the objection is restated; then, from "How could... onwards is the formal response.
Answer: If you do not observe [it], how is it that the Noble Ones (ārya) also observe the three periods of time? [The passage] "ghosts and spirits, etc.
cites the inferior to illustrate the superior. Question: How do ghosts know? Answer: It is fully explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Ghosts know the past and future minds of women.

You should realize that you do not understand the three periods of time within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) at all; how then can you observe the mind? As for those who see "tortoise hair" or "rabbit horns," your three...
In the world, there are no such things as those two objects. This takes the flying hare and the water-tortoise as metaphors;

for if they were a terrestrial hare and a land tortoise, it would be possible for them to have fur and horns. Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "Like the hair of a water-tortoise, like the horns of a running hare."
One should know that this concludes the section below. If one takes the minds of the three periods of time as the object, then one is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Why? Because it is not eternal, it is not real; because it is not annihilated, it can be observed. One does not say that what is unreal need not be observed; rather, precisely because it is unreal, it is therefore capable of being observed.

If one gives rise to inferior [states], it is a binding reproach; if one gives rise to annihilationism, the myriad practices will all collapse. Therefore, one must observe both the past and future minds.
Thus, your citation of the sutra shows that you are not conversant with its underlying intent.

"Below, the practitioner is exhorted to advance. This means that consciousness, having cognized the various movements, gives rise to contemplation accordingly; because it contemplates what has already arisen, it is called "reflective illumination.

Next, "passing through below" correctly clarifies the arising of contemplation. First, regarding the twelve matters, they are collectively discussed in relation to *dāna* (generosity). "Receiving" refers to the apprehension of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). "Acting" [refers to the subsequent engagement].
This refers to "performing. Question: What is meant by "performing silence"? Answer: To perform the sign of silence is not to depart from the ten realms.

Regarding the phrase "if there are [objects]," this correctly distinguishes the objects of contemplation; one contemplates the strongest first, setting aside those that are present for the time being. "Dust" (rajas) refers here to material wealth. If there is nothing [to distract], one contemplates the performance [of the rite].

Within this, one first accepts [the precepts], and next performs the three contemplations within the acceptance. First, in the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one first restates the movement of the object, then reverses...

Regarding the section on "Contemplating Below": In practicing contemplation, one likewise employs the four propositions to analyze oneself, others, and so forth, establishing that their nature and characteristics are empty.

As for the statement, "That which emerges internally does not depend on causes and conditions," this follows the immediate flow of the phrasing; it should rather be stated as, "The emergence from within without depending on conditions is called the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness. Question:

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That which is observed is equal to blindness. Now, why do you say that the observer is like one who is blind? Answer: The *Vimalakīrti* uses the object to reveal the subject;
this is the skillful artistry of the translator, who employs expedient means to explain that sūtra. Regarding the phrase "space, light, and each [of the other factors] are equal":

when the eye sees a form, there is a conjunction of five conditions—namely, space, light, the sense organ (the eye), the object, and consciousness. This applies only to the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue...
The body does not depend upon light; the rest is the same as for the eye. The current text follows the context as it arises and thus speaks only briefly;
therefore, it does not mention "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), which differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) view where the sense organs and consciousnesses contend with one another.

Below, concerning "causes and conditions," the next section clarifies the contemplation of the provisional (jia-guan). First, it restates emptiness as the object: [emptiness] serves as the universal cause for the ten realms.
Furthermore, with the mind that has just ceased as the cause, and the sense organs, objects, space, and light as the conditions, they combine to produce consciousness.

Regarding the statement that "visual consciousness arises conditioned by mental consciousness": this refers to the arising of visual consciousness based on the first moment [of mental consciousness]. Regarding the statement that "mental consciousness arises based on visual consciousness":

this means that immediately after the visual consciousness has ceased, it serves as the cause for the mental faculty (*manas*), and when it encounters other objects, visual consciousness arises once again.
Therefore, these two types of consciousness act as causes for one another. As for the statement that "visual consciousness is able to see," this is based on the Sūtra.

The school [of thought] may say that this is "conscious perception. In this manner, the ten realms arise in succession. Regarding "greed and defilement" and so forth: greed is the root of delusion; by violating the precepts, one falls into hell.

The details of violating the precepts are as clearly explained in the *Piānjù* (the *Śīla-skandha*). Is it not truly love? Therefore, one falls into flattery and deception. As for "calculating selfhood" and so forth—who does not suffer from this?
To speak of it as being "only among animals" is a case where the words are general but the meaning is specific; it refers to [those who treat] their own retinues as...
That which can be reckoned as "self" is what the sages who have severed [delusion] regard as such; this is a universal principle. Regarding "giving by another" and so forth:
taking what is given by another constitutes the avoidance of taking what is not given (*adattādāna*). The latter phrase clarifies the former, establishing the meaning of giving by another.

Since one does not take what is not given, it is called "not taking what is not given. To forget wealth through propriety is termed "giving. If, for the sake of one's parents, husband, or the Buddha-Dharma...
That which is prohibited is taking what is not given (*adattādāna*). Even when another has bestowed it, one remains detached; this includes improper timing, place, measure, and selling, and so forth.

While this is the specific analysis, the general meaning may be understood thus: all other [objects] such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so on are likewise [prohibited]. "Yang" (譲) means "to yield" or "to relinquish."

"Zheng (Rectitude)" means correctness. Movement that accords with the compass and square is "Li" (Ritual). "Ming" (Clarity) is identical to "Zhi" (Wisdom). The remaining names are the same as in the older [translation].

The five constant virtues are complete, the five precepts are fulfilled, and the ten wholesome actions are perfected while the ten unwholesome actions cease. This applies only to humans and devas dwelling on earth within the realm of desire; all others are omitted.

Below, in the section on "Contemplating the Four Periods," the four periods of the Two Vehicles are clarified. First, the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) reveals the Śrāvaka Vehicle:

because of impermanence there is arising and ceasing; because of impurity there is no abiding; because of suffering there are the three feelings; and because of non-self there is no sovereignty. The single phrase regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) spontaneously clarifies the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

"Observing oneself and below": the Bodhisattva is free from these three [faults]. The first refers to the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). "Compassionately pitying oneself" refers to observing one's own self; "pitying others" refers to observing others.

The following section explains the characteristics of the six perfections. The single phrase "abandoning that which cannot be extinguished" is used to exclude the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and to include ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), because the Śrāvaka-piṭaka is the same as that of ordinary beings.

Now, regarding the observation of the lower [realms] and the universal observation: as for the mention of "three things," the intent is that the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the sensation (*vedanā*) constitute the three;
