The Tiantai śramaṇa Shi Zhanran, at Fulong, here provides the second major section of his commentary:
the Explanation of Names. Now, the establishment of names varies; some have a causal basis, while others do not.
Nirvana is likewise; there are no causes or conditions for it, yet names are forcibly established for it. Calm abiding and insight are also like this:

that which is without cause is termed "having causes and conditions. For the sake of sentient beings, these designations are established according to their capacities. Furthermore, supramundane names are established based upon mundane names.
Thus, one should know that the noble ones establish mundane names as a skillful means to create supramundane names, thereby establishing calm abiding and insight.

The visible patterns of nomenclature and classification can be understood as follows: in general terms, these are referred to as "general and specific" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), or alternatively as "extensive and concise.
The former is concise while the latter is extensive for the purpose of explaining the meaning; the former is extensive while the latter is concise for the purpose of comprehensive retention.

Now, by expanding upon the previous conciseness, the meaning is made easier to understand; therefore, this extensive exposition is also presented according to the four *siddhāntas*. Because the causes and conditions differ, there is further expansion and contraction. First, the preceding section is concluded.

Regarding the phrase "After [the preceding], it is also called the general outline of the intent for coming" (*shōgo yaku mei raigi taizu ketsu zen fuku i shōgo taizu tō*), *tō* (途) means a path or way.

Since its specific tracks have not yet been discussed in detail, it is called a "general outline" (*taizu*). *Toku* (挾) means briefly; *gai* (槩) means to level or summarize. It simply provides a rough sketch of the main framework.
Therefore, within this general meaning, the causes and effects, as well as the practice and realization, of both self and others are roughly complete. Furthermore, by...

In what sense are "calm abiding" (*śamatha*) and "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) so named? I shall now further explain this by opening it into four gates. The first three are the designators (*vācaka*), while the last one relies upon the designated (*vācya*).

Regarding the sequence of the designators, they are sequential; regarding the designation itself, it is non-sequential. This brings together the differences. It brings together the different names of "relative" and "absolute. First, concerning the relative:

when things mutually influence one another, it is called "mutual form" (*xiang*); when things look toward one another, it is called "relativity" (*dai*). As Zhuangzi said: "And humans [have] seven..."
A foot cannot be called "supreme," yet an ant measuring seven feet can be called "large. What is meant here by "relative" (dai) is that there is only the relative where the coarse becomes the subtle;

there is no further relative where the subtle becomes the coarse. Since the present text follows the general outline of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it adopts the designations of "relative" (*xiang-dai*) and "absolute" (*jue-dai*) accordingly.
The same applies to the subsequent categories of "thinkable" (*si-yi*) and "unthinkable" (*bu-si-yi*), and so forth. Now...
In this passage, there is no preceding section to wait for; rather, the characteristic of "waiting" is established merely to manifest its ultimate transcendence.

All subsequent sections are exactly like this. Regarding the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*: although three names are opened up, these names remain general and comprehensive, encompassing the three truths (*trisatya*) without yet distinguishing their relative depths.

It is only upon reaching the section that clarifies the essence (*tattva*) that their superiority and inferiority are differentiated. As for the phrase "all evils" and so forth, while the terminology resembles that of the *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* [afflictions], its...
The meaning remains consistent throughout; all the scriptural citations adduced as evidence are likewise so.

If one wishes to preemptively borrow a passage from the "Exposition of the Substance" (*Xianti*) for the sake of clarification, it refers to the cessation of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the settling of the mind in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Ultimate truth itself is neither something to be ceased nor something not to be ceased.

According to the conventional explanation, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are likewise so. Thus, the subsequent text states: "The first three establish the next three; the final one possesses all three.

Furthermore, in the section on "stopping" (*śamatha*), it says: "the mind conditions the principle of reality (*tattva*)," and by citing the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*), it is understood that while this is general rather than specific, the analogy to what precedes can be known.

Regarding the third statement on "stopping" (*śamatha*), it says: "The words are common, but the meaning differs. These words appear to apply to the two preceding types of stopping, yet their meaning is entirely distinct.
Here, it is said that stopping is clarified by contrast with non-stopping; in the two preceding cases as well, cessation was clarified by contrast with non-cessation.

Because it does not cease by means of cessation through clarity, it is said that "the terminology applies to what precedes. Thus, in the former case, the subject and object are relative and their essences are distinct;

now, however, ignorance and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are identical in essence, and therefore its meaning differs slightly from what precedes. Regarding the phrase "now specifically concerning [the third]," this correctly introduces the third [category].
As for what is meant by "specifically": both types of cessation possess both wisdom and abandonment, yet they receive their names based on whichever is predominant.
Regarding the titles *Śamatha* (Calm Abiding) and *Vipaśyanā* (Insight): here we discuss only the principle of the Truths (*satya*). This principle is neither subject nor object;

it is only because of the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*) and their mutual relationship with them that the third [category] differs from the first two. Furthermore, while the first two are "calm abiding" (*śamatha*) established according to their own respective states, the third is neither threefold nor calm abiding;

yet, by way of contrast with the afflictions, it is provisionally designated by the name "calm abiding. This is done merely to conform to conventional thought, as it is necessary to distinguish these differences.
As stated in the sutra below, the citation proves that their essence is one: both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are neither arising nor ceasing.

Although in principle both are "neither," if one speaks of the dharma-nature, one must speak of it as "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirodha*); if one speaks of ignorance, one must speak of it as "arising and ceasing. Yet, by merely seeking these names, one does not know their distinct essences.
In the initial contemplation, the phrase "sharp pickaxe" and so forth should be read with the character *zhǔ* (to hew) rather than *shí* (stone). "Stone" is not the essence. Great.
Large stones are called *pan*; powdered stone is called *sha*; small pebbles are called *li*. Although these distinctions in carving are different, for now we shall follow the general usage.

The intent behind the carving of the *Lotus Sūtra* is likewise. Next, the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* is cited with the aim of reaching the ultimate limit; let us set aside its specific meanings for the moment. Third, it is explained according to the standard [exegesis].

Next, the explanation of "transcending dependence" (*juedai*) proceeds by first refuting the horizontal and vertical [dimensions], and then correctly elucidating transcendence. Regarding the initial passage:

by means of refuting the horizontal and vertical, one causes them to become horizontal and vertical, and causes one to know the horizontal and vertical; this is not yet called "transcendence. Because it involves the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as in the *Lotus Sūtra* and other texts, it is called "horizontal.

Because it involves the shallow and deep stages such as birth and so forth, it is called "vertical. Within the initial refutation of the horizontal, the first three [propositions] both state that they "illuminate the object."

As for the statement that "correct [practice] is for the sake of rectifying, while auxiliary [practice] is for the sake of removing delusions," what does this mean? It is intended to distinguish between their essential natures and their faults. First, one must recognize the auxiliary and the correct;

although both are abandoned through wisdom (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), they receive distinct names. From the correct, one falls into oneself; from the auxiliary, one falls into others. As for the phrase "illuminating the object," this is merely following the convenience of the phrasing; according to the underlying meaning, it should rather be said:
"Cultivating tranquility (*śamatha*) by relying on the truths, and removing delusions as the auxiliary. Only when reaching the explanation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) below can it be so stated.

Zhao [comments]: From the phrase "If it were not... onwards, he judges this to fall into the commonality (sādhāraṇa). Although the phrasing resembles the "double negation" (ubhayābhāva), the underlying intent actually involves a "double affirmation.

Therefore, he says: "It ceases because of the causes and conditions of wisdom and abandonment. Because it is dual and distinct from the previous two [positions], it is called "double negation. Third, regarding "neither cessation nor non-cessation," he judges this to fall into causelessness (ahetuka). It is simultaneously free from both the previous two;
it is not "cessation" because it is free from itself, and not "non-cessation" because it is free from the other. Contemplation (vipaśyanā) is also like this, and can be understood accordingly.

This is known through comparison. However, the names that express [these meanings] do not exceed the three teachings. Provisional attachments are closely tied to these names; one must eliminate emotional conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Under the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), one refutes dependence. That which can be conceived and spoken of is called "conceivable" (*cintya*). When attachment to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has not yet been overturned, it is called "afflictive fetters" (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).
Because afflictive fetters give rise to [existence], they are called "arising from afflictive fetters. Being struck down by transverse dharmas (*tiryag-dharma*), they are called "destructible."

The arising and ceasing, and the departing, are explained separately by means of the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation. However, only one instance of cessation and one instance of contemplation from the middle are cited;
because the middle serves as an illustration for what precedes and follows, they are not explained individually.

Furthermore, regarding "erecting the subsequent" and "erecting the refutation": that which arises from the previous four [conditions] is called "the arising of arising. The terminology of "established phenomena" (*dharmas*) must be understood in relation to the Three Truths.
If one still gives rise to attachment, even the initial contemplation will be non-existent. If one refutes this "arising," one immediately enters "non-arising.

Because it is designated in dependence upon arising, it is called "the non-arising of arising. Because it is designated in dependence upon the True [Truth], it is called "the arising of the non-arising. Because it is designated in dependence upon the extremes, it is called "the Middle. (2)

The "extremes" and "simultaneous arising" are called the two "non-arising. Each should possess three aspects; however, since only two types of cessation (*śamatha*) are established here, it is said that "cessation" refers to the stilling of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and abiding in the True Truth (*tattva*).

The subsequent cases may be understood by analogy, and thus are not explained separately. If the four transverse [delusions] are included within the first phrase, then once the vertical [delusions] are destroyed, both the transverse and the vertical are simultaneously eradicated.

All of these are "lower. Although they differ in being horizontal or vertical, their capacity for calculation is equal; therefore, it is said that they involve "relative opposition," "destruction," and so forth. Question:
Since the vertical progression has already reached emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, why is it said that "knots" and "delusions" arise? Answer: There are two reasons.

First, even when calculating both [the horizontal and vertical], one is still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); thus, logically, knots and delusions exist. Second, as they arise successively, each subsequent stage is entirely produced by what precedes it.
The fetters and afflictions have not yet subsided. To specifically refute them, one takes up the name of "mutual dependence" (sāpekṣa) to establish "absolute independence" (anapekṣa).

Having established this, one then uses the name of "dependence" to compare things with one another in turn; thus, although within mutual dependence it may be called "cessation" (śamatha), when viewed from the perspective of the absolute, it still becomes "non-cessation.

Therefore, among the three [aspects] of mutual dependence, before the absolute is established, the first two types of cessation do not even constitute cessation, let alone non-cessation. This is also the case for śamatha and vipaśyanā. This is the middle [section].

Although there is no dependence [in the ultimate sense], because they arise through causal dependence, the three truths depend upon one another; thus, none are yet called "absolute. Why is this? The following passage explains the intent of the previous refutation.
It explains that the elimination of attachments was not exhaustive. It explains the attachments to horizontal and vertical natures within the aforementioned dependence.

"The path of language," etc., explains the previous notion that characteristics are produced and are conceivable. "Karma" explains delusion; "fruit" explains birth. Alternatively, both karma and fruit may be [the objects of the refutation].
Regarding the statement that "birth does not cease," this explains what is subject to destruction.

Now, with the words "below," the text formally explains cessation. First, it clarifies that which is ceased: namely, all horizontal and vertical dependencies. Afflictions (*kleśa*) are merely the conceptualization of the nature of things within the four alternatives (*catuskoṭi*).
Because of this conceptualization of nature, there is karma and its fruit. By receiving the teachings and practicing contemplation, one realizes [the truth] in successive stages.
All of these are objects of thought; therefore, they must be shattered. "All below" clarifies that which can bring about cessation.

Although it is said that *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) reside in the capacity [to shatter], this capacity itself is still dependent [on conditions]; thus it is called *śamatha*. When even *śamatha* itself vanishes, it is termed "unattainable. *Vipaśyanā* is explained by analogy with this.
"Even cessation and contemplation do not exist" means that since the power of the mantra can sever even that which is "non-existent," how could there be anything else?

Therefore, the passage below concludes and explains the severance of intention. The phrase "all are unobtainable" indicates that all things—both the subject that severs and the object that is severed—are separately set forth;

once the duality of dependence and opposition is severed, it is the final summary. Because one has severed the expectation of dependence, that very dependence remains what is severed. This applies to both conditioned phenomena and...
Regarding "can be contemplated" and so forth: each of these is explained as "cessation" (jue) in contrast to the preceding "non-interruption" (dai).

As for "perversion" and so forth, the four permutations—both horizontal and vertical—are all termed "characteristics" (xiang). Furthermore, regarding "also the cessation of the conditioned" and so forth, the names differ according to the specific point at which cessation occurs.

Regarding "cessation and contemplation that transcend dependence" (*juedai zhiguan*), this next section distinguishes the benefit of others. Since one has personally realized the state of transcendence, one is able to teach according to the capacities of sentient beings;
therefore, it is said that "it can also be taught. If this is so, then the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is also entirely for the purpose of transforming others.

Thus, the four chapters correspond to the four *siddhāntas*. Question: Now you clarify "transcending dependence"; why do the four chapters correspond to the four [benefits] for the sake of others? Answer: One's own practice (*sva-caryā*) consists solely of transcendence.

The transformation of others encompasses all four [levels of teaching]. Thus, in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Texts), the coarse fourfold *siddhānta* is opened up to become the wondrous fourfold *siddhānta*. Now, in contrast to the four chapters, these are the wondrous fourfold *siddhāntas*.
As for those who say that [these teachings] are for the purpose of calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is because these four chapters are none other than calming and insight.

Below this, the two types of emptiness are established. First, the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is clarified; it is also not found below. Since the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) has been refuted, both the horizontal and vertical [dimensions of conceptualization] are severed, and the principle remains only as reality.
The essence of reality is precisely the substance of the two types of emptiness. Below the character "is" (是), the name is established.

It is also termed "below" (*adhaḥ*). This is an alternative name for "transcending dependence. Thus, from "as follows, below," the characteristics of transcending dependence are explained; the text consists of the dharma, the metaphor, and the application, the structure of which is clear.

From "the people of the world, below," erroneous views are refuted: when worldly sentiments speak of transcendence, such transcendence is ultimately not established; because things depend upon one another without end, this is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).

Transformation. If one attains the state of "descending from the mind," having reached the ultimate principle, there is no further discrimination. When conditions cease without obstruction, it is still termed "waiting. This is simply realization; it is called the opening of true wisdom.
Furthermore, "attaining the departure of the mind" clarifies that the ultimate is beyond discussion; "the departure of mental activity" clarifies that the ultimate is beyond thought;
"following the departure of wisdom" means that discourse regarding stages and levels ceases. It is also "not descending," which overturns the aforementioned erroneous understandings.
The term "etc. includes saṃsāra. From "various" downwards, it emphasizes the function of the stage of true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*).

As in the previous section, an analogy is cited: "the former" refers to advancing. Just as a fire-drill not only advances the fire but also consumes itself, and not only transcends dependence but also cuts itself off, it is said that "having cut it off, it cuts it off again."
"If that is so," and so forth, explains away a doubt. The doubt is as follows: "If true wisdom is opened, what benefit is there in the initial mind? Now, the following passage explains:
because it is explained in terms of the six stages of identity (*liuji*), there is no loss [of meaning].

Regarding the third point, "the convergence of different names": all distinct names are extinguished. By "convergence," it means that the extinguishing of distinct names is brought about by the convergence [of the three virtues].

In the section below on the various sutras, it explains the convergence of the distinct names for *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Although the specific names are universally extinguished, stillness and illumination remain perfectly distinct; yet, it causes all these distinct names to be none other than stillness and illumination.

Therefore, all the various distinct names are said to be "extinguished" and so forth. As for the question "Why is this so? and the subsequent section, it explains the intent behind the convergence of the differences: although they are all indeed distinct names for the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

"Those who do not know" refers to the section on the initial *prajñā* (wisdom), which brings together the various names for *vipaśyanā* (insight). "Liberation" refers to the section following it, which brings together the various names for *śamatha* (calm abiding).
"Like empty space" refers to the section following that, which brings together the various names for the non-duality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; these are the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

"Prajñā is a single dharma" refers to the verses from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* praising *prajñā*. "Liberation is likewise" and so forth refers to the passage on the hundredfold liberation from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
"Equal to space," etc., is also from the text of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. For example, space also has four names: first, space; second, non-existence;

third, immovability; and fourth, non-obstruction. If even emptiness, which lacks form and color, possesses these four names, how much more so for the inconceivable, which is neither cessation (*śamatha*) nor contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)?
Question: Why not simply synthesize the two names of cessation and contemplation? Why is it necessary to list two [syntheses] for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?
Yes. [The Master] answers: "Because cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are necessarily non-dual. The phrase "One should know" below concludes [the argument].

Furthermore, regarding "cessation and contemplation," since their mutual dependence has been severed, the name "severance" is established not by shifting the meaning of "dependence," but by returning to the breaths and so forth to bring them into self-concordance.
Cessation is also called contemplation, which is precisely "stopping"; contemplation is also called cessation, which is precisely "penetrating."

"Non-stopping" is precisely the non-stopping of stopping; "non-contemplation" is precisely the non-contemplation of contemplation. Thus, they constitute the perfect and absolute three stoppings and three contemplations.

Among the fourfold penetration of the three virtues, the first section clarifies the intent behind the names of their functions, while the second, through its repeated questions and answers, may also be understood.
Regarding "self and others, etc.": constantly contemplating *nirvāṇa* is the practice of self-cultivation; likewise causing sentient beings [to do so] is the practice of transforming others.

"Placing all children [in safety]" refers to the stage after transforming others; "I myself also abide [therein]" refers to the stage after self-cultivation. The former is called "cultivation" (*xiū*) and the latter is named "entry into a section" (*rù yī bù*).
This merely clarifies the sequence of self and others, beginning and end. As for "if one employs the following," this correctly clarifies their mutual correspondence. First, by means of these two...

Regarding the commonality of the three virtues in terms of characters: since various teachings may contain meanings such as "non-duality" (advaya) and so forth, it is necessary to establish non-duality by means of this commonality.
The question below explains away doubts. The doubt asks: "How can two dharmas be common to three? The answer is: "Only the Perfect [Teaching] can encompass them. Not... [text continues].
"Two yet two" refers to what is common to the two names. "Two yet not-two" refers to the Dharmakāya. In the lower section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it cites scriptural evidence;
since it employs both eighteen and one hundred and eight [dharmas] to prove śamatha and vipaśyanā, one should know that when one is empty, all are empty;

when one is settled, all are settled; when one is settled, all are settled; and when one is settled, all are empty. These enumerations are established according to phenomena, yet their underlying principle is such.

They are always identical. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* is cited to further substantiate that the meanings of these two names encompass the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). Chapter Twenty-five states:
"All sentient beings without exception possess the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; it is also called Prajñā, and it is also called the Vajra Samādhi."

It is also called the Lion’s Roar, and it is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Thus, among the five names, two refer to concentration (*samādhi*) and two refer to wisdom (*prajñā*), while Buddha-nature is non-dual.

Furthermore, below [this point], each term applies universally, because the names "calm abiding" (*śamatha*) and "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) possess one another; just as calm abiding possesses insight, so too does insight possess calm abiding.

There is that which is neither cessation (*śamatha*) nor contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); contemplation is likewise. Therefore, it can be said that cessation and contemplation each individually encompass all three [categories].
This is because they are "common" in terms of their names, yet "individual" in terms of their meanings, for cessation and contemplation each possess these three meanings.

Furthermore, [the text] below states that the three virtues (*guṇa*) pervade both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Question: The virtues are that which is pervaded; why, then, do they instead pervade the names of the pervaders?

Answer: It is not only that names summon forth principles; rather, principles also correspond to names. Furthermore, because the name is itself the principle, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* pervade the virtues.
And because the principle is itself the name, the virtues pervade *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Moreover, since both sets consist of three, they may thus mutually pervade one another.

Within this, there are first the collective and then the individual. "Collective" refers to that which is common to the three virtues; "individual" refers to each one being pervasive throughout the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation.
From "If one believes... onwards, it cites metaphors to exhort belief.

Regarding the phrase "while in the various sutras," this refers to cases where the names are partial but the intent is complete. However, it is only in the Perfect (Yuan) Sutra that one may say the names are partial while the intent is complete;

this is not the case for the three other teachings. One must understand this through profound insight and observe the purport of each section. If one discusses the Buddha’s intent, however, it is the same in all cases.
"Śamatha and vipaśyanā are also like this," and so forth, citing śamatha and vipaśyanā as examples for all the sūtras. Furthermore, regarding the three names that apply universally:
if one speaks in terms of their separation and combination, there could also be two, four, or even ten million; since the three names are immeasurable, they are called "all.
According to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Avalokiteśvara-mikkyō-gengi*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-ṭīkā*, all take thirteen as the standard. The verse says:
The nature of the path-consciousness is *prajñā*; the body of the Mahāyāna Bodhi; and the virtues of Nirvāṇa and the Triple Gem.

Now, these shall also be briefly correlated with those [categories]: the Jewel-nature is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); true wisdom is *prajñā*; and skillful means is liberation (*vimukti*). Regarding the three Buddha-natures: the causal essence (*hetu*) is the Dharma-body;
the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) is *prajñā*; and the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is liberation. Regarding the Triple Gem: the Dharma is the Dharma-body; the Buddha is...
Prajñā is liberation. Regarding the three paths: suffering is the Dharma-body; afflictions are Prajñā; and karma is liberation.

Regarding the three consciousnesses, there are also differing interpretations; here, we follow Paramārtha: the ninth consciousness is the Dharma-body; the eighth consciousness is Prajñā; and the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are liberation.
Regarding the three Prajñās: the ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā) is the Dharma-body; the contemplative illumination is...
Prajñā: syllables are themselves liberation. Regarding the three bodies as the ultimate destination, there are three types of nirvāṇa:
the nature-purity of the dharmakāya, the perfect purity of prajñā, and the skillful-means purity of vimukti.
The question "How so? below provides a detailed judgment on the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). Wishing to present the ancient interpretations, [the author] first cites the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

The question [that follows] constitutes the ultimate tenet of that sūtra and is also the fundamental aim of practice and understanding for this particular school; therefore, it must be examined in detail.

Among the ancients, there were three masters each within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions. Only after seeing these can one recognize the subtlety of our own school. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "It is like Maheśvara..."
On the face of Śiva are three eyes, which are the three dots of the letter *ī*. Thus, we now rely upon this to discern the essence of the Dharma. Zhan’an said:
"The Western *ī* is like the 'grass' radical (*艹*) character here in this land. Examining his interpretation, the meaning of the character is not established.
The ash-smearing heretics claim that Maheśvara also possesses three bodies; how could these three names cause the Dharma to be correct? First...

The Hīnayāna masters say: "One whose knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is perfected" means that perfection is achieved through the wisdom that abandons [afflictions] by means of thirty-four moments of mind.

Although the physical body born of parents remains as a fruit-bound state, this is merely a state of having remainder; therefore, liberation is not yet complete. One still relies upon substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Since such food is not singular, it is called "mixed. "One superior" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom); "two inferior" refers to the other two [bodies]. This is because the character for "one" is long.

The second [point] is because they are short. Next, "Furthermore, it says below" refers to the second master’s statement: "That which is first attained fulfills one hundred kalpas; that which is next attained refers to the thirty-four moments of mind;
and that which is finally extinguished refers to the eighty-fold entry into extinction. Therefore, it is said that [the conditions] are only then complete.

"If one enters below" refers to the third master. Regarding the initial phrase "if one enters": since there is still a body present, it is called the *dharmakāya*. As for "wisdom-consciousness" (*jñāna-vijñāna*)...
It does not proceed; this is called the absence of *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said to be "without wisdom. Regarding the statement that Arhats exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth:
once one has attained the meditative absorption of the formless and entered *parinirvāṇa*, they are termed an Arhat. There is only mind without form, which appears to possess *prajñā*.

However, if they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they are then called "bodiless. Since their wisdom is extinguished, they are "without wisdom. Because they possess liberation alone, they are called "solitary" (*ekavīra*). Each belongs [to its own category].

One person: their names are unrelated. Suppose three dharmas were present in one person: namely, emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), possessing the knowledge that severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and not abiding in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, this is called "possessing a body" (*sadeha*); it shall certainly be without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), and thus it is called "possessing liberation" (*vimukti*).

Therefore, they are provisionally called "concurrent. If these are accumulated in one person, obtained sequentially, they are further called "successive" (*paryāya*). These three minor masters [hold these views] forever.
There is no meaning in [the term] *ī*. Next, regarding the three [bodies] of the Mahāyāna: first, it is said that the *dharmakāya* is the primary essence because it is inherently existent;

therefore, it is placed at the beginning. The other two are to be attained; therefore, they are placed next. Between these two, *prajñā* must necessarily precede being free from impediments (*anupadhika*);
thus, they form a vertical sequence. As for the statement "these two, etc.," although *prajñā* and *vimukti* are pervasive and all-encompassing, even when cultivated...
The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and liberation are both partially attained. Because they are partially attained, they are pure; because they are not yet complete, they are defiled.

There is no difference in their arising within the world; it is merely due to the arrangement of the ornate prose. Because they follow the sequence of time, they are called "vertical" (*tiryak*). The former master says that there is no before or after;

from the perspective of the inherent completeness of the essence, they are called "horizontal" (*pārśva*). However, in terms of meaning, there must be a sequence of before and after, and thus they are called "vertical. The latter master says:
Regarding "neither being distinct": they are not distinct because both exist from the beginning; they are sequential according to their realization through practice.

Thus, it is said that they are hidden or manifest: the *dharmakāya* is hidden while within the bonds (*saṃkleśa*) and manifest once it has emerged from them. As for the other two virtues, they are hidden in their state as seeds.

Because they are ultimate, they are manifested; the three virtues are all likewise so, and thus they form a vertical alignment. These [previous interpretations] do not accord with the dharma and metaphors of the Great Sūtra.

Now, from "explaining below," our own school provides the correct interpretation, which alone accords with the intent of the sūtra. The three natures are fundamentally complete, and are termed the "Treasury of Principle. Regarding the phrase "all are inconceivable" and so forth:
it is because none of them can be described as being either three or one, nor as being different or identical, for they are beyond such conceptualization. [This refers to] the body.

Regarding "eternal" and so forth: one cultivates toward the treasury of principle (*li*), and only upon reaching the fulfillment of the fruit does one speak of the body as eternal. Because wisdom is perfected and severance is complete, and because these are inherently possessed by sentient beings, it is called "principle.

Regarding the statement that it is the cause of practice: among the six stages of identity (*liu ji*), it specifically pertains to the ultimate stage, while generally it pertains to the five preceding stages.
Now, in contrast to principle, it specifically pertains to the ultimate stage. Since the mind is not sequential, there is no vertical succession; principle proceeds from...

Cause and effect are simultaneous; they are fully present and mutually interpenetrating. Because they are fused, they are not horizontal [sequential]. As for the phrase "the characteristics are appropriate," this is spoken from the perspective of practice (*caryā*);

in reality, it arises from principle (*tattva*). Regarding "being able to manifest in various ways": the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are concurrent with the principle, and all possess the power of transformation;

therefore, they are all manifold. When transformation ceases and returns to quiescence, they become hidden; thus, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Next, regarding the single stroke below: if we analyze it according to the meaning of the characters, the three dots are one...

The letter *i* consists of one *i* and three dots; there is no sequence of before and after. How could it have further vertical or horizontal dimensions? One should know that throughout the beginning and end of the Great Sūtra, these are the three virtues (and so forth).

Questioning the lower [category]. This section consists of two question-and-answer pairs. The first text provides the formal judgment; the second text offers an opening for further understanding. The initial question asks:

"Since both the third and fourth [categories] reside in *nirvāṇa*, how are they similar or different? The intent of the answer is that *nirvāṇa* is not distinct, and the third and fourth are not separate;

therefore, they are now reconciled so that one may realize their non-duality. Furthermore, there are both general and specific aspects. As for the general aspect, all virtues fully possess the four [qualities], and thus they are common.

There are two further interpretations. First, because the body is eternal, the [other] two qualities are likewise so; the remaining three are also thus. Therefore, they are called "pervasive" (sāmānya).
Furthermore, one may use the two qualities as counter-examples for the Dharma-body: the Buddha is awakening (bodha), and awakening is wisdom (jñāna);

therefore, he belongs to Prajñā. Moreover, he is able to discipline others; therefore, he belongs to Liberation (vimukti). Thus, the word "Buddha" possesses these two qualities. Next, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is cited.

By the cessation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), all are endowed with the four virtues. If one relies on the "lower" [method], one further transforms the five aggregates and the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) so that they correspond individually to the four virtues;

therefore, it is called "distinct. Regarding "relying on the complete," etc., there are two types each for the general and the distinct; however, these merely concern the number of dharmas and do not yet involve the actual modes of practice (*ākāra*).
Therefore, they are now further distinguished: the initial contemplation is called "sudden," while the subsequent stage is called "distinct."

Next, regarding the "Opening and Penetrating" (*kaitong*): first, as for the questioner, it is as stated in the *Zhigui* (The Return to the Source). Both hindrances and virtues involve the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*);
ultimately, they are that which is to be remedied and that which is attained. Thus, these three hindrances all reach their ultimate limit.

Now, by aligning the three paths and four inversions with the three hindrances—since their names differ but their meanings are identical—they should both reach the ultimate limit. "Opening" means to open up obstructions; "penetrating" means to bring what is near to what is far.
The meaning of the response is as follows: for the sake of providing an opening, he first grants the premise that both may reach the ultimate.

He then proceeds to provide an explanation, wherein he again clarifies that the meaning of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) is universal; thus, they are finally and completely refuted. Therefore, it is said that they "reach the ultimate."

From the section "Furthermore, regarding the lower [realms]," it correctly demonstrates that the three paths and four inversions reach their ultimate limit. Regarding the retribution-obstructions (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*), they are divided into three;
since they have reached this ultimate limit, each opens up into three paths, for it is logically necessary that they reach the ultimate, as each respective land possesses its own three paths.

Since afflictions (*kleśa*) differ in depth and shallowness, it is logically appropriate that karma and retribution (*karma-vipāka*) should likewise be distinct. As for the division of each of the three afflictions into four inversions, these refer to the view-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the thought-afflictions (*saṃjñā-kleśa*).

There are four [views] such as permanence; there are four [views] such as impermanence regarding that which is not known; and there are also four [views] such as permanence regarding ignorance. Question:
Since both suffering and the afflictions are each divided into three, why is it not explained that karma is also threefold? Answer: Karma is included within those [categories];
it is naturally subsumed under the divisions, and can likewise be understood by analogy. Therefore, it is not discussed separately. Question: Why are there only four inversions?

"It is neither three nor five. [The questioner] asks: "In principle, names are fundamentally non-existent; they are established in contrast to error. It is for this reason that it is so. [The Master replies:
"When the Buddha first refuted the heterodox, he taught the four [marks] of impermanence. Subsequently, to refute the Hinayana, he spoke of the four [marks] of permanence, and so forth."
Next, in the explanation of the essence and characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), four chapters are established because the essence itself cannot be directly manifested.

Within these four chapters—namely, the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), the faculty of wisdom (*jñāna-cakṣus*), the ability to interpret (*vyākhyāna-śakti*), and the ability to overturn (*viparyāsa-śakti*)—the distinctions between gain and loss and the practice of conduct are clarified. Furthermore, four additional chapters are established to determine whether one has progressed according to the teaching or not, thereby using the means to manifest the end.

First, the purpose for coming [into this section] is explained; it is also called "concluding the birth. From the beginning up to "if one turns toward," the preceding two chapters are concluded. Once one knows... up to... [text continues].

As before, this concludes the general meaning of the preceding section. From "Names" up to "If one turns toward," it concludes the previous explanation of the names. From "One must recognize" onwards, it arises subsequently to reveal the essence.

Since the general meaning pervades both cause and effect, as well as self and other, it is described as "vast and open" (*hòudá*). Since the explanation of the names encompasses both the horizontal and the vertical, it is described as "broad and far-reaching" (*kuàngyuǎn*).

"Breadth" (*kuàng*) refers to horizontal extensiveness; "reaching far" (*yuǎn*) refers to vertical depth. This is as in the explanation of the names, where there is existence through mutual dependence.
The horizontal contains the vertical; when absolute, the horizontal and vertical are non-dual. This discusses non-duality by means of the horizontal and vertical.

Penetrating virtue is vertically distant, while uniting differences is horizontally vast. This discusses duality by means of non-duality. As previously mentioned, there is a slight distinction between "previously" (*qian*) and "toward" (*xiang*):
that which is slightly distant is termed "previously," while that which is somewhat near is termed "toward. One must understand this equality, and furthermore...

Regarding the essence (*tattva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in relation to the preceding two [sections]: the preceding two are both horizontal, whereas the essence and characteristics are exclusively vertical; therefore, they are described as "profound and mysterious" (*yuanxuan*).

Next, in the separate explanation of the opening chapter, that which is expressed—the principle of the truths (*satya*)—is taken as the essence, while their various distinctions are taken as the characteristics.

It is also said that this "reveals the essence," because the essence is that which is revealed. Now, from the words "The principle... onwards, it clarifies the basis upon which the four chapters rely and how they arise.

First, the teaching that expresses [the truth]; second, the practice expressed by it; third, the principle to be attained; and fourth, the discernment of right and wrong. If followed according to their sequential arising, these four chapters form a coherent whole;

if explained according to the intent of the text, each section stands out with exquisite clarity. Question: What is the difference between the characteristics of the teaching (*jiaoxiang*) and the explanation of names (*shiming*)? Answer:

The former distinguishes general names, while the present [section] clarifies the specific distinctions within the teachings. Question: Since you say this section "reveals the essence" (*xiantti*), why do you still discuss the teachings?

[The text] proceeds. [The author] replies: Because the capacity can manifest that which is manifested, as explained previously regarding the definition of the name, it is by means of the capacity that the object of aspiration is realized.

Next, following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the meaning of the chapter on "Function" (*yòng*) is clarified. Since the definition of the name already employed the categories of "provisional" (*dài*) and "ultimate" (*jué*) from the *Xuánwén*, we now rely upon the four meanings of "revealing the reality" (*xiǎnshí*).
The Sūtra says: "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. That which is known and that which is seen constitute the "oneness of principle" (*lǐyī*). [This reveals] the teaching of Bodhi...

The identity of the Dharma (dharma-ekatva) is the oneness of the person; the constancy of a single purpose is the oneness of practice; and preaching for the sake of sentient beings is the oneness of teaching.
The commentary further divides the oneness of principle (li-ekatva) into four aspects: the means by which it is manifested is the same as in the present text.

The four wisdoms are like the eye-wisdom; the four gates are like the characteristics of the teaching; the stages and positions are like the objective realm; and the contemplation of the mind is like gain and loss. Within this—

Regarding "the characteristics of the teaching" (*jiaoxiang*): it is called the characteristics of the teaching because it concerns the characteristics of the school of teaching. As for the terms "general" (*tong*) and "specific" (*bie*): since the preceding name is general, one distinguishes it by means of the teaching.

First, there is the clarification of the *sāsrava* (defiled) dharmas within the realm; these are the objects to be remedied by the cultivation of cessation (*śamatha*), namely killing, stealing, and so forth.

That which arises from practicing virtue refers to acts such as releasing living beings. Regarding the "four dhyānas" and so forth, this follows the classification of factors provided below; this is stated according to the majority of cases. To explain in detail:

in each of the four dhyānas, the single-pointedness of mind is termed *śamatha* (calm abiding), while the remaining factors are termed *vipaśyanā* (insight). Since they are now collectively categorized under concentration (*samādhi*), they are here simply called *śamatha*. Regarding the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*):
the first three have the characteristic of insight, while the fourth has the characteristic of calm abiding. Furthermore, compassion (*karuṇā*) is itself *śamatha*.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the contemplation of characteristics; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) possesses both. What is now referred to as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is not necessarily restricted to one [of these two].

As for the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākārā vipaśyanā*), it can also be understood such that the aversion toward the lower realms constitutes cessation (*śamatha*), while the aspiration for the higher realms constitutes contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Now, following this sense of aspiration and aversion, they are collectively termed "contemplation."
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, refutes this. Furthermore, when the three vehicles are compared with that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are called "not true knowledge.
If one considers the lower two vehicles from the perspective of their essence, they mostly belong to *śamatha* (calm abiding); this is also merely a general classification.

If discussed specifically, as in the case of the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*), the first seven belong to *vipaśyanā* (insight) and the latter three belong to *śamatha*; yet it can also be said that they are both insight, for all are described as being associated with wisdom (*prajñā*).

This is also determined by the general classification. Because the last three of the "unlearned" (aśaikṣa) stages are close to *śamatha*, the first three of the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) may also be classified as belonging to *vipaśyanā* and the last five to *śamatha*.

When comparing the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this classification is appropriate. Regarding the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*) and the refinement of the eight liberations, one may follow those [texts];
however, based on the general portion, they are provisionally classified as *śamatha*. Since there are such distinctions, it is said: "one."

Regarding the passage: "There are those who [practice] the wisdom of the Four Truths and so forth. Although, on the surface, these are categorized as *śamatha* (calm abiding) based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the nine visualizations in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* belong to the noble practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Since they are designated by the term "wisdom," they may also be called *vipaśyanā*. The following section criticizes clumsy methods of cultivation.

When skillful and clumsy methods are contrasted with one another, both are provisionally given the names *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; however, a detailed discussion reveals that each possesses its own distinct characteristics.
Next, we clarify that skillful means (upāya) pervades the sequential stages of the threefold sequence of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Tripiṭaka teachings are termed "clumsy," while the three teachings of the Mahāyāna are collectively termed "skillful. Thus, both the sequential and the non-sequential are called "skillful.

While the name "realizing the truth" (*tattva*) within the initial clarification of śamatha can be distinguished [from other contexts], a detailed discussion of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) requires further differentiation.
The second [section] concerns the two emptinesses. Regarding the second "cessation" (*śamatha*): what is realized by the three vehicles is largely the same with minor differences.

If one is at the level of the two vehicles, it explains that there is no need for the cessation of expedient means. Cessation is emptiness; movement is the provisional (*prajñapti*). Because the mind of emptiness enters into the provisional, it is said to be "always one."

Regarding the phrase "the third [stage] is called 'exclusive practice' (*piānxíng*) and so forth," the character *xíng* (practice) is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*). "Practice" (*xíng*) refers to the direction toward which the mind of the preceding two types of cessation (*zhǐ*) tends;

"function" (*yòng*) refers to that upon which the mind relies. In the "Contemplation of the Reality of the Body" (*tǐzhēnguān*), both [aspects] exclusively tend toward the True (*zhēn*), and one initiates practice based on the True.

In the "Skillful Means Contemplation" (*fāngbiànguān*), both exclusively tend toward the Conventional (*sú*), and one initiates practice based on the Conventional. Since neither of these contemplates the Middle (*zhōng*), they are both termed [exclusive].

"Partial. Furthermore, abiding in emptiness within *nirvāṇa* and proceeding toward the provisional (*upāya*) is called "partial activity. The movement [toward the provisional] is termed "partial function.

Moreover, knowing that the conventional is not the conventional meaning, one penetrates both types [of truth], relying on conditions to exercise skillful means (*upāya*). Since both types of the conventional are quiescent, it is said to be "tranquil.
That these three types of cessation (*śamatha*) are called "equal" is a term of humility and deference.

Next, I shall cite scriptural evidence to demonstrate that [the term "contemplation"] can be established in meaning not only with reference to *vipaśyanā* (insight), but also with reference to *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Regarding the expression "relying on contemplation," the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras everywhere list the two names of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in tandem. Since the three contemplations are already accepted, it would be futile to claim that [the term "contemplation"] refers solely to insight. Therefore, in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (The Jewel Ornament Sutra), the meaning of the three contemplations necessarily includes calm abiding;

the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) contains a chapter titled "Calm Abiding and Contemplation" (*Śamatha-vipaśyanā-parivarta*); and in the establishment of the teachings in the *Āgamas*, it is universally stated as "calm abiding and contemplation."

Next, to examine in detail what is stated below regarding their commonalities: previously, "stilling" (xi) was named as such because it stilled delusions; now, "true" (zhen) is so called because one realizes the reality of the essence.

Previously, "stopping" (ting) consisted in resting within principle; now, one likewise stops the mind within conventional principle. Previously, it was held that the *dharmatā* is neither stopping nor non-stopping.

Now, regarding the statement that [the three truths] differ because they rest upon the cessation of the extremes of "stopping" and "not stopping": in the previous [section], the three were one truth; now, the three are each a separate truth.
As for the statement that "the previous three establish the subsequent three," both the "subsequent" and the "latter" refer to the current text.

Because the "previous" refers to the "explanation of names," it reveals that within the essence (*tattva*), each and every element is provisional. Since there are three explanations of names, it is said that "the previous three establish the subsequent three. This is like the "truth of the true essence" (*tattva-satya*).

Cease. One must rest the views and afflictions and settle the mind in the true principle, thereby knowing the true *dharmatā*. It is not that there is no cessation when one ceases; the same applies to the other two.
Therefore, each of the latter three fully possesses the preceding three.
Next, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are explained. There are two explicit passages concerning them in the *Mūla-karma-sūtra*.

In the lower fascicle, the Buddha expounds the meaning of the three contemplations to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Sudhana, Dharmamati, and six other bodhisattvas; it is stated that these should now all be practiced together.
In the upper fascicle, at the section on the first stage (*bhūmi*), the sequential three contemplations are established in contrast to the two contemplations prior to the stages.

People do not see it and thus take it to be mere subjective opinion; therein, two parts are established: first, a listing according to the sūtras, and second, an explanation beginning with the words "That which is spoken.

Within the explanation, there are two sections: first, the formal explanation, and second, the differentiation of similarities and differences. The initial section itself consists of three parts, which correspond to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

First, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is divided into five parts. The first part provides a general discussion of the designations, treating both subject and object together. This is because without the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), one has no means to know the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Therefore:
One must rely on the two truths.

Next, he again brings together the subsequent section, which specifically takes the two truths as the subject to be explained (*abhidheya*). By using realization as an analogy for cultivation, one knows that the two truths are required.

This consists of the dharma, the analogy, and the application; first, regarding the meaning of the dharma: even at the stage of initial cultivation, one still perceives the two truths—having already perceived the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and perceiving the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
How could there not be the two truths? In the subsequent analogy, the clouds are the obstruction; the removal of the obstruction is called "arising," which is synonymous with "opening.

When the clouds are cleared away, the sky is revealed, and the myriad phenomena necessarily become clear. The upper part corresponds to the manifestation of the ultimate (paramārtha-satya), and the lower part corresponds to the clarity of the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). Because the ultimate merges with the conventional, both the ultimate and the conventional are revealed together;
how then could they not possess both truths?

Third, regarding the section on the conventional (*saṃvṛti*): this is explained in terms of the function of refutation. One must know that there are two truths; for whenever there is a conventional object to be refuted, there is necessarily a true (*paramārtha*) means of refutation.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish both.

Next, the section "Furthermore, distinguishing the lower" explains this in terms of emotion (*sattva*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). There must be two truths (*satyadvaya*), for according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there must be both sentient beings and so forth.

In terms of emotion, one speaks of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); in terms of wisdom, one speaks of the ultimate (*paramārtha*). The causes of the body being different is the conventional; that there is nothing other than liberation is the ultimate.
Just as in the Mahāyāna, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, a single dharma is established with various names, so too is liberation manifold.

"Names. These all refer to the meanings of the conventional and the ultimate as understood by ordinary sentiment and wisdom. Question: Since one has not yet seen the truth, one should merely follow sentiment;
how can there be equality with wisdom? Answer: This is explained generally and universally; why must it apply to a single individual?

The fifth section, "Brief Analysis," consists of eight parts in total. The first addresses the second [section’s] resolution of difficulties regarding the present provisional contemplation (*jia guan*).

Previously, the conventional was refuted to employ the ultimate; now, the ultimate is refuted to employ the conventional. Since both possess the function of refutation, should they both be termed "contemplations of the two truths"?

The intended answer is that, in principle, this is indeed so. Although both possess the function of refutation, the present refutation of the ultimate to employ the conventional is able to benefit others, whereas the former...
The conventional is sublated by the ultimate, which can only be practiced by oneself; therefore, it is now designated as "equality" based on its superiority.

Next, the third [level] is contrasted with the second. Because the second is superior when compared to the first, it specifically receives the name "equality. When the third is compared to the second, [it is likewise superior].

"Why not follow the superior [third]? [The opponent asks: "Why is the second not called 'equality,' given that it employs partiality while still being designated as equality? Why is the third not so called, given that it employs equality which is supreme and thus designated as equality?
The answer is as follows: The intention is that, in comparison with the latter, both of the former two are not yet equal.

While the second is equal when compared to the first, the principle of the middle one is now shown to be superior to the second. Although it is not formally called "equality," if one were to falsely claim it does not reach the level of the middle, then [it would be untenable].

The name in the middle [section] is even more excellent. Next, he asks a double challenge regarding the preceding two [sections]: since both [of the preceding two] involve contemplation, they could likewise both involve entry.

Why, then, does one first contemplate the True [nature] and only subsequently enter the Provisional? The answer in the middle [section] responds only to the first contemplation; by this, the second may be inferred. The two meanings are each distinct.

The observations of the entrances (*āyatana*) differ. Regarding the subsequent question: previously, the question refuted the identity of the ultimate and the conventional; now, it challenges the conventional from within the ultimate. Within the ultimate, that which is real may be called a "truth" (*satya*);
however, as for the conventional, since it is not real, how can it also be called a "truth"? Within the ultimate refers to the reality both inside and outside the realms (*dhātu*);

conventional truth refers to the conventionality both inside and outside the realms. Because the names "inside" and "outside" are identical, both are termed "conventional. This is the intent of the response.

[The first] questioner asks: "Ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is principle; it is called the *dharmatā* of principle. Conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is phenomena; it is called the *dharmatā* of phenomena.

Since both are *dharmatā*, they are both termed 'truth' (*satya*). The next questioner asks: "Since 'truth' (*satya*) means 'reality' (*bhūta*), are both [truths] identical to *nirvāṇa*? The intent of the answer is:

"Since the name 'truth' is the same for both, although they are distinguished as ultimate and conventional, they are both equally named *nirvāṇa*. However, there is a difference between the mundane and the supramundane. The next questioner asks: "Both are termed *nirvāṇa*..."

[Question: Regarding *parinirvāṇa* and the untainted (*anāsrava*): are they both untainted? [The intention of] the answer is this: to enter the untainted state, one must first possess right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

Although they share the same name, "right view," there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane. Next, [the questioner] asks: since the untainted is itself non-arising (*anutpāda*), they should both be non-arising.

In the answer, he likewise responds by pointing out that while the names are the same, their essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ. This is as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "In an ox there is no horse; in a horse there is no ox."

The mutual absence of one another is also termed "non-arising. Regarding the subsequent question—whether [the teaching] proceeds from conventional language to refute or not to refute—the answer is expanded into thirty-six propositions, as found below in the section on the objects of affliction (*kleśa*). Here, first, we shall address the four propositions within the text:

"refutation" refers to refuting the conventional; "entry" refers to entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "not refuting yet entering" refers to the realization of the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*); and "refuting and entering" refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The Dharma of the Arhat (aśaikṣa) is neither subverted nor does it enter [emptiness]. The non-Buddhists who have attained dhyāna are neither subverted nor do they enter [emptiness].

All ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), whether their views are subverted or not, likewise proceed from the conventional (saṃvṛti) and likewise enter into emptiness (śūnyatā); these correspond to the first two lines [of the verse].
Furthermore, those whose views are subverted or not subverted also proceed from the conventional, yet do not enter into emptiness; these correspond to the latter two lines.
Next, the second contemplation is explained in two parts: first the teaching (*dharma*), then the analogy (*upamā*). Regarding the initial phrase "equality at different times":

only by comparing the function of the former refutation with the function of the latter refutation does one attain equality. Following this, from "Now, furthermore" (*atha khalu*) onwards, there are two layers of analogies and their applications.

The first analogy illustrates entry into emptiness; the next reveals entry into the provisional. "Ordinary people and the blind alike do not see" refers to the two vehicles seeing the true and the conventional.

From "the provisional downward," the text correlates [the metaphors]: although they perceive the two truths, they are only able to employ the truth; therefore, it says they "cannot discern. The "four kinds of four truths" are termed "various.
"Herbs" represents the three types of grasses, while "trees" indicates the two types of wood. "Herbs" is the general term for grasses, comprising roots and stems.
The sparse branches and leaves within the text serve as metaphors for faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom. All four teachings possess these four dharmas of faith and so forth.

The four kinds of Path and Cessation are called "medicine," while the four kinds of Suffering and Origin are called "poison. When entering emptiness, one is unable to distinguish between them; this is termed "being unable to employ [the medicine].

Next, the analogy for entering the provisional (the conventional) shows that one also perceives the two truths; this is termed "seeing both emptiness and form," at which point one is finally able to distinguish the four sets of four.

Medicine and poison pervade the four sets of four truths; therefore, it is said that they "all" [pervade]. That which is applied to the nine realms is called "benefiting others. Below this is the analogy, followed by the application (*yōgā*).

Third, the contemplation of the Middle Way is explained in three parts: first, the direct explanation of the Middle Way based on the text of the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*); second, the analysis...

Briefly stated, there are three concluding summaries. Regarding the first section: following those two contemplations, it is immediately stated that by taking these three contemplations of emptiness as a skillful means (*upāya*), one enters the Middle Way.
One simultaneously illuminates the two truths; with every thought-moment extinguished, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience) and thus enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Now, for the first [point], explaining the skillful means, there are two different aspects: both "forgetting" and "illumination" are given the name.

This is by way of skillful means (*upāya*). The initial statement regarding the "emptiness of emptiness" refers to the emptiness of the provisional (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*); these are both "extinguished," meaning they are extinguished simultaneously.

By taking the prior extinction of these two as the skillful means, one now enters the Middle Way where both are spontaneously extinguished. Furthermore, from "Next, observing below" onward, it explains the skillful means of simultaneous illumination.
Because previously one employed emptiness and the provisional at different times, one now enters the Middle Way where both are spontaneously illuminated.

Therefore, it quotes a sutra, saying, "If the mind is in samādhi," and so forth. Arising and ceasing are simply the objects of the two truths. Next, the question-and-answer section for clarification has two parts:

first, the formal question and answer; second, the citation of sutras for explanation. The first part contains two questions and answers. Regarding the first question, which cites a sutra to resolve a difficulty:
the intent of the question is to ask how the specific characteristics [of the stages] are such that they are called "stages" (*bhūmi*) and so forth. The intent of the answer is as follows:
Regarding those who, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), mostly do not see the nature (*dharmatā*): this belongs to the perspective of gradual progression (*anupūrva*). Next is the objection.

Since the previous answer stated that they mostly do not see the nature, [the objector] again cites the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to challenge that previous answer: "If the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is present and can still be seen partially, why do you say that both [eyes] do not see?
This refers to the Buddha’s response to Siṃhanāda in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states: "The wisdom-eye sees..."

Therefore, it is not clearly perceived. The intent of this answer is as follows: according to the partial teaching (pāryāyika), neither [of the two] is seen; according to the perfect teaching (pariniṣpanna), the eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣus) is able to see.

The term "eye of wisdom" refers to the stage of the ten abidings (daśa-vihāra), where the abiding itself constitutes wisdom; it does not refer to the eye of wisdom that perceives emptiness belonging to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Next, there are two parts to the citation of scriptural evidence. First, it clarifies that the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is capable of seeing. If even the Buddha-eye can be designated as the wisdom-eye, how much more so the [wisdom] of those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)?
The phrase "such as this" refers to the aforementioned fact that the ten stages do not equal the World-Honored One. The phrase "like the night, etc. [refers to the following].
This is because the bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet exhausted their ignorance and afflictions. The same intent applies to the analogy of the geese in the sky and so forth.

Furthermore, the analogies of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding "digging and boring" are cited to prove that the third contemplation is seen only when it is perfected and established; here, "seeing" refers to seeing the water.

Following these two teachings below, the conclusion is reached that the two contemplations of the two teachings cannot see [this reality]. These two teachings are the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings.

Therefore, it is like dry soil where the center is not yet seen at all; as for those who are distinct from the "clay," this is because their paths of teaching are mixed. Because they first realize the center, only two [vehicles] are mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "the two practices do not reach [it]," this concludes the preceding point concerning contemplation: that is, the two contemplations do not see [the center].

This refers to the entry into emptiness by both the Shared and Distinct vehicles of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which are subsumed under the practice of emptiness by Bodhisattvas. For the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct [vehicles], there is the exit into the provisional (*upāya*), which is subsumed under the practice of emptiness by Bodhisattvas.

They are subsumed under provisional practice; therefore, it is said in general that the two practices do not reach [the goal]. In the subsequent mind of the Separate Teaching, one sequentially reaches the Middle;
hence, it simply mentions "two.

Following these three contemplations, the similarities and differences are distinguished by correlating them with the previous explanation of their names, which can be understood by reference to the section on *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Next, based on what follows below, the [three] fetters are judged. Although the skillful means of emptiness and the provisional both belong to the gate of expediency, these three contemplations take the meanings of "mutual dependence" from the teachings of the past as their general designation, and take the characteristics of the sequential teaching as that which reveals them.

Next, the third truth is taken as that which is revealed. For this reason, it is not the characteristic of the Perfect and Sudden; rather, the Perfect is revealed by borrowing [the meaning of] this [truth].
Furthermore, because it is neither general nor specific, the concluding passage follows below.

The stages encompass both the Great and Small Vehicles. Within this, there are two parts: first, it is determined to belong to the Great Vehicle; second, by means of its meaning, it is determined to belong to the gradual [teaching].

From the perspective of those who have not yet attained realization, it is said that they are "distinct" and so forth. By way of the gradual meaning, according to the characteristics of the sequence, each item is treated individually. This is a general indication of the characteristics of the teaching.
As for the passage beginning with "If one discusses," it explains the specific characteristics of the teaching's meaning from the perspective of the person of contemplative wisdom. It has not yet...
Fusion (róng) thus renders even contemplation (guān) unfused; this refers to the three provisional and one real, and the three turnings of shallow and deep.

Since it is so for the cause of contemplation, it is likewise so for the fruit of wisdom. Consequently, wisdom also possesses distinctions of priority and inferiority. While the Dharma is universal, individuals differ;

therefore, it encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the general and specific stages, subsuming them all within itself. Because it incidentally includes the Small Vehicle, the Small is not the primary focus.

Next, regarding the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]: the "absolute" (*juedai*) serves as the means of expression (*nengquan*), while the "three-in-one" (*sanyi*) is that which is revealed (*suoxian*). This section is divided into two parts: first, a direct explanation of the Perfect and Sudden;

second, the opening and clarification of various names. The first part further contains four sections: first, *śamatha* (calm abiding); second, *vipaśyanā* (insight); third, the simultaneous occurrence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; and fourth, an analogical conclusion.

The first of these [sections on *śamatha*] further consists of the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis. Within the initial section on the Dharma: *śamatha* is the subject of cognition (*nengyuan*), and the Truths (*di*) are the objects of connection (*suoxi*).

Therefore, the Sūtra says, "Binding the conditions to a single thought-moment," and so forth. Next, in the section on the analogy, both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *satya* (truth) are analogized as three and one, non-dual.

Regarding the section on *śamatha-satya*, in the passage where the teaching is applied to the analogy, the textual arrangement of "three, one, one, three" and "one, three, one, three" differs according to the convenience of the phrasing.
In summary, it is simply that the three and the one are non-dual. Next, with the words "Next, by means of *vipaśyanā* (insight)," the practice of *vipaśyanā* is clarified.

"Evil. Because it cuts off manifest evil, it is called an "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*). To explain its nature comprehensively: although it exists in both the past and the present, there are the latent (*mīng*) and the manifest (*xiǎn*).
