The third section provides three analogies, which are further divided into two parts: first, the analogies; second, their application to the doctrine (*yōjō*). The first part [the analogies] also has two sections: first, the Hall of Victory (*Shōdō*);

second, the Hall of Ultimate Excellence (*Zenjin*). Regarding the first text: Viśvakarman is the master artisan of the celestial realm. Because Śakra built this hall after achieving victory over the asuras in battle, it is named "Victory" (*Jishō*).

Furthermore, because it is the foremost among the thousand worlds, it is named "Supreme Victory" (*Saishō*). I shall not elaborate on its detailed interpretation here, as the subsequent text will provide the application (*yōjō*) itself.

Next, regarding "skillfully exhausting [the practice]," it is like those such as Zhang Yan who attained mastery in the subtleties of brush and ink. Below this section on the Ten Contemplations, these elements are combined;

by means of this single combination, two metaphors are joined together. Finally, the conclusion for both individuals is likewise the same. Now, first we shall contrast them with the two similes, and subsequently explain and combine the text.
First, regarding "the superior hall," the horizontal and vertical alignments correspond, as do the qualities of being neither too sparse nor too dense. This corresponds to the initial section below.
"Lofty and majestic," etc., corresponds to "the intention being perfect," and below that, it corresponds to "not the work of a clumsy craftsman," etc.

If one correlates this with the subsequent analogy, "horizontal and vertical," etc., corresponds to "perfectly true to the original," "subtle and wondrous," etc., corresponds to "pictorial representation," and so forth. "At first," and below, correspond to "possessing the vital breath," etc.;

this is not a correlation with the recitation of the text, but rather with the person who applies the colors. Next, the commentary explains the correlation of the text. Regarding the terms "horizontal and vertical," there are two meanings: the general and the specific; these refer to the ten dharmas.
To exhaustively penetrate the ultimate reality of objects is called "vertical"; to encompass the ten dharma realms is called "horizontal. To resolve to seek enlightenment above is called "vertical";

to transform sentient beings below is called "horizontal. To settle the mind so it penetrates the principle is called "vertical"; the sixty-four methods [of contemplation] are called "horizontal. If you grasp this meaning, [you will understand].
The subsequent text should be understood accordingly. If the ten dharmas are taken as a whole, their mutual relation across successive stages constitutes "horizontal" (transverse) progression;

when each reaches its ultimate limit, it is termed "vertical. To encompass all phenomena universally is called "comprehensive integration. Their principle being profound is termed "subtle"; being beyond all dependence is termed "wondrous.

Not being confused with others is termed "refined"; following the sequence is termed "skillful. Initially, the Perfect [Teaching] is taken as the true, while the three [other teachings] are pointed out as false. In the middle, the seventh [stage] serves as an aid, while the remainder...

All are correct. Subsequently, the ninth is patience (*kṣānti*) and the tenth is detachment from craving (*vairāgya*). Whether in contemplation or exposition, there is nothing lacking; this is called "perfection of intention" (*manas-pūrṇatā*).

Their orderly arrangement and synthesis is called "skillfulness in the Dharma" (*dharma-kuśala*). To encompass universally is called "pervasive inclusion" (*gai*), and to gather inwardly is called "comprehensive subsumption" (*kuo*).

Because of pervasive inclusion, it is all-encompassing; because of comprehensive subsumption, it is complete. Relying on this to explain and practice, there are the four teachings, the sixteen gates, and the five [periods].
At that time, the eight teachings all converge in the one mind; this is something that even the masters of the partial teachings cannot know, let alone those who possess only obscure realization.
Establishing the circle with the compass and the square, the Dharma possesses standards and rules. To distinguish between true and false states is the rule for the beginning.

To combine the primary and auxiliary practices is the rule for the middle. To abide in patience and non-attachment is the rule for the end. Upon reaching the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
From "The Tathāgata" downwards is the fourth section, the praise. Now, because it relies upon that wondrous One Vehicle, it praises it by means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* text.
As for the traces (*jì*), the Great Pervasion (*Dàtōng*) constitutes the accumulation of kalpas, and the site of enlightenment (*dào chǎng*) constitutes the wondrous awakening.

As for the origin (*běn*), the original practice constitutes the accumulation of kalpas, and the original fulfillment constitutes the wondrous awakening. Although the origin and the traces differ, these two are not neglected. Regarding Śāriputra and the others, [it refers to] the site of tranquility (*jì chǎng*).

The capacities of beings arise; further expedient means are employed, and through the maturation of samādhi, Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is finally opened. Therein, the "Four Ones" are pointed out and the chapter on the Five Buddhas is expounded.
Since the Dharma analogies and causal conditions reside within these ten dharmas, both the ten objects and the ten dharmas are likened to the great vehicle.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "It is precisely here. Yet the world still does not know this as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. This is exactly as it has been described.
Regarding practice, how does it differ from upholding and reciting? Whether with signs or signless, both serve as skillful means;
one should properly grasp their intent so as not to deceive oneself.
First, observing the mind below. Fifth, the extensive explanation. The text itself consists of ten sections. First, further clarifying the object: Question: At the beginning, one should...

[Question: It has been explained that [the mind] is luminous observation; why then is the object further discussed? [Answer: Although the mind was previously indicated, its objective aspect had not yet been shown.

Fearing that there might still be doubt regarding the existence of a creator and something created, [the text] further distinguishes the excellence of the observed based on the observing subject. Once the excellence of the observed is established, the observing subject is spontaneously perfected.

Furthermore, since the objects of cognition constitute the nine fundamental categories, they are explained in detail. Within the objects, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.

In the explanation, there are again two parts: first, the conceivable; second, the inconceivable. Regarding the first (the conceivable), there are four sections: first, clarifying the purpose of employing the conceivable;

second, clarifying the reason for employing the conceivable; third, the actual explanation of the conceivable; fourth, the summary. Regarding the first (clarifying the purpose): there are ten texts and ten meanings.

This indicates that the sequence is not fixed; thus it says, "First, clarify [the preceding]," and so forth. Having clarified what is conceivable (*saciṃtya*), it points to the one mind; therefore, it says it is "easy to understand.
Those who see the commentary and say, "This is not what is used here," and seek elsewhere, are far, far removed. It is like using the provisional to teach the real—the intent lies in the real;
or opening the provisional to reveal the real—the intent lies in the real. This applies even to the "provisional" and "ultimate" (dai-jue), all of which are...
Thus it is. Up to the point of "the ultimate aim," one can see this by reflecting upon it. Next, under "contemplation through thought" (*samsaya*), the reason for such contemplation is clarified:

because both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna state that "the mind gives rise [to all things]," and because their teachings are provisional (*upāya*), they have not yet spoken of [this reality] as being fully present; thus, it is disparagingly termed "contemplation through thought.

Third, under "if one contemplates," the actual characteristics of contemplation through thought are correctly explained: within the Buddha-dharmadhātu, all are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); there is nothing that is not the Dharma.
The realms dissolve and all phenomena vanish. Who is good? Who is evil? These are dissolved within the preceding realms of the three virtues and three evils. Who exists? Who does not exist?

These are dissolved within the preceding three realms of existence and the non-existence of the two vehicles. Who is saved? Who is not saved? This dissolves the four great vows regarding the savior and the saved.

Although the subsequent stage dissolves the preceding ones, because they arise from a gradual process, the beginning and end still constitute something conceivable; one takes up the latter while discarding the former.

Because the former two dharmas are both lost, the explanation follows below. This applies to all four sections. By synthesizing the understanding, one achieves the present inconceivable contemplation.
Below this "fourth," there is a general conclusion.

Next is the "Inconceivable" [chapter]. The phrasing differs and the meanings differ; its intent is not sequential. Within it, there are seven sections: first, a general clarification of the realm of principle; second, a clarification of the realm of one's own practice;
third, a clarification of the realm of transforming others; fourth, a clarification that summarizes the matters and principles of self and other to establish the three truths;

fifth, the presentation of analogies; sixth, a clarification of the functional power of the realm; and seventh, the convergence of the preceding matters and principles—both self and other—back to [the ultimate source].
The first section on "The One Mind" also has four parts: first, citing the authentic teaching; second, explaining the general name of the object;

third, clarifying the phenomena subsumed within the object; and fourth, concluding with the logical object. Regarding the first part: the preceding text states that "creation" means knowing that this is the forest of those who possess merit, and it extensively recites its characteristics.
Furthermore, what is created by the mind does not exceed three meanings. The first is in terms of principle (*tattva*); principle is...
It is complete. Second, regarding actual entities; third, regarding transformations. As for "regarding actual entities," they do not transcend the three periods of time.

These three periods, in turn, are twofold: first, past actions producing the present; second, present actions producing the present. Third, regarding transformations: the sages act in common with ordinary beings.
Furthermore, it is only through the principle being fully present that phenomena can manifest. Now, by contemplating the principle alone, one universally encompasses both ordinary beings and sages.

Next, from the section on the "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) below, the general name of the object is explained. Question: What is the distinction between the Dharma-realm and the Dharma-nature (dharmatā)?
Answer: They are merely different names for the same thing. To speak of the "Dharma-realm" means that all dharmas are demarcated; all dharmas take the three truths as their realm.
[This is] a division. To manifest the three truths, it is necessary to speak of ten. Therefore, the three characters are explained as being composed of three [truths].

First, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are explained as the basis (*āśraya*): the number ten is provisional; emptiness is the basis, and since the dependent relies upon the basis, all ten are empty.
Furthermore, below this, regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are explained as being distinct: therefore, each of the ten dharmas has its own specific domain.

From the passage "Furthermore, from these ten... onwards, the text provides an interpretation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) based on the Middle Way. Among these ten dharmas, there is none that is not the true principle of True Suchness.

If one reads this text, the three characters for "ten dharma-realms" (*shí fǎjiè*) are divided into phrases according to their meaning: in the first instance, the ten characters are read separately with the word "dharma-realm" (*fǎjiè*) joined;

in the second, the two characters for "ten dharmas" (*shí fǎ*) are joined with the word "realm" (*jiè*) read separately; and in the third, all three characters are joined together. It is according to this [interpretation].

Upon reading the text, the meaning of the Three Truths becomes manifest. All three are devoid of marks (*animitta*); they can be distinguished only by relying on phenomena. Because one relies on consciousness, the three thousand realms are easily discerned within emptiness.
Even if one turns them over a million times, the three dharmas remain unchanging. If one can attain this knowledge, the myriad dharmas will be harmonized and integrated.

Below the ten dharmas, the third section concerns the phenomena subsumed under the objective sphere (*viṣaya*). This further consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the three worlds; second, the explanation of the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*). Regarding the first, there are again two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the concluding indication. Regarding the first of these, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

second, the explanation of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); third, the explanation of the world of the environment (*bhājana-loka*). First, regarding the five aggregates, they differ according to the ten dharmas, which are as follows: [The text continues with the specific categories of the five aggregates.]
Three [sections]. First, the listing of the ten kinds of five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Second, citing treatises and other sources to prove the five aggregates within the Buddha-realm.
Third, summarizing the ten realms to establish the world. The first is as in the text. The second, citing proofs, also has three parts; the first cites the *Mahā-śāstra* to prove the Dharma.
Next, citing the *Anantārthika* [Sūtra] to resolve doubts. Third, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* to prove that the Buddha-realm constitutes the "Infinite Meanings.
Third, from "By means of the ten [factors]" below, the conclusion is as in the text. From "Gathering the five aggregates" below, the "sentient world" is explained.

It is like gathering fingers to form a fist. Within this, there are also three parts: first, the enumeration; second, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to prove that the Buddha-realm becomes sentient beings; third, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

"Below. This establishes the worldly realm (*loka-dhātu*), which refers to its specific distinctions. First, the scripture is cited: therefore, in the *Mahā-sūtra*, both the primary [sentient] and secondary [insentient] realms possess ten temporal distinctions.
Regarding the primary realm, it begins with *kalala* and ends with old age and death; regarding the secondary realm, it begins with the sprout and stem and ends with the ripening of fruit.

"Directly concerning the below," this concludes the formal summary according to the text. "The ten kinds, below," explains the world-realm of the environment (*bhājana-loka*) as the ten elements (*dhātu*).

The basis does not exceed the four lands (*bhūmi*). The text is also divided into three parts: first, the listing of the four lands; second, citing the *Ratnaketu-Parājitā Sūtra* (Renwang jing) to prove that the Buddha’s dwelling is called a land;

and third, noting that while the nine realms are termed aggregates (*skandha*) and termed births (*jāti*), there is no doubt regarding the existence of lands, and thus it only cites the Buddha as proof. Furthermore, the Buddha himself possesses all three lands.

Below the section on the three lands, the text concludes by establishing them as the mundane world. Next, under the section beginning with "These thirty," it provides a general summary showing that [the lands] arise from the mind. Question:
Why are the three worlds established within the teachings? Answer: Their names appear among the one hundred and eight samādhis in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, below the section on the "ten kinds," they are explained as the "ten suchnesses" (*daśa-tathatā*). Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The true reality of all dharmas is what is called the 'suchness' (*tathatā*) of all dharmas," and so forth.
Everyone reads this, yet everyone remains ignorant of its meaning. Therefore, we know that the ten suchnesses correspond to the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*). From [the perspective of] self...

Thus, it constitutes the Three Truths. For this reason, Nanyue read it with three distinct turns of phrase: first, taking "suchness" (rú) as the phrase, which signifies Emptiness; second, taking "characteristics" (xiàng) as the phrase, which signifies the Provisional;
and third, taking "is" (shì) as the phrase, which signifies the Middle. He usually reads it by taking "characteristics" and so forth as the phrases, wherein there are three:
first, the aggregates (skandhas); second, birth; and third, the lands. Within the first [the aggregates], the five aggregates and the ten suchnesses further comprise three parts: first, the heading.

Next, the three explanations are listed. Within these explanations, there are two parts: first, the general; second, the specific. The general serves as a heading for the specific. Both the general and the specific are "as they are" (yathābhūta). In the initial text, the ten "as-they-are" are divided into ten sections.
Regarding the first, "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), there are three parts: the phenomena (dharma), the analogies (upamā), and their correspondence (yoga).

These correspond to the text. In the analogies, it says "resting and declining. "Resting" (xiū) means joy; "declining" (fǒu) means evil. When the ten realms are compared with one another, good and evil can be known. Formerly, [the story of] Sun... [text ends].
Regarding the phrase "Sun Deng and others," this cites an actual event as proof of the signs. At the end of the Han dynasty, three men went together to consult a physiognomist.

The physiognomist recorded only the features of Sun Deng and did not record those of Cao Cao. When he lifted his robes to show them, the physiognomist laughed heartily and realized that the empire would be divided into three parts.

He noted that the physiognomy of Lord Cao was hidden like the eight realms (*aṣṭa-dhātu*), while the physiognomy of Sun Deng was manifest like the two realms (*dvi-dhātu*); thus, both the distant and the near were recorded.

Regarding distant [prophecies], there are those such as those for the pigeon, the sparrow, and the Dharma Master; regarding proximate [prophecies], there are those such as those for Maitreya and the prediction concerning the Bhadrakalpa.

Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* sets forth four kinds of prophecy: first, those who have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening; second, those who have just resolved their minds; third, secret prophecies; and fourth, those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Among the four [stages], three are distant; non-arising (*anutpāda*) is near.

Within this nature, there are further two parts: first, the correct interpretation; second, the refutation of ancient views. The first part also has three sections. The first [section] on the Dharma is as the text explains.
Regarding the analogy, it says "the *suiren* (fire-driller)"; this refers to the fire-producing wood. Because the *suiren* first produced fire in this land, later...
The name of this object is "fire-stirring stick" (*chui*). Contemplate the fire-stirring stick as the objective sphere; use dry grass to assist it and apply effort with the hands.

When delusion is severed, the nature is revealed—this meaning is like the emergence of fire. Furthermore, its ability to benefit all things is called "burning everything. The mind is also [like] the lower part; their union is as described in the text.
Next, below "The Mundane," the refutation of ancient [views] is divided into two parts: first, the general; second, the specific. The specific part is further divided into three sections.

First, from "Nirvāṇa" downward, he refutes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for its failure to clarify Buddha-nature. Second, from "There is a Master" downward, he refutes those who divide the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) into provisional and real, thereby rendering the nature of reality impermanent.
Third, from "Nirvāṇa" downward, he refutes the view that the characteristics of bodhi in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* are impermanent. [Finally,] he returns to list the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Thus, the accomplishment of impermanence explains the essence, as per the text.
Regarding the explanation of power, the phrase "afflictions and so forth" is used here provisionally to explain by way of the four powers of the noble ones.

If discussed generally, all sentient beings possess the functions of the ten realms; the six remaining [realms] are as explained in the text. "Successive classification" (*lei-jie*) refers to a specific explanation.

It further consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the exposition. Within the exposition, there are four sections of its own; fearing that they would be cumbersome and difficult to perceive, they are condensed into four categories.
Thus it is called "classification. The first three are the unwholesome, and the next three are the wholesome, as in the text. The third and second [sections] are as follows.

Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that "nirvāṇa is the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) among the categories of vehicles: nirvāṇa is precisely the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
That which is coarse in its dharma-nature is termed the "characteristic. Liberation is the bliss of the Dharma; that which is subtle in its dharma-nature is termed the "nature" (*svabhāva*).

Those who attain no-remainder represent the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), while those who attain the bliss of the Dharma have a nature that is necessarily immutable. As for the five factors being the essence (*tattva*):

It consists merely of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Taking precepts as form, the remaining four are mind. Regarding the "fivefold" [path]: the morality concomitant with the path, the matter of the path, the principle of concentration, and untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) constitute the two types of liberation.

"Liberation" refers to the knowledge of thorough deliverance. "Being unbound constitutes power" means that through the wisdom of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one is detached from the bonds of the three realms.
"Since it is subsequent existence," etc.: the aggregates (*skandha*) of future birth are called "subsequent existence. Subsequent...

The arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called the "field for future existence. Because the births of the two vehicles have been exhausted, they are said to be "non-arising. "Field" carries the meaning of "arising. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"First, that which is both fruit and retribution; second, that which is only fruit and not retribution. Regarding the statement that among the four classes of Bodhisattvas, the primary cause constitutes their essence:
Question: In the general [definition], it was stated that matter and mind constitute the essence. Should it not then be said that all ten realms consist of matter and mind?

Regarding this, why is the "correct cause" (hetu) taken as the essential nature? The answer is: To provide a complete explanation of the correct cause, it specifically refers to form and mind (*rūpa-citta*), because these constitute the path of suffering.

Within this, there are again three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the analysis of the inverse and the conformable; and third, a further discussion of causes and conditions according to convenience.

The six realms of existence follow [the flow], while the two vehicles within the realm follow against it. The two vehicles follow [the flow], while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas beyond the realm follow against it.

Since there are many types of Bodhisattvas, their following or opposing [the flow] is determined according to their respective stages and positions. As for what is called "comprehension," it refers to the three aspects of nature, characteristics, and essence, which collectively explain causes and conditions.

"Power" (*li*) is the functional capacity of causes and conditions; "activity" (*zuo*) is the operational application of causes and conditions; and "retribution" (*guobao*) is the habitual fruition of causes and conditions.

Thus we know that the brief [explanation] refers to causes and conditions, while the extensive [explanation] refers to the ten characteristics. Third, regarding the section on "discerning the lower," it discerns the presence or absence of the retribution body (*vipākakāya*). The Buddha possesses a retribution body, as fully detailed in the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning).

According to the *Dafoding rulai fangguang xianzhai pusa wubai qingjing xingyuan jing* (The Great Amulet, Radiance of the Tathāgata, Fasting and Vigil Sutra on the Five Hundred Pure Vows of Bodhisattvas), this results in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Next, the ten suchnesses of sentient beings may be understood by analogy with what precedes. Third, regarding the ten suchnesses of the lands (*kṣetra*), these are explained in detail through the four lands (*catvāri bhūmayaḥ*).

One should distinguish between their horizontal and vertical dimensions, as fully described in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* commentary on the Buddha-land. For now, we shall employ the four lands to subsume the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). The six realms are contained within the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahābhāsa-bhūmi*);

the remaining three realms—the third, fourth, and tenth—are likewise divisible into the two vehicles of the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and the Bodhisattvas of the Land of Real Reward (*dharmatā-niṣyanda-bhūmi*), as well as the Land of Tranquil Light (*prabhāsvara-bhūmi*).
In the Buddha.
Now, from "If one is single-minded" downwards, the fourth section establishes the logical context. Fearing that people might become confused by what preceded, it is reiterated here.

Within this, there are three parts: the principle (dharma), the analogy, and the application. First, the statement "it is simply mindless" clarifies that the mind is not non-existent; "a mere instant" (jì) refers to the very moment...
It exists; it merely differs from the state of mindlessness. The three thousand realms and the three virtues are all fully present.

Therefore, throughout his entire life, the Great Master’s teachings spoke of the three thousand only within the context of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight). Thus we know that although other teachings are called "insight" (*vipaśyanā*), they are not the primary teaching on insight;
for this reason, they are all treated briefly. Hence, the preface states: "I have explained the Dharma-gate practiced within my own mind," which is indeed the case.
Generally speaking, the reason why various explanations of the meaning fail to distinguish themselves from other teachings is truly because they do not speak of the three thousand [worlds].

The following examples illustrate this. For instance, regarding that which "transmigrates things through the eight phases": "phases" refers to that which causes the transition, while "things" refers to that which is transitioned. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

This refers to "arising-of-arising" and so forth. Among these eight, there are seven that arise within one [primary dharma]; the "eight" refers to the primary [dharma] itself, while the others follow the four characteristics.

Thus, the "great" name refers to the primary, and the "small" name refers to the followers. Because of these eight, they constitute the characteristics of existence (*bhava-lakṣaṇa*). As for "arising-of-arising," it means that the small arising gives rise to the great arising;
the same applies to the other three. These eight, in relation to the primary dharma, are neither prior nor posterior. The mind and the three thousand [dharmas] are likewise.

It is likewise so. Now, regarding "the mind below": it is a convergence. It is not consciousness; it is beyond thought. It is not speech; it is beyond deliberation. This concludes the section on the realm of principle.

Next, the question below clarifies the realm attained through cultivation. This also has two parts: first the question, then the answer. Regarding the initial passage: this refers to the realm of one's own practice.

Therefore, the initial inquiry was raised to establish the characteristics of the arising [of phenomena]. Since the defects regarding the nature of the previously mentioned rational essence (*dharmatā*) have not yet been discussed, it is now necessary to investigate it by means of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*).
This present inquiry, for its part, addresses the point of arising in order to refute attachments concerning that which is fundamentally endowed within the rational principle.

In fact, it is simply a matter of departing from the conceptualization of the intrinsically possessed nature. Therefore, in the subsequent answer, once the four attachments have been abandoned, one returns to the fundamental principle:

the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment. Furthermore, since it was previously stated that [the nature] is "intrinsically possessed" (*li-jù*) and also stated to be "cultivatedly possessed" (*xiu-jù*), it is necessary to employ this investigation to establish the characteristics of practice (*xing-xiang*).

Next, the response consists of two parts. First, the refutation of attachments by means of four sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to clarify the characteristics of practice. Second, the citation of scriptural evidence. The first part has two sections:

first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. The first section further contains four parts. The first is the horizontal four propositions, which is further divided into five: first, the citation; second, the treatise.
However, these refutations of [inherent] nature differ across the three teachings. Now, as for the rational nature (li-xing) being entrusted to the two treatises:

since the treatises preserve the path of the teachings, there is a fear that attachment to the teachings might obstruct the principle (li). Therefore, they are cited here to refute such attachment. Regarding the phrase "beginningless and inexhaustible ignorance" (wu-mo wu-ming):

because the ālayavijñāna exists eternally, it is called beginningless and inexhaustible ignorance. Next, from the passage below, the characteristics of each respective calculation are shown and categorized under their respective natures.

[This] is an error. To reckon the mind as "self" and to reckon conditions as "other" [is the fault]. Third, regarding the passage "If the dharma-nature... and below, this correctly refutes the attachment to [intrinsic] nature and establishes the error.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the refutation of the Master of the Earth (Dharmasubhūti). As for the claim that "the dharma-nature is not truly the condition," this again cites what he himself maintains and refutes it according to reason.

The nature of mind and the mind itself are both neither [existent nor non-existent]. Those of the *bhūmi* and *pudgala* schools hold the biased view that the dharma-nature is not the mind, yet they allow that the mind possesses [it].

Likewise, one might argue that while the dharma-nature is not a causal condition (*pratyaya*), it nonetheless possesses [the seeds]. How then can you not admit the *ālayavijñāna* as taught by the Master [Asaṅga]? Next, regarding the passage "if one says... and below, the refuter uses the opponent’s own position to refute them:
if there were an *ālayavijñāna* existing separately outside of the dharma-nature, and if one grants that the *ālayavijñāna* serves as the support (*āśraya*), then one must grant...

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) serves as their support; if it were not involved, the principle would further fail to be established. Fourth, "Furthermore, this contradicts the sūtras" below introduces scriptural authority to demonstrate the fault.
The sūtra referred to is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Chapter). Since the teaching is not fourfold, why do you each maintain [those four views]? Fifth, "Furthermore, regarding...

uses the analogy of a dream to refute the fault of [inherently] existing natures. Within this, there are three parts: the metaphor, the application, and the conclusion. The first part also has three sections. First, the determination of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Second...

If one relies on the lower [interpretation], it is refuted by the critique. Regarding the third and fourth lines below, they establish non-arising. As for the subsequent analogy of the mind, the application (*yōjō*) appears to be erroneous.

Since the analogy already contrasts "sleeping" with "mind," the application should state: "Mind is the metaphor for *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and sleep is the metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*."

The phenomenon of the dream serves as a metaphor for the arising of all dharmas. Regarding the phrase "even those who sleep," it should simply be amended to state that "sleep" is the metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*.
If one were to say that even a sleeping person has times when they do not dream, one merely takes the time of dreaming as the metaphor. Third, from "one should know" onwards is the conclusion.

Although the dream-phenomenon cannot be found upon investigation, the dream-event is not non-existent. If one explains this to others, one still relies on the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the three thousand [worlds].
A single thought-moment can be understood by analogy with this. Why stop at merely stating this? Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) likewise proceeds according to what is appropriate.
Therefore, in the *Śikṣānanda’s Treatise on the Mind* (*Guānxīnlùn*), each phrase gives rise to thirty-six phrases (the explanation of the horizontal refutation is complete).
Next, regarding the refutation of the "vertical" [position]: the previous "horizontal" position established its calculation by correlating the *ālaya* with the *dharmatā*.

This already differs from the *Kṣānti* and *Śrāvaka* vehicles, as those two do not possess the name "*ālaya*. Although they speak of "arising" and so forth, they are merely referring to the present mind and objects. As for the inference of the "both-and" [position]:

since the first two calculations of the single [sides] have already been refuted, one now shifts to calculating "both-and"; therefore, it must be refuted. Each has already been shown to be non-arising. Two.

That which does not arise cannot be conjoined; how then could it give rise [to anything]? It is like water and fire, whose intrinsic natures mutually destroy one another; how could they further produce dharmas?

As for those who refute the "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta), they claim that cessation is the producer and non-cessation is the produced. Since it is called "neither-nor," there is neither producer nor produced;
how then could it give rise [to anything]?

"Both horizontal and vertical" refers to the third set of four propositions. Fearing that one might conceive of these as being distinct from the two previous single propositions by way of being horizontal or vertical, they must be further refuted.
This involves conceiving of horizontality within each of the four vertical positions. The first proposition conceives of four [alternatives], which is the same as the preceding text.

Regarding the conception of four [alternatives] for "cessation," it states: "ceasing of itself," "producing the cessation of another," and so forth. The third and fourth propositions, as well as their refutations, may be understood by analogy.

This is the refutation by means of calculating [the production of phenomena] through horizontal and vertical succession. If one discusses this in general terms—that is, that all phenomena arise through both the horizontal and the vertical—the refutation should be understood accordingly.

"Neither vertical nor horizontal" refers to the fourth set of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Since both the single and the dual [positions] have already been refuted, one then calculates a "double negation," claiming that all phenomena arise by being free from both.
If even their conjunction has been refuted, how could their simultaneous separation possibly exist?
Next, following the section on "Language," the objects of cultivation are established. If it were not so, how could there be two concluding sections?

Next, following the section on the "Great Sūtra," the scriptural evidence is cited. Passages such as "transverse and vertical births" have already completed the discussion on the vertical; if one is to prove the transverse, [the following is cited].

"Birth" refers only to the eye; the remaining three [faculties] are to be understood accordingly. The third and fourth [points] can be discerned. Question: In the previous discussion on the nature-realm (*dharmatā-viṣaya*) and in Zhiyan’s questions, it was stated in all cases that [the nature] is "spontaneous" (*svarasa*).

Why, then, is it said here that the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā-viṣaya*) is established only by confronting conditions? Answer: When one analyzes the preceding factors as being the mind or the conditions, there is a fear that they might be grasped as constituting a fixed nature.

Therefore, they are analyzed in this way. To grasp what is without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is precisely what is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the signless (*animitta*). What cause for doubt is there?

Yes. Third, from "One should know" onwards, it clarifies the realm of transforming others. This section also has four parts: first, concluding the previous [section] and introducing the subsequent; second, clarifying the characteristics of transforming others;

third, clarifying that the Buddha’s intention, essence, and nature are mutually identical; fourth, clarifying the great substance of the teaching. The first part also has five sub-sections; the first concerns—

The two truths link what precedes with what follows: the former links one’s own practice, while the latter gives rise to the transformation of others. How could there be self-satisfaction without benefiting sentient beings?

Therefore, by means of multiple proofs, the characteristic of benefiting others is established. The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) links what precedes, and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) gives rise to what follows.
Therefore, for the sake of others, one must necessarily explain it in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). From "Next, as the Buddha told [below]" to the end is the conclusion.

This establishes the arising of the connection (*pratisaṃdhi*) by citing proof from the Buddha’s sūtras; this is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, where the virtuous woman answers the Buddha, and all these are the conclusion of what preceded.

The Buddha’s repeated statement "It is so" constitutes the subsequent arising. Third, the establishment of the arising of the connection is proven by means of Nāgārjuna’s *Madhyamaka-śāstra*; the term "arising" refers to the arising that follows.

Fourth, citing the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* to clarify that which follows the linking of existence (*pratisandhi*). Fourth, citing the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* to clarify that the linking of existence is ineffable.

Because there are causes and conditions prior to the linking, there are five [aspects] following the birth. Although the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) below explain the various linkings of existence, the four propositions are dark and quiescent;
they explain the preceding linking of existence. Compassion is not mere pity; it explains the preceding birth. Whether ordinary person or sage, whatever is spoken falls within the four propositions.

Once [the obstacles] have been destroyed, there is nothing that does not benefit others. However, this benefiting of others differs from the "arising of the teaching. That [benefiting of others] occurs during the eight stages of manifestation (*aṣṭamākāra*); this [destruction of obstacles], by contrast, pertains specifically to the initial mind.

Even if it were to extend to subsequent minds, it would still remain within the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*). Question: Why is it that the destruction [of obstacles] involves all four [aspects], whereas the benefiting of others has only one for each?

Answer: To know the capacities of beings and establish the transformation [through teaching], there is only one [aspect] for each. To prevent oneself from turning toward further conceptualizations, there are thus four [aspects].
Next, there are the manifestations of clarifying and transforming others. Each of the preceding four phrases possesses four *siddhāntas* (purposes), making sixteen sections;

the textual characteristics are easy to discern. For the sake of brevity, these are condensed into four, yet according to the capacities of beings, there are sixteen different ways in which they receive benefit.
Regarding the first set of four, concerning the world (*loka*): the mind’s inherent possession is "self," knowledge is "other," and mercury combined with gold is "common. This is simply so.
This is causeless. The four conditions conducive to joy constitute the world. Why "below"? They are the four for humans. According to faith, they are internal; encountering a Buddha is external.
Distinct from the internal is the water, which is both internal and external, and not internal etc., thus it is causeless.

Regarding the mention of Śreṇika: in the Buddha-dharma there is no attachment. If Śreṇika had attachment, even the Hīnayāna would find him difficult to convert, let alone the Mahāyāna. [End of] Treatise.
Since this is according to the Mahāyāna, the small is used as an illustration.

Second, below the Buddha’s intent, the third section clarifies that the essence and characteristics of the Buddha’s intent are mutually identical. The Buddha’s intent is fundamentally identical; it exhorts practitioners to train accordingly.

In accordance with this, there are again two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the mutual identity of the characteristics; second, the judgment of gain and loss. The first part [of the first section] further has three sub-sections:

first, the explicit clarification of the mutual identity of the two truths regarding their essential nature (*tattva*); second, the mutual identity of the two truths in relation to benefiting others; third, the summary conclusion on the mutual identity of the essential natures of self and others.
Regarding the initial statement "not abiding," etc., this refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Following the next four phrases, it concerns benefiting others.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the explanation according to the Dharma; second, from "If for the sake of the blind," etc., which is the analogy and its application. The phrase "if for the sake of the blind" and so forth is an analogy for the Buddha’s intention.

According to the explanation of Asaṅga, all [teachings] accord with the *siddhānta* (established tenets); therefore, it says "seeing milk. This concludes the analogy within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Third, from "One should know," etc., it concludes that the essential natures of self and other are mutually identical. Regarding the sūtras and śāstras, they have been cited as previously mentioned. Next, regarding Vasubandhu, etc.

Clarifying gain and loss. This section has two parts. First, clarifying the statement regarding "loss": as for "arrows and stones," it is like shooting an arrow at a stone; such a thing is ultimately impossible.
Second, from "if one attains" onwards, clarifying "gain" according to the text.

4. "If one follows what is appropriate" and below clarifies the general principle of the Buddha’s teaching. Although the application [of the teaching] to beings involves adaptations to changing times, the general principle of the Buddha’s teaching is that all things arise through causes and conditions;
thus, self and others alike all proceed from commonality. Therefore, we now speak again based on this general principle. This section further has two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the general principle of the teaching; second, the clarification of the excellence of the phenomena produced. First:

Regarding the statement that "the nature of dharmas is the dharma of ignorance," it is like the medicinal property of cinnabar (*dan*). Just as the property of coming [into being] resides in gold, the nature of ignorance can be understood by analogy with this:
it arises from its own defilement and arises from the purity of others; self and other are thus a synthesis of defilement and purity (and so forth).

Therefore, one should know that whenever the four propositions are investigated, they all investigate this synthesis; thus, once the four have been investigated, the synthesis remains perfectly manifest.
Next, following "one nature" (一性), the excellence of the dharmas produced is clarified. This section also has two parts. First, it clarifies that what is produced is precisely the nature of harmony;

therefore, it is called "nature. Thus it says, "Although 'one nature' is slight," and so forth. Because it arises from conditions, that which is born of conditions is empty; therefore, it says, "ignorance," and so forth.
Since this nature is fundamentally non-existent, once this nature is perceived, the wondrous principle remains. Next, following "What is it? and so forth, the [subject] is explained.
Birth is, by its very nature, ignorance; therefore, "many" is not many. Ignorance is, by its very nature, [the true] nature; therefore, "one" is not one. Thus it is called "below.
This concludes the section on transforming others.
If one understands the section below, the fourth [point] again relies on the essence of the teaching to conclude the various dharmas mentioned previously;

these are precisely the three categories (triskandha) and the three worlds (traidhātuka), which exclusively demonstrate the wondrous realm. The characteristics of the three truths (trisatya) will only be explained by way of analogy at the end of this fascicle.

Within this section establishing the realm, they are first summarized collectively to constitute the three truths. This further consists of two parts: first, the summary of the brief [exposition]; second, the demonstration of the three truths.

And so forth. Under "the first mind," one traverses the preceding minds that have created [them]. Under "one aggregate" (*skandha*), one traverses the preceding five aggregates. Under "one base" (*āyatana*), one traverses the preceding twelve bases.
Under "one element" (*dhātu*), one traverses the preceding eighteen elements. These three categories together constitute the world of aggregates (*skandha-loka*).

"First, 'the realm of sentient beings' (sattva-loka)" refers to traversing the aforementioned realms of sentient beings and the realm of the physical world (bhājana-loka). "First, 'the single characteristic' (eka-lakṣaṇa)" refers to traversing the ten suchnesses (daśa-tathatā) across the three aforementioned locations.

Next, "if it is the dharma-nature" (dharmatā) and so forth indicates the three truths (tri-satya) and so on; it demonstrates the various aggregates (skandha), births, lands, and suchnesses traversed previously. This is [the meaning].

The Three Truths and so forth. This is further divided into three parts: first, the summary of the Three Truths and so forth; second, the reconciliation of different names; third, the admonition and exhortation.

The first part [the summary] is further divided into five: first, the Three Truths; second, the Three Contemplations; third, the Three Wisdoms; fourth, the Three Phrases; fifth, the Three Realms. The first of these [the Three Truths] is further divided into two:
first, the explanation; second, from "In this way" onwards, the application by analogy.

If one dharma is taken as the basis, three contemplations are formed; there are also two [sections]: first, the direct explanation; second, the analogy. The first [section] has two parts: first, the specific [explanation]; second, the single [contemplation].
From "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) downward, there is the general enumeration. From "all" (*sarva*) downward, there is the analogy, as in the text.

If one proceeds from the causes and conditions below, three types of wisdom are established; these are also twofold: first, the distinct, and second, the general. The general is the illustrative model.

By using the provisional and the real as the model for contemplation, one should also first correspond them to the three dharmas and subsequently clarify their general characteristics; therefore, it says, "first, the provisional," and so forth.

If one follows the inclination [of the listener] below [the highest level], it is concluded as three types of discourse, or also two. First, the formal conclusion; second, the analogy. Regarding the first text:

that which can express is called "discourse" (*vāk*), and that which is addressed to an object is called "teaching" (*deśanā*). Furthermore, these are concluded by means of the three teachings, such as the gradual and so forth. Following the other [person's capacity] is the gradual; following oneself is the sudden; and both together is the indeterminate.
In the previous general meaning, three aspects were shown within a single perfect and sudden teaching; now, regarding the wondrous realm...

The middle section subsumes the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which together enter the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]. Therefore, by means of these three, one correlates them with the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the three terms, proceeding through the lower sections in sequence as the text describes.
If one understands the lower [teachings], they form the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The three vehicles arise from the gradual and other teachings;

in contrast to these three teachings, the "incomprehensible" (*asaṃprāpya*) and the "non-vehicle" (*ayāna*) are combined into the Perfect and Sudden (*ekayāna*). Within all dharmas, these are opened up into the remaining two.
Following the three contemplations mentioned above, there should likewise be corresponding examples, though the text is merely abbreviated.

Following these, the section on "Distinguishing Synonyms" (*nāman-paryāya*) clarifies that while the sublime objects (*viṣaya*) are not different, they receive distinct names according to their specific contexts; this can be understood by reflecting upon them according to their respective meanings.
Third, the section on "Various [Categories]" provides exhortations and warnings as stated in the text.
As follows. Fifth, the presentation of the analogy for the wondrous realm serves as a general illustration for the preceding passages concerning nature, cultivation, others, fetters, and so forth.

This section further divides into two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the three metaphors; second, the exhortation to believe. Regarding the first, the metaphor of the jewel: it is "in the heavens" because it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
It is a "superior treasure" because it is the reality of the rational nature (li-xing). It is "wondrous" because it is naturally pure without defilement and lacks anything external. Only...
In a single kṣaṇa, it fills the fruits of both self and others; thus it is called "mustard seed. Because it possesses the capacity to fulfill them, it is named "functional power" (kāritra).

Because it can fulfill the vows of others, it is called "desire" (icchā). Its essence is a jewel-torch, hence it is called "jewel" (ratna). True jewels are called *lin*, while those resembling jewels are called *lang*. As in the gate of the primary and auxiliary [practices], this principle does not go beyond these.
Because it is neither the nature of self nor other, it is not an internal division. From the point of departing from non-deliberation, it is fully endowed [with all qualities].
It is for the benefit of others. Because it is not sequential, there is no plotting of before and after; because it is not horizontal, there is no selecting of much or little.

Because it is spontaneous, there is no plotting; because it accords with capacities, there is no selecting. Although the five flavors follow a sequence, they are always secret and indeterminate; thus, it is not sequential.
Although the various teachings differ, they increase or decrease according to the timing; thus, it is neither much nor little. The response to capacities is never inappropriate.

Because it accords with both the provisional and the ultimate, it is neither coarse nor subtle. Because it manifests through contact with conditions, it is said to be "conforming to the mind" (chēngyì).

Because its abundant restraint benefits sentient beings without end, it is called "abundant" (rǎngrǎng). "Rǎngrǎng" signifies blessings. This extends even to the manifestation of the pearl as the primary retribution. The two characters [of "rǎngrǎng"] are pronounced in the departing tone (qùshēng).
It is not added because it was non-existent originally and now exists; it is not exhausted because it existed originally and now no longer exists.
The two subsequent analogies are brief in wording but identical in meaning; they may be understood by applying this principle.
Regarding the analogy of the three poisons: it is neither definitively existent nor definitively non-existent, as these are not the characteristics of the two extremes.

Next, regarding the three dreams: they are eliminated by being contrasted with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and ignorance; their relative extent should likewise be understood. "Xian" means to fly lightly.

The contrast between dreaming and awakening allows for their elimination to be known. How could the dream of peaceful conduct be any different? Next, "if one has faith," and so forth, is an exhortation to believe, as written in the text.
"Below this 'inconceivable' [section], the sixth clarifies the functional power of the object. It is for this reason that the following nine [sections] are termed 'sublime.
Below 'at the time of speaking,' the seventh collects all phenomena to enter the meditative object, wherein within a single mind, one's own and others' natures, etc., are fully present."

Next, the second arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is explained. The initial act of setting out toward [the goal] is called "arousal" (*utpāda*). It is not the "true one-mind" (*ekacitta*) of the three previous teachings;
rather, the Three Truths are the "correct," *bodhi* is the fruit, the objective realm is that which is traversed, and the mind is that which traverses it.

Compassion and so forth are the means employed. Because one relies on the teaching to reverse delusion, it is called "arousal. Because one restrains the mind to accord with the Dharma, it is called a "vow" (*praṇidhāna*). It is the aspiration of the mind.
Because it exists, it is called "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*). Question: It should have been presented first; why is the object (*ālambana*) placed at the beginning? Answer:
If there were no object of focus, the mind would have nowhere to direct itself. Furthermore, although it may have already been generated previously, it is now being taught again.

Within this [section], there are six parts: first, the general heading, as in the text; second, the formal explanation; third, the correlation of object and wisdom; fourth, the exclusion of what is not [the case]; fifth, the summary; sixth, the contemplation.

The mind. Having already descended deeply, the main text explains two [aspects]: first, compassion (*karuṇā*); second, loving-kindness (*maitrī*). First, compassion is explained according to its teaching; now, this is explained according to its practice.

The first [section on compassion] further has three parts: first, clarifying the object; second, formally arising the vow; third, the conclusion. The first passage has two parts: first, restating the aforementioned sublime object.

Therefore, it is called "one. It is termed "suffering" because it is designated by way of its causes and effects, such as suffering itself; yet it is called "all" because the three thousand worlds are present in a single thought-moment.

All instances of the term "all" should be understood according to this principle. Since it is precisely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that transforms into ignorance, compassion arises based upon that ignorance.

Next, from "one's own sorrow" (*ātma-śoka*) downward, one contemplates the various realms (*viṣaya*) as the basis for giving rise to the vow. This section consists of two parts: first, clarifying the nine types of non-mind;

second, clarifying the minds of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). These also rely on the sequence of taking oneself and others as objects. The first part further consists of two sections: first, clarifying suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*);

second, clarifying compassion for others. The first of these further consists of two sections: first, the three miserable destinies (*apāya*); second, humans and devas. The first of these [the three destinies] further consists of two sections: first...
This clarifies that suffering is the fruit of the cause of suffering. Next, it clarifies the vow. The first section has two parts; first, how the cause of suffering invites the fruit of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "Former suffering," etc.: "former" refers to the causes of the three miserable realms; "revolving and circling" below refers to the fruits of the three evil paths in the past. Next, "And now," etc. [refers to the present].

Now, within the fruits of this present life, causes arise once again. Following the passage "Next, [at] a hundred thousand [yojanas] below," there is an expression of astonishment that serves as the reason for making a vow.

Following the passage "Next, even if," it clarifies the realms of humans and devas. This section also has two parts: first, it clarifies that there is no path to cessation, using analogies such as market trade;

these all illustrate the nature of conditioned merit, which merely exchanges one for another among the three miserable realms, and is further changed in an instant. These successive exchanges are driven by merit, yet they only increase the burden of transgressions; hence it is said:
"Flipping and turning" refers to the act of catching fish. The mind is like the fish; the [karmic] signs are like the fish-trap. Merit is like the trap; the lamp is like the light.

Experiencing the fruit is like entering [the trap] or rushing toward it. Fabricating names in vain is like calculating worldly wisdom, which is called a "perverse dot. Binding oneself with thick [afflictions] is called increasing delusion;
suffering becoming deep is called going further away. Lacking the water of True Principle is called thirst; experiencing retribution while increasing desire is called drinking saltwater again.
To increase birth and death instead is called "even more severe"; it is precisely to damage the Path. Physical marks and blessings are like facial hair and skin;

the Three Studies are like the body. Mental marks are like fetters; receiving karmic fruits is like entering a direction. To retreat and follow the three evil paths is like [the fetters] becoming even firmer. Ignorance is like blindness, causing increasing pain.
Precepts and goodness are like entering; receiving karmic fruits is like eating dates. Mental marks are like being unsteady; yet one still obtains blessings.
It is like falling into a whirlpool;
next, it is like grasping a blade while descending. One sighs that those who lack the Way are extinguished, yet all shall proceed toward Bodhi. It is like handling a knife by its handle.
If one conforms to the marks of the mind, it is like grasping a blade or holding fire; when a Bodhisattva beholds this, it is as if treading upon the tail of a tiger.

Next, from "He then reflects for himself" onwards, he takes pity on others as described in the text. He reproaches ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and [those attached to] the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); the six perfections are like poison, and ordinary beings are like counterfeits.
This also includes those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Next, "Suppose, for instance, that [the mind] descends" clarifies that the minds of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) are themselves one liberation. The causes and fruits of the two vehicles also constitute the object of the vow. Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the absence of the great vow, wherein there are only the causes and fruits of the two vehicles; second, lamenting for others. The first part also has two sub-sections.

The first correctly clarifies the causes and fruits of the two vehicles: *su* means having died and being born again; because the Tripiṭaka does not immediately [attain the goal], it is like a narrow pass.
The Path. The Bodhisattva proceeds like a public official; the followers of the Two Vehicles depart like rebels. Birth-and-death and afflictions harm *nirvāṇa* as if with an enemy’s intent;
therefore, the three realms are all termed "kingdoms. To wander throughout the five destinies is like undergoing exhaustive trials;
that the three realms offer no peace is like enduring bitter hardship. Losing the Great Vow is called "collapse"; to again give rise to a lesser aspiration is called "revival."
Turning one's back on the Great [Vehicle], one enters the impoverished village of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Sweeping away filth while seeking the coins of wisdom is called "hired labor.
Birth-and-death is the night; *nirvāṇa* is like the sun. The place of rest in the minor fruits is called a "grass hut. Not yet having resolved upon the Great Mind is called "refusing to advance.
Using clumsy means to destroy delusions is called "lowly work."

Next, regarding the section on "lack of faith" and below: this is the cause for our astonishment and lamentation, and for our compassionate sorrow. It is because they turn their backs on the Great [Vehicle] that they still slander the Vaipulya;

thus, their lack of faith, lack of understanding, and lack of practice are termed "not recognizing. Because they do not recognize the specific delusions, they are pitiable; because they do not distinguish the distinct principles, they are to be regarded as strange.

Next, "contemplating below" refers to truly feeling compassion for others oneself; this contemplation is the beginning of the great vow, while the sense of "agonizing pain" (*keng-tung*) is the cultivation of compassionate aspiration.
Because one's sorrow reaches its utmost intensity, it is called "agonizing pain."

Next, the text proceeds to the section below, which explicitly clarifies the Great Vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). This section also consists of four parts. First, the vows are established based on objects; that is, the first vow is formulated in reference to sentient beings.

Next, the subsequent vow is formulated in reference to afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the bodhisattva’s unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-karuṇā*) has been cultivated throughout both past and present, these are both discussed in terms of objective phenomena (*vastu*) to explain the compassionate mind.
Having already made vows based on objects, one must now accord with the realm of principle (*li-jing*); therefore, all the subsequent vows...
In accordance with the three truths, the compassionate vows are likewise so. Following the section on "the assembly of beings," the characteristics of the vows are clarified;

these are also explained by relying on the sequential order of contemplation. First is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Under the phrase "although knowing," follows the characteristic of the provisional (*upāya*). Under the phrase "although knowing," follows the middle characteristic (*madhyama*). Each of these is elucidated through two vows.

Since the vows are vast, the suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are likewise extensive. Regarding the question "What are the three? and below, the characteristics are explained while refuting partiality.

First, he refutes the *Hīnayāna* (Zàng); next, he refutes the *Common* (Tōng); next, he refutes the *Distinct* (Bié). Because these two types of contemplation are still bound by ignorance, they are said to be "not liberation.

Fourth, from "Now, however," he reveals the correct [view]. Within this, there are two parts. First, regarding the Dharma: the Middle Way is a double negation, and thus it is neither poison nor falsehood.

Second, from "It is like a bird," he provides an analogy. This also has three parts. First, the analogy of flying through the sky without dwelling: just as [the bird] is identical with emptiness while...

"Provisional" (*prajñapti*). Although it does not abide in the past, it is like the provisional being empty; this is the "conjunction" (*yoga*) following the section on emptiness. From "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, it further applies the analogy of the "empty fist" (*riktamuṣṭi*) to the conjunction.
From "For these three reasons" (*trihetutvāt*) onwards, it is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

Furthermore, following the section on consciousness, the next part clarifies the compassionate vows (*maitrī-praṇidhāna*), which is divided into two: first, the object (*viṣaya*), and second, the vow itself. The first [the object] is further divided into two.
First, it reiterates the previously mentioned sublime objects; therefore, it says, "one happiness," and so forth.

Next, regarding "myself and those below," this specifically clarifies the objects of the vow. It clarifies that although they previously attained the Path and Cessation, they merely sought the realms of humans and devas, not knowing to seek the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Path and Cessation as ultimate bliss. In the analogy, the shards and rubble represent not recognizing cessation.
The light of the practice is like not yet knowing the Way;

now, as it is about to descend, one makes a vow based on the objective realm. This also has three parts: first, establishing the objective realm of the vow; first, initiating the initial vow in relation to the Way.

Next, regarding the sequence of cessation and arising, there is a subsequent vow. Although the section beginning with "Though one knows" [discusses] the inferior, it clarifies the characteristics of the vow;

furthermore, although they are sequential, they are distinguished as non-sequential. In the initial passage, "Emptiness" refers to the first vow. The section beginning with "Though one knows" refers to the provisional (the second vow). The section beginning with "Though one knows" refers to the middle.

Within the Middle Way, the Dharma-gate marks the first vow, while the Buddha-fruit marks the second vow. "Not cultivation, etc. explains the first vow. "Not realization, etc. explains the second vow; within this, "not cultivation" explains the middle [vow].
Realization can also be cultivated and realized; therefore, one makes a vow for both oneself and others.

Third, from "therefore" onwards, the text refutes the false to reveal the correct. One should distinguish the poisonous and the false by means of the three teachings [Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct], such as views of emptiness and attachment;
these are collectively termed "poisonous" even before realization. The nine [stages] of the two vehicles are collectively termed "false. The two vehicles and...

The various teachings that enter emptiness are all termed "emptiness," while the three teachings that emerge into the provisional are collectively termed "views and attachments. Since these proceed from the initial contemplation of principle, neither is rejected.
From "The three are thus" below, the object and wisdom are synthesized; first, it clarifies that the vow is identical with the object and wisdom, followed by compassion.
Below, it clarifies that wisdom and compassion are mutually identical. Wisdom is simply understanding; understanding arises based on an object, and the vow arises based on that understanding.
The object is the focal point (*ālambana*), and the vow is the subject that focuses upon it. By means of non-referential compassion, one takes this object of wisdom as its focus.
Because the object is called "non-referential" and the vow is called "non-conceptual," through the employment of this compassion, one is able to act spontaneously (*anābhoga*).
The four [vows] differ from those below; this is a general distinction rather than a refutation of the false. "Is named" (is below) refers to the fifth [section], which provides a summary.

The general meaning follows the previous [explanation], hence it refers back to what was above. To speak of them simply as "compassion" is merely a matter of linguistic convenience. Furthermore, these four great vows mutually support one another.

Being co-present within a single thought-moment is what is called the "aspect of the vow. This is the sixth [section], the Contemplation of the Mind. Regarding the four truths of non-arising within a single thought-moment, the third is the Settling of the Mind (*anxin*).
It is called "settling the mind" because one skillfully employs *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to settle that *dharmatā*. Within this, there is first the formal presentation.

Next is the explanation. Within the explanation, there are three parts. First, from "excellent" (*śubha*) downwards, the name is explained. "Superior deep penetration" (*shang shen da*) refers to the preceding section;

"inferior" (*xia*) links the preceding to the subsequent. First, the preceding object is concluded as being profound, hence it is said: "a deep abyss, vast and far-reaching. Below, the preceding vow is concluded as being extensive, hence it is said:

"pervading the canopy," meaning all-pervasive. It is not that the object is not extensive, nor that the vow is not deep; however, for the sake of convenience in explaining the name according to phenomena and principle (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), one must practice.

In the past, when one was born into this world, the capacity for which one vowed was merely an intellectual understanding of emptiness. Now, when the mind is settled within its object, it finally accords with that vow. Having attained such stability, one benefits others;
this fulfills the first vow. Having attained stability, afflictions are severed; this fulfills the second vow. With afflictions severed and the Dharma fully realized, the third vow is fulfilled.
Realizing the truth stage by stage fulfills the fourth vow. Thus, from these stages up to the primary and auxiliary practices, all are termed the fulfillment of one’s vows.

Regarding the three types of ignorance [listed] below, the explanation is divided into two parts: first, the general; second, the specific. This is done to accommodate those of sharp and dull faculties, to manifest past and present [afflictions], because of the lightness or heaviness of delusion, and because of differences in what is preferred.
Within the general section, there are again two parts: first, the clarification of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, the revelation of their identical essence.

The first section also has two parts: first, clarifying the objective realm of principle; second, clarifying *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The first of these also has two parts: first, the teaching; second, the analogy.

Within the teaching, it refers exclusively to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and no other path. Next, under the phrase "like cold," etc., an analogy is presented, adding the two conditions of cold and sleep.

This also refers to the ignorance within the realm of *dharmatā* itself as being the obstruction and concealment. Superficially, it appears as if the coldness covers the water of the mind from the outside;
however, in principle, this is entirely the water of the mind. Therefore, one should contemplate that prior ignorance is merely *dharmatā*, which is termed "fusion" (*rong*) and "awakening" (*jue*).

Next, we shall now briefly clarify *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) as the general characteristics of peaceful stability. This is further divided into two parts: first, *śamatha*; second, *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the first, *śamatha*, there are again two sections:

first, clarifying the application of *śamatha*; second, clarifying the perfected state. In the initial passage, the section beginning with "Although [the mind] is inverted" first correctly explains *śamatha*.

The section beginning with "The analogy for lack of faith" corresponds [to the application], while the statement regarding "mindfulness of the *dharmatā*" somewhat resembles *vipaśyanā*; this is because it serves to establish *vipaśyanā* through the binding [of the mind].
Mindfulness and cessation are concurrent; this is due to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Next, the characteristics of the perfection of cessation are realized through its essence.

Next, within the section on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there are again two parts: first, the application of contemplation is clarified; second, the characteristics of its perfection are clarified. In the first passage, there are also two sections:

first, the teaching; second, the analogy. The kalpa-fire is as described before. When the Ocean-Wisdom of the Empty Treasury (Kōzō kai-e) was about to enter the assembly, he first manifested this before the Buddha.

The marks serve to manifest one's own virtue while simultaneously demonstrating the benefit of others; thus, they cause those in the assembly at that time to see only empty water. The contemplation of dharmas is likewise:
the nature of dharmas has no exterior.

"Below 'a mere moment' (*jier*): the contemplation is perfected. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the perfection of contemplation; second, providing an analogy. Regarding the first part, the text concludes by establishing the two kinds of emptiness as the mark of perfection.
'A mere moment' (*jier*) is not false; 'momentary' (*chana*) refers to the one who calculates [the contemplation].

'Mere' (*jie*) means assistance, which is to say, subtle thought. When subtle thought is destroyed, it is called the emptiness of nature (*xingkong*). When the characteristics of emptiness cannot be apprehended, it is called the emptiness of characteristics (*xiangkong*)."

Next, as before, "lowering" refers to lifting the fire-drill wood; the non-existence of both agent and object serves as an analogy for the two kinds of emptiness. "The Dharma-realm lowers" signifies their merging into non-existence.

Next, "it is simply wisdom" and so forth reveals that the essence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is identical; because quiescence and illumination are simultaneous, it says "it is simply. "Causing" and so forth...

They may be separately established for the sake of identification; thus, the two characteristics of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are distinguished. Moreover, since their essence is non-dual, one should not allow them to have two distinct names.
Therefore, it should be known that herein they are distinct yet non-distinct. In the subsequent section on "separately establishing," they are non-distinct yet distinct.

Below the section on "non-movement," the characteristics are further clarified: first, it is shown that *śamatha* is itself *vipaśyanā*; below the section on "non-movement," it is shown that *vipaśyanā* is itself *śamatha*. Non-movement...

"Below 'Wisdom' (智), it clarifies that the two dharmas function in tandem. Because one attains the *dharmatā*, both are settled. Below 'Immovable' (不動), it further reverses this to cover [the previous point]:

because the upper phrase establishes stillness (*śamatha*), observation (*vipaśyanā*) is settled; because observation is settled herein, stillness is established. Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* says:
'Based upon the *dharmakāya*, there are great concentration and wisdom.'"

If both [methods] fail, one should practice separately. First, the specific intent is set forth. This section has two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the formal explanation. The first part has four sections.

First, a restatement that simultaneous application is inappropriate, serving as an introduction to the inquiry. "Both" means that neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā* can be established simultaneously. Next, from "Now, as for the mind and spirit...
onwards, the general characteristics of instability are presented as the basis for separate practice. "Obscure and dim" refers to *vipaśyanā*.

"Anxiously unsettled. [The character 怵 (chù) is composed of 止 (zhǐ) and 栗 (lì), meaning to stop the unsettled state. The character 怵 should be written as 這 (zhè) with 坐 (zuò) instead of 言 (yán). It means "swift. *Gǔ* (汩): pronounced *wéi* (為) and *bǐ* (筆) combined;

it also means "swift. *Shū* (儵): another term for "rapid," and also "startled. In the third section, "Strong Enemies Below," events are cited to illustrate the characteristics of being anxiously unsettled.
"Obscure dispersal is like powerful enemies; movement is subtle like weak strength. These events concern the Six States and appear in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. (2)

Since they have already competed with one another, I fear both will be manifested. Now it is the same: if the general state of stillness and the scattered state of darkness are mutually suppressed, then the former [stillness] prevails.

Cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) share the same meaning as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): both are equally extinguished. Even if one understands them partially, one is not yet capable of fully grasping them.

Fourth, regarding "martyrdom for the lower" (*xunxia*): this is generally described as the ritual for "peace through affairs. To follow life unto death is called "martyrdom" (*xun*); it refers to vowing to practice with diligence.

"To offer" (*jian*) means to present; "flesh" (*ji*) refers to the skin. Even if the skin and bones wither and decay, one should cultivate single-mindedly without slackening, firming one's resolve for a separate peace in anticipation of [the goal].
