Regarding the "Chapter on Entering" up to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), it is therefore called the "Skillful Vow.

Under the section on "Serenity of Mind," the text correctly clarifies the distinct serenity (*viśeṣa-śamatha*). This is termed "distinct" in contrast to the general [serenity], yet it does not imply a sequential progression. When viewed in light of the subsequent enumeration of categories, the distinct [serenity] still constitutes the general.
In contrast to the sequential [classification] below, this is named "one mind"; thus, both the general and the distinct are here designated as "one mind. Therefore...

To know that this is merely the general integration of cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), yet through their distinct applications, further augmented by faith and the Dharma, these four *siddhāntas* (purposes) mutually support one another to constitute the distinct characteristics.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the listing of the two gates; second, the detailed explanation. The detailed explanation has five sections:

first, the explanation of the one hundred and twenty-eight permutations of self and other; second, the sequential traversal of the three contemplations to calculate the total number; third, the opening [of the gates] by means of the four *siddhāntas*; [and so forth].

Manifesting. Fourth, [the capacity] by which that which is manifested is manifested. Fifth, citing an analogy. The first [section] has two parts: first, distinguishing the masters who determine the practice;

second, the formal explanation. The first [of these two] also has two parts: first, distinguishing the masters; second, determining the practice. The first [of these two] also has two parts: first, listing the two masters. Regarding "benefiting others":
The Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the mind is fundamentally for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.

[The passage] beginning with "The Holy Teacher" provides an explanation. This explanation is divided into two parts: first, the Holy Teacher; second, the ordinary teacher. The first part is further divided into three sections. Regarding the first section, which clarifies the "three powers":

these are the inconceivable wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*), the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and the path of transformation (*nirmāṇa-mārga*). Thus, within a single eye, one distinguishes between the wisdom of phenomena (*dharma-prajñā*) and the wisdom of reality (*tattva-prajñā*).
Next, as stated below in the *Kukuda* [text], it cites an example of an ordinary person to illustrate how difficult it is to encounter a holy teacher.

Thus, the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra* (付法藏) says: "These are all the teachings of sages. Regarding the one who climbed the tree, this is cited in the fourth fascicle. Regarding the one awakened by food: he was greedy for hot gruel;
when told to let it cool, he blew on it with his mouth, and it immediately cooled. The Venerable One said to him: "The fire of your desire is still hot; you ought to..."

By contemplating water, he eliminated the fever of his desires and immediately attained the realization of an Arhat. [The Buddha] rebuked him for claiming that his attainment of the fourth dhyāna constituted the fruit of the fourth stage (the Arhatship).
He frequently manifested in the form of a woman to test him; when [the monk] became aware of lustful thoughts, the Buddha again assumed the form of his Upādhyāya to rebuke him.

It was through this that he obtained the fruit. This was not a conversion of one who was not yet mature, nor was it a case where fame did not wait for the right time, nor was it a case where the capacity [of the recipient] was not yet ripe.

Transformation. The name "Not Missing the Time" follows. Below, a parable is raised: a holy teacher is difficult to encounter, just as in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* it is said that this turtle emerges once every three thousand years, while in the ocean there is but a single piece of wood with but a single hole. By what means could it possibly encounter such a rare hole?
Even the throwing of a mustard seed from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven onto a needle in Jambudvīpa is more difficult than this. The difficulty of encountering the Four Reliances is twice as great again.

In this regard, there are next four points concerning the ordinary teacher (*pṛthagjana-ācārya*). First, the opening of the ordinary teacher’s dispensation of transformation; second, the analogy for the benefit of the ordinary teacher’s transformation. Within the latter, first is the analogy:
although the holy one possesses three powers, they are of no benefit to the ordinary person. Therefore, the ordinary teacher is entrusted with the task, just like a worldly physician.

Regarding the Dharma: the superior physician examines the complexion; the middling physician listens to the voice; and the inferior physician diagnoses the pulse. The Sage observes the three leaves and manifests the transformations of the three wheels. The analogy of the "complexion" and so forth can be seen in their respective order.

If the obstacles are heavy and there is no receptive capacity (*indriya*), even the Sage cannot be of benefit; lacking the sharpness of a suitable recipient, it is said that [the medicine] cannot raise the dead.
Next, if one does not descend [to the level of the patient], this is the primary analogy: although the teacher who transforms and benefits others lacks [the need for] mental karma (*manas-karman*).

There may be two remaining [points]. The Great Master himself disparaged [this] by calling it the "teaching of an ordinary teacher. Because it occasionally provides benefit, he says "extracting and liberating" (*tiao tuo*).
To humbly defer to those who follow, he says "according to the words," and so forth; thus, in all subsequent texts, it is said that "the teacher should ask," and so on.

Below the passage concerning Śāriputra, the text cites a noble being to illustrate the case of ordinary people. If even a minor sage errs regarding the capacities of others, how much more so those who follow him?

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were not true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). This refers to how they failed their two disciples by misjudging their capacities and thus losing the opportunity for benefit;

it is like a washerman discovering that clothes are not clean, or a goldsmith skillfully knowing when to cease [the smelting process]. How could they have given such erroneous instruction? As for the term "those bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana*), it refers to those at the stage of the five grades of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

All possess ignorance; therefore, they are said to be "bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana*), as explained in the first fascicle. This is because [the text] refers only to those in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) as "sages.

Furthermore, since the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka still possess both types of fetters in their entirety, and [the text states] "now not descending," this is the formal conclusion, demonstrating that ordinary masters should transform others.

Next, regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore, others... the practice (*caryā*) is judged to be fivefold. First, two types of practice are briefly established. Second, two treatises are cited to provide a detailed discrimination. Third, starting from "However, as for the number...

it is judged that while two schools are preserved, they are not used in their entirety; rather, they are harmonized and reconciled. The completion of this practice occurs upon the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Skillful means (*upāya*) is the root-nature. The accomplishment of practice arises through skillful means; they cannot be considered distinct. Therefore, the reasons cited in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* differ.
Now, because the fundamental tenets of the various schools differ slightly—appearing as if they mutually support one another—the present school synthesizes and preserves them.
[The section] "Now, the Master" and below assists the Master’s intention by correctly explaining the two lines, clarifying that past causes serve as the seeds for the present. The present...

There exists reliance upon long-standing causes; these long-standing causes differ according to the principles of various schools, and the manifest effects likewise differ according to many treatises.

Therefore, we now discuss only how the past serves as the present. By verifying the seeds of hearing and reflection within the present, one knows of the past. To accommodate various capacities, it is stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:

"If [the Dharma] passes once through the ear, one shall not fall into the evil realms for seven kalpas; by contemplating its meaning, one will certainly attain Bodhi. This refers precisely to hearing over a vast period of time.

It is the seed of reflection (*cintā*). Regarding the five [faculties] below, their designations as "sharp" or "dull" are determined through mutual relation, which differs from the two treatises previously mentioned.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Having already explained," this correctly clarifies the distinct establishment [of the faculties]. This section further has two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the actual explanation. The actual explanation also has two parts:
first, clarifying that self and others are mutually exclusive; second, clarifying how they assist one another. The first part also has two sections: first, the actual explanation.

Next is the enumeration. This section also has two parts: first, transforming others; second, one's own practice. The first part also has two sections: first, demonstrating the characteristics of the phenomena;
second, the enumeration. The first of these also has two sections: first, explaining the two practices individually; second, explaining their transformation. The first of these also has two sections:
first, providing a general question-and-answer to distinguish their nature as the method for transforming others.

Next is the formal explanation. This section consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer, beginning with "That person," which describes what he values. Within this, there are again two parts:
first, the explanation of practice through faith (*śraddhā-pratipatti*); second, the explanation of practice through the Dharma (*dharma-pratipatti*).

Next, following the phrase "having known the lower," the formal explanation is divided into two parts: first, faith; second, the Dharma. The first part further has three sections: first, indicating the number of dharmas;

second, explaining the three fetters (saṃyojana); and third, as in the text. Within the explanation, there are eight sections, each of which contains three points: the first is to demonstrate the characteristics of the dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Next, the breadth [of the teaching] is indicated. Third, the three [points] establish the *siddhānta*. The initial statement, "O man! and so forth, correctly demonstrates the characteristics. What is cited here merely shows the formal manner of exposition;

although there are terms such as "Confucian," "Small Vehicle," "partial," or "gradual," the words are proximate while the meaning is profound, all serving to establish the practice of the four *siddhāntas* of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
In the following text, the enumeration of categories is separately established according to their distinct meanings. It says: "By..."
Regarding the first meaning: it is as stated in the *Laozi*: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil," and so forth.

The intent of Laozi is merely that heaven and earth, when unified within the Way of Yin and Yang, are termed "the One. Now, [in this context], both suffering and its origination are unified through their attainment of cessation (*nirodha*);
the six obscurations are unified by means of the other shore (*pāra*); and this is the ultimate of the Three Vehicles.

Therefore, it is said to be "the most excellent. The section beginning with "skillful means" below points to the detailed exposition; the section beginning with "this name" below provides the conclusion. The seven sections following "siddhānta" consist merely of seven textual passages.
Next, regarding the statement that humans are like the gods and so forth: "kàng" (亢) also means drought. "Huì" (卉) is a general term for grasses.

By citing their failure to grow, it reveals what they are capable of producing; this refers to the arising of wholesome qualities (*kuśala*). As for the *Bhaga* Dragon King, the text appears in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
the present mention of the "four directions" refers to the *Anavatapta* Dragon King. "Humans" are also below [the gods]. "Joining yet not joining" refers to the seven days and the four [periods].

[The text] is square. It combines the rivers and ponds and adds the factors of the path (*mārga*) and trees. At first, when reversed, they do not arise; if one can descend [into them], they arise through combination. One may also teach and explain them through contemplation.
As for those who produce the various dhyānas like rain, it is because they can serve as the causes for all dharma-gates. The stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth belong to the Tripiṭaka-vinaya.

The "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and so forth are as previously explained in the section on Turning the Wheel of Dharma. The "Patience of Accordance" (*anuloma-kṣānti*) and so forth are common to the teachings of the Shared Vehicle (*pāryāyika-śāsana*).

This is the Dharma. It is quiescent extinction and non-arising; it is the roots of goodness of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles]. These all arise from *dhyāna*, which is precisely the arising of goodness.

Regarding the "intoxicated elephant" mentioned in the section on counteracting [afflictions], it is as previously explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da lun) concerning the *Ṣaḍdhātuvibhaṅga*.

As for the "five obscurations," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "For example, the sun and moon do not appear when obscured by five things: smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and the hand of the *asura*. Here, we take this in its general sense.
Because they are able to obstruct, they are collectively termed "obscuring" (*tāmisra*). Wind stirring up dust is called "dust" (*reṇu*); the rising of smoke and clouds is called "haze" (*nīhāra*).
"The Radiant One" (*yāolin*) refers to the sun and moon; it is also said to be the light within the void. Since these are obscured, they must be counteracted.

Regarding the phrase "the eyelashes being too close," etc.: "xiāo" means near the heavens. When the red vapors are thin, the clouds can form completely; thus, they become red vapors that cannot be seen.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both contain eight points that are difficult to perceive; yet while these are all close at hand, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is like a star descending from the heavens.
Both treat the evils remedied by the cultivation of emptiness. As for the "Golden Scalpel," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Nature" (*Dharmatā-parivarta*), states:
"It is as if a group of blind men went to a physician. The physician used a golden scalpel to clear away the cataracts from their eyes and showed [them the way]."
[The practitioner] holds one, two, or three fingers. When asked, "Do you see [the moon]?", he answers that with one finger held he does not see it, but with two or three he does.
The Sūtra itself states: "In the Ten Abodes, there is slight seeing. This means that in the Perfect [Teaching], one sees the Three Truths during the Ten Abodes.

Regarding the passage in the *Prathama-artha-samādhi* (First Meaning) which says "if the mind is equal," it means that the world is the dharma of arising, and the world is the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing; all of these depend upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Non-arising and non-ceasing are themselves the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Ultimate truth is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

The Tathāgata’s attainment of the Way is likewise the primary meaning; so too are permanence, bliss, and stability. Regarding those who possess meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is like the "Lightning Flash" from the *Teaching Left Behind* (*Yōgyō*);
seeing the Path is also the primary meaning. Regarding the phrase "shattering countless billions," this concludes the shattering [of delusions] and the realization of principle.

Regarding the passage "That person, below": this refers generally to the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) as observed through the stage of faith (*śraddhā-carita*). The first question extends its application to this point.

The phrase "I have heard" and so forth serves to exclude those who practice the Dharma through mere formal adherence (*dharma-carita*). The mention of the "three evil realms" and so forth cites worldly suffering to illustrate that while the suffering of being scorched by fire or the burden of heavy loads has limits, the obstruction of ignorance regarding the Truth (*satya*) extends even to the stage of True Reward (*samyak-phala*).
Therefore, it is called "great suffering. This analogy of direction and region illustrates the principle of the provisional and the real (*upāya-tattva*).
Furthermore, it may be that within each of the truths of the internal and external realms there are distinct directions and divisions. Regarding the phrase "much learning" and so forth:

"delight" refers to aspiration; "hearing" refers to practice through faith. These can be contrasted with the mundane world; thus, terms such as "evil" and so on follow accordingly. Regarding the phrase "as taught" and so forth:

the fourfold path-factors constitute the Path, while the two types of death constitute the non-Path. Within the internal realm, the three miserable destinies serve as pits and chasms; as for the external realm...
Taking the wholesome within the realm as a pit or trench, one distinguishes the various differences such as the paths; this is the worldly intention.
Regarding the statement "among humans, it is like the moon opening [the lotus]," the blue lotus depends on the moon and the red lotus depends on the sun. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"Just as when the sun shines upon a red lotus, there is none that does not open and flourish. Regarding "the eyes arising," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "All activities..."

All must await the clarity of the sun. The master, the glue, the fire, and the guide are all metaphors for contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The merchant, the painting, the unbaked clay vessel, and the blind man are all metaphors for practice (*caryā*).
Practice is itself goodness; the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the most excellent among all forms of goodness. Therefore, it is followed by way of its preeminence.
Regarding the section on "raising the antidote": the enemy is evil itself; recognizing the enemy is the contemplation that serves as the antidote.
A military commander who possesses strategic planning—such as Wang Jian of Qin or Wu Qi of Wei—is skilled at breaking through enemy formations and obstructions, and thus it is like destroying evil.
Next, regarding "clouds, heat, fire, darkness, fuel, and bondage," these are all the evils to be destroyed.
As for the phrase "a well and so forth" within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "It is like a dark room containing various kinds of treasures."
Because it is dark, one does not see; because the sun shines, one sees. One cannot say that what was originally non-existent now exists.

Nirvāṇa is also like this. It must be understood through departure. This is the intent of the Prajñāpāramitā verses: all dharmas are truly equal, which is the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Equal contemplation" refers to entering the ultimate truth by means of causal contemplation. Thus concludes the section below.

The person below [is next]. Next, the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*) is explained in three parts. First, the faculties and dispositions (*indriya-gotra*) are again examined. "Silence upon silence" clarifies that thought does not shift;
"diminishing it yet further diminishing" is a phrase borrowed by Master Zhaok from the *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes), used here because the ultimate truth is named "Non-action" (*wuwei*).

This excludes the practice of faith and hearing as being "action" (*sawei*), and thus [the latter] is like galloping while sitting still. Now, I borrow from Zhuang Zhou’s "sitting and forgetting" (*zuowang*).
Regarding the term "forgetting" (wàng): by means of forgetting words, one contemplates principle through the text; as one follows the text, the mind races.
Next, there is the formal explanation, which also consists of eight sections. The first four concern cessation (zhǐ). [The character] huà is pronounced hùguài.

Among the qualities of a person, what dharma is not fully present? At the very least, one must possess the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). Within each perfection, all dharmas are complete; how could anything be superior to this?
Therefore, it is the most excellent among all virtues. The first six can be seen [directly]. As for those beginning with "stopping" (*śamatha*), stopping is the state of non-duality.

This is due to skillful means (*upāya*). Within *śamatha* (calm abiding), all vows are complete; hence it is called "all-encompassing. Because it possesses the power to eliminate delusions, it is termed "power" (*bala*).

Since this is the wisdom of the middle way, it is called "non-dual. Regarding the term "wall-like concentration" (*kuṭī-pratisaṃyukta-samādhi*) mentioned in the context of antidotes, it refers to a dwelling that shields one from the eight winds.
Having attained cessation, one is able to depart from both the eight [afflictions] within the realm and the eight outside the realm.

Regarding "dew and so forth": dew is like scattering; the sun is like cessation; *xi* means to dry. Cessation is great compassion (*maitrī*), just as compassion treats anger. Regarding "the Great Bright Mantra" (*mahā-vidyā-mantra*):
the great wisdom of Prajñā is itself the "Great Bright"; Prajñā is the mantra, hence it is named the "Great Bright Mantra. It upholds all...
The Dharma treats all things universally; therefore, it is said that "all are dispelled. Regarding the phrase "cessation is the Buddha, etc.":

mindfulness of the Buddha treats obstacles [to the path], whereas here, through the Dharma-Buddha, cessation treats the obstacle to the wondrous path. As for "Agada, etc.," these are among those capable of treating [obstacles].

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), "cessation" refers to the realization of reality (*tattva-bhāvanā*); by employing sequential terminology, this constitutes the wondrous cessation. Regarding the phrase "the Mother of Buddhas, etc.":
The true mother and the provisional father together constitute the Buddha’s sons. The quiescent illumination of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is the Teacher of the Buddhas.

The Buddha-body is the manifestation of the Dharma. Cessation (*śamatha*) and cause-and-effect are the eyes; concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are able to adorn it. Now, since cessation belongs to concentration, it is called "marks and signs" (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Possessing the Dharma is called the "Treasury" (*kośa*); that which is relied upon is called the "Abode" (*sthāna*). To fully cite the preceding [sections] is "appropriateness"; to exclude the citation of the preceding [sections] is "remedy. This is to generate goodness based on principle.

To destroy evil. Regarding that person’s inferiority, it is explained by observing the four *siddhāntas*. First, concerning the phrase "right awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and so forth: when in the causal stage it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), and when in the resultant stage it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).

"Rightly contemplating the Great [Vehicle]" and so forth is a praise by borrowing the terminology of the result. Regarding "that which can produce" among the generation of wholesome qualities: it is able to produce the fivefold [wholesome] factors.
Among the production of wholesome states, this is the foremost.

Among the methods of transformation and guidance, it is next to bestowing medicine as an antidote. That which can illuminate immediately destroys darkness; that which attains reality immediately eliminates poverty. Regarding the phrase "one should simply...

within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these four are all the intent of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*). This is fully explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Contemplate accordingly.
Commentary on the Mind. The phrase "The four are the lower" is the conclusion, as in the text.
Furthermore, regarding the section below that clarifies the "turning back," the two initial treatises speak of "beginning and end.

Both treatises [previously] used "beginning and end" for the benefit [of others], whereas here they are not the same. Within this, there are again four parts: first, the general statement of the purpose; second, the citation of the two treatises; third...
"Now, 'to clarify below'" correctly clarifies the present intention. "Fourth, 'if a dharma-practice' below" correctly clarifies the turning back.
"'Turning and not turning' below" is the second summary of the number, as in the text.

Next, the practice for oneself is explained. Practice for oneself involves the simultaneous exposition of both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Practice for others involves the distinct exposition of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Since teaching others takes speech as its foundation, the practice of faith is explained first. Since practice for oneself takes reflection as its foundation, the practice of the Dharma is explained first.
Furthermore, there are two aspects: first, teaching others to each practice separation; second, practicing oneself through unification. Within this, there are again two parts:

first, directly clarifying the mode of practice; second, clarifying the turning back [of the mind]. Regarding the first, there are three sections: first, the inquiry; second, the indication of the two modes of practice, as stated in "If one wishes," etc.;

third, the formal explanation, beginning with "Delighting in tranquility," etc. Within this, there are again two: first, the Dharma; second, faith. Regarding the first of these, there are again two: first, the explanation.
Next, regarding the sequence of the bonds: the first four each constitute a pair, with one *śamatha* (calm abiding) and one *vipaśyanā* (insight) for each.

Within the first [pair], that of "desire" (*chanda*), the former is *śamatha* and "if one desires" (*yadi kāmayeta*) and below is *vipaśyanā*. Because it occurs at the beginning, the arising of faults has not yet been discussed.

Next, from "his mind" (*tasya cittaṃ*) downward, the three [sections] beginning with "for the sake of others" (*parārtham*) all first discuss the arising of faults due to the preceding [desire], and subsequently apply *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to remedy them. From "moment by moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*) downward, these are the remedies.
The section on "Cultivating *śamatha* (calm abiding)" below [the first] is the primary meaning; this constitutes the conclusion, both of which are evident.

Next, the clarification of the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*) also has two parts: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are also four sections, namely the four *siddhāntas*.

The initial passage concerning the faults of not yet having generated the aspiration for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, etc., is in meaning as explained previously. The following three [sections] also concern faults arising previously. Next, the application of *śamatha*.
Contemplation. Regarding "listening to contemplation": for the sake of people, or at times, as an antidote; or regarding "listening": it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha). This is the conclusion.

Regarding the section "If the Dharma is Inferior": next, the turning back [of the mind] is explained as in the text. Regarding the section "Next, one's own practice": the enumeration is concluded as in the text. Furthermore, regarding the section "Next":

next, the mutual support [of the two aspects] is explained. This also has three parts: first, the actual explanation of mutual support; second, the citation of an analogy; third, the refutation of errors.

The first section also has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion regarding the number of dharmas associated with faith. The first follows the text. Within the explanation, there are two further parts:
first, clarifying that the dharmas assist faith; second, clarifying that faith assists the dharmas. When the dharmas are many and faith is few, it is called "dharmas assisting faith.

When faith is many and the dharmas are few, it is called "faith assisting the dharmas. These are also termed "primary" and "auxiliary. Since the initial "dharmas assisting faith" are said to assist one another, they are mutually [dependent].

This is further augmented. Each of the two sections contains two parts: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, *śamatha* (calm abiding); second, *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the Dharma" within the initial section on *śamatha*: since faith serves as the support, it is designated by the name "Dharma. This first part generally clarifies that faith is the supporting factor.
Below the "Crown" (guàn) are the four *siddhāntas*. If explained in full detail, each *siddhānta* would begin with the phrase "upon hearing a single phrase," and so on, up to "all are dispelled.

To avoid excessive textual verbosity, only the initial phrase of each is indicated. Returning to below the "Sitting" (zuò), there is "Joy" (lè). Next, below that, are three. Furthermore, "upon hearing" is followed by three *siddhāntas*.

Next, regarding the phrase "furthermore, one hears": within the contemplation of the four *siddhāntas*, faith serves as the support for the Dharma. In the first two phrases, there is the term "hearing"; the latter two are to be understood by analogy.
[The first two] constitute the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*) for destroying evil; [the latter two] are for the purpose of awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This concludes the section below. Question: Why does it not say "awakening" but rather "desiring"? Answer: Here, the four *siddhāntas* are established and distinguished by means of practice. It is not yet a matter of having destroyed evil views.

This is the truth. However, unlike the previous three [categories], this belongs to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the preceding section merely indicates such states as "vast and clear.

The subsequent sections—beginning with "faith and practice" and continuing through "the Dharma relies on faith" and "fourth, sitting upright," etc.—correspond to the four *siddhāntas*. In the text, the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is omitted.
This constitutes the lower section of the *knot*. Next, prior to this, the third *knot* concerning the enumeration of the Dharma of Faith is established;

both are as stated in the text. Next, under the phrase "Now, as for the ground of the mind," an analogy is presented. This also has three parts. First, regarding the textual passage on the Dharma: it differs from the preceding general [section], hence it says "according to one's vows.
Under the analogy, it further employs the three pairs of analogies—food and drink, pills and powders, and Yin and Yang—each of which pervades the meaning of the preceding [sections].
These form the four *siddhāntas*, which accord with the aspirations and inclinations [of beings]. Food and drink produce wholesome roots; pills and powders provide remedies.
Yin and Yang represent the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This concludes the third and eighth sections.

The third section, "One Kind," below, refutes the error of lacking mutual support through signlessness (*animitta*). Therefore, how could these two masters be taken as a standard for partial application?

Since they entirely lack the factors of faith and so forth, there is likewise no basis for their verses on "one cessation" and "one contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); these are cited to establish partiality. Since the masters themselves are thus choked with contradiction, their students must surely be wrong.
If even the realms of humans and devas are absent, how can one achieve the truly sublime? Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is cited: "Whey is [the stage of] humans and devas; curd..."
[They] transcend the world together.

Next, if one proceeds from the lower [level], one enumerates the figures by traversing the three contemplations. The phrase "if one proceeds" (*jù*) is a term used for establishing a distinct classification.

Although the text speaks only of the sudden (*dùn*), if one further relies on the gradual (*cìdì*), there are likewise one hundred and twenty-eight iterations for each. Because these are recounted again based on the previous [explanation], it says "furthermore" (*yòu*).

Thus, the preceding analysis comprises five hundred and twelve sections. As in the subsequent "Refutation of Pervasiveness," where each phrase is examined and each chapter is contemplated, it is stated that faith and the Dharma mutually support and revolve around one another; thus, each individual section contains sixty-four variations.
Furthermore, the non-duality of the horizontal and vertical dimensions is likewise a single mind consisting of one hundred and twenty-eight variations. Therefore, it should be known that herein...

Furthermore, let us speak according to the truths. If one explains by making the characteristics manifest based on the preceding and succeeding [moments], this is also a manifestation of sequence within non-sequencing.
If that is so, then within the inconceivable, each of the three may individually constitute one, and each of those three ones may further constitute one.
This also inherently consists of four sections totaling one hundred twenty-eight [items]. Question: How are they distinguished within the "Perfect" (Yuan) [classification]?

Answer: As stated in the sixth fascicle below: "Many enter Emptiness; few enter the Provisional," and so forth. Regarding the single [triple], the double [triple], and the complete [triple], these combine into seven layers.
If categorized sequentially, they are simply three. Although there are five hundred twelve variations, they are merely...

Regarding the teaching of the Dharma through faith, there is nothing that is not encompassed by either *śamatha* (calm abiding) or *vipaśyanā* (insight). To distinguish between the provisional and the ultimate, it is further analyzed according to four categories.

The third section, concerning the three *siddhāntas*, relies on the four *siddhāntas*. As for the text, it concerns what is treated by worldly physicians; it borrows from the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* to establish its present meaning.
That which pertains to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is designated as the worldly physician. The three *siddhāntas* mutually generate and require one another, following...
Obtaining one *siddhi* necessarily requires the other three *siddhis*; therefore, it is said that "rebirth" leads to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Even if there has not yet been an original birth, realization must proceed by means of this; hence, it is called "non-birth. Furthermore, because it is eternally distinct from the preceding three, it is called "non-birth.

Thus, the conclusion below states: "The mundane and the supramundane mutually accomplish and manifest each other. Therefore, every single practice should correspond to the four *siddhis*. This is why it is called the ultimate truth.

If one has not yet reached the ultimate, one must further ascend through the three [stages]. Within this, the fundamental is inconceivable; thus, the four [aspects] allow the characteristics to become manifest.

If these four were separated from the lower [stages], they would merely use what is manifested to repeatedly indicate the prior object. Now we know there is no distinction. If the mind rests in the lower, [the higher is attained].
A doubt arises. The doubt asks: "Must a practitioner necessarily employ all the preceding phrases? Therefore, it is explained: "It is sufficient to simply place one general phrase as before.
If one does not place [the general], one sets aside the general and follows the particular; thus, even when reaching the various phrases, one can still place the single general phrase.
Since this does not even require two, how could it require sixty-four? Therefore, an analogy is cited: 'One who catches birds uses but a single mesh of the net.'"
Fifth, "under the eye": this provides an analogy for the numerous preceding instances of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within this, there are three parts; first, the analogy:
it may be that one accommodates many people, yet because each individual has their own sequence of before and after, they must each find an entry point accordingly; hence it says "catching birds.
Since the practices of a single lifetime are not limited to a single eye, if one can find such an entry point, even many people may share a single one—how much more so when there are many?
Because many people use it, the conclusion below states: "As it is for a multitude of people, so it is for a single person. *Luo* (羅) refers to a bird net.

Following the section on the multitude of people, the analogy is joined [to the teaching]. Regarding the third point, "it must be broad," the analogy is raised and then joined to the teaching. *Fu* (蒱) refers to a land snail.

The fourth section, "Clarifying the Universal Destruction," is divided into two parts. First, a brief clarification of the purpose; second, an extensive clarification of the universal destruction. The first part is further divided into two:

first, clarifying the intent of the destruction in relation to the wondrous object; second, clarifying the intent of the destruction in relation to the settling of the mind. The first of these is further divided into two: first, citing the preceding object to raise the inquiry.
Thus it says, "The nature of dharmas, etc. "Convergence" refers to a single thought-moment; "dispersion" refers to the three thousand [realms]. Next, "but sentient beings... [and so forth].

[The Master] replies, clarifying the intent of the refutation: In principle, it is neither appropriate to refute nor not to refute; yet even [the position of] "peace" (an) is not truly peaceful. Therefore, a refutation is necessary.

Since beginningless time, who can calculate the extent of one's inversions? It is said to be "few" merely because one has previously practiced the first three [stages]. Because one’s own [position] has not yet been refuted, it is further called "refuted.
The former [stage] is called "peace" (an) because it causes one to reach the principle; the present [stage] is called "refutation" because it investigates according to the teachings.
Refutation. The refutation proceeds according to the practice.

Since the mind and its objects are one and the same, [the text] following "Next, the skillful means" below clarifies the intent of the refutation by contrasting it with the aforementioned "settling the mind. This also has two parts; first, it restates the preceding "settling the mind."

If [the mind] was already settled previously, then that settling itself constitutes a breach [of the meditative state]. Now, it is further clarified that the breach arises because [the mind] was not yet settled previously.

Next, if [the mind] has not yet descended [into concentration], this explicitly clarifies the intent of the "breach. As for the statement, "one who possesses wisdom based on concentration": how could the two gates of settling (*sthāpanā*) and breaching (*bhedana*) be applied in isolation?

If one is suited to possess wisdom based on concentration, one should employ settling as before; if one is suited to possess concentration based on wisdom, one should clarify the breach as now explained. One should take pleasure in this.
They are not the same; thus, names are not established in vain.

However, following the refutation of phenomena (*dharmas*), there is a broad refutation which is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the gates upon which [the refutation] relies; second, the actual broad refutation. The first part is further divided into two:

first, a general presentation of all the gates; second, specifically selecting the gate of the teachings (*śāsana*). Because one wishes to rely specifically on non-arising (*anutpāda*), [the text] cites [the general] for the sake of universal application.

The first section also has two parts. First, the teachings, practices, wisdoms, and principles as they appear in the sutras and treatises are listed; these mutually cause one another to enter, and do not exceed these four.

"Texts" refers to the teachings, specifically the forty-two letter gates. Regarding Mount Nanyue’s two interpretations: the first is general to the Three Vehicles, while the second is specific to the Perfect [Teaching].
Now, setting aside the general for the immediate [Perfect Teaching], each of the forty-two letters is fully endowed with all others.

One school may perhaps liken this to the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Now, regarding "teaching" (*śāsana*): as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, "speech and so forth, letters and so forth"—from speech comes teaching.

Alternatively, below the section on "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā*), it clarifies that "practice" (*caryā*) serves as the gate; samādhi is itself practice. Alternatively, below the section on "wisdom" (*jñāna*), wisdom serves as the gate.
Alternatively, below the section on "principle" (*tattva*), principle serves as the gate. Subsequently, based on "teaching," it clarifies the mutual interpenetration of their arising.

Regarding the teaching on contemplation (*guan*), that which stands at the beginning is what is currently employed, because the teaching can lead to the wisdom of practice and the principle of reality. Therefore, this present teaching is now being glorified and made manifest.
Following the three gates below, the gate of the teaching is specifically selected. This section further divides into two parts: first, clarifying what is to be excluded and what is to be adopted;

second, under the heading of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), the gate of the teaching is formally adopted. Within this, there are again two parts: first, a general enumeration of all teachings; second, the specific application of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Regarding the initial statement about first refuting the "viewers" (*dṛṣṭi-carita*): these were originally disciples of the Buddha. Some had severed [afflictions] through wisdom and practice or were weary of them;

some were *svāgata* (welcomed) or *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning); others severed [them] simultaneously through thirty-four moments of mind. This is largely the same as the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), except that for the Buddha there is no simultaneous severance.

In the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), stages are established sequentially; the inversion of the remaining [stages] can be seen [there]. As for the statement that they do not pervade horizontally: they cannot universally encompass all dharmas at every stage.
Next, "Now, not descending" means to employ the Perfect [Teaching] separately; this further consists of two parts. First, by restating the preceding mind and objects to reveal the Perfect Gate:
"one object, all objects" refers to the aforementioned wondrous objects; "one mind, all minds" refers to the aforementioned settling of the mind.

Since the arousal of the mind still relies on this for its refutation, it is called "refuting the pervasive. Next, under "the remaining gates," the Perfect Gate is properly employed. Within this, there are again four sections, the first of which is...

First, distinguishing between the pervasive and the non-pervasive; second, "Next, so-called 'below'" refers to the formal listing of the four gates of the Perfect Teaching; third, "Third, now, for the time being, below" clarifies the process of selection and rejection;

although in principle they are mutually identical, because one follows the teachings and the majority, the gate of Non-arising is provisionally retained within the Perfect Teaching; fourth, "Fourth, below the section on Non-arising... [and so forth].

This section clarifies the functional capacity of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It consists of two parts: first, a clarification of the characteristics of horizontal and vertical inclusion; second, a detailed demonstration of these characteristics and an explanation of their functional capacity.
The first part further divides into two: first, a brief clarification of the horizontal and vertical; second, the conclusion. The first of these again divides into two:

first, the vertical; second, the horizontal. The first of these (the vertical) further divides into two: first, the presentation of the two meanings of luminous manifestation; second, from "What are they? onwards, the explanation of the aforementioned two meanings. Within this [section]:

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, clarifying the cause of arrival; second, clarifying the fruit of arrival. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying that the teaching-gate is able to lead one through;
second, clarifying that it is able to illuminate and manifest. The first of these also has two sections: first, directly clarifying that the teaching-gate leads one through to the cause;
second, citing the two stages of dwelling as proof. In all cases, leading through to the cause begins with non-arising.

Next, following the section on "Cessation and Contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it clarifies that cessation and contemplation are capable of manifesting [the truth]. This further has two parts: first, the teaching; second, the analogy. Regarding the initial passage:

although this teaching exists, it must necessarily be manifested through practice until one reaches the stage of the first dwelling of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Next, as for the presentation of the analogy: "person" refers to the practitioner.
"Position" refers to entering and abiding. If the gate exists in vain, what would the gate serve? If the person exists in vain, what would the person receive?
Only when the person and the teaching correspond is it called "coexistence. It is like a person who must enter the gateway of characteristics before they can receive the manifest [teaching].

Next, the explanation of the "fruition of penetration" (*abhisamaya-phala*) is also twofold: first, explaining that the gates of the teaching can penetrate; second, explaining that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* can manifest it.

In the first section, the object of penetration is first presented: namely, the non-arising of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the two dharmas of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are only fulfilled upon reaching the fruition.

Regarding the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: although in principle there is no coming or going, it is nonetheless named after the Buddha. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* should be understood accordingly. Below, under the section on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*...

It can manifest. Furthermore, there are two parts; the first correctly clarifies the capacity to manifest. Because the fruition is fulfilled, all things are simultaneously fulfilled. "Elevated" (*weiwei*) and so forth refers to the appearance of rising high.
"Majestic" (*tangtang*) refers to the countenance. The *Baihutong* states it means "luminous. This refers to the fruition-wisdom being as lofty and bright as the moon emerging from the stars.
Now, this refers to the fulfillment of fruition being able to benefit others. "Illuminating the Ten Treasure Mountains" refers to the place where the fruition-moon resides.

Emptiness illuminates the mountains of the ten stages, its reflection reaching the four seas; this is the arising of the response (*yìng*). The fruit likewise descends to accord with [sentient beings].
Those who draw the water of the four capacities—wherein the water is like the capacity and the reflection is like the response—the four teachings and four gates are all termed "response."

Next, the scriptural evidence is cited. Regarding the statement "paying homage to a bone stūpa": within the midst of the assembly, a stūpa suddenly appeared, and the Buddha himself arose to pay it homage.
Because there were the śarīra relics of the Buddha’s former bodies within this stūpa, he arose to pay homage due to the principle that causes elicit their corresponding fruits.
Is this not, indeed, a manifestation of glory? Therefore, it is cited as proof.

Next, the horizontal inclusion (*pārśvagrahaṇa*) is explained. This also has two parts: first, from "Furthermore, there is no arising" (*punar-anutpāda*) onwards, which concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one;

second, from "The Great Chapter" (*mahāparivarta*) onwards, which is the formal explanation of the horizontal gate. Question: For what reason are forty-two characters cited for both the horizontal and vertical [approaches]? Answer: Previously, one entered vertically through a single gate.
This is the gateway of the letter A (*akṣaramukha*). Now, because each of the forty-two letters is mutually related [to one another], it is called "horizontal" (*tiryak*).

Both horizontal and vertical [dimensions] are entirely contained within the gateway of the letter A, and thus extend even to all forty-two letters; therefore, there is no contradiction in citing them together.
Following the section on "horizontal and vertical," this concludes the summary.

Below this section, the characteristics of the gates are explained in detail, and the functional significance of the horizontal and vertical meanings is elucidated. This text is divided into three parts, which further consist of two sections.

First, the purpose of the preceding discussion is indicated and listed; thus it is said that [the meaning] is difficult to perceive. However, as explained previously, the underlying intent remains unmanifest.

Therefore, the text next cites the *Buddhapiṭaka* and other sources to explain the three intents. These three intents are further divided into three. First is the *Buddhapiṭaka*, which is divided into two parts. The first concerns the phenomena (*vastu*).

Next is the principle (*li*). Principle is precisely the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the initial "phenomenon" (*shi*), there are two parts: first, directly citing the sutras to clarify external application;

second, synthesizing it with the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). As for external application, the sutra states: "Within that which is without name or mark, one provisionally speaks by means of names and marks;
all of these are the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata. It is like a person chewing Mount Sumeru, flying through space, or even [enduring] until the end of the kalpa when all is consumed by fire."
At that time, with one sleep the kalpa-fire is extinguished, and with one breath the world is formed. There are eight matters in total;
among these eight, the meanings of "breathing" (blowing) and "sleeping" accord with non-arising, such that the internal and external correspond. Therefore, these are cited.

Below that sutra, next is the section on the Gate of Non-arising (*anutpāda-dvāra*), which correctly establishes the correspondence [of phenomena]. If there are those who claim for themselves to have attained non-arising, they must rely upon external application (*bāhya-prayoga*).
Next, "must descend" refers to the reason for external application according to principle: a single moment of arising is termed one sentient being; this is precisely what arises.
The cessation [of this state] is termed a single kalpa. Within every thought-moment, the three poisons constantly arise; this refers to the intent of the three calamities at the end of a kalpa.
Of the three poisons, greed is foremost; of the three calamities, fire is primary. One should contemplate this through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
If wisdom and severance are perfected, there will necessarily be external efficacy.
Next, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is cited to explain the meaning. Since all sūtras contain the statement that nothing surpasses nirvāṇa, it is now cited here to establish this principle.

This principle does not go beyond [the categories of] one's own and others' wisdom and abandonment, the agent and the object, phenomena and principle, the conceivable and the inconceivable, and so forth.
All are non-arising. This text is found in the nineteenth fascicle of the sutra. It is divided into two parts: first, citing the sutra to provide an explanation;

second, a detailed analysis. The first part is further divided into two: first, explaining the four propositions; second, explaining the six propositions. The first of these is further divided into three: first, briefly citing the scriptural text; second, briefly clarifying the inclusion of all phenomena.
The sutra lists the four propositions beginning with "not hearing what is heard," followed by the listing of "arising" and so forth to serve as an explanation.
The terms "hearing" and so forth are listed first, followed by "arising" and so forth to explain them. Here, we speak from the middle [of the sequence] to encompass what precedes and follows it.
Furthermore, this accords with the name "Non-arising" used within our own school. Although there have been many ancient interpretations, we shall set them aside for now without further discussion.

When the Sūtra wishes to expound this, light shines throughout the ten directions to summon the Bodhisattvas; only then does it preach to the assembly. This is no easy matter. Other texts likewise employ terms such as "arising."

If one applies this to the four teachings, the principle is established. Now, selecting the teaching of non-arising (*anutpāda*), it simultaneously elucidates the meaning of the sutra; therefore, I shall list them according to the sutra. First, I provide the standard fourfold classification;

next, following this, I briefly illustrate their mutual inclusion. This consists solely of the causes and effects of one’s own practice (*svayam-pratipatti*) and the means and objects of transforming others (*parānugraha*), as fully explained below.
If it were not so, how could it be called "universal"? Thus, the meaning of the "Gate of Universal Destruction" (*paryādāna-mukha*) is also included.
One section. This one section concerns only the causes and effects of self and others.
Next, following "the non-arising of arising," the third part extensively explains the meaning of the sūtra to clarify the inclusion of all phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*).

Within this, the four phrases constitute four distinct sections. The first phrase is divided into two parts: first, citing the sūtra for explanation; second, presenting the present interpretation. Following each of these phrases, generally...

Regarding the "Explanations of the Sūtra" (*Sūtravibhāṣā*), these were all explained by the Buddha himself. Whenever it says "Now I explain," this refers to the Great Master’s explanation of the Buddha’s own interpretation;

in all such cases, he concludes by citing the *Buddhapiṭaka* and the "blowing on saliva" (*kheṭa*) analogy. Only the first sentence lacks a concluding phrase, but according to the established pattern, one would expect it to be present there as well. In the opening passage, the text first cites the words of the sūtra.
"Abiding in the lower. This concludes the explanation of the sutra.

Next, in this current explanation, we praise the clarity of that which is abided in; therefore, we first explain conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and subsequently clarify the "one who abides" and so forth to explain "abiding.
Since in principle there are no two distinct dharmas, it is provisionally called "common. The same applies to the producer and the produced, as well as the one who abides and that which is abided in.

This is so. Through the stabilization provided by *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the wondrous realm is finally perfected. When this contemplation first arises, it is called the stage of "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā-bhūmi*).

This contemplation relies upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and is termed the "sacred gestation" (*āryagarbha*). Because the sacred one takes up residence within the womb, it is called "reposing in the sacred womb.

Furthermore, because one is born from within the lineage of the sacred, it is called "reposing in the sacred womb. Upon reaching the stage of the first abiding (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is called "emerging from the sacred womb," for one is born from the sacred. This accords with...
Because it is partially based on principle, it is called "not seeing. This "not seeing" constitutes the non-arising of wisdom; this explains the term "non-arising.

The passage beginning with "attaining the Buddha... explains the term "arising. To cite the treatise: all dharmas are the worldly truth of ignorance, while Prajñā is the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The commentary on the following section explains the second phrase, which also has two parts. First, the scripture is cited, wherein the phrase is first restated; next, from "does not give rise to" (*na utpadyate*) onwards, the scripture provides the explanation.

From "named Great Nirvāṇa" (*mahāparinirvāṇa*) onwards, there is a general heading. From "the characteristic of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*) onwards, the two types of non-arising are explained: because the characteristic of arising is exhausted, wisdom and abandonment are perfected;
because it is attained through the path of cultivation, the cause accords with the fruit.

Now, the middle two [sections] are explained. First, the causal relationship is established; next, it is concluded with the Buddha-treasury (*buddhagarbha*). The initial passage concerns the perfection of the two virtues, which explains the exhaustion of the marks of arising;
this refers to wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) as the fruit of quiescent extinction (*jimiemo*). Following the section on cause and effect, the conclusion is made with the Buddha-treasury.

Next, the third phrase also has two parts. First, the third phrase is listed: "In the conventional truth," followed by the scriptural explanation. Next, the present explanation is clarified in two layers.
The first of these also has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the conclusion with the *Buddhagotra*. The first of these also has two parts:
first, the direct interpretation of this phrase; second, using this phrase to interpret the first phrase. Regarding the first text: because of ignorance and...
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) gives rise to all phenomena; therefore, ignorance is called the root.
When the root is destroyed, phenomena do not arise; this is termed "death."

This explanation follows below; next, this phrase is used to explain the first phrase, further clarifying the intended meaning of what is employed here. This uses the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) to explain the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*);
since it is the abandonment belonging to wisdom, it is employed for this explanation. If the virtue of wisdom in the first phrase is thus established, [the explanation is complete].

This refers to the character "not-arising" (a-utpāda) in the lower part of the first phrase. If the perfection of the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*) is established within this phrase, it refers to the "not-arising" in the lower part of this very phrase.
Regarding the term "identical" (*sama*), it serves to distinguish the "not-arising" in the upper part of the first phrase from the "not-arising" in the lower part of this phrase;
though the names are identical in both places, the phenomena (*vastu*) and principles (*tattva*) differ. In the first phrase, the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) is the object of focus.

"Principle" (*li*) is named "non-arising. This phrase refutes phenomena; when phenomena are exhausted, non-arising is attained. When principle is viewed in relation to delusion, delusion is inferior; therefore, it is called "refuting the inferior.
When principle is viewed in relation to delusion, principle is superior; therefore, it is called "taking the superior as its object."

Next, beneath the first phrase, two instances of the term "arising" (*jāta*) are distinguished. The "arising" beneath the first phrase belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*); the "arising" above this phrase belongs to affliction (*kleśa*).

Although the names of these two "arisings" are identical, their bondage and liberation are not equal. The wisdom of the first phrase is liberation; the affliction of this phrase is bondage. Therefore, they must be distinguished.
Since the third [phrase] has already been used to explain the first, the first may likewise be used to explain the third. This is because...
This is because these two virtues are simultaneous. Nevertheless, one must first exercise wisdom; how could delusion be severed first?
Following the first phrase, the *Buddhapiṭaka* provides a conclusion. Since this has already explained the first [point], it likewise uses the identity of the first phrase as its conclusion.
Next, the sutra re-explains the third phrase, which also has two parts: first, the citation of the sutra; this is the initial restatement of the phrase. Second, the present commentary.

Since the sutra provides two interpretations, the Great Master adjudicates them. This section has two parts: first, the formal explanation. Previously it was said that "severing" refers to the extinction of one's own afflictions (*kleśa*);

now it is said that the "four abidings" (*catuḥ-vihāra*) refer to severing the four abiding afflictions and being able to arise with mastery. This is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), which severs the four [categories of affliction].
If one is already able to exercise mastery even while abiding in the [preparatory] stage, how much more so when reaching the true stage of the first *bhūmi* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*)?

Therefore, the inferior is used to manifest the superiority of the Perfect. Alternatively, "extinguishing the lower" is also concluded with the "Buddha-treasury. These are two interpretations; alternatively, "extinguishing the fetters" marks the beginning, while "the arising of transformation" concludes it.

Next, the fourth phrase is explained. This also has two parts: first, the citation and conclusion; second, the current explanation. The current explanation further has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the supplementary discussion.

In this text, following the previous section, the four stages of Bodhisattvas are again distinguished. In the initial passage, only the formal explanation is provided while the concluding summary is omitted. As for the meaning of the following section:

The preceding passage is restated here as the "capable transformer" (*nirmāpaka*). That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is birth; because its continuity is uninterrupted, it is called "birth-of-birth," which is precisely the object to be transformed.
Therefore, the subsequent section restates the intent of the capable transformer. The phrase "this constitutes" serves to conclude the demonstration of its functional capacity.
The first three phrases refer to the wisdom and abandonment that constitute the cause and fruit of the ability to transform others; this present phrase refers to the objects to be transformed.

Next, regarding the re-explanation of the four abodes (*catvāraḥ vihārāḥ*): the Great Master again uses the six abodes from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* (Dichizhi) to explain the understanding of the Buddha’s four abodes.
This explanation consists of two parts: first, citing the treatise to provide an explanation; second, explaining the intended meaning of the sutra. As for the first part:

the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* corresponds to the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). Since it is already used to manifest the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyavyavahāra*), how could it not also contain the Distinct? Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* is employed to interpret the sutra.

To clarify the meaning: regarding the six abodes (*ṣaḍ-vihāra*) discussed in the treatise, those prior to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are not included in the count of six; these refer specifically to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Because all six are non-retrogressive, they receive the name "abode.
They are called "non-retrogressive" because one has already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).

As for the phrase "one person," this refers to the first individual among the six, through to those on the path of practice and the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), all of whom are situated herein; therefore, it is said that they "progress numerically. The third is the Abode of Pure Mind (*viśuddha-citta-vihāra*).
The first stage (*bhūmi*) destroys the view of identity; hence it is said that one is "free from self. This refers to the distinct path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

The stage of abiding in the traces of practicing the path refers to the distinct stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The stages of "certainty" and "finality" likewise refer to the distinct stage of cultivation.

The phrase "the Sūtra says" introduces the Master’s subsequent explanation of the Sūtra’s intent. Reaching the point where one dwells on the traces of the Path is called "truly emerging from the conventional.
Next, he explains the six phrases in two parts: first, the direct refutation of the "ineffable"; second, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to show that it is indeed "effable.

The first four phrases directly clarify that cause and effect are non-arising, yet they have not yet refuted [the notion of] non-arising; therefore, the Sūtra clarifies this again. Thus, beneath each and every phrase...

It is unspeakable. First, there are four [sections]. First, the direct refutation of the six phrases as being unspeakable; second, the conclusion that establishes the universal refutation; third, the conclusion by means of the *Buddhaguhya*;

fourth, the citation of the *Laṅkāvatāra* to explain and establish [the point]. The first [of these four] has two parts: first, listing the six phrases to demonstrate their universality; second, the explanation. Regarding the first text:
while the preceding four phrases pertain only to the Perfect [Teaching], these current six phrases refute both the partial and the perfect simultaneously. This is as follows:

The primary intent of the current text’s refutation of pervasiveness (*pòbiàn*) is that all six propositions concern one’s own practice (*zìxíng*). Following this, "demonstrating pervasiveness" refers to the meaning of these propositions.

The section beginning with "If one refutes... provides the explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, the Great Master’s (*Dàshī*) interpretation of the sutra; second, the Great Master’s interpretation of the Buddha.
The commentary consists of two parts. The first part also has two sections: first, the actual explanation; second, the conclusion of the pervasiveness. The first section also has two parts:

first, the judgment regarding the conceivable and the inconceivable (which should be termed "delusion and awakening"); second, the actual explanation. The actual explanation also has two parts: first, the conceivable; second, the inconceivable.
The first [section] also has two parts: first, delusion; second, liberation. The first [of these two] has two sentences, which also have two parts:
first, an individual explanation to manifest what is conceivable; second, a general explanation to manifest the ineffable. Regarding the first passage:

because the sequential and non-sequential are mutually dependent as subject and object, both liberation and delusion are termed "conceivable and inconceivable. Question: Why is the inconceivable also refuted? Answer:
Principle is neither partial nor complete; one must break through attachment to completeness. Therefore, it is further said that "one does not destroy what the sages have attained," and so forth.
Regarding "beyond the realm" (*dhātu*) and so on: the essence of principle is non-arising, yet delusion is arising; hence, it is called "arising from non-arising.

Delusions within the realm are called "branching and terminal" because they have already arisen beyond the realm and arise again upon that arising; hence, it is called "arising from arising. There are thus distinctions such as the internal being coarse and so forth.
It is called "conceivable. Next, below this delusion, it reveals that which is "inexpressible.

The statement "all are equal" means that since all births are objects of transformation, all causal capacities are inexpressible. That which is "inexpressible" precisely reveals the meaning of refutation.

Next, the refutation of the conceivable understanding is also twofold: first, the individual explanation of the two phrases to establish that it is conceivable; second, the explanation of the ineffable.
Regarding the first section on the understanding beyond the realm (*dhātu*), the term "simultaneous elimination" (*ubhaya-prahāṇa*) is so named because it incorporates the preceding [category].

As for "eliminating the limited分段 [birth]," this is a case of speaking of the fruit within the context of the cause. Question: If the delusions beyond the realm are those capable of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), what is their distinction from the understanding within the realm?

Answer: The objects of aspiration differ, yet the person remains the same. This explanation below demonstrates the attainment of the marks; because there are sixteen distinct gates, they are called "various.
From the shallow to the deep, all belong to self-cultivation (*svayam-pratipatti*). From the perspective of transforming others (*parārtha*), there are many causes and effects.
The principle is even more inferior. It is explained that it is inexpressible. The four kinds of the Truth of the Path are the practices by which one approaches;

the dharma-nature of the Truth of Cessation is the principle toward which one approaches. Since the nature of principle itself does not exist, how could there be various distinctions? Therefore, it is inexpressible.

Next, the "inconceivable" (acintya) is refuted. This also first addresses delusion and subsequently clarifies the perfect principle through understanding. Alternatively, it is called "inconceivable" because it does not distinguish between the internal and external.
Regarding the initial section on delusion, there are two parts: first, the explanation; second, the clarification of its ineffability (*anabhilāpya*).
As for the first passage, it first establishes the inconceivable nature, hence the words "it is merely," etc. From "ignorance" (*avidyā*) onwards, it concludes with its ineffability.
Next, regarding the refutation: it also first demonstrates the inconceivable aspect; thus it says, "it is merely. Herein, the perfect cause and perfect fruit are established.
Since the principle does not descend [to the level of words], it is clarified that it cannot be spoken of. Since the principle is entirely beyond speech, both modes of explanation are untenable.
Next, taking up that intent, the conclusion is reached as pervading [all cases], as the text states.

The Buddha himself descended. The Great Master [Vasubandhu] explained the six phrases elucidated by the Buddha; the text itself is divided into six parts. The first phrase also has two sections: first, he cites the Buddha’s explanation;
second, he clarifies his own interpretation. This interpretation further has two parts: first, he explains "non-arising arising," hence saying, "relying on this intent of the Buddha";
second, "arising" follows below, clarifying that it is ineffable.

"How is it that [the second phrase] is inferior? This explains the second sentence in two parts. First, the scriptural passage is cited and explained; next, "Now, the explanation of the two" follows. First, "birth of birth" (*jāti-jāti*) is explained. Regarding "birth of birth," the following clarifies that it is inexpressible.

The initial statement regarding the "eight characteristics" (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*) is as previously explained. Question: In the treatise (*śāstra*), among the eight characteristics, the "birth of birth" gives rise to the "great birth" (*mahājāti*).

Why is it here that the "great birth" gives rise to the "small birth" (*parīttajāti*)? Answer: The "birth of birth" gives rise to the great principle (*mahat-tattva*). As for the numerical category (*saṃkhyā*) of the small, it is as follows: [text continues].

This is indeed so. This is because the Great Arising (mahābhūta-utpāda) gives rise to the small, and the Great Arising initiates [the process].
