Next is the refutation of continuity (*saṃtati*), which can be understood by analogy with what preceded. Now, I shall briefly divide this into three parts: first, the intent of the introduction; second, the actual refutation; and third, the conclusion.

If it does not cease, we shall refute three points regarding the analysis of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*). First, we distinguish it from the two preceding provisional [positions]. Second, we refute the ancient [view].

Third, we provide the formal inference. The first [section] has two parts. First, the brief reason for the distinction: because it is reckoned as existing. Second, "by the establishment of the cause" and below, which explains the characteristics of the distinction;

namely, that while continuity is distinct from cessation, this [existence] is distinct from sentient beings because mental factors (*caitta*) cease, and it is further distinct from that empty space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, it is distinct...
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); furthermore, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not a mental factor (*cetasika*).

The designation "continuity" (*saṃtati*) is obtained solely in relation to specific mental states (*sattva*), whereas the name "cessation" (*nirodha*) is common to both. Because it is common to those three [types of phenomena], it is called "relative" (*apekṣika*).
Although they are not equal, because the name "cessation" signifies non-arising and non-arising is the same for all, it can be extended [to apply] universally.

Once the superior [position] has been refuted, the next section refutes the ancients, which also consists of three parts. First, it restates the old interpretation of Kaishan, borrowing their term "simultaneous cause" (*yin jian*) to explain "mutual dependence.
Because the former [cause] is simultaneous with this one, it is called "simultaneous cause. Previously there were only two layers; now we arrive at the third.

Therefore, it is said that this surpasses [the previous]. Next, "furthermore, because it also encompasses the subsequent" refers to the correct interpretation of our own school (Jinjia). This is because within the "mutually dependent" (xiangdai) [truth], both of the aforementioned two [aspects] are present.

Regarding the second, "after the provisional" (*jia*): although the [delusions] have not yet been destroyed, there is an understanding of the non-arising of conditions. This understanding corresponds to the mental faculty (*manas*). This is the aspect of "causality" (*yin*) within the mutually dependent truth.
When one proceeds from the two aforementioned provisional aspects to the mutually dependent truth, this constitutes the aspect of "continuity" (*xiangxu*) within the mutually dependent truth.

Because it leads from the preceding [section] to this point, it is called "cause" (*hetu*). Because it encompasses the two preceding [sections], it is called "inclusive" (*yān*). The explanation of "cause" is the same as the old [commentary];
the inclusion of the faults is slightly different, which can be understood by comparison with the old version. Having finished the threefold explanation, he concludes with a critique.
Now, examining the section below: within the third part, the "Correct Refutation of Mutual Dependence," there are two sections. First is the actual refutation;

second, from "In this way" onwards, is the conclusion establishing the two emptinesses and the eighteen emptinesses. Therefore, one should know that the preceding mention of "the absence of the eye of wisdom" and so forth is merely an abbreviation of the text.
Furthermore, the fact that "all-knowledge" and so forth are not mentioned is likewise an abbreviation.
Next, from "not only [the inferior]" downwards, the various views are refuted by analogy.
From "this is called" downwards, the conclusion is established. The passages on "illuminating and manifesting" are all as they appear in the text.
From "if one does not awaken" downwards, the second major section consists of fourteen pairs concerning faith and the other factors; this is further termed the "distinctive" section.

Setting aside the preceding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, this applies analogously to the subsequent stages such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth. If the [false] views are suppressed, they remain only within the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so on;
therefore, they are called "outflowing" (*sāsrava*).
Once they have been suppressed below that point, in the third stage, the views undergo transformation. Although some may be suppressed, they still transition into the "peak" (*mūrdhan*) stage.

Next, regarding the refutation of the lower [view]. The refutation of the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*) also has two parts. First, establishing the two practices and three faculties, which concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.

Second, the actual refutation. This first part also has two sections: first, clarifying the two practices; second, "if above or below," clarifying the three faculties, which is the basis for the refutation.
Based on the calculation of non-arising, they establish the inferior faculty (*mṛdv-indriya*). Below this, each instance of faculty and practice is refuted. Regarding "or non-existence":

it refers to those who, having heard briefly, give rise to views such as [the notion that] arising is real; thus, because they regard the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as substantial, it must be refuted.
Next, there is the correct refutation, which is also twofold: first, the general; second, the specific. "General" refers to the direct cultivation of the contemplative method;

"specific" refers to the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). This general section is the same as the initial text. In the preceding text, it was called "general" in contrast to the four views; here, it is called "general" in contrast to the single view.
Next is the general refutation below. This explanation is further divided into three parts. First is the general refutation of the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*).

To begin with, a scriptural passage is cited to clarify the nature of this refutation. The initial citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) is used because consciousness (*vijñāna*) discerns that which has arisen as "existence" and that which has not arisen as "non-existence.
Since both existence and non-existence are refuted, they are used as mutual analogies. The repeated statement that "neither can be apprehended" uses the profound to illustrate the shallow.
Using the shallow to illustrate the profound, one can see this upon reflection. Next, he cites the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to corroborate the preceding general refutation.
The sūtra states: "If one gives rise to the view of emptiness, one is called a nihilist; one falls into [the extremes of] self-nature and commonality. That sūtra’s refutation of views is extensive.
Third, from "However, no [such thing] arises" onwards, he rebuts errors.

Next is the specific refutation, which also has three parts: first, the direct refutation; second, the sixty-four rounds [of debate]; third, the transformation of views and calculations. The first part [the direct refutation] also has two sections: first, the sequential narration of the intent for the discourse;

second, the actual refutation. The first of these [the narration] also has three sections: first, a brief demonstration of the view of emptiness; second, a comparative determination of the two types of emptiness—the false and the correct;

third, a demonstration of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) within the view of emptiness. The first of these [the demonstration] also has three sections: first, restating the aforementioned views and refuting them.

The characteristic of the provisional serves as the basis for non-seeing; because it is suppressed by the real, the present "non-existent object" is established. Through the three refutations—of the whole, the parts, and both—the functions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are realized.

Not seeing the three types of provisional constructs, one perceives that nature and characteristics are empty. One enters emptiness in a state of total dissolution, seeing neither internal nor external.
The first, "seeming to refute the cause," establishes that there is no priority or posteriority; the second, "seeming to refute continuity," shows there is no mutual dependence of characteristics;

the third, "seeming to refute dependence," clarifies that below the phrase "next, silently," there is no essence or characteristic of seeing; and the fourth, "thirdly, arising," rebukes the error of perceiving characteristics.
Next, the commentary below explains and adjudicates between the two types of emptiness—erroneous and correct. This section has two parts: first, it clarifies the erroneous emptiness of non-Buddhists;

second, it clarifies the correct emptiness of the Buddha’s disciples. The first part also has two sections: first, it clarifies how erroneous emptiness gives rise to afflictions (*kleśa*); second, from "In this way" onwards, it concludes by returning to the nature of erroneous emptiness.
Next, it clarifies correct emptiness: one knows that craving itself is the source of faults because of a mind of attachment; if such a mind of attachment arises...
Knowing one's errors, one must depart from them; departing from them, one must cultivate contemplation—how could one calculate "non-arising"?

Third, "How so? and below, this demonstrates the three types of false views regarding emptiness, which are further divided into two parts: first, it reiterates the reasons for turning away from calculations to become the view of non-existence;
second, from "Non-arising" downward, it demonstrates the characteristics of the three types of provisional designations (*tri-saṃvṛti*).

Next, the subsequent section should be examined. This section correctly elucidates the application of contemplation, which is divided into three parts. First is the correct contemplation itself; within this, it first refutes establishment by causes.
Next, from "one should know" onwards, it concludes by establishing the two types of emptiness and so forth. Finally, from "not only" onwards, the third part provides an analogy to refute all views.
Next, if [the realization] has not yet descended, there are sixty-four stages. Third, through diligent cultivation, it descends; one sees that the conceptual calculations of transition turn away.
Regarding the third [section], "both existence and non-existence," there are two parts: first, the sequential narration; second, the formal explanation of the cultivation of contemplation.

The first [of these] also has three parts: first, explaining the signs of vision; second, citing people as examples; third, briefly indicating the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*). The first [of these] also has three parts; the first reiterates what preceded as...

First, the origin of the arising of views; second, from "or advancing downward," the correct demonstration of the characteristics of views; third, from "arousing this mind," the demonstration of the faults of views;

next, from "like the long-nailed [monk]," citing others as examples. Within this, there are three parts: first, the direct citation of the Long-nailed [monk], who claims that everything can be refuted.
This [view] is also non-existent. To reckon that this view exists is itself an existence. As for the statement "one attains awakening," it is because of the Buddha’s instruction.

Next, following the development of the view, he cites the case of Dīrghanakha as a parallel. Third, from "How so? onwards, he extensively demonstrates the characteristics of the view; herein there are two parts, the first concerning suffering.
Next, the Collection. First, regarding the "five non-appropriations," the Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva practices Prajñā, they do not appropriate practicing;
they do not appropriate non-practicing; they do not appropriate both practicing and non-practicing; they do not appropriate neither practicing nor non-practicing;
and they do not appropriate even non-appropriation. Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "For what reason is there no appropriation? He replied: "The nature of Prajñā..."
Because [the first two] are not accepted, why do you accept the third proposition? Next, from "Furthermore, I" below, the collection [of the aggregates] is shown.
Thirdly, from "Moreover, this" below, the characteristics of the three types of conceptual construction (prajñapti) are briefly indicated.

Next, the following section refutes [the opponent's view] and correctly elucidates the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This also has three parts: first, the correct elucidation of the cultivation of contemplation;

second, the elucidation of the sixty-four permutations; third, the observation of the transformation of conceptual reckonings. The first part also has three sections: first, the correct elucidation of the application of contemplation; second, from "In this way" onwards, the conclusion establishing the two kinds of emptiness;
third, from "This is precisely" onwards, the conclusion regarding eye-wisdom (*cakṣur-jñāna*). The second and third parts are as stated in the text.

Next is the refutation of the view that things are neither existent nor non-existent. This also has two parts: first, clarifying the sequence; second, correctly clarifying the application of contemplation. The first part also has two sections:

first, a brief clarification of the characteristics of the view; second, demonstrating the three types of provisional construction (*prajñapti*). The first section also has three parts: first, clarifying the causes for the arising of the view; second, clarifying the characteristics of the view; third, clarifying the faults.

Regarding the first cause, there are two further divisions: first, the actual clarification of the cause; second, the explanation [of the following passage] beginning with "Because... (or "Therefore...").
If it is not fixed as inferior, next the characteristics of [wrong] views are explained. This also has two parts: first, the actual characteristics of the views;

second, from "What is... onwards, the explanation. From "Three firm attachments... onwards, the faults are clarified. This also has two parts: first, the direct refutation; second, from "The mind of self...

onwards, the ten mental formations and the delusions produced by them are clarified. Regarding the phrase "寧起" (寧起, *nìng qǐ*), the Sūtra says: "It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to harbor [hatred toward] the Dharma."

To harbor views and increase pride is but a minor fault; one should rather say: "I would sooner give rise to the view of self pervading the entire dharma-realm than wrongly grasp at emptiness even to the extent of a mustard seed.
Regarding "poisonous weeds" and so forth: poisonous weeds represent suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), while the path of medicine represents cessation (*nirodha*).
Next, each item is presented one by one to demonstrate the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Within each of these instances, all three provisional designations are present.

"If one refutes the lower" correctly clarifies the application of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which is further divided into three parts: first, the direct clarification of the application of contemplation; second, the clarification of the sixty-four permutations.

The third [section] is the extensive exposition on the transformation of conceptualization. This, in turn, has three parts: first, the direct clarification of the refutation of the provisional; second, the analogical refutation of various doubts;

and third, the conclusion establishing the two kinds of emptiness. The first part further has two sections: first, the direct explanation of the application of contemplation; and second, the pointing out of the Four Noble Truths. Within this [second section], there are again three parts.
First, from "Furthermore, below" onwards, the Four Truths are correctly demonstrated; the preceding text concluded without explicitly stating suffering and so forth.
Next, from "Now, moreover," onwards, the function of the Four Truths is clarified. Third, from "The Tathāgata," onwards, the Lesser Vehicle is used as an analogy for the Greater Vehicle.

Since the merit of destroying [wrong] views truly resides in the Tripiṭaka, the initial turning of the Wheel of Dharma was precisely for the purpose of destroying such views; thus, in all the Āgamas of the various schools, the Buddha and his disciples...
Whatever is taught is all said to be the Four Noble Truths. If even the teaching on arising and ceasing is thus, how much more so the latter three teachings?

Next, if it is not inferior, one refutes various views by analogy. Third, one establishes the two kinds of emptiness. If it is not inferior, the sixty-four rounds of views and calculations shift accordingly, as detailed in the text.
Next, "therefore" concludes with an exhortation. Regarding the term "unmixed," it means that the characteristics of the views and their provisional manifestations are each distinct and not the same.

...Furthermore, there are three parts to the subsequent refutation of "wordlessness. First, it demonstrates the characteristics of the view. Second, from the phrase "Briefly... onwards, it again uses numerous instances of ineffability to provide a comprehensive critique.

Regarding the phrase "If one says... and so forth, it judges that [the opponent's position] does not transcend the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). This refers to the view that does not transcend the fourfold alternatives. First...
The second phrase is precisely the "neither-nor" phrase; its expression is complete and exhaustive. The first phrase refers to the initial four phrases.

Within these, there are four phrases, namely: existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and also the first phrase within the fourth phrase, which is "neither existence nor non-existence, yet existence.
Third, the *Lotus Sūtra* cites scriptural evidence below this point.

Next, regarding "further possession" (*punar-bhoga*) and "possession below" (*adhobhoga*), the cessation of speech follows the previous pattern; one should likewise extensively or briefly investigate and establish the characteristics of their formation and so forth.
The present text is extremely concise; it merely first clarifies "further possession."

Next, the explanation of the transcendence of words. This transcendence of words is further divided into two parts. First, from "Furthermore" (*fù*) onwards, the characteristics of views are first presented.

Second, from "In this way" (*rúcǐ*) onwards, they are refuted. This refutation is also twofold: first, the refutation itself; second, from "Why is this? (*héyǐgù*) onwards, the explanation. This explanation is also twofold: first, the horizontal (*héng*); second, the vertical (*shù*).

The preceding instances of comparing various forms of transcendence of words constitute the horizontal. Now, comparing cause and effect in terms of temporal sequence constitutes the vertical. Furthermore, the vertical is threefold. First—
This clearly explains the vertical [classification]. Next, from above to below, there is a re-evaluation of the horizontal and vertical [classifications].

For example, within the category of "that which has visibility," the three provisional [categories] and the four propositions constitute the horizontal; progressing through them until the fourth constitutes the vertical. Within that which has visibility, "causal formation" is horizontal, while "continuity" is vertical.

The two [categories] are mutually dependent. In each of the views, there is first a general refutation before distinguishing between the horizontal and vertical. Regarding the phrase "the general course" (*dàtú*) and so forth:

as previously stated, the horizontal and vertical do not transcend the horizontal. Why? Because all views are horizontal; since they are further refuted by means of the horizontal, they all collectively constitute the horizontal.

Next, we shall now proceed to clarify the "vertical refutation" (*shuppa*). It is called "vertical refutation" because it employs vertical principles to conduct the inquiry. Regarding "vertical principles":

they are termed "vertical" because they refer to the progressive depth of the doctrinal formulations, beginning from the five *śamatha-vipaśyanā* practices of the Tripitaka and culminating in the wondrous enlightenment of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
These states arise; therefore, they are called "arising. If you say there is arising, what kind of arising is it? Each of these is interrogated.

Now, since there is no [valid] position, let them form their own views as they please. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the four propositions regarding the vertical dimension (*ūrdhva-catuṣkoṭi*);

second, clarifying the transcendence of words regarding the vertical dimension. Regarding the first four propositions, there are two sections: first, refuting the proposition of arising. Within this, there are three parts: first, the interrogation, as in the text.
Below this, four teachings are enumerated, each consisting of four sections. The first is the Tripitaka; below "this is dry wisdom" (śuṣka-jñāna) is the stage of commonality (pāṭha-sthāna);

below "this is the three worthies" (tri-pudgala) is the stage of distinctiveness (viśeṣa-bhūmi); and below "this is the iron wheel" (ayaścakra) is the stage of perfection (pariniṣpanna). In the distinct teaching, the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) is not separately listed.
That Zhiyuan does not list five grades is merely an abbreviation. Regarding the term "repeated contemplation" (*chóng lù*): "contemplation" (*lù*) refers to mental reflection;
because one repeatedly observes the preceding Truth, it is called "reflection. The phrase "Third, using this... concludes [the section].
Next, if one calculates according to the lower [level], there are two parts to the vertical refutation of the "phrase of non-arising" (*anutpāda-pada*):

first, the actual refutation; second, distinguishing the differences by way of the master of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. The first part also has two sections: first, the interrogation; second, from "for this reason" (*ataḥ*) onwards, the enumeration of the charges.

This does not differentiate the characteristics of the teachings, but rather establishes the name "non-arising" as a general principle whose meaning applies across all teachings. Within this, there are three further sections: first, clarifying [the meaning] by means of the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

"Birth. The three—view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-moha*), thought-delusion (*saṃjñā-moha*), and so forth—are the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "For the sake of practicing the lower" refers to breaking [the hindrances] by means of phenomena and principle.

Because one breaks the three hindrances, one attains practice and principle; when practice and principle are fully perfected, it is called "non-arising. "Ordinary people below" refers to breaking [the hindrances] by means of the three Buddhas.

Within this, there are again three parts. First, the refutation of the old [interpretation]: if it were only the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*), then the activity of gathering and transforming beings would be unnecessary. However, this non-arising is itself non-arising.

One must not read this with a heavy or indistinct tone; it should be clearly set down in writing. That which does not produce [a subsequent term] above constitutes the end of an upper clause; that which does not produce [a preceding term] below constitutes the beginning of a lower clause.

Now, the explanation of the "lower" section follows, which is the correct interpretation. This text has four layers: first, the selection between the hidden and manifest aspects of phenomena and principle. As for the Dharmakāya being primordially existent...

The "hidden" [nature] is revealed because the "retribution" (vipāka) is broken or because it has utility. Thus, the three "alternatives" (vikalpa) are paired with the three bodies (trikāya). The exhaustion of ignorance and the perfection of knowledge are called "retribution.

The dust-like hindrances obstruct the Dharma-gates, while the hindrances of views and afflictions obstruct the path of transformation; only when these two alternatives are broken is the "response body" (nirmāṇakāya) perfected.
Next, below the section on ignorance, the three delusions are selected for their antidotes, as they correspond to the three bodies. Therefore, they are paired with the three.
Because the body corresponds to the three delusions, the manifestation of the body according to those secondary delusions should also be understood accordingly.

Third, regarding "karma, practice, stage, and wisdom" below, this is explained by way of the antidotes and that which is manifested. Karma, practice, stages, and wisdom serve as the antidotes; True Suchness (tathatā) and the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) are what is manifested.

Furthermore, through the destruction of the three afflictions—karma and so forth—the retribution is accomplished. Because it is accomplished, the principle is manifested. Fourth, there is the individual correspondence with the three.

The commentary explains that because both cultivation (*xiū*) and nature (*xìng*) are thus, they are applied in contrast to one another. Both are common to the Separate (*bié*) and Perfect (*yuán*) teachings, yet the intent lies in the Perfect.

Thus, the first three [explanations] appear to be Separate, while the second and fourth support the Perfect; by using the Separate to manifest the Perfect, the meaning of the inquiry is collectively established.

Regarding the text, the first three explanations concern the arising of the three Buddhas based on the non-arising of all phenomena, while the fourth single explanation concerns the arising of the three Buddhas based on the arising of all phenomena. This is the intended meaning.

In the general discussion, it was stated that while all phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-arising, the three Buddhas arise; thus, the conclusion states: "Arising is precisely non-arising, and non-arising is precisely arising.
If one were to consider only the *Dharmabuddha*, the underlying intentions would not be seen. Now, this text primarily addresses non-arising to explain the meaning of the three Buddhas.

Because it refutes other [views], it clarifies their mutual identity (*paraspara-saṃbheda*). Within this section, there are three parts: first, the conclusion regarding their mutual identity based on principle.
Next is the citation of evidence and the conclusion. Third, from "As for all those below," comes the reprimand; since there is nothing comparable or equal, is this not seeing?

From "There is someone below," next follows the divergent analysis by the Master of Treatises (Śāstrin). This also has two parts: first, the refutation of the old [interpretation]; second, using that error to manifest the correctness of the present [position].
In refuting the errors of others by presenting alternative interpretations, the first part also has two sections: first, citing the objection of another; second, the Master of Treatises.

[The Master] rescued [the teaching]. The masters of the *Śāstra* were erroneously refuted by him; although they offered many interpretations, they did not clarify the boundaries [of the doctrine], and thus he was able to refute and censure them using the perspective of ordinary beings and those of limited capacity.

He added characters to provide a comprehensive explanation so that [the meaning] could be reconciled within the assembly. If this were so, it would not be the arising and ceasing of transformation, nor would it have reached the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

For now, we provisionally grant it the side of "neither arising nor non-arising," and thus it is called "supporting the Middle" (*madhyama-upastambha*). Because it does not reach far enough, it is criticized.
It is said that this harms the meaning of the text;

thus, the present school refutes it in three parts. Furthermore, there are two sections: first, the brief refutation from "This interpretation... onwards; second, the detailed explanation from "For what reason... onwards. This explanation also has two parts.
First, the meaning of the error is explained; next, the flaw in the text is explained. The first section has three parts. First, the meaning of what was lost is clarified:

namely, the loss of the meaning that integrates the general with the specific. Since the "Perfect Doctrine" (*yuanzong*) in the treatise already contains diverse implications, how can you be reproached for failing to acknowledge the Middle Way?

Just as you have been refuted according to the actual text of the treatise, the "general and integrated" *piṭaka* (scriptural collection) is precisely what is contained in the opening passage. If [this] arises...
Below, for the sake of clarifying the distinct meanings contained within the treatise, if one proceeds to the section "Below," it presents the main body of the treatise.

Regarding the statement "to refute the twenty types of *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity)," the various sūtras and śāstras differ; this need not be recounted here. The five aggregates (*skandha*) each have four [aspects], forming twenty propositions.

One calculates whether form (*rūpa*) and the self are identical or different in size; the same applies to the other four aggregates. By refuting these, one attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Next, according to the text below, the conclusion is reached.
The demonstration includes both [aspects], which constitutes the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) Piṭaka.
Third, beneath the Dragon Tree, he demonstrated the correct text and its meaning. How did he, attributing the merit to the Master of the Treatise, propagate this treatise to refute errors?
Next, the opening of the "Lower" section refutes the textual error of the injury. In the ninth chapter of the *Lunyu*, Jieyu saw Confucius leading his disciples and sang to him:
"O Phoenix! O Phoenix! How has your virtue declined? This was intended to reproach Confucius for failing to find his proper time.
Thus, Deng Ai replied to the Wei ruler: "O Phoenix! O Phoenix! You are but a single phoenix; you needlessly add 'not' [to your title] and yet remain as such."
"Loss of meaning. [The author] sets down his pen. He severely criticizes the writing of the treatise. "The previous criticism concerned the loss of meaning in what was said.

"Hanging warts" below: he uses a metaphor to reprimand him. A wart is a remnant of flesh; it is an extra piece of flesh that grows out of place and attaches to the body as a赘 (superfluous growth). [He adds a dot.]
The meaning is like a redundant growth or a wart appearing upon what already exists.
Next, as for the present interpretation, it uses those [previous] errors to manifest the present correctness; this is done to support the inclusion and clarify the manifestation.

Does it preserve the original or not? Does it arise based on your addition or not? There are also many instances where it does not arise. Therefore, one must inquire: what kind of thing is this "seeing-mind"? Regarding this—

Within this, there are again two parts: first, the actual exposition; second, the conclusion and refutation. The first part consists of ten sections. First is the heading; second is the enumeration and explanation. The explanation is further divided into three parts.

The first two clarify that it is not merely by refuting "arising" that "non-arising" is also refuted; thus it says "not non-arising. This uses the correct refutation of the false to clarify the "not non-.
From the third to the ninth, all [sections] demonstrate that the two do not refute either of the two alternatives regarding arising. That is to say:
Therefore, the single character "life" (sheng) is contrasted with the preceding two instances of "non-life" (busheng). To open [the explanation], "two lives" means "two non-lives.
As for the concluding phrase which simply says "not non-life," this is merely an abbreviation; the same applies throughout what follows.

In the tenth stage, the wisdom of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue-zhi*) is eternally fulfilled and complete, and thus there are "two non-lives. All three explanations coexist within the stage of wondrous enlightenment. Furthermore, from the third...
The first nine [positions] have all been refuted. Next, the subsequent phrases are generated. In the initial text, Dīrghanakha constitutes the fourth phrase;
as for those who advocate the "inexpressible," all such refutations are like the speech of "neither-nor," which can all be turned back. That which resembles the inexpressible is correct;
thus, one thesis has four variations—namely, the latter three phrases and the inexpressible. Now, these are collectively refuted. It is like the non-arising of the one. Not...

They give rise to wrong views; therefore, they must be refuted. This is called "non-arising" (anutpāda), which is like the stage below the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Regarding "desire-delusion below," we shall first take one grade as an example; each possesses the three types of provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

First, within the "accomplishment through causes" (*hetusiddhi*), there is also the desire directed toward the mind. By the power of causal conditions, the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) that arises is called a "produced dharma. [There are] six desires.

Regarding this, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), in its commentary on the nine meditations on repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*), states that these can counteract seven types of defiled desire in practitioners:
first, some are attached to colors such as blue or yellow; second, they are attached merely to physical form; third, they are attached to deportment and movement;

fourth, they are attached to eloquence and quick-witted speech; fifth, they are attached to smoothness and softness; sixth, they are attached to human characteristics, namely male and female; seventh, they are attached to people in general.

The seventh [category] subsumes the six; it does not exist now. Nanda’s practice of desire is fully explained as previously analyzed. Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts, they cite the light to illustrate the heavy; they even prohibit mere conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
As for what are called the "characteristics of desire," they are as described in the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: receiving, desiring, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.

Among the celestial realms, those dwelling on earth engage in physical union; in the Yāma heaven, they embrace; and in the three higher heavens, they proceed respectively by holding hands, laughing, and gazing.
One is already detached from internal perceptions, let alone regarding looking or smiling.

If one takes the following [passage], it correctly clarifies the establishment of causes: the six movements of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) establish the continuity of the phenomena produced therefrom.

Within this, the phrase "engaging in activities" refers to the restraint of internal continuity in order to prevent such activities; it is a provisional, general understanding of the unreal, which is called the principle (*nyāya*).
If one still relies on provisional mental projections, how much more so when calculating the details of wedding ceremonies? This is called being inferior to the non-Buddhist outsiders of the West.
Next, regarding the correct analysis of the establishment through causes, first the phrases are listed: if one proceeds from below using contemplation, there are four phrases;

at the bottom, the two emptinesses—emptiness of the nature of desirelessness and emptiness of the marks of phrases—are absent. For those of sharp faculties, the conclusion is as explained in detail in the "Refutation of Views."
If it is not yet in correspondence with the lower [stages], one likewise employs sixty-four cycles.

If it is purely lower and continuous, it is explained according to the *Hetuvidyā* (Treatise on Causality). Next, regarding the lower [levels] of the first category, the remaining categories and remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) are taken up by analogy according to the explanation in the *Hetuvidyā*.
At the lower level of the nine categories, one establishes non-arising (*anutpāda*). Non-arising is simply the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

Next, in the section on "Distinguishing the Essentials," the question is as stated in the text. In the response, the two treatises provide a definitive distinction because the paths differ. If one proceeds from the lower perspective, the two paths are distinguished;

next, the views of those who prioritize form and those who prioritize thought are refuted. First, the difference between wisdoms is clarified: that which is called "worldly wisdom" relies upon the six practices, whereas [supramundane wisdom] takes the Truths as its object and is untainted (*anāsrava*).

If one begins with the lower stage, one distinguishes their nature: the body and its requisites in the desire realm are termed "afflictions of phenomena" (*vastu-kleśa*), while the afflictions within that same realm are termed "obstructions of nature" (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*).
Within the first dhyāna, the initial passage refers precisely to the signs of the arising of the first dhyāna.
Next, regarding the middle and lower [levels]: among the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna, those of the middle and lower grades are [eliminated].

If they are not eliminated, the mental faculty (*manas*) is destroyed; now, by employing the lower, there are sixty-four cycles. From the second dhyāna onwards, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a lower stage serves as the causal condition for a higher stage.

The higher [stage] arises with the lower as its condition, which is precisely the phenomenon that is produced. Regarding the third dhyāna, it is said that equanimity (*upekṣā*) is difficult to achieve.

Regarding this: the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*) contemplates the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Among the meditative realms (*dhyāna-viṣaya*), five of the nine abodes of the dhyānas are clarified as the "five *anāgāmin* abodes" (*pañca-anāgāmi-sthānāni*);

these are the five noble dwellings (*ārya-vihāra*) named the five *anāgāmins*. The state of non-ideation belongs exclusively to worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), while the [other] three are common to both worldlings and noble ones (*ārya*), because they include those who "leap over half" (*ardhapluta*).

Regarding "universal submergence" (*paryādāna*): because the cultivation of dhyāna (*bhāvanā*) has five distinctions, it is divided into five stages (*bhūmi*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this cultivation extends through nine stages.

As for what is meant by "cultivation," it refers to the permeation of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) into the outflowing (*sāsrava*). From many instances of the outflowing and many instances of the outflow-free, they are each reduced until only two moments remain;

this is called the completion of the preparatory application (*prayoga*). When they reach a single moment each, it is called the completion of the fundamental [attainment] (*maula*). These are the five distinctions.
This refers to the lower, middle, and upper grades, each further divided into three—namely, the superior, more superior, and most superior—thus totaling fifteen grades.
These arise sequentially in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). Regarding the term "interlaced perfuming" (*sāṃvāsa-paribhāvita*):

because the untainted (*anāsrava*) states at the beginning and end perfume the tainted (*sāsrava*) state in the middle, it is called "interlaced. As for the "five heavens," they are: Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha.

[The section on] the ultimate [cessation]. Next, the destruction of the formless [realms] is discussed. Regarding the phrase "those with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and so forth in the middle [of the text]: these three groups of three exist within the realms of form and desire;
they enter the formless [attainments] as a means of cessation. The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "First, the visible with resistance; second, the invisible with resistance; third, the..."

One sees the non-obstructive (*apratigha*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Transcending all form, one extinguishes it. First, form is extinguished; that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) is immediately extinguished.

Next, by not recollecting various characteristics of form, form is extinguished. Regarding the third form: the first form is [ordinary] matter; the second form refers to the five sense organs and the four objects;
the third form refers to the *dharmāyatana*, specifically a small portion of non-manifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*). According to this principle, one should recite as follows:

Among the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), these refer to the eight types of form (*rūpa*). When the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is accomplished, even the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is destroyed.
The methods for extinguishing form are fully detailed in the *Dharmamukha* (The Gate of Dhyāna). One contemplates the body as being like a steamer or a basket, gradually becoming empty and void.

Question: Does the formless concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*) possess form or not? Answer: According to the Hīnayāna (*kṣudra-śāsana*), it certainly does not; according to the Mahāyāna, it must exist. For now, we shall follow the [Hīnayāna] view that it does not.
At this point, the text below clearly elucidates the contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita). Next, within the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it first refutes ancient errors.
A question is raised in the *Chanmen*: "How can one enter meditative absorption by taking 'nothingness' as an object? The answer is: "It is not so; one simply takes nothingness itself as the object."

It is merely that the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters those mental objects (*dharmas*), giving rise to a slight perception of consciousness; it is not by grasping the conditions of that slight consciousness that one enters meditative absorption.
Therefore, [the text] now refutes "that which exists" (*sat*) and "that which has utility" (*upayoga*).

Following the description of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), the non-percipient sphere (*asaṃjñāyatana*) is next explained. Regarding the statement "relying on the eight noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*), the text here is abbreviated;

it should have stated that the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is like a disease, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) are as described [in the sūtra], and the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is like a judgment.

That these are not mentioned here is because they are currently categorized as "superior meditative absorptions" (*adhi-samādhi*) based on being with outflows (*sāsrava*). If one were to strictly rely on the noble lineages, then there would be four [categories]: illness and so forth, as well as the [absence of]...

The four [immeasurables] beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are the antidotes for the first four [hindrances]. The latter four take the Four Noble Truths as their objects. Furthermore, there is both a general and a specific contemplation;

those four aggregates correspond respectively to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Question: The four dhyānas consist of only six aspects (*ākāra*); why must the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) have eight? Answer:

Because it is subtle and difficult to abandon, the *Abhidharma* (below) explains the name "perception of non-perception" (*asaṃjñā-saṃjñā*). The citation is very brief. The *Lokadhātunirdeśa* states: "It is not like the four form realms or the three formless [attainments], therefore it is called 'non-perception' (*na-saṃjñā*);
it is not the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-deva*) nor the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), therefore it is called 'non-non-perception' (*na-asaṃjñā*). [End of] human [realm].

The Master himself did not even permit citing the Heaven of Non-conceptualization within the Form Realm, let alone citing all four dhyānas. Since this is a passage from the treatise (*śāstra*), there is no fault in adopting it;
therefore, both are preserved here. Now, we shall explain by means of a sequential progression through the three emptinesses.

The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "First, there are always those with outflows (*sāsrava*). This [text] of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) judges the *Mahā-śāstra*. Question: Why are there no [beings] without outflows (*anāsrava*)? Answer:

Because they are not suitable vessels for the field [of merit]. Those in the state of being without outflows are neutral; their desires are indeterminate, and they are deluded regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). It is because of these factors that [the beings with outflows] exist.

This concentration is inferior; it is not free from the afflictions associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. As for what are called "subtle phenomena," that stage still possesses ten kinds of subtle phenomena, namely:
feeling, perception, formations, contact, volition, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. These ten arise in conjunction with the feeling and other factors of that formless realm.
One who wishes to enter the attainment of cessation must first destroy them.

One should know that the following section employs the perspective of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Having understood that the subtle perceptions of those stages consist of the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*), one cultivates contemplation to exhaustively destroy them;

this is called "non-arising in terms of phenomena" (*dharma-anutpāda*). When the ultimate principle of the True Dharma is fully realized, it is called "non-arising in terms of principle" (*tattva-anutpāda*). How could one, by virtue of these stages, continue to abide in outflows (*āsrava*)?
If one uses the lower [classification] to judge wisdom, it is called the "lower" [category], which concludes the pervasive destruction of thought.

Regarding the three knowledges (*vidyā*) that destroy the stages, the first three belong to the *piṭaka* stage. All schools outside of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Treasury) are termed "different sects" (*nikāyāntara*). First, explaining the Śrāvakas:

as for the phrase "provisionally relying on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth," herein the Great Master uses the old *Vibhāṣā*, which does not accord with the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.

There is no distinction regarding the "small" [category]. A detailed explanation of the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family), the "single-seeded" (*ekabījika*), and so forth, is fully set forth in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Having abandoned two or four categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm, one is a *kulaṃkula*; having abandoned up to five, one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one is a once-returner. This refers to sequential abandonment.
The present text speaks of "leaping over," which refers to those who surpass others. Originally situated in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they have not yet attained [the fruits].

Regarding the concentration of form (*rūpa-dhyāna*): when the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāma-kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted, one who, upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, transcends and abandons five categories [of afflictions] is called a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*).

This transcendental abandonment of five is for the time being the same as the four [categories]. Depending on the number of categories abandoned according to their original state, one receives such names as "family-to-family," "seed-stage," or "candidate for the fruit.
Regarding those of the six types of *anāgāmin* included therein, the *Mahā-śāstra* states that there are five types of *anāgāmin*, namely:

Regarding the intermediate-attainer (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and the one who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), there are further six types when added to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*).

Having attained the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), they are destined to be born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); these five or six types are distinguished by differences in their faculties (*indriya*) and conditions (*pratyaya*). As for the ninth unimpeded [path] and so forth:

Each of the [ten] stages has one unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇa*) and one liberation (*vimukti*). Severance is termed "unimpeded," while realization is termed "liberation. It is also called "subduing and severance.
Regarding the phrase "forming non-arising below the three realms": as for the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the *Abhidharma* states: "I know suffering."
Up to the path, the one with the knowledge of non-arising thinks: "I have already known suffering... up to having already known the path; I shall no longer practice further.
This is also called mundane knowledge and untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and it is also called the two liberations (*dvividha-vimukti*).

Next, the explanation of the common stages (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "common with the śrāvakas and others," this refers to the stages prior to the seventh bhūmi. If that is so, then beyond this point they would not be common. The answer is:

from the initial establishment of the name, they differ from the distinct and perfect [stages]. Within the Tripiṭaka system, because the bodhisattva does not sever [the afflictions], they are not common;
yet because their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) is not different, they are not uncommon either.
Regarding the term "inferior" (*hīna*): this briefly explains its meaning. Although the specific terminology differs, it ultimately refers to the same stage.

Regarding "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*): this is the formal explanation. First, the five cessations (*pañca-nivaraṇa*) and the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) are both designated as "inner" and "outer" in relation to the Tripiṭaka.

Nevertheless, although they differ in skillfulness or clumsiness, their function in treating and contemplating desire is the same. It is called "dry" because it lacks the water of principle; having a slight understanding of the nature of things is termed "nature" (*prakṛti*).

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the cause. "Seeing" (*darśana*) means seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*). "Slight" (*tanu*) means attenuated; "separation" (*viveka*) means total exhaustion. "Accomplishment" (*niṣṭhā*) means the completion of the task.

These three distinctions are designated within the stage of general penetration (*sāmānyaprativedha-avasthā*). First, regarding the differences in refutation and establishment, we first generally refute the [opponent's] failure to understand the stage of general penetration.

As for the phrase "Why is it that...": this is a specific reprimand. Why are the two stages not the same? Subsequently, one should not fail to enter or emerge from meditative contemplation (*samādhi*).
"Human Teacher" (下): Refuting those who do not understand the meaning of the sūtras. "Now it is said" (今言下): A brief indication. "Separate views" (別見下): A brief explanation.

"However, named" (然名下): A definitive judgment. "For example" (例如下): Citing an illustration. These sixteen mental states share the same path yet differ in their specific designations; the judgment regarding these views is illustrated by this example.
In summary, if one knows that these positions use specific names to designate what is universal, because they occupy specific stages, then [the universal] is now [established].
Because they are not the same, this format is established to demonstrate it for later learners, so that the differing explanations of past and present may be clearly seen.

Regarding the phrase "borrowing from the distinct [stage]," this correctly clarifies the borrowing of stages. First, one borrows from the distinct stage; what is called "universal" (*sāmānya*) refers to its beginning and end.

Since there is no formal stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) in the Universal Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya-yāna*), the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is used here to correspond to the first two grounds. Since there is no formal stage after the grounds, the dharmas of the distinct teaching are borrowed.
The ninth is the Cloud of Dharma stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Because the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is not definitive, it uses the word "or" (*vā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that the ten stages are like the Buddha, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states that reaching the distant goal of Buddhahood is the Buddha-lineage (*buddha-gotra*).

Since these concern the lineage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), are they not merely employing alternative names? Furthermore, if one were to simply borrow the alternative name of the ten stages, it is merely because the stages are being correlated with the stages.
Regarding the four specific names that apply generally to the stages of a Bodhisattva: since these are compared stage by stage, their application ought not to be fixed.

From "In this way, below" onwards, the Bodhisattva stages are used to refute the views of the former masters. From "Thin, immediately below" onwards, the stage of contemplating the [four] truths is correctly identified. From "The former [masters] say, below" onwards, the discrepancies among the former [masters] are introduced.
From "But the six grounds, below" onwards, the present school’s critique follows; first, it critiques the six grounds, asking: how could they merely abandon the delusions of desire? How...

[The opponent] equates [the practitioner] with an Arhat. Next, [the author] refutes this by stating that even if one is said to "arbitrarily" face the third fruit or be on the path toward the fourth fruit, they are still termed "one who has abandoned desire" (*vītarāga*);

how could such a person be equated with an Arhat? Next, he refutes the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). If it is argued that the final category being exhausted is what constitutes the seventh stage, then that may well be so; yet such a person is also termed "one who has abandoned desire.

If [the term "abandonment of desire"] were to belong exclusively to the fruits, then the first dhyāna’s single category would already belong to the "already accomplished" (*kṛtāvin*), while the remaining category would not yet be accomplished—how then could they be equated?
"Arhat. Now, if [the term] were placed below, the present school would provide an explanation: it is for the sake of convenience to pair the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) with the fruits.

Although the sūtras frequently employ other meanings by pairing them with the thousand [perfections], those who establish this interpretation also fear that later generations might not understand the intent behind the universal application of these names in the sūtras.
Following this, all [terms] are placed below to attribute the merit.
Regarding the subsequent question: it is generally understood that the Bodhisattva may be established either through shared or distinct [characteristics], yet there appears to be no definitive proof.

In response, both the sutras and śāstras each contain explicit clarifications in two locations. First, citing the śāstra: "The three places of the burning wick" refers to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*);

this is distinct to the Bodhisattva and does not apply to the initial flame of the shared [stage], because the initial flame has already been severed. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are twofold: first, the Bodhisattva..."

The first stage (*bhūmi*) constitutes the initial "flame. Second, the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) of the śrāvakas constitutes the initial flame; therein, even the path of subduing through dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) serves as the initial flame for the bodhisattva.

What is there that is improper in subsequently attaining the stage of abandonment? In the sūtra below, the text itself establishes the distinct status of the solitary (*pratyekabuddha*) and the bodhisattva as separate positions.
Regarding the three types of bodhisattvas, they are those who share the same stages as the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
It is severed in the third and fourth stages.

Furthermore, the lower section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this comprehensively: "If even at the limit of the Buddha-stage there still remains the Bodhisattva-stage, how much more so for the preceding nine?

Therefore, each may be established separately. As for the term "adjacent to the ultimate" (*linji*), it refers to that which is distinct from the Buddha-stage yet transcends the ten stages; it is called "adjacent" by way of metaphorical borrowing.
"If there were no [separate stage] below... [This section] proves that at the limit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there exists a solitary Bodhisattva.

Regarding the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): it is said that at the limits of the ten stages, one "cultivates the karma of the stages. Next, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it establishes names such as "patience" (*kṣānti*) at the limits of the ten stages;

the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is likewise. From "In this way, below... onwards, the author formally presents his current intention: since he allows for a separate establishment [of a stage], he also borrows a distinct name to designate that distinction.
[Objection: How can this be reconciled with the fact that the sūtras and śāstras contain such meanings? [Response:

Next, it is explained that while the categories of abandonment are few, the fruits are many; this answer is evident. Next, the questioner asks: "The afflictions are heavy and the teachings are numerous; their meaning is one and the same.

Since there are many regulations regarding the fruits, there should be many established meditations (dhyāna), for meditation prevents distraction. [Response: The intention of the answer is that this is also due to distraction.

Most are not associated with dhyāna. Regarding the subsequent question: "Why is the name 'patience' (kṣānti) established for the Bodhisattva in those [stages] prior to the sixth and seventh grounds, which are shared with the two vehicles?
The answer is given based on three meanings. First, citing the examples of the fifteenth and sixteenth moments of mind, it shows that patience is the cause and wisdom is the fruit.

Within these fifteen moments, they are designated as "distinguishing cause and fruit" because the fruit has not yet been realized; this is because both cause and fruit pertain to the same realm. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
For those of the Bodhisattva vehicle, both the cause and fruit of the two vehicles serve as causes; the other two [vehicles] may be understood accordingly.

Next, the distinct teaching (biejiao) clarifies the stage of destroying thought; whereas the preceding section revealed the commonality (tong), this now specifically distinguishes the stages to further manifest the meaning of vertical progression.

Therefore, they are explained next. Question: At the beginning of this chapter, there was no mention of the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles; why are they explained here? Answer: They were not listed previously because they had already accomplished entry into emptiness.

Furthermore, according to the intent of the treatise, they are all explained together here. As for the Ten Practices (daśabhūmi) which involve emerging into the provisional (the conventional world), they no longer concern what preceded them;
since even the stages of the Separate Teaching do not concern emptiness, how much less so the subsequent Shared and Tripitaka teachings? This is precisely why they were not listed before.

Next, regarding those who exhaust the residual habits (*vāsanā*) during the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages of faith within the stage of perfection: the term "residual habits" does not refer to the *sands-of-the-Ganges* [countless] afflictions or ignorance (*avidyā*), because these are attached to the internal realms;

therefore, for now, it is said they are "exhausted. By extension, one should also say that they no longer concern the preceding stages, as they have been permanently separated from them, though this is not discussed here.
As for citing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is because one fears that people might not understand that gross delusions are first eliminated when one initially realizes the first *bhūmi* (stage), yet...
One looks forward to the ten stages of faith; hence it is said that "the habitual tendencies within the realm [of desire] are exhausted.

Next, regarding the passage from the *Avataṃsaka* below, it serves as proof of the first stage (*bhūmi*). Modern scholars all claim that the afflictions are merely suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), yet how can this account for the passage concerning the "transcendence of the Sage" at the stage?
This constitutes the second section, which demonstrates the perfect meaning of the text. Regarding the phrase "How... and so forth, it explains the intent of the *Avataṃsaka*.

The initial passage provides a brief explanation. From "Named thus" (*er*) onwards, there is an inquiry. From "However" (*ran*) onwards, there is the answer. The Buddha-way belongs to the stages of the Distinct and Complete [Teachings] (*bie-yuan*);
even those at the stage of *bhūmi* or *vihāra* surpass the two Buddhas and let alone the Bodhisattvas. This is explained according to their respective levels.

Furthermore, the following section distinguishes similarities and differences, clarifying the specific distinctions in attaining the names [of the fruits] through the severance of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions).

This also analyzes the previous refutation of the provisional nature of the severance of afflictions, showing that the functions of wisdom (*jñāna*) differ at each stage of the Buddha’s career; it is also a remote judgment regarding the various wisdoms and severances taught in the scriptures. The initial passage concerns the contemplation and wisdom of the four teachings.

Regarding the phrase "If one says... [it] judges the similarity and difference between them. The initial passage refers to the Shared (Tongjiao) Teaching; when the three vehicles are compared, [they are seen as] similar.

Regarding the phrase "If one says...", this uses the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct (Biejiao) and Perfect (Yuanjiao) Teachings to compare with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Tripitaka (Zangjiao) and Shared Teachings. While they are similar in severing the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava), their wisdom and function are not equal.

One might further say that both wisdom and severance differ; this refers to the fact that in the Shared Teaching, the distinct delusions (biéhuò) are not severed. At this point, the distinct delusions have not yet been discussed.

Therefore, it is not discussed. Furthermore, regarding the mutual comparison of those who have attained the three vehicles: it may also be said that their wisdom is identical while their abandonments differ, because there is a difference between the abandonment of the fundamental afflictions and the abandonment of residual habits.

Regarding the question below: the first question and answer can be seen clearly. Regarding the phrase "although not below": this clarifies that although the fruits may be transcended, the stages [of cultivation] remain.
The stage is not lost. For example, when a person travels, how could there be no distance measured in *li*? Regarding the next question: "Advancing toward the goal" is called "transcending.

When Śāriputra first heard the Three Truths, why did he only attain the first fruit (*srotāpanna*)? The answer is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "It was said that he attained it while listening to the Buddha debate with his maternal uncle;
others say it was while listening to Aśvajit preach the Three Truths; and some say he attained it seven days or fifteen days later."
[He attained] the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Is this not indeed transcendent? As for Ānanda serving as the attendant:

according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when the Buddha sought an attendant, his heart was set upon Ānanda, just as the sun rising in the east shines upon the western wall. When the time came for the First Council, he was rebuked by Mahākāśyapa; only then did he attain the state of no-more-learning.
Because an Arhat is not fit to serve as an attendant, [the Buddha] himself did not accept him. [This concludes] the section on the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). Part One.

Previously, it was explained that there is no skipping [of stages]. Therefore, it is said that there should also be skipping. Because Bodhisattvas bear the burden [of all beings], skipping is not discussed.
Whether there is skipping or no skipping, the afflictions of thought (思惑) must be severed.

Below the section on "Transcending the Fruit," there is a detailed analysis. Regarding the phrase "originally severed": this refers to what was originally severed by non-Buddhists through mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*).

Because the extent of what was originally severed varies, it is not the same in the present case. That which was originally attained as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is already severed;

thus, one does not speak of the eight lower stages as being directed toward Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*), but rather as being directed toward Anāgāminship (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*), because the power of their contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) is inferior. This applies if one has originally attained the dhyānas.

...and so forth. These shall be determined and explained by comparison, perhaps in three or two chapters, as previously stated. Regarding "the one whose practice is perfected," this refers only to the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka.

As for the person of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanren) being called "supreme" (*zui*), the question is asked: "The previous [text] spoke of 'shouldering the burden' (*hefu*); why is it now called 'supreme'? The answer is: It is called "supreme" in relation to what preceded it. Therefore...

The *Śrṅkhalā-sūtra* (or *Śrṅkhalā-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*) provides evidence for whether [the stages] transcend or do not transcend [the ordinary]. In that sūtra, the Buddha answers Śrīśūra, saying: "There is only the sudden, no gradual.

The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) judges this to be the First Abode (*prathamavihāra*), which is likewise a stage of suddenness. As for the term "stainless" (*vimala*), it is categorized according to the "Six Identities" (*liù jí*). Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
This is also the stage of the first abiding (*prathamā-bhūmi*). It is below the principle of true reality (*tathatā*).

Regarding the fourth phrase, as for the analytical examination (*vicāra*) of the three and four gates: first, to clarify the intent of the gates, sixteen gates are required in order to penetrate the principle.

Furthermore, since these sixteen gates equally refute both the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they are subsequently analyzed once more; this is also for the purpose of clarifying the severance of views.

The basis for this reflection lies in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). As distinguished from others in the "Refutation of Pervasiveness" (*po bian*), one takes only the gate of the perfect non-arising (*wushengmen*);
the gates of the other three teachings follow as secondary.

In the initial explanation of the section on the "Gate of Existence" (*sadvāra*) within the Tripiṭaka: regarding the five companions, namely Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bāṣpa, Daśabalakāśyapa, and the Prince Kolita—these five had been his original attendants, and therefore he delivered them across [to liberation] first. They were all individuals belonging to the Gate of Existence.
As for Aśvajit preaching the Three Truths: it was because he observed the majestic and orderly deportment of Ājñāta that he asked, "Who is your teacher? and so forth.
"What dharma did he teach? He replied, "Prince Siddhārtha is my teacher. Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya was taught by him that all phenomena arise from conditions.
'Suffering' is a phenomenon; he taught its cause and condition, as well as its cessation and extinction. This is how my teacher spoke. Only the Path was not mentioned;
yet where there is cessation, there must be a path."

In the second volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it clarifies that those who employ the gates [of practice] must be skilled in expedient means; that is to say, they must be free from attachment. This applies to all such gates.
In the second volume of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, it cites those who have attained benefit.

Next, regarding the gate of emptiness, as for the question "Who is it that ages and dies?"—the treatise cites the *Saṃyukta Āgama* to show that within the twelve links of dependent origination, no master over ignorance or aging-and-death can be found;
thus it is called "who. This is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). That there is no such thing as aging-and-death is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Although the names of phenomena exist, from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, this refers merely to the emptiness of persons.
Regarding Subhūti and the others: although they had attained arhatship, what prevented them from excelling in particular ways?

When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he alone did not enter the assembly but sat upright in a stone chamber, contemplating only the emptiness of all phenomena and thereby perceiving the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body consists of five aspects.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, also clarifies the gate of application. The expedient means are the same as before. [This section] washes away the third gate.

In comparison with what is said in the fourth gate, regarding the mention of Chandaka: when the Buddha was in the world, he was obstinate and difficult to tame; the Buddha now dispatches him to be governed according to the Brahma-punishment, which is precisely silent ostracism (*tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya*).
If one contemplates the object, it should likewise be said that it is "provisionally non-existent," as before, for it is not [ultimately real].

Ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) is fully endowed with both existence and non-existence; therefore, this "neither-nor" is itself the objective realm. "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the name for observation. Regarding the term *gotrabhū*:
since ancient times, translations have been inconsistent due to a lack of linguistic proficiency, leading to its being translated as *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer).

Guṇavarman criticized and contested this, asserting that one enters the Way and attains the fruit by relying on the gate of existence (*astitva-dvāra*). His intention was that the attainment of the Way does not arise from contention.
Section on the Gate.

Why, below, is there a discussion regarding the existence or non-existence [of the Buddha] and the classification into Great and Small Vehicles? This is now applied universally. To follow the principle, there is necessarily no [conflict];

it is because one loses the principle that conflict arises. Regarding "Śākyamuni first encountered," etc.: the *Abhidharmakośa* states, "Throughout incalculable eons, he made offerings to various Buddhas."
Seventy thousand. Furthermore, he successively made offerings to five, six, and seven thousand Buddhas, meeting in reverse order the Buddhas Vipasyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin.
Regarding the first, Śākyamuni, his name differs from that in the treatise; their respective pronunciations are distinct. The six perfections are as cited in the third fascicle.
As for the reference to Śākyamuni and others as the "causes" (*hetu*) in the treatise, it explains the meaning of "bodhisattva" within the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, clarifying the causal stage.
"Referring to Śākyamuni" means pointing to his three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas*. "Clarifying the fruition" refers to Maitreya’s future attainment.

Why is this? Because Śākyamuni’s fruition has already been realized; therefore, one must point to his causal practices. Since Maitreya’s causes are already fulfilled, one points to his future fruition.

Thus, by observing the cause one knows the fruit, and by seeing the fruit one knows the cause. For this reason, many sacred teachings extensively clarify the causes of Śākyamuni and distinguish the [fruition] of Maitreya.

Regarding the statement, "Nāgārjuna refutes [the idea that] going and so forth are results," this is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) is primarily elucidating the Mahāyāna vehicle;

thus, it cites the definitions of bodhisattvas found in the *Vibhāṣā* and other Hīnayāna works to extensively refute them. Since those teachings are merely provisional (*upāya*), how could they be worth refuting?

Next are the four gates of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). First, regarding the gate of existence (*astitva-mukha*): "Yet there is illusory transformation" is the main body of the gate of existence;

"Thus... concludes it. "If one says... is the main body of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*); "In this way... concludes it. "If one clarifies... is the main body of the gate of both emptiness and existence;
"In this way... concludes it. "Since it is said... is the main body of the gate of neither-nor (*ubhayābhāva-mukha*); "In this way... concludes the main body of the gate.
Regarding the statement "discussing the essence in terms of refutation," this serves as a general response to an anticipated objection. The objection states:

"If one universally observes that all things are like illusions, and that which is fundamentally unarisen is called the 'essence' (*tattva*), then since the essence is not something to be refuted, why do you speak of 'refutation'? The answer is: "Discussing the essence in terms of refutation.

Although the term "refutation" is the same, its application here differs fundamentally from its use in the process of analytical deconstruction. To support this, the treatise cites the example of "flames and so forth," which serves to demonstrate that the teachings of the four gates are all ultimately ungraspable.

Furthermore, the explanation of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) states that all four propositions regarding reality and so forth differ; entering the pool through the four gates and so on are all the intended meaning of this gate.
If one does not descend [into this], it clarifies that the essence of the gate is free from contention.

Question and Answer, Part II: Distinguishing from the [Hīnayāna] Pitaka. *Dang* (pronounced *ding-lang*): to obstruct; to block a faction. Mutual refutation and mutual obstruction are not the primary intent of this gate. It is also called "As It Truly Is" (*yathābhūta*), etc.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, two analogies of skillful and unskillful physicians are used for these two stages:

like needles and medicine versus incantations; and like crossing to the other shore by means of a grass raft versus a boat. [This refers to] the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) of the Śrāvakas and the Bodhi...

The Bodhisattva contemplates the true mark of dharmas. This refers to the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* concerning the three animals crossing the river. The three types of persons are like the animals; the ultimate truth is like the water.

Although the elephant reaches the bottom, it is still distinguished [from the others] by its depth of perception. One distinguishes between those of sharp and dull faculties based on whether they perceive emptiness or non-emptiness.
Next, regarding the four distinct gates: the lower section of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* distinguishes between similarities and differences.

In the *Śūxing shiqian*, concerning matters such as the sequence of hearing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and so forth—for instance, precepts, concentration, and wisdom involving birth-and-death (*saṃskṛta*) are entirely identical to those in the Tripiṭaka;

only the three [levels of] non-arising (*anutpāda*) and so forth differ from the Tripiṭaka. Since these are explained first, it is said they are "not different. This is the explanation of the hundred phrases of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Excluding the Chinese text. That text consists entirely of the meaning of the Separate and Perfect Gates. Regarding the ten metaphors for the Tathāgatagarbha, the title reads "The Vaipulya Tathāgatagarbha";
although there are ten textual passages, they constitute only nine meanings, because the first two passages share a single meaning.
1. Like the fruit within a flower; 2. like honey among the trees on a mountain cliff; 3. like rice within the husk; 4. like gold within impurities; 5.
like a treasure trove in a poor man’s house; 6. like the seed within a fruit; 7. like an image wrapped in tattered cloth; 8.
like a noble child conceived in a woman’s womb; 9. like an image within a mold—these correspond to the ten matters set forth in the *Nirgrantha Sūtra*.

It is sufficient. It is like gold within stone, fire within wood, water within the earth, curd within milk, oil within sesame seeds, grain within the husk, an image within a mold, a fetus within the womb, and the sun within the clouds.
Regarding the statement that *nirvāṇa* is not existent and so forth: it is neither the designator nor the designated; therefore, it is said to be non-existent.
Yet, because it is provisionally established based on conventional reality, it is called "existent" as *nirvāṇa*. Since it is not form (*rūpa*) or any such [sensory object], how...
Why is it said that one sees the existence of a "wondrous form" (rūpa), yet hearing the name of *nirvāṇa* is like [the case of] a water-jar, a wine-jar, a curd-jar, and so forth?

This is also from the "Hundred Phrases" (*Śataśāstra*). The Sūtra says: "Liberation is called 'not empty' (*aśūnya*), just as a jar that contains water and the like is still called a 'water-jar' and so forth even when it is empty. In such cases, the jar cannot be described as either empty or not empty.
