As previously stated, the former [position] was refuted; therefore, it was said that [the opponent's view] is untenable. Now, however, we clarify that [our teaching] accords with the capacities of beings; thus, while the words are the same, their meanings differ.
Regarding impermanence in contrast to permanence: impermanence is "other" (parāyatta). Therefore, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, when refuting the non-Buddhists, it says:
"In your doctrine, the cause is permanent while the fruit is impermanent; what prevents my doctrine from having a cause that is impermanent yet a fruit that is permanent? Thus, it may be followed.

It arises as the Truth through conditions. Furthermore, the passage below uses the analogy of "other-arising": *eranda* (a thorny plant) represents ignorance (*avidyā*), while *candana* (sandalwood) represents the *dharmatā*.
Thus, King Ajātaśatru described it himself, saying: "Now I have seen that from an *eranda* seed grows a *candana* tree.
This *candana* tree is my own rootless faith; it is the seed of the *dharmarāja*'s nature itself, for it has grown from a grain."

It is called a "seed" (*bīja*). Because the seed of grain does not change, it is called "nature" (*prakṛti*). Arising from my own mind, its meaning is like that of a seed; being beginningless and unchanging, it is called "nature.
Because it is not the same as [the nature] derived from the Buddha, it is called "self" (*sva*). Next, regarding the statement that "because of the cessation of causes, etc., it is common":

because one externally observes others by means of the nature of one's own phenomena (*svadharma-prakṛti*), it is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). Or, as stated below, it is distinct from what is non-... [text ends].
It is not the internal nature of phenomena, nor is it external, nor is it produced through conditions. At the end of each phrase, one should conclude by saying: "One attains this wisdom.

Regarding the statement "there is no attainment," etc., this concludes the preceding contemplation having been perfected; because it has achieved the state of being free from intrinsic nature, it is called "no attainment.
Because one attains this wisdom, it is called "attainment. Attainment is itself provisional; non-attainment is emptiness. That attainment is non-attainment is precisely the Middle Way.

Below the section on "The Bodhisattvas," the treatise establishes the gates. In Vasubandhu’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is established as intrinsic; the remaining three [treatises] are to be understood by analogy.

In Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, emptiness is established; the remaining three are to be understood by analogy. If one grasps the intent of these gates, then when the four natures give rise to the capacity for awakening, there will be no room for contradiction.

The character "牟" (*móu*) should be read as "矛" (*máo*), meaning a spear—a weapon. It should also be read as "盾" (*dùn*), meaning a shield—a side-plate. This is like the saying that in the state of Chu, there was a merchant selling spears.
The "Shield" (Phalaka) refers to self-contradiction.
If one employs the lower [method], it relies on the middle gate, wherein all practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā are cultivated. Regarding the sūtras and śāstras below, this explains the efficacy;
thus, in the middle gate, it clarifies that the merit of contemplative practice is in full accord with reality.
Question on the lower [level]. An analysis follows. Regarding the first question: since the two are mutually identical, they should both be negated and revealed simultaneously.

The meaning of the answer is this: although both are provisionally established, they ultimately do not coexist; yet, because ignorance remains even though they do not coexist, the two names are provisionally established.
When the *dharmatā* arises, both names are extinguished. Regarding the second question: since the two dharmas do not coexist, why are they mutually identical? It should be established as follows.

Regarding the "opposite gate," the text addresses only one side for now. The reason it does not further discuss the other side is that it intends to demonstrate the principle within the state of delusion.
In the response, there are two analogies. The meaning of the first analogy is as follows: although both pairs of factors are fully present, they are like something unrecognized.

The first phrase serves as a heading for what follows, while the second phrase refers to the individuals; because each is deluded, they must be shown to one another. If one were to speak from the perspective of a single person alone, it would ultimately remain only one side, which is feared [to lead to error].

[The opponent] is confused regarding ice and water. He further cites the analogy of the jewel. Why? Because the two phenomena of ice and water mutually displace one another, it is easy to give rise to divergent conceptions.

Therefore, the essence of the jewel is cited as superior to that mutual displacement. Thus, although fire, water, and the jewel arise from conditions, even though they follow the analogy of the jewel, the [analogy of] ice and water should still be maintained; this can be understood by combining the analogies.

Regarding the sequence of stages: since the initial explanation of cultivation and realization preserves the sequential order, the stages prior to the first bhūmi are taken as the two preparatory means (*upāya*).

Upon reaching the first bhūmi, one spontaneously integrates cessation and contemplation; therefore, the preceding and succeeding phases of cessation and contemplation constitute the means for ascending to the bhūmis.

Next, the practice of the lower [stages] is cultivated to refute the provisional. First, three types of persons are established: those who have attained the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), those at the first stage of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), and those at the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

If one connects the Distinct Teaching downward, it clarifies that [the Distinct] reaches up to the eighth stage; only when those being grafted [into the Perfect] realize this can it be said that they are discussing the cultivation of the seventh stage.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* provides scriptural proof: if the third fascicle speaks from the perspective of those with inferior faculties, then one hears [the Dharma] at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), suppresses ignorance (*avidyā*) at the ninth stage, and destroys ignorance at the tenth stage. Herein, for those of middling and superior faculties, the transition may also occur at the fourth or fifth stages.
Since the teaching generally proceeds from the inferior, their respective positions are fixed.

The phrase "as follows" below refutes both the general and specific [interpretations]. Although this [stage] also destroys ignorance, it is provisionally taught as being of high rank; therefore, it must be refuted.

Regarding the statement that "a beginner cannot cultivate *śuklavidarśana* (dry wisdom)": Question: One who has attained the general [realization] may cultivate *śuklavidarśana* at the stage of a beginner.

Why, then, do you refute it by saying it cannot be cultivated? Answer: This is an instance of citing the inferior to illustrate the superior. Within the teachings of this school, *śuklavidarśana* itself possesses the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Worthies). At the beginning...

Since the mind is first made to practice the five *sthāpanās*, one has not yet attained the practice of the *smṛtyupasthānas* even from one's own perspective. Next, regarding the refutation of the distinct stages:
having established faith for sixty *kalpas*, how could one possibly discuss the dedication [of merit] within the context of cultivation?

Next, the section "Now Explaining the Lower [Levels]" correctly elucidates the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*). The first part consists of five sections: it cites the *Lotus Sūtra* to explain and establish the three contemplations (*sanguan*).

It explains that the seat is emptiness (*kong*), the clothing is the middle (*zhong*), and the chamber is the provisional (*jia*). Furthermore, it uses meditative concentration (*ding*) and wisdom (*hui*) to assist in explaining the clothing and other elements. Because the seat is ultimate, emptiness is perfected.

The robe is circular because it represents quiescence; the chamber is circular by way of metaphor because it represents great compassion. Furthermore, since both are called "Tathāgata," all three are circular;
this constitutes the stage of similarity.
Seeing the crane descending is an analogy. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of seeing: first, seeing by resemblance; second, clear seeing.
Therefore, seeing the crane is called "seeing by resemblance" because it is like the visual perception of form.
As for "clear seeing," if even the mental observation of the eye perceiving form is still considered seeing, how much more so is seeing by resemblance? Next, an example is cited.
This can be understood. Now, below the five grades, the text correctly clarifies the middle stage. Next, it cites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to testify to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

Within the stage of the six sense faculties, one exhaustively destroys the boundaries of the internal realm; this is provisionally termed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Only by advancing to destroy ignorance does one truly transcend the Sage (*muni*). This is the teaching of the Tripiṭaka school.
This meaning is entirely absent; therefore, ignorance is shattered. Regarding the teaching, it is said that this is an error.

Starting from "below," the functional capacity of contemplation is revealed. The phrase "without waiting for" etc., excludes the seventh stage of the *Pāramitā* (Common) vehicle. The phrase "how could there be leisure to contemplate joy?

excludes the first stage of the *Vihāra* (Distinct) vehicle. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Once the Bodhisattva dwells in Suchness (*tathatā*), they ascend to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). How could this be the seventh [stage]?
If [the stage] were the same as that of the Two Vehicles, it would contradict one's own teaching; this has never been a neglected principle. Regarding the preceding teaching:

the more substantial the teaching, the lower the stage; the more provisional the teaching, the higher the stage. Therefore, in the Shared [Teaching], it extends to the eighth stage; in the Distinct [Teaching], it is the first stage;

in the Perfect [Teaching], it is the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the passage on "Expedient Means" serves as proof for the provisional, while the section on "The Real Matter" serves as proof for the real.
This is the verification.

Furthermore, below this, there is another classification of the teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*). Previously, upon entering the Middle Way, three pairs of currents were enumerated; now, following the names generally, the Three Piṭaka Teaching (*tripiṭaka-śāsana*) is included as well.
Thus, in the Three Piṭaka Teaching, the names "emptiness" and "existence" are applied, and their position is situated within the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*).

Although it is stated that the stage of perfect reality (*yuan-shi*) is clarified within the words [of the teaching], next an analogy is raised, followed by an illustrative explanation. If this were to be applied analogously to the entry into dhyāna, there should be many categories;
as for the two preceding contemplations and the subsequent equality, it is only upon reaching this sequence that the conclusion should be pressed home, as has already been discussed above.

Now, descending to the Middle Way, the two kinds of emptiness are established: ignorance concludes the first section; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) concludes the next section; and "not relying" and so forth conclude the third.
Not relying on the four propositions, its nature is empty and without dependence; it is the emptiness of non-attachment.

Next, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is cited because it possesses these two kinds of emptiness; therefore, one bows in prostration. Since emptiness is used as a metaphor for emptiness, it is said to be "like space. It is without [intrinsic existence].
Furthermore, because its nature and characteristics are restored, it is called "without dependence.

Next, regarding the horizontal gate (*yōmon*): within the initial "intention for the teaching" (*raimyū*), there is first the Dharma and then the analogy; because they proceed from the shallow to the deep, it is termed "direct."
Because the meanings of each gate are equal, they are called "aligned" (齊). Because their meanings are listed together, they are called "parallel" (並).
Regarding what it means for them to be "horizontal" (橫), the meaning of the gates is explained next: although horizontal and vertical differ, there is nothing that does not reveal reality.

Regarding the "Horizontal Gate" (hengmen): this is the sequential formal explanation. First, the eight negations are listed; since the *Śāstra* possesses all eight, they are enumerated here. The text of the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo) is identical.

The phrase "the *Śāstra*" below refers to the extensive *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. Below, the *Śāstra* is cited to subsume the characteristics, using two to encompass six, as well as the arguments concerning defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*).
Question: All phenomena (*dharmas*) are immeasurable; for what reason are eight enumerated? Answer: Although phenomena are immeasurable, these eight subsume them.

[The eight categories] are exhaustive. Thus, one should know that although the names in the various teachings differ, they do not transcend these eight. In the treatise itself, the first two have already been shown to encompass the remaining six.

Question: Why are the other six required? Answer: It is for the sake of establishing the first two. Speaking from this perspective, they are mutually inclusive in pairs; therefore, all [categories] here now enter into non-arising (*anutpāda*).
As for the others entering into one another in turn, it may be understood by analogy with this. Regarding the first point, "if there is no arising..."

"Entering the gates is also like this" means that from within the "Gate of Non-arising" (*anutpāda-mukha*), the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the various sense-bases (*āyatana*) emerge in pairs to enter the various gates.

Next, if one refers to the section below the "Gate of Non-arising," it refers to the initial passage concerning the ten dharmas that constitute the vehicle (*yāna*), as well as the inconceivable realms and suchnesses numbering three thousand;
these are abbreviated here and simply referred to as "various. Next, if one refers to the section below the "Gate of Arising," it refers to... [the text continues].

"Settle your mind and come forth. Next, "if there were no arising below," introduces the section on "pervasive refutation" (*pòbiàn*). This is precisely the point where one enters through the gate of pervasive refutation;

therefore, the textual exposition here is the most extensive, while the others follow suit by being abbreviated. "Whether this consciousness exists or not below," introduces the text for entering emptiness;
this merely refutes [the view of] existence, while the rest is all omitted. Next, "if there were no arising below," introduces the entry into the provisional (*jiǎ*).

The passage beginning with "knowing and seeing the provisional and the heavy" is cited from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; the remainder is abbreviated. Next, the passage beginning with "if there were no arising" is cited from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* as a textual source for entering into the Middle Way.
Next, the passage beginning with "extinguishing by itself" is cited from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* as a textual source for entering into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

From the passage beginning with "depending on itself," this is cited as a textual source for contemplating true conditions; the preceding text contemplates ignorance and so forth in terms of being self-originated or other-originated.

In the preceding Middle Way contemplation, one grasped the prior [realms of] emptiness and the provisional as the three truths; therefore, now each and every [phenomenon] constitutes the three truths.
Previously, one investigated the absence of explicit textual evidence for the four propositions; now there are only the four [propositions] such as "arising from itself" and so forth.

Briefly stated, the nature of phenomena in the prior contemplation was the "continuity-provisional" (saṃtati-prajñapti); this is why it is now said that they arise from themselves, others, both, or neither. If one speaks of "arising," it is in contrast to what preceded.

This is inconvenient. Next, regarding the passage on "mutual dependence" (*pratītya*), it says: "that which depends on itself. This mutual dependence of the four propositions is also applied as a critique of self, other, and so forth.

Next, the section beginning with "if there were no arising" introduces the concluding summary of the pervasive [analysis]. According to the sequence of the text, this should properly follow the three observations (*trividha-darśana*).
Therefore, the present entry [into the teaching] occurs precisely within this context. Next, "if there is no arising" and below concludes the section.
"If one attains" and below next clarifies the entry into the two sūtras. First, it generally clarifies the characteristics of entry; therein, it first clarifies non-practice (*apracāra*).

The initial mention of "truth" (*satya*) refers to the object (*viṣaya*). Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the arising of understanding based upon that object. "Bodhisattva" refers to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the settling of the mind (*citta-vyavasthāpana*).

The passage on "shattering views" and so forth constitutes the "universal shattering. "Birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) is a general reference to the beginning and the end. "Practices," "stages," and so forth correspond to the subsequent sections of the text.

The stages from "pervasive and obstructed" (*tsū-soku*) up to "correct and auxiliary" (*shō-jō-i*) constitute the sequential stages. These sequentially encompass "patience" (*nin-nin*) and "detachment from reception" (*ri-ju*).

Beyond this, one is necessarily able to teach; therefore, it is called "teaching" (*kyō*). Next, regarding the "Vajra": first, it generally leads to non-abiding; next, below the section on "object and wisdom" (*kyō-chi*), [it proceeds].

This refers to the ten modes of practice (*daśayāna*). From "not abiding in object and wisdom" up to "viewing and contemplating" and so forth, only the first three passages are cited here because there is no need to refute [the notion of] universal penetration through these stages.
It states that one does not abide even in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), further citing the scriptural passage on non-abiding;
since one does not abide even in the stages because they have not yet reached ultimate perfection, how much less could one abide in objects, wisdom, and the like?

Below this section on "Non-abiding," the stages are again re-evaluated. Therefore, in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), the explanation of the evaluation of stages states that all three locations equally destroy ignorance;
thus, one partially attains the non-abiding diamond [wisdom]. Below the section on Śākyamuni, there is the ultimate diamond [wisdom].
"If that is so," and so forth, explains away the doubt. Generally, it is said that because one is at the stage of subduing [the afflictions], it is called the "path of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-mārga*);

however, there is no "Vajra[-like Samādhi]. Since the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang jing) states that Śākyamuni possessed it, the path of abandonment must exist [therein]. Furthermore, the statement that the path of abandonment exists does not exclude the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);

its meaning applies to both the beginning and the end. Regarding the phrase "crossing the melodies": it is like secular wind and string instruments, where the various melodies are innumerable, and the pipes and strings are like...

Horizontal. All the curves are like verticals. This initial chapter is the essential destination of fundamental wondrous wisdom. At the beginning of the melodic modulation, its vastness is such as this.
Taking entry into the Way as the principle, the remaining three belong to phenomena (*dharma*). A thousand interpretations follow from this; I have set forth but a small portion as words.
Next, the further analysis may be understood as follows. In the response, the first chapter is designated as "two meanings" in contrast to the others.

The first part correctly demonstrates the gate through which one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*) attains universal penetration; thus it says, "The world, etc. The section beginning with "If one says... presents the interpretations of others. The subsequent section beginning with "Furthermore, others...

explains that prior to transforming others (*para-parāvṛtti*), each enters [the path] individually, thereby constituting one's own practice. This is the praise of the gate. The section beginning with "How... provides the concluding reply.
Furthermore, regarding the four *siddhāntas* within the gateway, the correspondence between the [four] joys and the four *siddhāntas* can be seen from the textual structure.
Next, in clarifying the single mind, all attachments—whether internal or external, partial or complete—are refuted. Because they are refuted, this simultaneously elucidates all sutras and treatises;
thus, the stages for destroying the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*bhava-kleśa*) differ between the Great and Small Vehicles.
"If there is no arising" below explains the gates of the transverse and the vertical, leading into the single mind. "Although there are various kinds" below concludes by establishing the single mind.

"But the single mind" below provides a detailed explanation by dividing the gates; first, it explains the general gate in contrast to specific states such as greed. Within this, the initial section demonstrates the method of contemplation.

The phrase "if one does not attain" and so forth clarifies the intent of leading into [the single mind]. The term "suspended transcendence" (hsüan-ch'ao) indicates that this is not the same as the transverse or vertical approaches. It is a double [gate].

Regarding "entering from the periphery": because one's own practice has not yet reached full mastery, it is like being distant; because one discriminates for the sake of benefiting others, it is like being repetitive.

Having departed and then returning is called "entering from the periphery," also termed "returning entry. Because the reckoning of one's practice has not yet been exhausted, it is called "returning entry";
this is because one has not yet reached the ultimate. Furthermore, as the three truths are successively entered into a single mind, it is called "wondrous emptiness" and so forth.

Below this and so forth, next, based on the single mind, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) are opened up. Knowledge and vision are merely alternative names for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
In every thought-moment and instant, there are no sentient beings who do not penetrate [reality] through stillness and illumination (*jìzhào*). Stillness and illumination serve as the cause.
The fruit is the wisdom of the eye. Why must it necessarily be called "opening" only at the first stage?
Just as the three vehicles are opened, this too merely demonstrates that the grasping mind is quiescent and luminous; how could there be any difference in intent here?

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the mental faculty (*manas*) is cited because the mind subsumes the other [faculties]. The "Benevolent King" (*Rājan*) is cited because one only attains the name "Pure" upon reaching the Buddha-stage where there is no longer retribution;
since this is discussed here in a general sense, the Buddha is also called "retribution. Next, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is cited, which likewise proves the reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
Next, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* is cited to explain the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Next, regarding "successively traversing the remaining one mind": this means that, intending to proceed toward the single mind, one traverses the remaining minds.

Since all that possesses mind is nothing other than ignorance (*avidyā*), one first observes them collectively. If this is not appropriate, one departs from the collective to emerge in the particular.

Question: Previously, you spoke only of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); why do you now speak of "desire and other states of mind"? Answer: What was previously called "consciousness" refers to the consciousness that belongs to all mental states. Now, [we speak of]...
"Desire and so forth" refers to the various mental states belonging to the category of consciousness. Question: Why are afflictions such as greed called "aggregates" (*skandha*)? Answer:

Although they are afflictions, they are subsumed within the aggregates of the wholesome and unwholesome; furthermore, they are not aggregates of karmic retribution. Therefore, they are designated as "greed and so forth. Because they are not retribution, [the text] subsequently proceeds again to examine the remaining aggregates.

Next, proceed downward. This pattern applies to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. Question: When observing the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), this should logically follow each of the ten stages (*daśa-yāna*).
Why is it placed here? Answer: Because it serves to break through [delusions] universally (*póbiàn*), it is convenient to apply this pattern at this point.

Therefore, from here downward until the section on "detachment from craving" (*li-ài*), one observes the five aggregates to discern their pervasions and obstructions (*tōng-sè*), as well as to examine the truths, conditions, and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The primary [practice] is the direct aid, while the auxiliary practices consist of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). In the lower three stages, one merely contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.
Next, in the section on questions and answers, the initial question is as stated in the text. In the response, the causes and conditions for entering emptiness are addressed.

First is the general response; "Which ones... and below is the detailed enumeration. "Now, regarding birth and death... and below is the specific explanation. This can be understood by comparing it with the five [aggregates]. One should know that this must be combined with the great [entry into] the provisional (*saṃvṛti*).

The same applies to liberation from oneself, which is identical to great compassion; liberation for others, which is identical to the original vow; the life of wisdom, which is identical to beneficial knowledge;

the untainted state, which is identical to skillful means; and the various stages, which are identical to diligence. Because they provisionally dwell after the realization of emptiness, it is said that they "follow the subsequent.

Regarding the section on the contemplation of emptiness below, the answer concerns the four gates of the provisional and the non-existent. Whether in the Small Canon or the Great Expansion, whether partial or perfect, all involve the destruction of view-delusions and thought-delusions to enter into emptiness.

[This concludes the] section on the stages. However, because the gates [of classification] differ, one must distinguish between them. Regarding the "obstruction of wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), I shall cite the interpretation of this term by an ancient master.
Dharmottara—translated here as Fashang—personally compiled the essential meanings of various sūtras, titling it the *Ekottarāgama-saṃgraha*.
The Great Master cites many refutations [of this view]. Since these are the positions of others, he briefly relies upon their explanations.

First, he raises an objection: "Wisdom has departed. He answers: "Realized wisdom resides in the Buddha; consciousness belongs to the two vehicles. That which cuts off delusions is called wisdom; that which is shallow and superficial is called consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "realizing the essence," "essence" refers to the true principle (*tattva*). Even a minor wisdom that contradicts the principle is still termed a "conformable perception" (*anuloma-saṃjñā*). Furthermore, it [is distinct] from that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

Because wisdom acts as an obstruction, it is called the "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the Buddha’s statement concerning the two obstructions—namely, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and [the obstruction] to wisdom—the text next cites the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* as proof;
"mind" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*), and "realization" refers to realized wisdom. Next, citing the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it explains the meaning of *nirvāṇa*:
they are merely different names for wisdom.
The subsequent section below further explains the "wisdom-liberation" (prajñā-vimukti) of the *Bhūmisaṃgraha*.
That is to say, ignorance obstructing realized wisdom is termed the "obstruction to knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa). Because one destroys ignorance, one attains wisdom free from obstructions.

Next, the introduction of the Mahāyāna establishes that ignorance (*avidyā*) has the meaning of being an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Below the section on the "two obstructions," a difficult point is raised;

from the section on "ignorance" onwards, it is explained. Next, examples are cited to explain the obstruction to knowledge. Regarding the two types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), the points where they receive their names are distinct.
Ignorance is also like this. As with the birth-and-death of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the explanation below regarding "craving" shows that afflictions (*kleśa*) are distinct from ignorance.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself wisdom (*jñāna*). Because their natures and characteristics are mutually exclusive, it is said that delusion and awakening do not coexist.

As for what is called "unconditioned birth-and-death" (*asaṃskṛta-saṃsāra*), it refers to the "birth-and-death of expedient means" (*upāya-saṃsāra*) among the seven types of birth-and-death discussed in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra-śāstra*. Both this and the "birth-and-death of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-saṃsāra*) are unconditioned.
For the time being, we borrow the category of "expedient means" as an analogy for the relationship between wisdom and delusion.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Next, below" explains that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is classified as an affliction (*kleśa*), and thus is distinguished from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it arises from a fruit and the cause again reaches a fruit, it is called "continuous," which refers to its functional capacity. The phrase "It can cause... explains the name [of craving]. Although the passage beginning with "Even though ignorance...
explains the function of ignorance, since the two operations are distinct, the two meanings are not equivalent.

Below "Ignorance" (*avidyā*): This correctly explains that ignorance is an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Although both [ignorance and afflictions] are liberated together, their names differ because the branches and the root are distinct.
Next, under "The nature of ignorance is delusion": This re-explains that ignorance is directly able to obstruct knowledge, thereby receiving the name "obstruction to knowledge."
Therefore, it is said that "the meaning is manifest.
Next, regarding the passage "Ignorance is of two kinds," and so forth, this distinguishes the names and natures as distinct, such that their obstructions differ. First, the intent of the question is:

although the objects of delusion differ, they are both equally named "ignorance" (*avidyā*); why then is ignorance alone termed the "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? Next, he cites the *Bhūmivastu* (The Stages of Yogic Practice) to provide a comprehensive response.
The names of the treatises are the same, yet their specific arguments must differ; since the subject and object are not identical, their designations cannot be the same.
"If this were so," and so forth, explains that the person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*) held by the *Dharmadhara* school are both objects of delusion and are both termed "principles" (*tattva*).

The wisdom of the two types of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya-jñāna*) is both termed "pure wisdom. Afflictions (*kleśa*) and [ignorant] cognition (*jñāna*) are both obstacles to the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, "wisdom removes... and so forth.
Because the wisdom regarding phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*) is obstructed, it receives the name "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If this is so, [the text] below raises a challenge to the preceding interpretation. Starting from the phrase "from the illumination of phenomena," it reconciles the two preceding interpretations; for there were two differing explanations by ancient masters:

some held that all phenomena are what are obstructed, while others held that ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which is capable of obstructing. The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) evaluates these views, and therefore...
It is said that there are no two [kinds of wisdom]. Although the objects illuminated differ, the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) is not distinct.

Furthermore, below the section on "Mind-Wisdom" (*citta-jñāna*), different interpretations are presented. First, under the section "There was a person," the intent clarifies that delusion regarding principle constitutes an obstruction to wisdom (*jñānāvaraṇa*).

By means of the cessation of thought, it cites the Lesser Vehicle for comparison; the vehicle of the cessation of thought is also called "cessation-wisdom" (*nirodha-jñāna*), yet this is a cessation through annihilation. Now, as for "cessation-wisdom" (*nirodha-jñāna*): [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Because the obstructing mind cannot be extinguished, the discriminating mind is in fact truly unextinguishable.
Furthermore, from "nor is it separate" (*na ca pṛthak*) onwards, there is a further explanation: within the Middle Way, wisdom is not separate, because their essence is identical;
therefore, it cannot be severed. Next, from "this is" (*ataḥ*) onwards, there is a citation of scriptural authority: merit is like ignorance, and bodhi is like wisdom.

The phrase "the person acts below" breaks the worldly attachment to views; it sees that whether there is cessation or non-cessation, the essence of wisdom is without distinction. The subsequent question explains away potential objections.

The *Ratnavali* (Yingluo) states only that the three contemplations manifest at the first stage (*bhūmi*). If this is so, why were they previously explained as a "dual flow" and now divided into three?

The answer is: they are established through mutual reliance on their meanings. Because the "agent" and the "object accomplished" stand in relation to one another, there are three. Although individually...

Regarding the provisional [teachings]: the *Ābhūṣaṇa* (Necklace) is the ultimate samādhi. By means of the textual structure of this samādhi, there are established levels of high and low. Because the high is borrowed to form the low, there is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

Because the lower stages borrow from the lower to form the high, there is the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-śāsana*). This single question-and-answer regarding the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is included here because it supplements what was omitted;
it does not concern the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). What follows is not sequential.

Essential Notes on the Subsidaries to the Practice of Calming and Contemplation, Fascicle Seven.

In the initial explanation of "penetration and obstruction" (*tong-sai*), first is the brief title; next, within the "purpose of the coming," there are the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.

Within the Dharma, first is the purpose of the coming, followed by the summary of birth. The refutation of pervasiveness concludes the preceding section. One should enter the following section on birth, which then employs the three names together regarding the faults in the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*).

It is necessary to now examine these three names through penetration and obstruction; if one does not so examine them, one fears falling into the same errors as the various outsiders (*bāhya*). If [this] were not the case...

Regarding "loss," it refers to the refutation based on prior progression. As for the term "unilaterally," it means one should not constantly maintain the refutation of pervasion without further investigation;
therefore, this section is established to examine the prior refutation of pervasion.

What follows below clearly explains the purpose of this coming section. Since those who can give rise to attachment are similar to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they should be examined and refuted by means of the four propositions regarding penetration and obstruction.
Therefore, one must employ the four propositions and the three types of provisional designation (*trividha-prajñapti*) to refute the mind that clings.

Just as the wisdom that clings is refuted in the same manner as the delusions it clings to, it is said that "the refuting [wisdom] is like that which is refuted. Although one does not cling to the subject (*grāhaka*), one still clings to the object (*grāhya*); hence, it is said:

If one is not attached to [the subject] and so forth, then one can break that which is not as it should be broken; thus, one merely employs the "pervasive breaking" (*pòbiàn*). For this reason, one must distinguish by means of two phrases:
first, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which can pervasively block what is to be blocked, as in the aforementioned pervasive breaking;

second, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which pertains to that which gives rise to attachment, as in the present case of pervasion and obstruction. Therefore, the text says: "The characteristics of dharmas may, according to their nature, involve either pervasion or obstruction."

How much more so when one gives rise to [notions of] suffering, its origin, and so forth within that state. Within this, there are four aspects: first, the horizontal; second, the vertical; third, the distinct; and fourth, the single mind.
While there are four textual divisions, they convey two meanings, with the intent resting upon the single mind.

Within each of these meanings, one employs a fourfold analysis: first, attaining penetration within obstruction; second, obstruction within penetration; third, obstruction remaining as obstruction; and fourth, penetration remaining as penetration.
This is the general principle. The first two cases pertain to the present; the latter two belong to what precedes. By entering into the current text, the first two phrases are established.

Next, in the section presenting the analogies, the "removal of cataracts" serves as a partial analogy, while the "defeat of bandits" serves as a comprehensive analogy. The bandit leader can be protected by the jewel, but the cataracts cannot be so protected.
"If that is so," and so forth, is the synthesis. First is the formal synthesis; next is the explanation of the meaning of "five hundred *yojanas*.

This is because the meaning involves both penetration and obstruction. Thus, the Sūtra says: "One who well understands penetration and obstruction may employ refutation and establishment to fulfill the present intent. Question:

Regarding the refutation of the first master, it was stated that [the stages] are not the seventh or eighth grounds, as these properly belong to the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Why, then, do you say they are not? Answer: This employs the intended meaning of the *Śāstra* (Treatise) to explain. By means of...

The exhaustion of afflictions within the boundary constitutes the six stages; exiting and entering the city constitutes the seventh and eighth stages. Therefore, for now, the seventh and eighth stages are used to refute [the opponent's position], which they claim contradicts the treatise.
This master uses the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* as a general authority but does not understand the intended meaning of that citation; thus, he cites it to refute [the opponent].

The latter two schools both calculate the afflictions (*kleśa*) to total five hundred. The former school does not count the *rajas* (dust-like secondary afflictions), while the latter school does not count the views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, in the "Discernment of Errors," these points are no longer further refuted.

Below this, the text refutes the ancient masters according to the Sūtra. Regarding the section "The Various Masters," it distinguishes their errors: first in general, then in detail. Within the general discussion, the specific points are as follows:

[the fault of] being too expansive is like a square that is overly large; [the fault of] being too pervasive is like a circle that is overly large; the *dāna* practice of the Two Vehicles is like excessive movement; and establishing a city within the realm is like excessive stillness.
Although each [interpretation] relies on a single meaning, the points of error are many; thus, it is not yet permissible to judge the intent of the Perfect Sūtra.
For instance, those who hold to the "single milk" analogy and others are each biased toward two views, making it difficult to explain the general principle.
First, regarding the first school’s distinct judgment: it judges only the first four [stages] and omits the latter two. The judgment of the first school states:

"The establishment of the city at the fourth hundred" refers to the seventh and eighth stages (*bhūmi*), which also belong to the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As the Sūtra says, "the establishment of the city at the third hundred";

according to this master, in relation to the fourth hundred, this constitutes the "establishment of the city at the fourth hundred. Regarding the "Inclusive School" (*Shèjiā*): Master Shè established seven kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), but he only employs...
The first five [stages] do not include the latter two, as you have explained. Beyond the Jewel Island (*ratnadvīpa*), there still remain the latter two;

therefore, it is called "severed" (*cheda*). Just as that which lies beyond the frontier regions is called "beyond the wilderness," the furthest lands are designated as "remote wilderness," like the Jewel Island.

Next, regarding the classification of the stages: as for establishing cities within the boundaries, those who dwell therein face the two hundred [afflictions], and their dwelling consists in severing the views and the afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Is it not the case that [the previous masters] established the "city of transformation" (nirvāṇa) at two hundred [yojanas]? Furthermore, the second school takes the two vehicles as the basis for four hundred or five hundred [yojanas], yet they speak only of abiding at three hundred;
now it is said to be four hundred. Is this not because the practice of *dāna* (giving) opens up the provisional (*upāya*) so that one may advance?

Moreover, before the provisional is opened, there is no mention of the name "two. Thus, prior to the opening of the provisional, it is called *dāna*. How much more so once it has been opened—how could it then be contrasted with three or four?

[The section] "The Master of Men" (Renshi) below explains away doubts. Fearing that those who see this treatise might harbor suspicions—specifically, wondering why the initial school’s argument, which correctly identifies the two vehicles as four hundred [yojanas], is being refuted—he first sets forth the text of the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "two passages," the beginning of the treatise also states: "One wishes to pass through a perilous road of four hundred yojanas.
At the beginning of the treatise, the desire realm is taken as one hundred, and so on up to the two vehicles as four.
One hundred. Furthermore, it is said that another four hundred [yojanas] constitute the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), continuing down to one hundred for the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Beyond these four hundred, one approaches the City of Bodhi. Now, following the general explanation below, I shall set forth the meaning of the treatise.

Now, following the section "Clarifying the Lower Part," the formal explanation begins; only then can it be called an exegesis of the sutra. If that were so, five hundred *yojanas* would be the very place of the treasure, yet the sutra says one must "pass beyond" it.
Therefore, we now rely on the sutra and explain it through three meanings. If explained in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), only then can it be said that one "passes beyond";

the other two [meanings] do not involve passing beyond. Thus it is said: "The wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness knows three hundred [yojanas]," and so forth; here, "knowing" is itself "passing beyond. First, this is explained in relation to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

All five hundred [types of fetters] are thus transcended. Therefore, they are not treated as separate from the "peaceful" (śānta) first. Next, regarding the afflictions: because views (dṛṣṭi) pertain to all three realms, they constitute one [category].

Because the lower-tier fetters (avarabhāgīya) bind one to the lower [realms], they constitute one; because the upper-tier fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya) bind one to the upper [realms], they constitute one. As for the lower-tier fetters:

The lower fetters are: the view of a self, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will. The higher fetters are: restlessness, pride, ignorance, attachment to the realm of form, and attachment to the formless realm.

Furthermore, the phrase "all those below" is a concluding censure. Because the teachings of these various masters are provisional (*upāya*), their status is high; yet within those provisional teachings, they fail to provide a complete explanation.
Therefore, what follows correctly uses the categories of horizontal and vertical to judge them, thereby clarifying the dharma practiced by those who rely on the provisional.

Whether horizontal or vertical, both are refuted as being five hundred [kalpas] away; however, because they are not realized in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), they are judged to belong to the provisional. To be far removed is to be distant; this refers to the two extremes.

This is because [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] establishes five hundred [stages] separately from the external [stages]. Therefore, according to the first master and the *Yogācārabhūmi* masters, these [five hundred] are subsumed within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

according to the Master [Vasubandhu], they are subsumed within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If that were so, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would be excluded from them. If those five hundred were exclusively for noble ones (*ārya*), the Sūtra should not have said, "in order to cause sentient beings [to attain enlightenment].

If they necessarily all reside in the [ten] stages, then those who have received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) as belonging to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) should no longer be in the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). Now, based on the True Teaching (*saddharma*), there are six...
They then divided it accordingly. Thus, the Dharma Master did not disparage those of the Two Vehicles; the Dragon Girl did not indiscriminately confuse their respective merits;
and each of the eight Ganges-sands of beings maintained what they had attained.

Now, the discussion below provides the formal explanation. First, the transverse and vertical; next, the single mind. The first [section] has three meanings: first, the transverse; second, the vertical; third, the distinct transverse. Regarding the first, the transverse, it is as the text states.
Regarding the second, the vertical, there are two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the vertical; second, using the transverse to interweave with the vertical.

The three aspects of the vertical are like the warp of a cloth, while the three aspects of the transverse are like the woof. By weaving them together, the textual pattern of the Three Truths is formed. These three include suffering, its origin, and so forth.

If there are no warp threads, there are likewise no woof; this is also a matter of inspection. It causes each of the three [realms] to be free from the three [truths] such as suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
Entering into emptiness is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the reduction to emptiness, beginning with suffering and its origin, followed by the phrase "neither...

nor" regarding causes and conditions. Third, from "not extinguished" onwards, it addresses the six obscurations (*āvaraṇa*); it mentions stinginess alone as a representative example. Next, it cites the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to prove the six obscurations. An obscuration is precisely a blockage. [The preceding...]

The same applies to the second [category]. Zhanran’s *Jingpan* (Judgment on the Sūtras) states: "These are the bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas. If one is at the lower level of the three penetrations (*santong*), one should employ the lower [level] for inspection and management.

Regarding the phrase "one by one" (*yi-yi*): this refers to not distinguishing between subject and object, nor even the mental factors (*citta-dharma*). Where there is an obstruction, it must be broken. Regarding the phrase "mental factors and so forth": "mind" (*xin*) refers to the analysis of the essence;

the "mental factors" of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) refer to the contemplation of the provisional (*jiaguān*). These correspond to the three [contemplations], such as "knowing the illness" (*zhībìng*).
Furthermore, within the Madhyamaka [system], the three factors such as ignorance (*avidyā*) each possess both a subjective capacity and an objective referent.

Moreover, the mind that acts as the perceiver and the phenomena that serve as its objects must both be scrutinized. Next, below [this point], the characteristics of initial penetration and obstruction within the emptiness of essence are shown.

As in the section on the Arhat, how much more so [for others]. If one calculates [the following], it demonstrates suffering and its origin: karmic activity is the origin (*samudaya*), and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is suffering (*duḥkha*). If not... [the cause].

Regarding the conditions: if one descends into craving, there are the six obscurations; here too, only the single function of stinginess (*mātsarya*) is cited. "Immediately empty" below refers to the investigation [of emptiness].

"In the context of illness" below refers to the investigation of emerging into the provisional (*upāya*). Question: When entering into emptiness, it is called "mind" (*citta*); when entering into the provisional, it is called "dharmas" (*dharma*).

Why, at the beginning, is it said that each and every thing is "mind-dharmas"? Answer: As previously explained, both interpretations contain this meaning. If discussing mind and dharmas separately, it corresponds to the first interpretation.
Next, regarding the investigation: returning to the middle path, it is approximately as explained in the "Pervasive Destruction" (*póbiàn*). Within this, the discourse is abbreviated;
it simply states that ignorance and the dharma-nature are truly conditions, and one must investigate each point accordingly.
The passage beginning with "In this way" (如此下) refutes the provisional [teaching]. The six stages (六地) belong to the Shared [Vehicle], while the first stage (初地) belongs to the Distinct [Vehicle].

How could one reach the other shore of the five hundred [kalpas] by such means? The passage beginning with "The Great Sūtra" (大經下) establishes the provisional [teaching]. Altogether there are four textual passages: the tenth says, "After such kalpas, one shall attain Bodhi";
the nineteenth says, "one arrives"; the twentieth says, "one attains"; and the twenty-first says, "one abides. Although the words differ...
All [the preceding] differences have already been enumerated.
Next, the horizontal distinctions are explained: first the principle (dharma), then the analogy. Within the principle, the characteristics are first distinguished by means of three types of persons;

for each, the characteristic of contemplation is first clarified, followed by the analysis of investigation. These three horizontal distinctions exist because, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there is one person for each category.

The passage beginning with "In this way" below refutes the provisional [teachings]. It further cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to prove the horizontal distinction [between teachings]. First is the analogy, followed by the application. In the analogy, the *Śāstra* says:

"For example, when traveling on a road, one may ride a sheep or other [animals]; because they differ, the destination reached is not the same. Now, [the text] substitutes "walking" for "riding a sheep," yet it is no different from walking.
Only by relying on the True Teaching (*saddharma*) can the provisional be refuted. Next, regarding "one mind": first, the horizontal [distinctions] are refuted.
Vertical. Next, the single mind is correctly elucidated. First, the two aspects of "penetration" (*tong*) and "obstruction" (*se*) are listed again; these correspond to the first two contemplations.

Within their respective stages, they are termed "penetrating" as each has its own object to be shattered. However, insofar as they have not yet shattered ignorance when viewed from the perspective of the middle [contemplation], they are considered "obstructions. Next, the middle contemplation excels the other two. Since the middle...
Separated by two [stages], the middle again becomes obstructed; this can be inferred by analogy for the horizontal [directions].

Below, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), let alone the emergence of obstruction within what is currently described as penetration—where the characteristics of penetration and obstruction have already been established—even if one gives rise to obstruction within that which is penetrating, and even if, in relation to the perfect penetration, both are obstructed.
Next, the single mind is correctly elucidated. The preceding refutation of the pervasive [view] has already established the single mind; herein, too, one should maintain only the single mind.
This also establishes the preceding sequence through its own sequence, and likewise achieves the preceding single mind through the single mind itself.

Furthermore, this is also a horizontal equality. To manifest the single mind, there are again the three types of horizontal equality; these, when compared to the refutation which is purely vertical, lack the internal horizontal [distinctions]. Thus, by means of the single mind...

Regarding the statement that "the single mind and three contemplations destroy the vertical, while the three contemplations and the single mind destroy the horizontal," this is spoken for the sake of convenience in order to refute both the horizontal and the vertical;
it is also the case that the one and the three together destroy both the horizontal and the vertical, with no other separate path.

"Excellent and below. This is a formal praise of the functional capacity [of the two gates]. Regarding "able to destroy the various māras such as the horizontal [māras]," *māra* refers specifically to celestial *māras*, while *dao* (path) refers to non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
Alternatively, the names "māra" and "path" may be applied broadly, as they encompass both the partial and the small [vehicles].

Regarding "ultimately not equal," this follows the sequence where foot-soldiers and cavalry follow the barbarians, and supernatural powers avoid those below; likewise, the two contemplations follow the barbarians, while the Middle Way avoids those below. Now, it is not so.
It is the same as that [preceding case]. Therefore, it says "never" (*zhōng bù*). The two characters "never" govern the following two sentences.

Regarding the phrase "if one, below," this clarifies the intent of the "one mind. Although the one mind does not correspond to the horizontal [delusions] and so forth, if one gives rise to obstruction and attachment within the one mind, it conversely becomes the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). How then could one eliminate them? Therefore, it says "not only," and so forth.
If one examines with single-mindedness at the lower level, this constitutes the lower-level correct judgment.
Next, regarding the detailed analysis: first, the differentiation of alternative names. The question is self-evident. In the answer, there is first a general explanation followed by a specific one.

Within the specific explanation, there are three parts. Regarding "words based on understanding": understanding arises from the teaching. Regarding "words based on practice": practice arises from understanding. These words are precisely...
Regarding the teaching: although the three meanings derived from it differ, they are mutually dependent, such that their substance is identical while their designations vary.
The passage from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* below collectively validates these three meanings.

Next, the distinctions between the pervasive and the obstructed are clarified. Regarding the four questions posed [in the text], these are formulated based on the initial horizontal and vertical dimensions.

To make this clear, the preceding text is cited again: the Four Truths and so forth constitute horizontal pervasion; Suffering, Accumulation, and so forth constitute horizontal obstruction; Emptiness, Provisionality, and so forth constitute vertical pervasion;

and the Views and Afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and so forth constitute vertical obstruction. These are paired with one another to form the four questions. Although the phrasing is thus, [the underlying principle remains the same].

However, the intent of this question is as follows: although the three delusions and the three wisdoms constitute vertical penetration and obstruction, it specifically points to ignorance (*avidyā*) and the wisdom of the Middle Way as the vertical penetration and obstruction, because they represent the highest and ultimate state.
If one were to horizontally identify the vertical, then although it is said to reach the Middle, when explained from the beginning, it remains merely within "immediate emptiness.

Therefore, in the subsequent text, the three—view-delusion, thought-delusion, and the three [delusions]—are pointed out as horizontal and vertical; that is, immediate emptiness is the True Truth (*satyadharma*).
He considered this to be a horizontal penetration (*tiṅtōng*).

The question was posed in a general manner, but the answer divided it into two parts: first, he established two paths; second, he explained the two meanings. First, he provisionally accepted [the premise], stating that whether it be horizontal or vertical...
They alternate between being mutually penetrating and obstructive; in principle, this corresponds to the Sudden [teaching]. Thus, it may be said that the single nature is likewise so.

If one follows the previous question and still perceives the remaining two [aspects], then one should further state: the horizontal, the middle, the truths, the conditions, and the means can also destroy ignorance.

The horizontal obstructs while the vertical penetrates; the truths of suffering and its origin veil the middle principle. Regarding the statement that there are two natures, the horizontal and vertical differ, each having its own penetration and obstruction.
Because one wishes to open up the subsequent answer, the former is termed "provisional."

Next, the explanation of the *mārga-varga* (Chapter on the Path) first enumerates the four characteristics. There are four aspects in the text and four meanings; the intent is to achieve balanced harmony. Generally speaking, these apply to both the Great and Small Vehicles;

specifically, the third [characteristic] pertains to the Small Vehicle, while the remaining three pertain exclusively to the Great Vehicle. As for the "distinctive" (*pratyeka*) aspect, this is because the seven categories of entry into the path do not depend upon one another.

This is stated as "the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and so forth from the perspective of the distinctive meaning. If considered from the general perspective, each teaching has its own distinct application.

Regarding "mutual inclusion" (*xiāngshè*): each section and category encompasses the others. Regarding "stages" (*yuèwèi*): as in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), where the four teachings differ.

Regarding "arising through characteristics" (*xiāngshēng*): the seven categories unfold sequentially, with the former giving rise to the latter; for this reason, the subsequent text is also termed "arising through characteristics.
Although there are these four types of textual divisions, they do not contradict one another across the preceding and following sections.

The reason for coming down [to this level] is as follows: first, it briefly clarifies the breaking through of pervasiveness and the penetration of obstructions. If one does not awaken to this, it is because there is no meditative adjustment (*pratipakṣa*).

Regarding the "True Dharma" below, it explains what is realized through the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*): the stages prior to abiding, the stages of abiding, and the partial fulfillment and full fulfillment of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. Therefore, from the perspective of the stage of names (*nāmadheya*), it serves as the cause for the First Abiding (*prathama-vihāra*).

The meaning within the parable is as follows: the True Dharma abiding in delusion is like water; the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are like a fermented brew that, when blended, produces the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

Next, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) to prove its function as the outflow-free: the *Śāstra* opens the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) through impurity, up to opening nirvāṇa through the three liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Nirvāṇa is termed "outflow-free. Although the wording of the treatise appears to belong to the Hīnayāna, it is not exclusively so.

Next, in the section on critical analysis (*liaojian*), first there is the analysis of the Great and Small Vehicles. This initial question and answer appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Dazhidu lun*).

The subsequent text also answers according to the intent of that same treatise. Next, three sūtras are cited to assist the treatise. Since the intent of the answer states that "attaining Buddhahood means seeing one's nature," how could the "Jewel Torch" (*Ratnolkā*) possibly belong to the Small Vehicle?

Following the passage "If [you say it is] the Great Sūtra," the text refutes the claim that it belongs exclusively to the Small Vehicle, and subsequently grants a concession, stating that it is common to both the Great and Small Vehicles.

[The path] is small because the gate of the teaching is thus; how could it be restricted by human sentiment? This also serves to resolve a doubt. The doubt says: "Since the directions are immeasurable and vast, the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) should be small.
The resolution says: "Although they are immeasurable, they are nothing other than the factors of the path; therefore, one knows they are not small. Next, he cites the [Four Noble] Truths:
since the factors of the path are one among those four, he cites them as an illustration. Regarding the phrase "nail-clipping dust," the Buddha took a small amount...
He placed the earth on his fingernail and asked Kāśyapa, "Which is greater: this earth or the earth of the ten directions? Kāśyapa replied, "It cannot be compared to the earth of the ten directions.
Now, using these words as a means of comparison for the Four Noble Truths: although they are immeasurable, they do not transcend the Four Noble Truths.
As for what are called the sixteen aspects, each aspect fully possesses them all.

Furthermore, there is the "outflow" (āsrava) category below. This is determined according to the five flavors (*pañca-rasa*). Since the preceding objections were applied throughout sixteen gates, it is said to be "immeasurable.

Therefore, it is determined by means of the five flavors; these five are immeasurable. Regarding the initial mention of "with outflows" (*sāsrava*): since they are all subsumed within the realms (*dhātu*), they belong to the category of being with outflows. Regarding the "twenty-two," etc., the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there are twenty-two [factors], excluding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the path (*mārga*). [This excludes] the threshold state (*anāgamya*)."

Thirty-six [factors]. Excluding the awakening-factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). In the first dhyāna there are thirty-seven; in the second dhyāna there are thirty-six. Excluding right application (*samyak-pradhāna*), which is identical to right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

In the third and fourth dhyānas, as well as the intermediate dhyāna, there are only thirty-five. Excluding right application and the three [factors] beginning with joy. In the formless realms (*ārūpya*) there are thirty-two.

Excluding the awakening-factors of joy and right application, as well as right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), right resolve (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). In the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) there are twenty-two, the same as above.

Having previously excluded the factors of awakening and the path, [the text] next—following the words "or" (*vā*) and below—discriminates between the primary and auxiliary practices to resolve doubts regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The doubt is as follows:

"Previously, Aśvaghoṣa was cited as an auxiliary practice; why is he now further presented here as the primary? Therefore, the general meaning of the teaching’s approach is used to answer this. It is not merely...
Because it is focused on one [aspect], it now achieves perfection. Therefore, how could the text concerning the five flavors be restricted to only one kind?

Furthermore, the phrase "if one says" below distinguishes between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), because the five flavors were initially established based on the tainted; thus, this objection is raised.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The seven factors of enlightenment are exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Now, for what reason is it said here that they are all contaminated?

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is cited to establish their uncontaminated nature. Regarding the passage beginning with "How so," this further challenges the text of the *Vibhāṣā*: since the seven factors of enlightenment belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they ought to follow the eightfold noble path.

This should be moved down. [The author] answers: Because this is indeterminate, it is separated [from the others] to form three categories. First they are listed; next they are explained. First, there is a brief explanation of the *sāsrava* (with-outflows):

"All are... and so on. Next, the *anāsrava* (without-outflows): "From the beginning... and so on. This may be taken as the formal treatise (*śāstra*). However, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* explains the third point:

"If the eight [liberations] were all *sāsrava*, then those preceding them would also be *sāsrava*. If the eight [liberations] were all *anāsrava*, then those preceding them would also be *anāsrava*. [Thus,] the Sūtra...

The general principle of this treatise belongs to the second intention. Furthermore, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, from the foundations of mindfulness up to the Eightfold Noble Path, each possesses two meanings.

Within the section on the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), the correct exposition of the factors of the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga*) constitutes the primary intention here; it is further employed to harmonize with the initial text.

The intent [of the passage] is also termed "taking and rejecting. There are seven textual sections and seven meanings; the underlying purpose lies in benefiting others according to their needs. This is a general clarification of the intent; the specific discussion follows later.

This transformation involves both the simultaneous inclusion (*sahabhū*) and the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, regarding the contrast, if one refutes that which is being contrasted, then one must transform; if one does not refute it, then the simultaneous inclusion and so forth must be applied.

Therefore, these are collectively presented as the "transformational formulas" (*parivarta*). As for what is called "transformation," it refers to the progression from the *śīla* (precept) to *prajñā* (wisdom), whether by sequential or skipping methods;

skipping from one to four, alternating between reverse and direct order, until the afflictions are eliminated, which constitutes "crossing over. With the five perfections as the primary heads, they merely transcend their original positions; the rest are the same as in the case of *dāna* (generosity).
This is a treatment where the affliction itself does not transform, but the treatment transforms. One perfection has five phrases; thus, the six perfections constitute three [sets].
There are ten phrases. When the remedy and the disease both proceed simultaneously, there are thirty phrases consisting of both "confrontation" (*pratipakṣa*) and "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*).

There are another thirty phrases where there is transformation but no confrontation. Furthermore, there are cases of skipping or intervening, which vary according to the specific circumstances. If the transformation extends to the fourth [stage], it is termed "transformation with combined names."
If it proceeds to five, it is called "proceeding" (pravartana) but not "complete" (samanvāgata). It is not called complete because it proceeds by way of individual dharmas.

If all six functions are present, only then is it called complete. If it proceeds to five and is not called complete, then "proceeding" is single-functioned, whereas "completeness" involves simultaneity.
If the illness shifts while the medicine does not shift, it is not a case of shifting both together;

rather, it may be treated in a single direction, or within the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of illness, there are also variations of transcendence, conformity, and alternation. Accordingly, for each single illness, these shift into five obscurations, which likewise comprise thirty phrases.
A single phrase is the treatment. As for what is called "comprehensive," it encompasses from one to four; when the four phrases are distinguished individually, they form twenty-four.

Taken together, there are only six phrases. This concerns treatment according to phenomena (*dharma*). The three teachings should be understood accordingly. If it pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one employs only a single principle to treat manifold ailments;
this should also be understood as the teaching employing the principle of its own school to constitute the ultimate truth—this is termed the "comprehensive meaning" (*sāmānya-artha*).

They are distinct. Those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan) also employ the principles of the three vehicles as their counterparts; thus, one knows that the four teachings unfold sequentially, with each preceding one assisting the subsequent.
Furthermore, although the principle of the Perfect Teaching is itself termed the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha), it is also called a "counterpart" due to its function of remedial application.

Below the section on "Aiding the Six Perfections," there follows a further general clarification of the method for practicing them in unison. In all four teachings, one practices in unison according to the principles of each respective teaching.

Under the heading "Some people," the author intends to clarify this unified practice; however, he first presents alternative interpretations, clarifying that the ten [perfections] and the six [perfections] are merely different ways of classifying and combining them, lest they be confused.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* explains this through its religious doctrine: the Sūtra states that for those who study the Three Vehicles together, there is both realization and teaching;
taking realization as the "essence" (*zong*) and teaching as the "doctrine" (*jiao*). Ancient scholars did not understand this and divided it into the Great and Small Vehicles.
Next, two sūtras are cited to prove the sixfold inclusion of dharmas (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-saṃgraha*). "If one attains... and below briefly indicates the meaning of the text. "As in dhyāna...
and below correctly demonstrates the opening and closing [of the categories]. Because they are combined, it is like the union of phenomenon and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*) in practice;

when separated, they are merely explained as distinct phenomena and principles. Furthermore, *ni-ra* and *jñāna*, and *bra-hma* and *bala*, differ only in sound. The two passages concerning dhyāna and wisdom both use the term "guarding" (*rakṣa*).
As for the "root," once it has been opened up according to its nature, it retains its own original name.

Next, to clarify the inclusion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃgraha*): this is truly due to the practice of integration (*saṃprayoga*). If there were no practice of integration, how could the qualities of the fruit (*phalaguṇa*) and the principle (*tattva*) be included?

First, regarding the clarification that the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) include the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*): even in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which represents the Hīnayāna, eleven [factors] are used to include the thirty [factors].
7. Now, these eleven [factors] are subsumed into the six perfections; their meanings merge and harmonize. This can also be understood by comparing the great [categories] with the small.

Therefore, in the *Vibhāṣā*, the seven factors of enlightenment are taken as the basis, and all classifications are included within the seven. Furthermore, the two types of faith are combined into one.

Right thought constitutes one [factor]. Of the three—vocal action, bodily action, and livelihood—their substantial entities are only two. Together with these, they total eleven. As for the remaining factors included within the seven, reflect upon them according to the present principle.

It is clear that within the perfection of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right application (*samyak-pradhāna*) should be properly combined. Therefore, in the text, there is an extensive treatment based on the ten realms. Regarding "the physical body" (*rūpakāya*) and so forth:

One simply contemplates these three matters: within the dharma-realm and the ten realms, these three matters naturally vanish. The environmental retribution is "wealth"; the primary retribution is the "body";

and "life" refers to the continuous sustenance. This is so for each of the ten realms. What is here called a single thought-moment is the complete presence of the three truths within the three matters of the ten realms.

"Why is this? [The text] below provides the explanation. Within this, first there is the explanation, followed by the citation of scripture; first the citation, then the explanation. Regarding the term "indestructible" (*abhedya*):

it refers to penetrating the body of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and perceiving the principle of eternal abiding (*nitya-dharma*). It serves as an antidote to stinginess (*mātsarya*) and further reveals the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since the body is thus, [it is indestructible].

Wealth and life are to be understood accordingly. Next, because the Vajra-holder possesses the three types of *prajñā*, the *dharmatā* (ultimate reality) sustains the body, whereby he relinquishes all bodies;
contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*) sustains life, whereby he relinquishes all lives; and the written word (*vyañjana*) sustains wealth, whereby he relinquishes all wealth.

Thus, the written word sustains contemplative insight, and contemplative insight sustains the *dharmakāya*; all three are real. Furthermore, by practicing these three, one accords with the three aspects of principle.

Therefore, the manifestation of principle depends upon the three relinquishments, and the three relinquishments depend upon the manifestation of principle. All of these take the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as their basis.
How could the four propositions possibly be compared to the body of relinquished phenomena?

The passage beginning with "In this way" below refutes partiality. Because partiality lacks integrated practice, such faults arise. Furthermore, when these two faults are compared, the former is superior in principle while the latter is inferior in fact.
Now, I urge you to practice; I fear that both may be lost. Regarding "carving the body," etc.: it refers to carving one's body into a thousand lamps to seek half a verse.
The verse says: "Born from heaven, one dies suddenly; this extinction is bliss. This "bliss" is a minor principle when compared to the present [practice], which involves both principle and fact.
"Caressing" (fǔ) means striking. "Protecting those below" refers to being unable to relinquish wealth; "refraining from speech" refers to being unable to relinquish one's body;
and "greedily cherishing" refers to being unable to relinquish one's life.

Now, regarding the section below: "Establishing practice and requesting empowerment. Only when one possesses the four factors, such as self-restraint and so forth, can empowerment be conferred. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From refraining from killing oneself up to the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), it is likewise for the three [other] actions—teaching others and so forth.

When one performs these practices, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) become thin. Therefore, one should practice these four kinds of superior conduct; the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fulfill them. These four are explained at length in the treatises.
[This] clarifies that if any of these four factors are mutually lacking, the ultimate fruit cannot be accomplished.
