Furthermore, the characteristics of the five practices are explained in detail in the commentary (*śāstra*). Among the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these correspond to the stage of the five *sthāpanā-citta* (stabilizing the mind) in the Tripiṭaka system.
Why is this? Because one removes doubt and distraction by following the principle; one removes miscellaneous seeking through recitation and chanting;

one removes delusion regarding the principle through all six perfections (*pāramitā*) by teaching the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); and one removes obstacles regarding phenomena through correct practice. If that is so, then [this] is common...

What is the distinction? The answer is: the distinct [teaching] merely stabilizes the mind through concentration and wisdom; the common [teaching] requires seeing all five aggregates as being like an illusion.

Furthermore, below this, it is explained again by way of the stages of the aggregates and sense bases (*skandha-āyatana*). Although the previous [explanation] was exclusively the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the present one applies to all teachings. Regarding the "five types of persons":

these refer to the two vehicles at the stage of fruition, and the latter three, or those Bodhisattvas who have severed [the afflictions]. Since these latter four virtues correspond to the semblance [stage],...
[The preceding stages] were all subsumed under the three bodhisattvas.

Next, regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*): because the five grades [of practice] completely suppress [the afflictions], the coarse delusions are first eliminated; thus, this specific stage is established.

Since there is no other stage called "Ten Faiths" in various treatises that involves the severing of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), a detailed explanation is provided in full in the *Yuan si nian chu* (Perfect Four Foundations of Mindfulness). Now...
This merely explains the initial stage of faith. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-vyākhyā* (Pusa jie shu) correlates this with the ten stages of practice through both horizontal and vertical correspondences;
one should understand that the sequence in the present text is slightly different from that work.

Next, regarding those who enter the stage of reality (*bhūmi*): this has been explained in detail in the *Śāstra on the Bodhisattva Precepts* and the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness*. Nevertheless, the stages of the sages are not to be conflated;
they are not within the scope of observation for ordinary beings. Therefore, in the various accounts of the sage-stages, only their functional capacities are set forth.
In the ninth section on patience (*kṣānti*), there is a combination of the Dharma, a simile, and their unification. Regarding the term "shuang" (爽) in the Dharma section, it means clarity.

In the simile, "fengren" (鋒刃) refers to a blade; furthermore, flying frost is used as a metaphor for this blade. "Cong" (聰) refers to being skilled at listening; "xinmin" (心敏) refers to a mind that is agile in affairs; and "rui" (叡) refers to profound clarity.
As for the "Chan masters of Ye and Luo," Ye was located in Xiangzhou, where the Qi and Wei dynasties were established as capitals and where the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly.
The flourishing of Chan patriarchs reached its peak here; however, out of consideration for the sentiments of the people of the time, their titles were not made public.
As for Wujin: he was a native of Wujin in Xingcheng, Chenzhou, on Mount Nanyue. At the time of his death, the Master Zhiyi consulted him regarding the essentials of Chan.
The Master then expounded for him the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), which left Zhiyi’s mind and eyes filled with wonder and awe. Zhiyi said, "I fear that the Master’s rank..."
"Ten Stages. The Master said: "I have merely purified the six sense faculties; the vow-text I composed is currently circulating in the world.
However, these four interpretations are intended to correspond with three methods, yet this is likely not the case. My intention in citing them now is to admonish future students:

they must exercise diligent discernment and apply themselves tirelessly. Thus I have stated it four times. The Great Master regarded Nanyue as a person of supreme excellence and bequeathed this [instruction]."
The *Yangui* may be taken as a mirror [for this].

Next, regarding the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the section on the *Dhyānapāramitā*, it asks: "If a bodhisattva manifests transformations for the sake of sentient beings, why does he remain in stillness and abandon them?
The answer states: "Though his body is far removed, his mind is not far removed; this is like the analogy of physical illness. (Thus it is said.)

Regarding the phrase "up to the purification of the six sense faculties" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), this statement initially relies upon the ultimate final stage. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Possessing afflictions, etc.

Regarding the "great elephant," here it is designated as "great" because of its long-standing practice; it is not the same as the "great" mentioned in the preceding text, which refers to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. "Hàn" means to resist or repel.

The character for "gé" (obstacle/resistance) should be written with the "earth" radical. The *Book of Rites* says: "If one waits until after [the transgression] has already manifested before attempting to prohibit it, it cannot be resisted or blocked."

The commentary states: "Hàn-jié" means firm and impenetrable. Since the five stages (*pañca-vastu*) were previously designated as the "small elephant," they must now be understood as the "great elephant.

Having transcended the bonds of the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*), neither favor nor opposition can be applied. The power of the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā-jñāna-bala*) is like the sun illuminating the world;
beginningless suffering is like vast ice. When the faculties (*indriya*) ripen and one attains benefit, it is called "self-governance."

If one is "equalized," it means that causing the observation of phenomena to disperse and perish is called internal invasion, while causing all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to be destroyed is called external exhaustion.
"Worms" refers to insects that harm things. Regarding the "three methods," they are as listed above: first, not receiving; second, shrinking virtue.

Within thirty thousand *li*, there are three methods, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*). External obstacles are "soft thieves," referring to things such as fame and reputation;
internal obstacles are "strong thieves," referring to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. Therefore, the methods employed internally and externally differ. *Vilana* refers to a violent wind;
if it were to blow upon Mount Sumeru, it would be like [blowing upon] withered grass. Wenju criticized the deficiency of meditation, regarding minor evils as either contraries or conformities.

"End. Therefore, one should examine oneself to ensure that [the vessel] does not break. Both the "broken vessel" and the "monk's robe flower" appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as metaphors for the beginner's mind.

"Heap" means a mound of earth. The monk's robe flower has few fruits. If one attains this meaning and so forth—meaning if one attains patience regarding the objects of the aggregates and purifies the six sense faculties—one has already contemplated and shattered the realm of the Bodhisattvas; how could there still be afflictions?
Is it equal? For such a person, one does not differentiate the lower nine stages.

Regarding the statement in the *Dharmāloka* (Ten Dharma-Love) that "practicing the upper nine matters breaks internal and external obstacles," although one may attain a semblance [of realization], [the obstacles remain].
Not yet having entered the true stage, there is indeed a state of attachment; being attached to this semblance is also called "falling from the summit" (*mūrdha-pāta*).
To fully traverse the four teachings and discern the stage of falling from the summit, one sees that all are merely the path of semblance (*sādṛśya-mārga*).

The first section, "Entrusting to the Three Teachings," begins with the phrase "Since they do not enter... and below that, it correctly elucidates the present stage. Regarding the first point, the Tripitaka [teaching]:

in the text, one first excludes those who are not in the stages of "Summit" (mūrdhan) or "Falling" (pātana), namely "Heat" (uṣmagata) and "Patience" (kṣānti). Since "Heat" invariably involves regression, whereas "Patience" is a stage free from regression, these two positions are neither "Summits" nor subject to "falling.

This is understood by analogy for the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), this occurs at the Ten Practices (daśa-pratipatti), where there is likewise no sense of falling, even if one has not yet entered [the Ten Dwellings].
"The ground is ultimately without the commission of faults.

(From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "Below," it indicates the stage resembling the Perfect [Stage], which possesses the characteristics of craving. "People of today," etc., clarifies that this is not related to other teachings.)

The six sense faculties merely "fall" by virtue of abiding at the summit; this is certainly not a retrogressive fall. Therefore, this stage of the summit differs from that in the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings].
Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two meanings for "falling from the summit": first, falling from the summit is called a fall; second, abiding at the summit is called a fall.

The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) also has two [stages], and even in its stage of abiding there is regression. Now, within the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), there is only one principle: abiding without regression.

Below this, in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is concluded and demonstrated: "Beyond this, these are not essential to this practice; therefore, they are set aside and not discussed. Thus it says, "up to this point.

Consequently, while various sūtras and śāstras extensively discuss the characteristics of the Buddha’s manifestation of transformative power (*nirmāṇa*) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they speak of them less frequently.

This explains the ritual for practicing the path of self-cultivation. Regarding the subsequent re-explanation, although its meaning refers specifically to the sphere of the Bodhisattva, as far as the vision of that sphere is concerned, other deficiencies are not discussed here.
This has already explained the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) through the Dharma-exposition; now, the text of the parable of the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is cited to further clarify them.

First, they are listed; next, they are applied [to the parable]. To understand the application of the text in full, one should consult the commentary (*vṛtti*). In summary, these are merely the ten dharmas, which fully employ the aforementioned meaning;

this is a brief correspondence. Next, regarding the conclusion of the stages: since the single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) is itself the great vehicle, it is thus complete within a single thought-moment.

The carriage possesses three virtues; its true nature is the vehicle-body, fully equipped with the means for accomplishment. The white ox is Prajñā, which begins from original existence and culminates at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

The six stages of realization are complete without deficiency. "Now" refers to those below [the stage of Buddhahood]. To "reject" (xie) is to borrow the character *xiè* (pronounced *jiě* in the ancient reading).
This establishes the name of the vehicle and its function of transporting one to the three evil realms; for its cause does not transcend the various views.

Below "the True Dharma" (saddharma): It is called "True Dharma" because it reveals that the correct [teaching] is not the same as the evil emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Controlling the Dharma without destruction is named the "Vajra City.
Being endowed with all dharmas is named the "Jewel Treasury" (*ratnakośa*). The explanation of "Jewel Treasury" is complete;

the explanation of "Vajra" is without deficiency. Emptiness refers to the principle (*tattva*); this is what is termed "bald emptiness" (*tuccha-śūnyatā*). Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is cited to refute and reject that view, for its principle lacks adornment.
It is called "ruination" because it is not subsumed within the three vehicles; it is called "donkey" because its grasping views are sharp and acute;

it is called "southern journey" because it constantly sits and contemplates the mind—this last point merely indicates the beginning of the four types of samādhi, hence the term "sitting upright," though the Dharma actually applies to all ritual postures.

Regarding the phrase "next, traversing conditions" (*kramena pratyaya*), this refers for now to the six types of sensation (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*). Therefore, all postures other than sitting upright are termed "other observances.
Regarding the three samādhis, these terms also apply generally to the beginner’s practice of the ten dharmas. This is a summary based on the lower [level].

Next, once the procedure has been performed, the remaining rituals follow by analogy. Next, the three [procedures] are performed three times each to resolve doubts. Next, within the section on confronting the objects: first, regarding the eye and form, ten factors are present;

next, this is extended by analogy to the other sense-objects. Within the section on the initial objects, as for the non-Buddhists striking skulls and so forth, in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha spoke with five [disciples].
One hundred bhikṣus traveled together to the Great Fear Forest. Taking all the skulls, they had Deer-Head strike them, whereby he fully knew the causes of death and the places of rebirth for each.
If even external dharmas are thus understood, how much more so should a Bodhisattva who has emerged from the provisional [teachings] regarding all dharmas? They are pure.

The phrase "characteristics of non-coming" and so forth refers to the six types of action (*kṛtya*), wherein one does not perceive characteristics in their performance. The phrase "perceiving through faculties and objects" refers to the six types of sensation (*vedanā*);
since both action and sensation are the Dharma-realm, the six [aspects] following the arousal of the mind can be understood through the power of intention.

Regarding the eight successive stages, if one perceives them gradually, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "If one can rectify the mind and rectify the intention, one will gradually see the Buddhas of the eastern direction with the eye of the mind;
first seeing one Buddha, and subsequently seeing all the Buddhas of the eastern direction, and so on until the ten directions.

Regarding instantaneous perception, the *Namo-aśoka-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging) states: "When that bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard the sūtra and received [its teachings]..."

"Maintaining [the practice] results in the purification of the six sense faculties; therefore, it is not called 'gradual. As for 'entering through the eye' and so forth, this refers to one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*).

Next, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* refers to one's own practice. That which transforms others is termed 'Buddha-work' (*buddha-kṛtya*). Next is the analogy. Regarding the disparagement of the black viper and so forth:"

The lizard and the long serpent merely snap their jaws; one who does not cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is like the long serpent, while one who skillfully understands *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and harbors the jewel is like the other.
Next, an analogy is introduced, each consisting first of the illustration followed by its application. "Shackles" (*xiè*) is a general term for weapons, and "jǐ" refers to a short spear.

Among the halberds, there is a small prong called the *xióngjí*. As for the passage concerning "the state's *qū* and *sàmi*" and so forth, this refers to the text from the appointment of Fúyuè by Yīn Gāozōng, the Minister of Revenue.

If one were to produce wine and sweet spirits using you as the *qū* and *sàmi*, the intended meaning is that the governance of the state is coordinated together, just as rice requires *qū* and *sàmi*.
*Sàmi* is also a type of *qū*. Regarding the frequent use of the term *bǐ*: *bǐ* means "to deviate" or "to be inconsistent."

Furthermore, when an army flees, it is said to be heading "north. Regarding the phrase "untying the hair-knot" (*jieji*) and so forth, the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "When virtue is eminent, confer office upon them;

when merit is eminent, confer rewards upon them. "Eminent" (*mao*) means "to exert oneself. The present "actual reward" (*shichang*) is the ultimate among rewards, as if bestowing a pearl. As for the "wild sorceress" (*yewu*), a male teacher is called a "sorcerer" (*wu*), while a female teacher is called a "seer" (*xi*).
*Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll Seven;
*Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll Eight.
Recorded by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Zhanran at Fulong.

First, the objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are explained. Regarding the six subsequent objects, one need only have a general understanding of the characteristics of the afflictions and so forth to prepare for their arousal;

once they are aroused, they may be understood by analogy, and thus cannot be shown in detail. As for the remaining three [objects], they have already been briefly discussed and distinguished previously.

Furthermore, those resembling the nine objects that do not lead to arousal are all subsumed under the category of the aggregates (*skandha*). Moreover, since it was previously clarified that the nine pairs mutually trigger one another, this is sufficient to establish their attainment.

[This section] is missing. Within the initial general explanation of the purpose for [this teaching’s] arrival: the phrase "the upper aggregate" concludes what preceded; the phrase "while observing the lower" gives rise to what follows.

Next, from "reproaching desire" onwards, the purpose for its arrival is clarified. First, this is distinguished from the previous reproaching of desire; second, it is distinguished from the abandoning of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Next, distinguish them from the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*). These three all possess deluded perceptions and are by no means produced through cultivation; how much less could they be objects of rejection?
This is a preliminary knowledge of their faults prior to entering meditative observation, as well as the discernment of the retributive aggregates (*vipāka-skandha*) from the afflictions (*kleśa*).

From "observing from now on" downward, the afflictions are correctly identified; this differs from the previous three cases. Regarding the subsequent analogy: the iron is like the aggregates (skandhas), and the fire is like the contemplation.
Because its habitual manifestation differs from before, it is described as "blazing."

Furthermore, in the section on the "Dharma of Retribution" below, the difficulties and ease [of practice] are distinguished. By citing the three preceding passages and comparing them with the present one, we know that the former three are not characterized by excessive wrath;
thus they are described as "ordinary."

What is "inferior"? This is explained separately as distinct from what preceded; first the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy. Within the principle, the former is the retributive dharma (*vipāka-dharma*), and therefore it is easily stilled.

"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to delusion (*moha*). Regarding the phrase "dead horse": according to the first precept in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Māra took the form of a woman, led [the monk] to the place of the horse, and vanished after concealing his own form.
Because his desire was so intense, he did not discriminate. Below this, the secondary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are further analyzed.

The following is an analogy for the subsequent stages. These all illustrate the arousal of the object-field, further augmented by external conditions. Regarding the analogy: flowing water is like the aggregates (*skandha*);
contemplation is like leveling the wood; practice is like the ripples arising. As for "ripples" (*lianyī*): when the wind blows, the flowing water forms patterns; this is also like successive waves.

The analogy of the strong man is the same. "Defilements below" [indicates] the application [of the analogy]. It is like touching a sleeping lion; this also clarifies the preceding analogy. If one does not descend [to the level of the defilements], it serves as a warning and exhortation.
It is not merely that one descends; faults arise due to objective conditions.

Next, in the main explanation, first regarding the explanation of the characteristics: there are two interpretations of the name. First is the interpretation by combining the characters; second is the interpretation by dividing the characters.
In both cases, the agent and the object are distinguished.
This section proceeds downward to distinguish between the sharp and the dull. Even the sharp faculties arising in ordinary beings belong to the category of the dull.

"Crawling creatures" refers to those with consciousness capable of movement. Regarding the mention of the *āṭaka* and others: it resembles a crab, though one of its claws is disproportionately large; how does it differ from a cricket? "Hairy" refers to the hair on the neck. This citation uses inferior examples to illustrate superior ones.
"The lowest of the low" points to the dull faculty that possesses sharpness. "The five sharp [faculties] at the bottom" clarifies the middle level of sharpness.

There is the dull [faculty]. For example, regarding the three poisons of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), if one has not yet attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth, a question is asked:

"The first fruit (*srotāpanna*) possesses no meditative absorption; how then does he sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*)? Answer: Here we are distinguishing what is currently manifest (*samudācāra*), not what is latently dormant (*anuśaya*). Even if the various non-Buddhists have severed the dull underlying tendencies (*mṛdu-anuśaya*), the active manifestations of the delusions of views still persist;

moreover, the eighty-eight underlying tendencies still belong to the category of the aggregates (*skandha*). If, after attaining meditative absorption, one perceives them—even if they do exist—[they are severed].
The three poisons likewise belong to the category of views.

As in the passage beginning "Just as two students... and so forth, an example is given: attaining the words is like being dull-witted, while attaining the meaning is like being sharp-witted; yet both equally conceive of a self.
Those who have attained dhyāna obtain benefit. If [the faculty] is inferior, although it previously possessed eighty-eight [defilements], they are now present in the current object.

If [the faculty] is superior and inferior, one distinguishes the categories of faculties. First, the objection is raised: if there were dullness within the superior, then when the superior proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned, that dullness should remain;
if this is not so, it is not dull. Although they coexist with one another, their respective classifications are distinct because each is governed by its own category; thus, the body departs.
"All follow.

Regarding "if [the doors] are opened," etc., this next section distinguishes between opening and closing. For now, we shall only examine the state of closure; the eighty thousand [afflictions] may be inferred from this.

Below the section on the "three poisons," it clarifies that the obstructions are not uniform: thus, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) does not constitute an obstruction, as it still belongs to the sphere of the aggregates (*skandha*). If it were to act as an obstruction, [it would be different].
The two categories differ, namely "arising" and "non-arising," as already distinguished previously.

The passage beginning with "The Sūtra says" cites scriptural evidence that the indeterminate [state] refers to the concentrated mind and the distracted mind entered by the Buddha-sons and others; this is based on the Abhidharma-piṭaka (Vibhāṣā).
The commentator states that all four parts can obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), referring specifically to delusion associated with the mind (*saṃprayukta-moha*).
If this is so, [the opponent] objects: according to the established doctrine, what affliction is not present within the delusion associated with the mind? Why then do you speak of "delusion" alone?

The current explanation below serves as a general clarification. To say that there is a specific intention [behind the distinction] refers to the fact that items such as the upper cover vary according to the individual;

therefore, they should not be definitively listed among those arising within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). How could what is being discussed here—the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*)—possibly pertain to them?

However, below [the section on] the afflictions (*kleśa*), the characteristics are distinguished as objects, and the intent is to distinguish them for the purpose of eradication; there was no opportunity for exhaustive detail, so the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is cited here, and its meaning can now be understood.

As for the "twenty years," this refers to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*). The abandonment of views consists of one path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
the abandonment of thought consists of nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.

"If that is so," and so forth, explains away a doubt. First, the doubt: "Is it for the sake of maintaining [the Dharma]? Below this, the explanation follows: fundamentally, from the point of entering the Path, one distinguishes and refutes external views in order to sustain the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, below [the text] correctly clarifies that these delusions are at the beginning of the ten contemplations; one must distinguish between the general and specific aspects of the "inconceivable" and so forth.
Since it states that each possesses [all aspects], yet here we focus only on the dull [aspect], the dullness thus aroused is what is currently being contemplated.

Regarding the initial analysis of the four parts, the statement that they are "combined into four parts" is made in contrast to the previous classification into eighty thousand; here, we simply speak of the four parts. [This concerns] the realm (*dhātu*).

The external correspondence is such that while the principle is identical, the entities are distinct; this can be understood through reflection. If one speaks of "mutual correlation" (*xiāngguān*) and so forth, it is subsequently distinguished from "contemplative deliberation" (*sīyì*) and so forth to clarify the preceding distinction between the general and the particular.
According to the different teachings, mutual correlation constitutes the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*).

Just as the roots and branches of a tree cannot be identified with one another, if they were mutually identical, they would be like ice and water or flowers in the sky, which can be grasped by the mind; therefore, it is called "contemplative deliberation."
Since all non-deliberative [afflictions] universally take pervasive afflictions as their objects, they are now categorized below. They serve as the fundamental objects for what follows;
thus it is said that if they act as causal conditions, there are three types, as will be explained later—namely, the three beginning with "habitual practice" (*abhyāsa*).

"Arising of characteristics" (*xiāng*) and below: this enumerates the phrases to distinguish their characteristics. As in the previous opening and closing [sections], it does not go beyond "profound benefit" (*shēn lì*). Therefore, this profound benefit differs from the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.

"Causes and conditions" (*yīnyuán*) and below: this correctly clarifies causes and conditions. The causal factor (*hetu*) is the "habitual cause" (*xí yīn*); the conditioning continuity (*vāsanā-saṃtati*) is the "condition" (*pratyaya*). Mental karma (*manas-karman*) serves as...

The body and speech serve as conditions (*pratyaya*), while the activities of Māra serve as causes (*hetu*). Because these three exist, when one now cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), these three arise once again;

therefore, they are called "conditions. This can be seen from the initial collection [of terms]. As for what is called the "factors of enlightenment," it refers simply to right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
To follow the current is called "drifting downstream" (*anuloma*); because one does not contemplate the aggregates (*skandha*), one follows the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

If one cultivates the path below [the stage of insight], observing the aggregates (*skandha*) gives rise to habitual tendencies; to flow against the current is called "upstream. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the twenty-five states of existence, as previously explained.
*Wei* means *cuīwei*, the appearance of rising high. Next, regarding the clarification of karma: *na* means "what"; *zhuó* means "rising high.
When karma arises, it is termed "accomplishment," and thus the stages and ranks are not established. In the analogy, the aggregates are like a river in stillness, while contemplation is like...
The wind arises; delusions erupt like waves. One lets loose body and speech like casting out sails; one loses single-mindedness like letting go of the rudder. Thus, the boat is wrecked.

Although one possesses karma, if the sails and rudder are strong and upright, one will surely reach the other shore. Regarding the "ten armies" mentioned among the māras, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"Where is it taught that afflictions are māras? It answers: "As in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Māra:"
It is said: "Desire is your first army," and so on, up to the tenth army. It is the Māra of self-exaltation that causes them to arise; for this reason, they are called "captured.
Although these are afflictions (*kleśa*), they all fall under the jurisdiction of Māra. Even if one lacks the former two [armies], Māra can still strike and disturb the mind.

If such things exist, ordinary wholesome virtues (*kuśala*) cannot restrain them; thus it is said they "cannot be resisted. Only the tranquil illumination of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* [can do so], just as the exclusive invocation of the Buddha [averts] fire.
For example, as in the passage "The deeds of Māra are inferior," which distinguishes between the two types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Next, it clarifies that the methods for cultivation differ according to the Great and Small Vehicles. Next, it judges the Great and Small Vehicles by means of the *siddhāntas*. Within the Small Vehicle, these are first enumerated.
Next is the section on "Discrimination. It indicates that where the text is incomplete, there is a slight lack of treatment regarding the hindrances to the Path.

The first [point], namely the five items below—such as the obscuration within the objective sphere of karma, the hindrance and non-hindrance, and the antidote—is fully explained in the *Zhudao* (Aids to the Path). Here, one additional phrase, "antidote for non-turning," is added; its numerical sequence follows the previous pairings.
As for the mention of "twelve," this refers to the detailed explanation of their characteristics within the seventh "Antidote" among the ten contemplations below. Not...

The pure reality-observation (*śuddha-tattva-vipaśyanā*) is also explained within the context of the Path. The conceptualizations (*parikalpa*) are as explained in the section on the meditative objects (*dhyāna-viṣaya*);

they differ only in their cultivation and manifestation. Compassion (*maitrī*) and the others are likewise clarified in the section on the meditative objects. Regarding the statement "the illness does not shift, but the treatment shifts":

after applying one treatment, one subsequently employs the remaining three. Regarding the statement "finite or infinite": because this mind has sunk into depression (*laya*), it is treated with reflection (*vitarka*); this constitutes the sixty-second [topic].

To perceive the characteristics of the present and future within the midst [of objects] is originally a perverse thought; now it has been transformed into a remedy. If one applies this to the "turning back" (pratyāvatāraṇa) and so forth, it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Next, to clarify the Mahāyāna: from a general perspective, it supersedes the Hīnayāna, yet it is not a universal remedy for all characteristics. One should, accordingly, contemplate desire according to its own nature (*svasaṃtāna*).
In the middle [section], fearing that there might be the same errors regarding teacher and disciple as mentioned in the preceding text, he warns: "One must skillfully grasp the underlying meaning.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "The Lesser Vehicle mostly uses... and so forth, this is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn). It provisionally relies on the four *siddhāntas*, yet it does not yet encompass all perspectives.
In that treatise, the four *siddhāntas* are distinguished by contrasting the Great and Lesser Vehicles against one another.

Next, one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Since the aggregates themselves have not yet been examined, phenomena (*dharma*) appear to be distinct; however, because they arise from distinct objects, their observed aspects seem different while the essence of the phenomena remains undifferentiated.
Within this, first the ten contemplations are correctly explained, followed by a reconciliation of alternative names.

Regarding the first object, within the section on "contemplation through reflection," it is said that pride takes shamelessness as its root, hence it is called the "king. Since reverence fundamentally resides in the person, it is said that [pride] causes one to lose the person.

"Also stingy with others' households" means being stingy regarding the objects belonging to others, not wishing for them to be encroached upon. Since ghosts take flattery as their fundamental nature, they are likewise stingy with others.

Regarding "poisoning and causing ruin": to cause ruin for others is like using poison (*viṣa*). "Marriage" (*hun*) refers to *hun* (darkness/confusion); it is so called because the rites are performed at twilight.
"Betrothal" (*ping*) refers to taking a wife; it denotes the interval during which wealth is sought. Furthermore, observing the lustful mind below, one discards it as one would discard a parasol.
In the middle, one rebukes desire as one would rebuke a scorpion; from this, dhyāna is produced. Although this is superior to Nanda’s [practice], it has not yet transcended the realm of form.
Furthermore, if one contemplates the lower [realms], one briefly cites the first and last of the six obscurations.

Next, regarding the "Inconceivable": first is the formal explanation; second is the exegesis that clarifies and applies the sutra text. Within the first [section], the objective sphere is established based on the sutra.

Within the second [section], the explanation begins with a brief clarification of progress and failure. Next, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other texts are cited for the initial explanation. Regarding the use of the *Vimalakīrti* to explain "non-practice": [the text follows].
Delusion is itself ignorance; ignorance is itself clarity. It is not like the Two Vehicles, which must first sever [delusion] before attaining liberation.

Rather, without severing ignorance, one gives rise to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*); without severing delusive craving, one gives rise to the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). Thus, regarding both clarity and liberation, all dharmas are fully perfected.

Therefore, this differs from ordinary beings, the followers of the Small Vehicle, and Bodhisattvas on the path of teaching. Regarding the explanation of "Vimalakīrti" (Pure Name) as "non-abiding," the following phrases are first set forth:
As for the reason for this, the commentary explains that the initial section follows the opening phrases of the sutra: first four lines, followed by eight. Regarding the first four lines:

the sutra initially rebukes errors, and its primary intent lies in addressing the bodhisattvas while concurrently rebuking those who are biased or heterodox. Now, since one wishes to clarify the objective realm, it is necessary to first rebuke such bias and heterodoxy.
Next, the sublime object is correctly established; therefore, it is judged that the ordinary and Hinayana practitioners fall into the errors of the first two phrases.

Following "next, not severing," the text rebukes those with deviant abidings for falling into the errors of the third and fourth phrases. Regarding the initial rebuke of the ordinary, the term *hen* (佷) denotes stubbornness.

"Contention" (zhēngsòng) means "to dispute. "Lì" (戾) means "to deviate. "Yóu" (由) means "to follow from. "To instruct" (xùn) means "to harmonize. The phrase "the two vehicles below" (èrshèng xià) is a censure of the Lesser Vehicle. The phrase "Arhats below" (āluóhàn xià) is a further, repeated censure of the failings of the Lesser Vehicle.
Below [the section on] the "Three Realms," he explains the meaning of "untrained mind. It is called "untrained" because it differs from the Mahāyāna;

it is called "untrained" because its crude wisdom cuts off afflictions only to the extent that they are exhausted within the realms. This very state of being untrained is, in truth, what is meant by "training. Having moved on from the "scorched seeds," he further rebukes the faults of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the section "The Bodhisattva Descends": this uses the superior to illustrate the inferior in order to distinguish attainment. First, both are established; next, both are explained.

First, explaining "possessing courage," the phrase "like a flower in the mud" and so forth means that while the high plateau of *nirvāṇa* lacks the flower of great compassion, it is within the mud of *saṃsāra* that such a flower grows.
This is analogous to the similarity with the physician.

Next, regarding the explanation of "not relishing" (*asvāda*), it says, "like birds, etc. Mud is a metaphor for suffering (*duḥkha*) being unstained; illness is a metaphor for the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) being undefiled.

Now, one does not cling to the Path (*mārga*) or Cessation (*nirodha*). Here, the primary clarification concerns the inconceivable provisional (*prajñapti-asambhava*). This is because one practices the Middle Way within the wondrous realm.
To verify this, the citation from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* must reside in non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), wherein the true and the responsive are sovereign.

"Continuously below," it refutes the heterodox and the spurious. At the beginning, it correctly refutes the faults of the third and fourth lines without remaining [in them]. Regarding the first part, it first distinguishes the faults of the third and fourth lines;

subsequently, it further distinguishes the fault of the fourth line. In the initial passage, the author first sets forth the characteristics of that which is deluded, thereby concluding the preceding section while simultaneously giving rise to the subsequent faults.
Now, in this degenerate age, [the author] rebukes those who have lost [the truth]. Regarding the term "harsh scrutiny": when one eats fruit, one preserves the seed by leaving it behind;

the fruit is sweet while the seed is bitter. To crush them both is to lose everything. To turn one's back on the Buddha’s skillful means is like losing the fruit; to let it go without observation is like losing the seed.

This constitutes the fourth point of error: namely, not abiding in either the disciplined or the undisciplined. Because of hearing [the teachings], one enters the "double negation," meaning that one is not obstructed by abiding in both.

To act willfully according to what is unrighteous is to lose the third intention regarding the first [point]. As for abiding in both [extremes] within nirvana, it is merely to abide in the undisciplined.

This is the inferior [view], a conclusion that constitutes a failure; it refutes those who are unimpeded yet malicious toward emptiness—those who, like one who overeats salt, do not understand moderation and instead focus exclusively on consuming much.
Therefore, it is called "excessive. While they claim all dharmas are empty, how can there be emptiness alone?
Next, it further cites the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to demonstrate the error of deviating from the Dharma. Next, it cites the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to provide evidence through past practice.

"This person" and below is a general refutation. "Furthermore" and below is a repeated refutation showing that the person of the fourth phrase shares the same error as the person of the second phrase.
Neither of the two abides; yet in seeking the Middle Way, one merely incurs the fault of abiding in the second position.

Below, in the northern section, both the faults of the third and fourth positions are fully present. Although the text concludes by summarizing the faults of abiding in the first and second positions, these faults fundamentally arise from the third and fourth.

Furthermore, regarding the section on "The Beginner" and below, which concludes with the characteristics of failure: first, as for the failure of abiding in both [the two gates], there is no such thing in the holy teachings.

Since one who has severed desire and dwells in the stage of cultivation is already neither distinct nor perfect, how much less so for one who indulges in evil? In the section on the Zhou family and below, cases are cited as verification;

for instance, all those cited in the *Suiziyi* (Following One’s Own Intent) fail at the fourth [stage]. Furthermore, those who abide in "equanimity" (*tiao*) and so forth are abiding in "neither-of-the-two" (*shuangfei*) and "both" (*shuang*).

Regarding "abiding": for one who has lost the cultivation of learning, abiding in tranquility is of no benefit; that is to say, it does not bring the benefit of being tamed. If one does not abide in either [tranquility or exertion], one merely achieves the lack of being tamed.
Combined with the previous case, this constitutes the two types of "neither-nor. As for the phrase "what relevance is there," this refutes the fault of the "neither-nor" position.
This is called a "great obstacle," which refutes the previous error of abiding in the fourth [state] of non-obstruction. Is this not a failure on both counts regarding the intent of the two sutras?
Thus, the following summarizes the four phrases to form the second fault; hence it says "undisciplined. Since even the minor [attainment] is not achieved, how could there be a sublime object?
Next, the eight phrases beginning with "Now it is said" expand upon the previous four to designate the sublime object. First, two sets of four are listed. Why?

Therefore, below, we first explain the four propositions regarding non-abiding. The first two are readily apparent. As for the third and fourth propositions, they consist merely of the simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination of the preceding two.
Although what follows does not descend [into further detail], it clarifies the fourfold formulation of abiding, which is identical in nature to the preceding.

Regarding "abiding" and "non-abiding," one should first explain the first two [of each] and so forth, applying this to the remaining two; subsequently, one should analyze their mutual identity. To avoid prolixity, the mutual identity is explained immediately here.
If one follows the interpretation of "abiding" by means of "non-abiding," it should likewise be seen as applicable when explained in relation to the three truths.

Question: What is the difference in meaning between abiding and non-abiding? Answer: Abiding refers to the function (*vṛtti*) of the truths, while non-abiding refers to the essence (*svabhāva*). Both function and essence are present; this can be seen through reflection.
Since these eight phrases are complete, one should know that craving is the great ocean of the *dharmadhātu*. Why is this so? [The following] explains.

The Dharma-realm. Next, by this [definition], the Dharma-realm is established as the essence. Furthermore, because it is the basis for expedient teachings, all ordinary people and their minor delusions are subsumed herein.
Relying upon this, one explains and practices with unimpeded mastery.

Regarding such passages as these, the gain and loss of the eight phrases are explained by way of the person who rides [the vehicle]. First is gain, followed by loss. At the beginning, it clarifies the benefit of not abiding in what is proximately gained.

As for the section beginning with "How so," it provides the explanation. Why are all four phrases regarding this dwelling referred to as "benefits"? Because within each individual phrase, all the other phrases are fully contained.
The same applies to non-abiding and abiding; where the text does not explicitly state them, they are omitted for brevity.

As explained below the section on the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), the following clarifies "attainment from afar": even those who merely hear slander [of the Dharma] still attain it, let alone those who believe and practice it.

Below the section on "skillful observation," the marks of attaining benefit are summarized: "near" refers to the householder who hears and attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); "far" refers to Vimati, who attained benefit only after a long time.

If not so [as described], one conversely incurs loss as the conclusion. One's own practice does not transcend the wondrous realm; for the sake of benefiting others, the Dharmakāya manifests according to the capacities of beings.
It is acceptable; it corresponds with the eight phrases.

If one descends into a single thought-moment, the wondrous realm is precisely established. Regarding the analogies of the tree’s shadow and so forth: first, it illustrates that within the obscurity of the principle-nature (li-xing) there is clarity;

second, it illustrates that within the luminosity of the cognitive hindrance (zhi-zhang) there is obscurity; third, it illustrates the light of the Middle Way wisdom within the divine pearl. These three illustrate [the three aspects] together.
The non-duality of light and darkness is precisely the wondrous realm. Regarding the first passage, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Kāśyapa raises an objection, saying:
"In darkness there are trees, yet there are no shadows. The Buddha replies: "There are shadows, but they are not visible to the physical eye.

This means that even in darkness there must be light for shadows to exist; just as within ignorance (*avidyā*) it is not that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is absent, yet it is not perceived by the four eyes.
What can be seen: although the two types of wisdom are luminous, they are entirely ignorance; likewise, the dharmatā of the Middle Way is entirely affliction.
This also serves as the first lamp analogy for the obstruction of wisdom, as explained below; the intended meaning can be understood accordingly.

Thus, below, one contemplates the nature of light and darkness. In the initial analogy, it is first established [as follows]. "Why is this so? and below, it is explained: the essence and its characteristics are fundamentally identical;
by relying on the principle of the two grasps, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is designated as ignorance (*avidyā*), which is interpreted as "darkness coming.

Yet, in reality, darkness does not come. The two wisdoms are designated as ignorance, which is interpreted as "the lamp being extinguished. Furthermore, it is indicated that the two wisdoms can destroy the two delusions, which is interpreted as "darkness."
[The opponent says: "Darkness does not go; when one seeks darkness, there is no darkness. [The Master replies: This refers to the essence of illumination itself.
Although there is neither going nor coming, the two meanings of "merging" and "the essence being non-dual" are nonetheless distinct in their capacity to break through obstructions and cover.

Regarding the phrase "not receiving [the defilements]," etc., this clarifies the objective sphere and its mode of activity. First, the terms are listed; then, below, they are explained. Here, "new" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and "old" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Internal" refers to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and "external" refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*). If worldly wisdom departs, it is compared to a pearl; because it differs from the former two, it is said to be "ever-luminous.
This intends to clarify that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the wondrous object; therefore, the passage concludes by summarizing the afflictions.
"Equal to the above" refers to taking the aggregates (*skandhas*) as an illustration.
"Likewise below" concerns the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), which again takes light and darkness as the objects of the great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).
Since light and darkness each correspond to two of the great vows, light and darkness constitute four vows simultaneously within a single moment of thought.
To fulfill the section below on "settling the mind," first the sequential [arrangement] is presented; next, under "skillful means," the general and specific modes of settling are shown.

If one looks at the section below on "pervasive penetration," the textual characteristics are largely abbreviated. Regarding the section below on "immediate emptiness," it concerns the "penetration" and "obstruction. As for the term "contrived inversion," it precisely accords with the meaning of the penetration and obstruction of the specific characteristics.
Furthermore, regarding the lower [realms] in the *Dharmapada* (Section on the Path): if one obstructs the lower, it serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

Although the text omits the combined practice, there are twelve antidotes for external greed and so forth, as indicated in the preceding passage; this very text is that reference. Since there are three for each of the four parts, there are twelve.

By contemplating the bodies of others, the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are accomplished as the external liberations (*bahir-vimokṣa*). By contemplating oneself, one knows the antidotes for the internal spheres of mastery (*adhyātma-abhibhv-āyatana*). Because these are superior to the former, they are able to function together.

To remedy transgression of the Dharma: those who harbor anger toward others do so because they fail to accord with the Dharma; therefore, one should contemplate sentient beings as being in accord with the Dharma. Those who harbor anger toward others do so because they violate the Dharma;
therefore, one must contemplate emptiness and the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Anger arises from delusion regarding the single reality;

therefore, one should contemplate the absence of objects and the two conditions, as well as the two periods and the three periods of time, in full accordance with the seventh [chapter]. As for the term "a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*), it refers to the final moment when one performs good or evil deeds.

Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), cause and effect are fully present; therefore, their nature is reckoned as real. Regarding the four types of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in the *Abhidharmakośa*, a "single thought-moment" refers to a *kṣaṇa*.

"Shortly before opening," refers to the successive stages [of the womb]. "The squeaking of a rat" and so forth: this refers to the strange sound of a rat; it is also like the strange bird making the sound "kōng-kōng.
It is merely called "squeaking in the void," having no substantial reality at all. "Tāo" (叨) means greed.

If one is inferior in both internal and external [aspects], yet attains patience, this is called "inferior. Even when free from craving, it is compared to a great carriage, as was previously illustrated by the analogy of the joints.

Some may still be obscure regarding this; thus, it is termed "inferior. This concludes the section on the inferior. Furthermore, it is termed "inferior" as a summary of the various alternative names for the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*).

The following section provides an extensive explanation; having removed the superfluous, it follows the essential points by briefly indicating these three. Furthermore, according to the *Mūla-śāstra*:
"If one contemplates the Buddha’s Prajñā and Nirvāṇa in accordance with the Dharma, these three are of one single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*); the three are the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

First, expanding upon the phrase from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, "Entering nirvāṇa without severing afflictions," results in thirty-six phrases. As for why they are called "thirty-six": [the text continues].
Furthermore, speaking in terms of one type of fundamental [structure], according to the initial textual arrangement, two fundamentals are required.

Therefore, the first fundamental is designated merely as the "entry" (入), while it is only upon reaching the exit into *nirvāṇa* that it is designated as the "exit phrase" (出句). Question: For what reason are two fundamentals listed? Answer:
Because the subject and object are distinct, if one wishes to establish a single fundamental proposition, then the entry and exit [phrases] intermingle to form a single set of four propositions.
If there are two fundamental propositions, then the entry and exit [phrases] each constitute four propositions.
However, since the two fundamentals each reside within the four sets of four propositions for both entry and exit, it is known that the actual propositions are but thirty-two.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, it is easy to see by careful investigation. Nevertheless, fearing further confusion, I shall briefly set forth the characteristics of those points that are somewhat difficult to perceive.

In the first four phrases, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) is taken as the "non-abandonment. In the second set of four phrases, the essence (*svabhāva*) is taken as the "non-abandonment.
Within the second set of four phrases, there are two pairs that are mutually inclusive: first, the pair of essence and abandonment; second, [the pair of]...

That which has already been severed is called "severed"; the remainder is called "not severed. As for what is termed "entry" (*praveśa*), it refers to the attainment of the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*);

it may also refer to the realization of the essence of the stage beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*). I suspect this text may be erroneous. Regarding the "neither-nor" [category], entry is defined by the principle of merging with the Truth (*tattva*). In the third and fourth phrases:
Regarding the first phrase, one must not follow the previous method by providing a dual interpretation.

First, having already analyzed "both" as the essential nature, one then takes the state where the analysis has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) as "both. The remaining three phrases are to be understood by analogy.

Regarding the fourth set of four phrases, one applies the dual interpretation from the second set of four phrases by analogy. Throughout the sixteen phrases, wherever the term "entering" (*praveśa*) occurs, it refers exclusively to entering.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitutes the method for establishing the verses. For the time being, the first four lines are taken from the perspective of ordinary people (*bāla-pṛthagjana*); these are what is negated by emptiness. The subsequent lines that emerge likewise constitute the establishment of the verses;

they are spoken in contrast to entering into emptiness. However, this emptiness and its provisional nature pertain to the *Zàng* (Āgama) and *Tōng* (Pratyekabuddha) teachings, while their meaning also encompasses the *Yuán* (Perfect) and *Bié* (Distinct) teachings, as shall be explained in the later text.
As for the fact that the entry into and emergence from the fundamental [nature] have each been explained above, yet are explained again below, it is for the following reason:
Because they are shown to be identical.

Next, the explanation of those who "emerge" [from saṃsāra] is as follows: Regarding the third phrase of the first set of four statements, even those of middling faculties do not emerge because their great [afflictions] are also severed;

yet, because they are capable of emerging, they are also said to emerge. Regarding the first phrase of the second set of four statements, it is established based on the meaning of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The second...
Regarding the first phrase of the third and fourth lines: the "dual-aspect" (*liangyi*) refers to the simultaneous application of the gate of essence (*ti*) and the gate of refutation (*zhe*).

As for the initial inability to emerge, it is called "not emerging"; as for the subsequent ability to emerge, it is called "emerging. Since the method of refutation is not the primary [method], it is termed "simultaneous" (*jian*). The Two Vehicles are also like this.
In the third line, the "dual-aspect" is likewise established based on the refutation of the essence; both cases refer to the Two Vehicles. Therefore...

It is said that [the fourth] does not emerge. Within the fourth phrase, the principle must necessarily be a double negation. The first phrase should state: "The essence is refuted; the principle is true.

To say "one who realizes the dharmas" is an abbreviation. The three subsequent phrases should all refer to "principle": the middle and lower [capacities] follow from principle, while those of superior capacity take principle as their condition.
The third and fourth [sections] may be understood by analogy with what has been explained.

Furthermore, in the subsequent question-and-answer section, it says that "the meaning is pervasive" because it pervades the three teachings; when divided, they form four, yet in meaning they pervade both the Perfect (Yuan) and the Distinct (Bie).

Therefore, I shall further summarize this: the essence [of the teaching] is resolved by means of the "beyond-the-boundaries" (jie-wai) method. Each point follows the previous pattern, with the only difference being that the Distinct (bie) and Complete (yuan) vehicles replace those previously mentioned.
Next, beneath each of these, one opens the gates from within the gates to form sixteen categories, and these should be applied according to the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* (*sīxī*).
Understood. Take, for example, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): because it takes delusion as its essence, it does not sever [delusion]; because it has not severed it, one does not enter [the path].

The same applies to the other three [gates] regarding the meaning of non-severance. Regarding the "person" (*pudgala*): because wholesome states arise, one enters; within the context of treatment, because it is a treatment, one enters; that which is not a treatment, one does not enter.
The ultimate principle may be understood by analogy with this explanation; the remaining three gates are all identical in meaning.

If one were to correlate gate with gate, it would be as explained in the four fundamental propositions (*mūla-catuṣkoṭi*) mentioned previously. Although the fundamental [propositions] and those that are expanded are equally "empty" and so forth, because each instance of the term "empty" and the like possesses its own distinct meaning of emptiness and so forth, they constitute sixteen [propositions]. This can also be correlated with the four [propositions] such as "not interrupted" (*anuccheda*).

The meanings of the gates of "within the realm" and "beyond the realm" are established by themselves. "Entering" means arriving at the principle; it is necessarily so. Not entering means that there is no principle to enter.
The third [gate] uses the principle to illuminate both simultaneously; the fourth uses the principle to negate both simultaneously. Both take the three virtues (*triguṇa*) as the truth.

"Exiting" refers to the arising of function. "Entering" means merging with the principle. Regarding "severing" and "not severing," the four meanings are the same as before. Within "exiting," there is also...

This should further be correlated with the four *siddhāntas*; where the text lacks them, they are omitted. Following this, the section below again employs the Distinct and Perfect [teachings] to encompass the Shared [teaching], as the Shared vehicle brings forth persons whose names for "refutation" and "essence" are identical.
Regarding the next thirty-six phrases on *prajñā*: although they follow the questions of the treatise, the answers are given by way of different names with identical meanings.

These are derived by expanding the single phrase from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "the non-arising of form through to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the arising of *prajñā*," into thirty-six phrases.

The intent of *prajñā* and all phenomena (*dharmas*) is fundamentally long-reaching. *Prajñā* is wisdom (*jñāna*), and all phenomena are the truths (*satya*). Therefore, their characteristics are now [examined].

Each of these is further divided into three, which mutually give rise to one another. If one were to say that the names differ while the meaning remains the same, it would merely be a substitution of "all phenomena" (dharmas) for "afflictions" and "prajñā" for "nirvāṇa.
Since wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) are distinct, their conceptual dynamics differ accordingly; therefore, this is clarified once more.
Furthermore, the sixteen aspects of all phenomena each encompass the thirty-six preceding phrases; this is because every phrase is explained from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching].

Furthermore, if one follows the sequential order, then the Small and the Expanded are contrasted; since the Expanded contains all three [vehicles], one first performs a preliminary analysis to distinguish the Separate and the Perfect.
The fundamental principles of opening and closing may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Within this, first are explained sixteen propositions on mutual arousal, followed by sixteen propositions on mutual illumination. Regarding what is called "arousal," there are two meanings: first, the inconceivable...

Consideration: Second is the arousal of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, if objects mutually arouse cognitions, one may discuss them as being due to past habituation. When cognitions mutually illuminate objects, there are again two distinctions:

if it is the transformation-cognitions (*pariṇāma-jñāna*) that mutually illuminate one another, they are not considered to be the arousal of habituation; if it is the [subsequent] cognitions that follow the objects and mutually illuminate them, this constitutes the arousal of habituation.

Furthermore, the mutual illumination of the empty and the provisional applies to Bodhisattvas of the three teachings; the mutual illumination of the middle [the true] applies only to the Distinct and Perfect [teachings].

The "semblance" [teaching] is generally included within the process of being received and transformed. Therefore, one should explain this with mastery according to the various teachings and stages, the relative heights of truth and wisdom, the presence or absence of the provisional and the real, and whether the sequence is gradual or non-gradual.
In general discussion, it is simply that the wondrous wisdom and the wondrous object mutually illuminate and mutually evoke one another.

Next, the thirty-six bodies are explained. According to the treatise, the questions and answers regarding their similarities and differences are the same as previously stated; they are not distinct, yet they are distinct, being precisely the virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Therefore, the bodies themselves are directly categorized into thirty-six. Transformation (*nirmāṇa*), response (*sambhoga*), retribution (*vipāka*), and dharma constitute the four fundamental [bodies].

Regarding the terms "entering" and "exiting," these refer to the arising and ceasing of transformation. Question: We have only heard that the three [bodies] arise from the Dharma, but we have not heard that the Dharma arises from transformation.

Second, [the response] arises from what is appropriate (*yathāyogam*). The Dharma [body] arises from retribution (*vipāka*). Answer: Because of giving, the superior arises from the inferior; because of opening [the gates], the superior arises from the inferior.
This should be understood through the thirty-six phrases of the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) regarding resonance and response. The Dharma body is hidden; the three bodies are manifest.
Alternatively, the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is hidden because it is for one’s own use, and manifest because it is for the use of others.

Next, regarding the explanation of the object of the sick person: first, the provisional and the real are briefly clarified. Within the Real, the four snakes serve as metaphors for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Among these, those whose nature is ascendant are like wind and fire, while those whose nature is latent are like earth and water. A "thicket" (*sū*) refers to a place where no people dwell, but only grasses and waters gather;
this serves as a metaphor for the principal subject of suffering being composed of a multitude of dharmas, as detailed in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. As for the "four countries" and so forth:
The "heavy" is likened to the four great elements; though near, it is yet distant. "Vast" means weak. "Mounting" means seizing an opportunity.
"Rest" means excellence. "Stagnation" means decline.

Regarding the phrase "the various Buddhas inquire after his health," etc.: there are two types of illness [as explained below]. Next, the provisional and the real are distinguished. First, "if he is prostrate," etc., refers to the provisional illness.
The kings, elders, and commoners represent the multitude of ordinary people. To disparage the small is as in the "Chapter on Disciples";

to rebuke the great is as in the "Chapter on Bodhisattvas. "On what does it arise? asks for the cause. Based on this, he further provides an extensive explanation; using illness as a pretext, he speaks of cessation and the eternal.
As for this: because the Buddha announced his passing into extinction and the great assembly requested him to remain, the Buddha consequently expounded at length upon the principle of permanence.

"Actual illness" refers to the actual delusions of sentient beings; "expedient illness" refers to manifestations displayed in high positions. All such matters as these are not what is being examined here.

Now, looking at the section below, it is judged that although this is indeed a real illness, one must still cause it to arise. If it does not arise, the illness remains within the hidden realm (*guanjing*). Regarding "superior wisdom" and so forth:
this is an analogy for when the previous hidden realm has already entered the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), there is no need to reach this stage;

therefore, the preceding text states that the other nine [stages] are unnecessary. Regarding "like felling a great tree": *dì* (躋) means to topple or overturn. Because the faculties are dull and heavy, the method of contemplation (*guanfa*) must be explained in detail.

Regarding "chronic illnesses" and so forth, this generally refers to all obstacles. Why must it necessarily be "long-term" in this context? Once an obstacle has arisen, one must immediately apply contemplation.

As for the phrase "the four *siddhāntas* at the conclusion of the passage," the first part concerns the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly convention). The passage beginning with "The Sūtra says... addresses the *puruṣakāra* (human effort).

The term "Three Vehicles" implies that one should give rise to wholesome intentions. The section beginning with "If [wrong views] arise... distinguishes the faults, thereby demonstrating that [right view] gives rise to [wholesome states].
Excellent meaning. Furthermore, below this is the "Counteractive Treatment" (pratipakṣa). Again, below this is the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha).
These correctly explain the five gates. First, regarding the "Disease": previously, the reason for examining the pulse was briefly distinguished therein.

"To indicate" means to observe. To now briefly clarify it: the pulse is the path through which blood and qi circulate. As the *Majing* (Pulse Classic) says: "The text is easy to understand, yet... [the remainder of the citation follows].

The following difficulties are difficult to clarify; even veteran physicians remain confused regarding them, so they cannot be fully detailed here. As for the characteristics of the five viscera in this text, they do not concern the cycles of mutual generation or mutual conquest;

rather, they refer to when a particular viscus becomes excessively increased. For example, although the nature of wood is straight, if it is now excessively tall and straight, fire and the others should be understood by analogy.
The mutual overcoming [of the elements] can be understood by relying on the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*).
When the face lacks luster, the internal organs corresponding to that element will diminish, thereby causing illness.
Since wood governs the liver, if there is no luster, it is like wood lacking moisture. Fire and the other elements may be inferred in the same manner as wood.
The white substance on the liver departs because of the mutual affliction of the organs. The treatment is based on the six qi to regulate the five viscera;

the methods of treatment are as clarified in the section on "Methods of Treatment" below. Because they correspond to what is somewhat convenient, they are listed here in advance and will not be listed again later.

However, one must not adopt the characters in their entirety; rather, it is sufficient that their tones and sounds correspond, for this constitutes the essential characteristic. Since these belong to the five [viscera]...

[The spirits] act accordingly; as their forms arise, they treat the five viscera. What is now described in the text regarding those emerging from the viscera is precisely the qi of the primary viscera, which assists in nourishing them.
Why is this? Since other viscera have been afflicted, [the spirits] are summoned to return to their source.

As for the disease-demons, such as the Lord of the Hearth, they are simply black in color. When the kidneys are harmed by the spleen, kidney disease ensues; the disease-demon then follows the course of the illness.
The color of the spleen is yellow; therefore, the first version lists all five colors as the ghosts of the five viscera (*pañca-kukṣi*).

This text should originally have appeared within the section on the causes and conditions of disease, but for the sake of convenience, it is placed here. Regarding the explanation of the spleen, the phrase "its color is *lǒngtǒng*" refers to the yellow *lǒngtǒng*.

From "Furthermore, there are many states of profound confusion" onwards, [the text] describes the symptoms of the six deities' illnesses. For the time being, following worldly conventions, each deity guards one treasury and presides over one faculty (*indriya*).

The "Yin" (the subtle essence) is the foundation of the body, pervading both the faculties and the treasuries. The *Jinglü yixiang* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) also borrows worldly metaphors, with each claiming its own merit;
thus, the six faculties and the six deities each contend for their own virtues.
Furthermore, there are six causes and conditions for illness. First, regarding lack of moderation in diet:
as the *Bowuzhi* states, "If one eats a mixture of foods, they become a locus where a hundred ailments and demonic influences gather."

Next, the characteristics of impairment and benefit are explained. Regarding the phrase "from the three apertures of the waist," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The waist has three apertures;
wind successively disperses the oily fluids into the hundred vessels, where they combine with the prior blood, coagulating and transforming into flesh.

That which arises from this is called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and it continues until the five sensory faculties are produced. Regarding the phrase "heavy like sinking downward," these are the characteristics of the eight types of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*).

Furthermore, below these eight tactile sensations, one distinguishes the sensations in relation to the breath. If they accord with the four great elements, they correspond to the eight tactile sensations.

The five constants and five phases involve mutual generation and mutual overcoming; their respective governing correspondences are distinct, as detailed in the *Baihutong* and the *Bowuzhi* regarding the five directions and the five [phases].
The Emperor, the five ministers, the five deities, the five beasts, the five notes, the five stars, the five flavors, and the five vital energies—each of these corresponds to one another.
Thus, these nine and five categories all possess the characteristics of mutual generation and mutual overcoming. The same applies to the five sounds: calling out belongs to wood;
speaking belongs to fire; laughing belongs to metal; chanting belongs to water; and singing belongs to earth. As for the five tactile sensations: the hardness of wood and the warmth of fire...

Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): the western direction belongs to wind, and therefore it is light. This follows the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*. The five vital airs (*prāṇa*) are as previously described.

As for the term "infant" (*ying*), the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "That which is first born is called an infant (*ying*); 'infant' refers to the chest. One receives [the child] at the infant's chest and nourishes them with milk.
Regarding "like a king," etc.: "folding the hands" (*gongshou*) means joining the palms. It is also like when Zhang Hua treated Li Ziyu’s illness; the spirit of the disease—

[The illness] was in the *gāohuáng* (the vital point beyond medical reach), yet [the physician] refused to treat it. Huá then fled. This shows that worldly customs also clearly recognize the existence of "demon illnesses" (*guǐbìng*).

Demon illnesses are likewise afflicted by the eight poisons. Demons do not descend upon and afflict people at random; this clarifies that the origin of demon illnesses lies in deviant thoughts (*xiéniàn*).
The *Dōuhuǐ* demon is precisely the "five-colored demon" mentioned in the preceding text.
Within the five demonic diseases, first is the discrimination [of them], followed by the causes of the diseases.

Within the six karmic diseases, regarding those such as the sin of killing and so forth, it is fully explained in the preceding text. Because the five precepts govern the five viscera, each disease afflicts its corresponding root-organ;
the treatment likewise follows this principle. If one maintains the precepts, thereby moving the habitual tendencies of the diseases, one should also investigate according to the respective roots.
Regarding this: if one employs it for treatment, it is the "treatment by contemplating the mind.

Next, the method of treatment is clarified. Within the initial clarification of similarities and differences, the phrase "it is not possible," etc., means that if one loses what is held, it is like grasping a knife by its blade instead of the handle;
it will instead injure one's hand. *Kou* (怐) means "equal" or "uniform. As for "the *xi* belt being at the navel," it refers to the mother’s navel while in the womb.

It is focused on the child's navel. Food enters through the navel to nourish the child; the vital breath (*prāṇa*) functions in the same way. Within the womb, the mother’s breath and the child’s breath are interconnected.
As for the mind frequently being directed toward the upper [regions]: the upper part is hot while the lower part is cold;

the upward-moving *prāṇa* assists this, making it easier for food to be regulated and moved downward. This portion belongs to *yīn* (yin) with little *huǒ* (fire). Thus, Jiang, Wu, and Mao: Jiang Tianwen, Wu Mingche, and Mao.
Xi was a high-ranking official of the Chen dynasty; both received the method for regulating the breath, and their foot ailments were cured, as detailed in the *Bai lu*.

Next, regarding the "Five Elements" of the Emperor: descending from Metal, they transform according to the sequence of mutual generation (*xiang sheng*); descending from Fire, they act according to the sequence of mutual overcoming (*xiang ke*). When Water encounters Earth, it does not flow.
The character "flow" (*xing*) is read here according to its phonetic value (pronounced *hù láng fǎn*).

As in the case of metal overcoming wood below, one should correctly employ the therapeutic method. If one perceives illness and identifies the afflicted organ (*kośa*), one should entirely bring the mind to rest within the organ capable of overcoming it, thereby subduing its strength.

Furthermore, it is used to suppress and treat the four great diseases that each contravene their own nature, preventing them from increasing. Regarding what is called "ordinary exhalation and inhalation":
in the regular practice of seated meditation, one first exhales to remove coarse breath and inhales to take in tranquility. Regarding what is called "relying on the breath":

this relies upon the retributive breath while simultaneously employing mental visualization (*parikalpa*). For instance, when one is angry, the breath becomes coarse; when one is calm, the breath becomes subtle. Mental visualization is likewise so.
Regarding Master Bian: the first edition states he was a person from Goryeo. To treat goiters using visualization (*saṃjñā*), one visualizes them as being like a bee’s nest;

by coughing out the air, one gradually causes them to burst. For ailments such as internal tumors (*gaṇḍa*), one visualizes piercing them with a needle; once the tumor is pierced, the illness is cured. Regarding the use of ghee (*sarpis*) according to the *Āgama*:
one visualizes the ghee at the crown of the head, flowing through the entire body down to the marrow; after many days of this practice, the ailment is cured. As it says: [text continues].
Regarding "swallowing a snake": it is like a person who, while eating, mistakenly sees the reflection of a snake in their food and takes it for a real snake, thereby falling ill.
