Once others recognize this, they administer a purgative; first, a dead snake is placed in a basin below, and when they report that the snake has come out, the illness is cured.

Regarding treating through the contemplation of the mind: it is like Nan-yueh, who suffered from swelling and focused exclusively on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), neither accepting nor clinging [to the affliction].
The illness will naturally be eliminated.

Among the various therapeutic arts, the treatment for pharyngitis and fear resolves itself. Regarding the treatment for toothache: the original text states that one faces the Big Dipper (Beidou) and says, "Mutu teng" (reciprocal pain).
The Big Dipper treats it, and it is immediately cured. As for the practice of pressing the thumbs and so forth: each of the five fingers governs one of the five viscera.
The thumb governs the liver; the index finger governs the lungs; the middle finger governs the heart; the ring finger governs the spleen; and the little finger governs the kidneys.
The mantra possesses the four *siddhāntas*, as explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra). Nowadays, it is mostly used for the purpose of remedial treatment (*pratipakṣa*).

When one whose life depends on the inhalation and exhalation recites this mantra, they must still verbally utter "ānāpāna. Regarding matters such as severe beating, I have frequently observed these occurrences since residing in Eastern Zhejiang.

Next, to clarify the nature of loss and gain: when the faculties are sharp and the afflictions are light, there is sudden benefit; when the faculties are sharp but the afflictions are heavy, there is gradual benefit.

When the faculties are dull and the afflictions are light, there is gradual loss; when the faculties are dull and the afflictions are heavy, there is sudden loss. Nevertheless, even though the faculties are dull, if one skillfully contemplates the Dharma, loss may also become benefit.
Regarding the phrase "the world laments those who are mediocre": "mediocre" (yōng) means "constant" or "ordinary.

As for those of superior talent, it is like the artisan Qiang Bo who laid down his adze before the man from Ying, or Boya who snapped his strings before Ziqi. If Zhongqi cannot be encountered, who can discern the notes within a melody?
Since the methods of treatment are so subtle, those who believe in them are rare. "Zhen" means a pillow.

If one cultivates the four samādhis, then whatever treatments are applied, provided they possess these four [conditions], the illness will surely be cured: first, the power of the Path; second, the addition of spiritual resonance.
Third, the method of curing; fourth, the sacrifice of the body. Chen Zhen was the lay elder brother of the Great Master. The Dharma Master Zang of Kaishan Temple cited a person to verify this matter.
A physiognomist told Chen Zhen that his death would occur after the next new moon. At that time, the Great Master instructed him to perform the Fangdeng Repentance.
Upon inspection, he saw a signboard for the Heavenly Palace that read: "The Hall of Chen Zhen," and it granted him fifteen additional years of life.
It is like the hall of Śakra; it draws forth a heart of courageous exertion. It is like the separate practice site (maṇḍala) of Śakra;

it is like the guardian deity of the hall of Śakra’s practice site, protecting [the practitioner] like a supporting general. Minor obstacles and various non-virtuous factors are like minor demons. As for the "city lord" and so forth, they are terrified.
This is the nature [of the practice]. The body is like a city; the mind is like the ruler; the guardians are like the [defenders of the] body. The spirit (*śen*) is born together with the body;

although it constantly protects a person, it must rely on the mind for stability. Only when the spirit is guarded does its protection become strong. Therefore, guarding the *dharmodāna* (place of practice) also relies upon diligence (*vīrya*).

Regarding the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* about demons sticking to the five places, etc.: there was once a man traveling through the mountains who encountered a *rākṣasa* demon. The demon stuck to his hands and feet, and...
[The ghost] asked, "Do you submit? He replied, "Even in death, I shall not submit. The ghost was astonished and released him entirely.

Next, regarding the practitioner who cultivates contemplation: the text in the section on "Contemplating the Meaning" is very brief; it should be compared with what was explained previously for those who fear birth and death.

Due to illness, fear increases; consequently, one further cultivates [the contemplation of] impermanence and so forth. As in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha had the bhikṣus visit the sick bhikṣu Kṣema and asked:
"Can one who contemplates the five aggregates attain the fruit of arhatship? He further instructed them to contemplate the departure of the disease.
Regarding the realm of the Pratyekabuddha: as it is feared that seeking [the path] would be difficult, it must be divided into five parts.

First, by inferring the present fruit, one knows the past cause. Second, by inferring the present cause, one knows the present fruit. Third, from "If one is crazed and thirsty" onwards, one contemplates the present fruit to cease the present cause.

Fourth, from "If not... onwards, because the present cause has ceased, the twelve [links] cease. Fifth, from "Since one cannot obtain... onwards, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha is established. The first is as in the text; the second is also...
Second. First, one contemplates that existence extends down to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Next, one contemplates below this, tracing name-and-form back to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The first [section] is as stated in the text. The second also has two parts: first, tracing form; second, tracing consciousness. Regarding the first [tracing form], there are again two parts: first, tracing that form lacks intrinsic nature because it arises from conditions;

second, tracing that form lacks intrinsic nature because it arises from the mind. Regarding the first [of these two], there are again two parts: first, tracing the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); second, tracing...

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): the first [of these] further consists of two parts—the horizontal and the vertical. The five aggregates likewise first follow the horizontal and then the vertical. Next, proceeding from the mind (*citta*), there is again first the horizontal and then the vertical.

As for the initial horizontal aspect: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise from the mind; therefore, they do not perish, because they are sustained by the mind. Thus, the four great elements resemble the mind.
Following this, in the vertical analysis, one examines how the mind arises in successive stages; therefore, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Next is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
From below: first, one infers consciousness from karma;

next, one infers the present fruit within the cessation of the present cause. First, there is the inference by way of analogy; next, again "downward," there is the analogy of cessation. "Running south" refers to the synthesis of the inference.
Likewise, "downward" refers to the synthesis of cessation. If it does not go downward, it is due to cessation. Since it does not go downward, the twelve cessations differ from the gradual [process].
"Breaking" means "not obtaining. The Tripiṭaka gives rise to Śrāvakas; the Common [Vehicle] gives rise to Pratyekabuddhas—just as they each emerge from within the *pratītyasamutpāda* [teachings].

Furthermore, regarding the passage "observing below": the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka first [practice] the six obscurations, followed by aspiration and practice; therein, aspiration comes first, then practice. Aspiration...
The "Four Great Vows" are the aspiration; the "Six Perfections" are the practice. Their general and specific aspects are as stated in the text.
Regarding the phrase "merely hearing [the name]" within the section on the "Inconceivable Object," the *Vyādhicikitsā-parivarta* (Chapter on Treating Illness) states:
"At that time, the Elder Jalavāhana, seeing the suffering of illness throughout the city, went everywhere within the city and spoke these words: 'I am a physician. Merely..."

Upon hearing these words, all the sick were healed. This is like hearing of the wondrous realm and immediately entering the First Abode (*prathamābhūmi*). What is called "the initial contemplation" refers to the object of that initial contemplation.

Furthermore, the phrase "there are others below" serves as a metaphor for the nine lower dharmas. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose suffering from illness is so deep and heavy that it is difficult to eliminate or cure."

He went to the elder’s residence and bestowed upon him a wondrous medicine, whereby he was restored to health. After the nine [periods] had passed below, he was likewise able to enter and dwell there;
his six sense faculties were purified, as previously described.

All that follows concerns the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*). First, the characteristics of this arousal are clarified by initially relying on the three successive contemplations (*krama-vipaśyanā*), each of which consists of four parts:
first, self-discipline through vows; second, the manifestation of birth through compassion; third, the benefits gained from such manifestation; and fourth, the conclusion by naming the contemplation.
"Thus, below," concludes the formation of a single mind. "Only he, below," introduces the person. Relying on the illness to give rise to a vow, the meaning is identical to that of Vimalakīrti.
Abiding in the eternally quiescent light, one manifests transformations within the three lands; all *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas are likewise so.

Only those such as Mañjuśrī, being naturally proximate [to the Buddha], are able to strike the opportune moment. Receiving the mandate to go and inquire, they first transmit the Buddha’s intent, and subsequently recount their doubts.

[The Master] says: "End. [The disciple] answers: "Below. This is the layman’s answer. First, he answers regarding the arising of the cause. "The multitude of beings," etc., he answers regarding the duration.
"The illness of the multitude of beings," etc., he answers regarding how it is extinguished. Because Great Compassion first arose simultaneously with the illness, the illness exists;

since beginningless time, Great Compassion is likewise so. Since the illness is thus, there is no priority or posteriority in its healing. "As for the multitude of beings," etc., he uses the manifested to reveal the manifestor, such as the "Square Chamber" and so forth.
All of this is due to his former vows; thus, having attained the Way, he possesses such supreme power. As for "the city of grass" and so forth, it refers to the city of Kuśinagara.
Desiring to proclaim his parinirvāṇa, he first manifested back pain. The reasons for his illness are explained in detail as previously stated in the section on "The Power Spoken of Due to Illness."
The vow proceeds; beginning and end are non-dual, and only at the final moment of mind is it fulfilled. Regarding "compassion descends," this refers to the power of the vow.
As for "Dharma-joy and so forth," this is the private commentary of Zhanran. The first edition states: "When the aspiration is true and real, whatever is thought of is immediately eliminated;
if one looks toward what is deficient, it is called unreal. Master Xi (Huiji) together with twenty-seven others made their aspiration at Guangzhou; among his disciples...
Master Zhongxi is the eldest. If his resolve is inferior, then the judgment of gain and loss must rely on the Three Jewels and so forth; this would not be genuine.

Lacking personal diligence, he instead defers to and looks up to the Buddha; thus, that which he seeks is unsurpassed. If his mind were truly sincere, he would have attained the first stage (*bhūmi*), let alone merely recover from his illness.

Next, regarding "settling the mind" (*citta-sthāpana*), as for the phrase "realizing the essence" (*tattva-avabodha*) and so forth: first, one must cause the object to be understood; based on that object, one gives rise to the vow, and only then does one discuss settling the mind.

Therefore, the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*) is clarified. Furthermore, the preceding two [points] are reiterated: "realizing the essence" refers to the object, and "arousing the thought" refers to the vow.

First comes correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), followed by the sixty-four cycles. As for the "great medicine," it is the remedy of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); there is no need to apply counter-measures, as it possesses both qualities simultaneously.

Next, regarding the refutation of pervasiveness: first, one investigates that the illness originates from the mind; next, "now observing below" correctly clarifies the application of contemplation. First is the refutation of establishment through causes;

second, "cannot be obtained below," refutes continuity and mutual dependence—the text for both is abbreviated. Regarding the initial refutation of establishment through causes, it says "not earth, etc.":
because it arises from the mind, it is not earth; yet because it is the body of the illness, it does not exist apart from earth. The same applies to the other three elements. Therefore:
This illness is not a combination of body and mind; its pervasion and obstruction can be seen.

Following the section on the "Factors of Enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa), the meaning of the middle [truth] is also the same as before. Regarding "not pure, etc.," this is explained in terms of the refutation of extremes.

Regarding "having reality, etc.," this is explained in terms of the realm of the truths (satya). The illnesses of both myself and sentient beings are all like this; it is also the union with the Middle Way while contemplating illness.

In this context, the discussion of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and so forth refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); the discussion of withering and flourishing and so forth refers to that which is manifested. This is fully as explained in the preceding text following the "Chapter on the Path" (*mārga-varga*) regarding the objects of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Regarding the statement in the "Aids to the Path" (*bodhipakṣa*) section that "one briefly cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā," this means that the six [categories], beginning with the objects (*viṣaya*), constitute the primary practice (*maula-prayoga*). If there are hindrances (*āvaraṇa*)...

Excluding [those cases], one should practice the six correct aids in combination, such as the techniques of śamatha, vipaśyanā, and breath control. One shall then enter the first stage (prathama-bhūmi). How much more so regarding the diseases of the four elements?

Regarding the successive stages, as in the case of that lapis lazuli and so forth: it is seen because the water is clear; it is not yet attained because the depth has not been reached. This may be understood accordingly.

The sixth [point] clarifies the beginning and end of attainment. Regarding the phrase "not yet escaping various calamities": if it refers to the three minor calamities, since the fruit-body still remains, one has not yet escaped them.
If, however, there is no portion [of these calamities] at all, how could one indiscriminately claim that the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna) is visible?

Next, regarding the objective realm of karma: "Now, as for those who practice samādhi," it is like this: calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) are like sunlight, while the characteristics of karma are like the myriad forms [reflected therein].

Next, the doubts are resolved. First, two sūtras are cited to prove the characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles; next, the *Lotus Sūtra* is cited to prove the characteristics of the ten realms. The same applies to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
If both the Great and Small Vehicles exist together, why is it said that [the Small Vehicle] does not exist?

Next, regarding the detailed explanation: first, concerning the causal conditions, the internal and external conditions are shown initially. Within the initial section on the internal, the phrase "the mind gradually" and so forth may also be called "clarity and stillness.

The two characters "clarity and stillness" correspond to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). As for the statement that "good and evil each have arising and ceasing," this is because they span two time periods;

furthermore, evil has degrees of lightness and heaviness, while good has distinctions between the heterodox and the orthodox. By practicing both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one stirs the past roots of goodness.

Evil. Regarding how good and evil arise and perish through cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*): it is because of contemplation that one sees [the truth], yet this does not arise from that [contemplation] alone.

Therefore, an analogy is offered: the object is like that which is polished; the rational nature (*dharmatā*) is like a mirror; darkness and distraction are like dust; cessation and contemplation are like the polishing; and the manifestation of karma is like the image.
Next, the external conditions are explained: these are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Although the texts speak of them separately, their meanings necessarily complement one another;

this constitutes the fourfold relationship between the responsive capacity (*yōki*) and the response (*ōō*), comprising both the hidden and the manifest. Regarding "sentient beings and so forth": only when there are the four *siddhi* (the fourfold suitability) can resonance and response occur. Because of the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they manifest [themselves];

this is called "meditation on good and evil. What is seen is clearly revealed, like a flower shown to a person. As for "now, however, only those who... and so forth, this establishes the objective realm.

Next, the actual explanation of the arising of karma is presented. Regarding the "six intentions," these consist of only two categories of phenomena: the first two arise individually, the third and fourth are explained in mutual relation, the fifth is simultaneous, and the sixth is mixed.
Although each subsequent item possesses all six intentions, in the following commentary only the two [categories] are distinguished.
The characteristics [of these] are as follows. For the remainder, one should simply follow the preceding examples; the details of their mutual intermingling can be understood through reflection.

Within this, first the causes of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) and the fruits of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*) are clarified, followed by the explanation of the causes of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*) and the fruits of retribution (*vipāka-phala*). Although the text does not explicitly establish the relationship between the fruit of habituation and the cause of retribution, it must nevertheless be addressed because there are two underlying meanings.
This is explained as follows. First, by way of contrast; second, by way of mutual designation. Therefore, we now cite two treatises to provide a comprehensive explanation.

Regarding the statement that the "cultivation cause" (*abhyāsa-hetu*) is the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*), etc., the new terminology uses "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these six are accepted as the causes. This is explained in detail within that treatise. If [it refers to] the Great...

The treatise states: "That which is produced is common to its own part; it is universally associated with retribution. This was translated by Fu Gong, and it is sufficient to serve as a model for transmission.
How much more so for the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), which is what our school employs; and how much more so for these two treatises, which still retain their original names.
For now, I shall briefly set forth the general principles according to the text to prepare for further understanding.

Regarding the phrase "How so? and below: first, there is the explanation; next, the characteristics of its arising are distinguished. In the initial passage, there is first the explanation and then the judgment. As for the statement that "the nature depends on the fruit," this is because it relies on the *abhyāsa-hetu* (habitual cause);

thus, it is a *niṣyanda-phala* (outflowing fruit). This is stated in terms of a single moment (*kṣaṇika*). Next, in the section beginning with "This meaning... and below, the nature is judged; this also proceeds from the standpoint of a single moment.

If, however, one speaks in terms of the beginning and the end, it is then an untainted (*anāsrava*) fruit and does not apply to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Next, in the section beginning with "The treatise author... and below, [it is compared] with the above.

Regarding the "mutual correspondence" and, next, the "retributive cause and retributive fruit": since the two types of habituation together constitute the retributive cause, these four meanings are reduced to three.

Within the category of "habituation," what is called "fruit" is viewed as the cause for the subsequent "retribution. Next, regarding the section beginning with "now," the commentator further explains that it is only when habituation continues across successive lifetimes that it is designated as the "habituation-fruit."

Regarding the section on the *Abhidharmika* (Śāstrakāra) school: they judge that the two fruits are distinct. Although their judgments differ slightly, their explanations of the underlying meaning do not vary.

The *Abhidharmika* rely on the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, and the treatise follows the previous explanation. Furthermore, regarding the section "Now, below": the treatise school offers a different interpretation, whereby the two causes and two fruits are all separated by an interval of time (*vyavahita*). They judge the two causes based on whether karma is completed;

that which arises after such an interval is then designated as the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*), while that which compensates for a prior cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*) is termed [the fruit of retribution].
Regarding "retributive fruit" (*vipākaphala*): these four names possess four meanings.

Following the section on "sitting in meditation," the subsequent passage clarifies the manifestation of signs. Within the initial clarification of retributive fruit, it is stated that among the manifestations of signs, they are "mutually designated."
Upon a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), two names—cause and fruit—are established. Because it previously acted as a cause, it is now called "fruit.

Since its retribution (*vipāka*) will exist in a future life, it may further be designated as a "cause. Furthermore, when this characteristic manifests, it acts as the cause for retribution. Now, [the text] merely... [judges].

Regarding the statement "descending within the sitting" and "the appearance of the characteristics of the causal practice," it is also said that they "mutually receive names. This means that in relation to what precedes them, they are called "fruits," and in relation to what follows them, they are called "causes.

Thus, they are said to "mutually receive names. All such statements are made based on the manifestation of characteristics; therefore, this explanation differs from the interpretation provided in the *Abhidharma*.
"Below, 'The characteristics of goodness are manifold' and so forth, separately judges that the manifestations of the characteristics of the six perfections differ.

However, the characteristics of the six perfections are merely categorized by analogy as being subsumed within these six. Whether they are practiced (*śikṣā*) or retributive (*vipāka*), they are distinguished by their function and manifestation.

For instance, regarding giving (*dāna*), the objects may mutually manifest all [the perfections], yet retribution occurs only when it arises from the internal mind; this is what is called 'practice. As for 'Dharma-gates,' [this refers to] the past and the present."

Either it is analyzed individually, or, for the sake of giving, this mind of giving is distinguished; both are termed "cultivating causes" (*vāsanā-hetu*). The same applies to the following five [perfections].

Next, regarding the section on precepts, the mention of the "ten masters" is merely based on the Central Kingdom (China). The first source states that there was a person from Chenliu who, through the arousal of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), was able to lecture on the Vinaya himself.
In the *Zhixiang lun* (Treatise on the Characteristics of Wisdom), it speaks of the "object of the Bodhisattva," wherein three types of Bodhisattvas are contrasted with the Perfect [Vehicle].
All are matters [of practice]. Excluding those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), the rest are all subsumed under "matters.
Regarding the section on the Six Perfections below, it provides exhortations; the preceding text on "ascending" says, "Be cautious and diligent," and so forth.

Regarding the section on various masters of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) below, it clarifies the different judgments regarding the necessity of repayment. The character for "loan" (*dài*) should be written as *tè* (with the phonetic *tāidé*). It means to seek goods from another. Previously, at the third...

If the treasure has not yet been returned, even in the Hīnayāna it is permitted that the debt remains unpaid; in the Mahāyāna, where the primary aim is benefiting others and saving sentient beings, it is likewise permitted that the debt remain unpaid while one is dedicated to entering the Path.
Although there may be old debts, one must never create new ones. Once the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) has been resolved, one must immediately bestow [benefits] upon others;

how could one who currently encroaches upon others be called a follower of the Mahāyāna? The character "觝" (dǐ) should be written as "抵" (dǐ), meaning to resist or reject. Next, the six [perfections] are explained.
Regarding the characteristics of obscuration: first, concerning stinginess, "蝃" (dì) means exhaustion; "詬" (hòu, with the *xù* and *dòu* rhymes) means shame and humiliation.

Within the breaking of precepts, there are only the seven natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the one prohibited transgression (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*), which is alcohol. Killing occurs due to hatred; sexual misconduct occurs due to greed.
These two, together with theft and the four verbal transgressions, constitute the seven branches. If speech is counted as a single category, they are the five precepts.

Furthermore, below the section on "the inner mind," the characteristics of the causes for practicing the four divisions are briefly cited; the remainder is omitted for brevity. Next, regarding the analytical examination:

first, the presence or absence of hindrances is examined by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Second, within the judgment, there is first a judgment based on the arising and ceasing of phenomena, followed by a judgment based on the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).
As for the term "initially good" (*ādau kalyāṇam*), it is because the outflowing (*sāsrava*) is contrasted with the three truths; thus, the outflowing [is situated]...

First, regarding the distinction between manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to non-manifest action. As for the causal condition of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*), it pertains to the mind, which is easy to understand.

As for the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*), it relies upon signs (*nimitta*), which are difficult to discern. The passage beginning with "If good or evil... correctly distinguishes between nature and non-manifest action.

Manifest action necessarily depends on the mind, as it coexists with the physical act; thus, when the sign appears, both the mind and the sign appear together. After the manifest action has ceased, non-manifest action remains constantly present throughout one's entire life.

Therefore, when the manifest [unmanifest] arises, it does not depend upon the mind. This is based on its coexistence with form (*rūpa*) and its being of the same nature as the action (*kriyā*). Thus, it is likewise difficult to determine.

However, because it contradicts the teachings and contradicts the original [Abhidharma] intent—since the term "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) exists in the original essential texts—it is called "contradiction regarding the unmanifest. Therefore, after the unmanifest...
Furthermore, one should examine this by means of ten dharmas and three characteristics.
Next, below, it is judged according to the three periods of time. The text states: "Initial anger followed by subsequent joy is the characteristic of the extinction of evil.
By analogy, one should further establish three propositions—joy and anger, and so forth—to judge the characteristics of the arising of goodness and the extinction of evil.

Regarding the phrase "As for generating the mind, [the text] below" (*fàxīn xià*), this distinguishes based on understanding and practice (*jiěxíng*). Regarding the phrase "If one is correct oneself, [the text] below," this distinguishes based on the teacher and realization (*shīzhèng*).

Since it is not easy to distinguish others, one uses realization as verification. As for what is called "not being personally moved" (*zì fēi qīngǎn*)—this means using one's own experience to verify another;

if one has never been personally moved, there will ultimately be no teacher. One should verify the signs of good and evil through this passage and within the *Cánmén* (Dhyāna Gate), and compare them with oral instructions (*kǒujié*).
I append this judgment. Otherwise, simply treat them with the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) and dissolve them thoroughly;

then all obstacles will be powerless against it, as is the case with the understanding and interpretation in the preceding text. The reason for my frequent warnings is the fear that those lacking discernment might rely on [my words] to deceive themselves and others.
Since ancients took their teachers' names as their surnames, they were called "Shishi" (Teacher-clansmen).

The question regarding "below" serves to distinguish it from the suspicion concerning the manifestation of present signs. The original question within the inquiry concerns the manifestation of various evil signs;

the intent of the answer is that such is indeed the case. Karma is the actual object of retribution; it is not protected by a deity. As for the term *yuhou* (虞候): these were officials who patrolled and monitored for transgressions within the army.
*Yu* means "exclusive" or "solely devoted"; *chan* (覘) and *hou* (候) both mean "to spy" or "to watch."

Furthermore, the following section explains the doubts regarding omissions. As for the term "mutual omissions": the *Abhidharma* lacks the methods of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* lacks the characteristics of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*).

Now, by providing both meanings, there is a surplus in one's own practice. When compared to those two schools, although this does not yet match the dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the *Abhidharma*, it establishes contemplation based on the dharmas;
thus, that treatise is sparse and neglectful in this regard.

Next, the actual explanation of the cultivation of contemplation begins with the section on "contemplating through reflection. Regarding the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), the text is abbreviated. It then concludes by stating that these "summon forth form and mind";

here, "form" refers to the six elements. The cases of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas may be understood by analogy. The reason no Bodhisattvas are mentioned is that the method of contemplation applies universally to all.
Within the "Inconceivable" section, the first section provides a comparative judgment. Regarding the citation from the *Lotus Sūtra*:

since the subsequent text mentions both the "primary" and "secondary" retributions (*niṣyanda*), if it refers to the primary retribution, it signifies that the ten [realms] are each the ten realms; if it refers to the secondary retribution, it is because the three thousand [worlds] do not transcend the ten directions.

Next, in the section clarifying the correct meaning, first the realm is delineated, followed by the citation of scriptural evidence. Question: The scriptural evidence cited previously was specific; how does it differ from the present "perfect" (yuan) perspective?
Answer: The words are the same, but the meanings differ. Previously, one took the producer and the produced as the focus; now, one takes the inherent nature of the earth as being fully complete.

Furthermore, within the mutual inclusion [of the elements], solidity itself is the solidity of earth. Since both the producer and the produced are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is no distinction.

Having already deeply penetrated the lower [stages], the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is for the purpose of following karma; this applies to both good and evil, and likewise first manifests the sequential before the non-sequential.
The settling of the mind (*anxin*) is also thus: good is followed and evil is stilled. *Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are merely different names for this.

Next, regarding the "Refutation of Pervasiveness": although various individual tenets are cited to collectively establish the three times as the object of contemplation, when one contemplates below, the subject that contemplates likewise first proceeds sequentially, taking the three times as its firm basis.
Next, regarding the phrase "if one says": in the past and present, time and space are taken as relative opposites and treated as horizontal; all four permutations are thus categorized as horizontal.
Furthermore, "the three periods of time" refers to emptiness; "the words" refer to the provisional; and "because of this" refers to the middle.

Regarding the four phrases within the section on "Penetration and Obstruction": first is the contaminated (*sāsrava*), second is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), third is the provisional (*prajñapti*), and last is the middle (*madhyama*). Examining the subject and object is fully detailed as in the section on the aggregates (*skandha*).

Next, within the section on the Path (*mārga*), from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* up to the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), these are precisely the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

When mental action (*manaskarma*) arises alone, this is mind (*citta*). When the mind attains real dharmas, this is feeling (*vedanā*). When it perceives conventional designations (*prajñapti*), this is perception (*saṃjñā*). From "formative factors" (*saṃskāra*) downward, these are the formative perceptions;

together they constitute the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Together with bodily and vocal actions, they constitute the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). According to the Sautrāntika school, these are attained sequentially.
This is the explanation. Regarding the Abhidharma, it follows the text as written. From this point onward, we shall examine the "unmanifest" (avijñapti) foundations of mindfulness.
As for the term "homogeneous" (sabhāga), it is so called because the ten realms, such as form and the rest, share a common designation.

Next, regarding those who assist the path: mindfulness of the Buddha treats the hindrances. These hindrances are karma. To destroy both the habitual causes and the evil karma—namely, the evil habitual causes—one must employ the thirty-two marks and the merit of retribution.
Because these are evil habitual causes, they are intensified by form (*rūpa*). Since they are habitual causes within the mind, one must practice mindfulness of the Buddha of Retribution;

thus, for mere habitual causes alone, the formal marks are not required. However, if it concerns the fruit of a virtuous retribution, that retribution is a phenomenon of form (*rūpadharma*); therefore [the marks are necessary].

It is simply a matter of contemplating form. While the retribution for good and evil should correspond only to their respective causes of habitual practice, when both contemplate the retribution of form yet speak only of the "Dharma-gate," this is said from the perspective of what is preeminent.
Furthermore, the term "Dharma-gate" encompasses the meaning of the retribution of form as well. As for the statement that "the obstacles of evil karma are transformed":
Both good and evil act as obstacles; for now, I shall speak of them according to their gravity.

Next, I will clarify the realms of Māra. Regarding what are called "māra-activities," the celestial Māras primarily take the task of causing one to regress from bodhicitta and becoming jealous of one's retinue.

The "hostile" (宿) refers to Māra; because Māra uses these [obstacles] to obstruct, they are called "māra-affairs. This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Māra-Affairs" (*Māravastu*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Within the initial intent [of this practice], all four *siddhāntas* are fully present. For one who cultivates samādhi, this restates the previous general cultivation; as evil is about to depart, [the obstacles arise].

This reiterates the three previous objects. As the unwholesome matter of the event is about to subside and the wholesome principle of the truth is about to arise, Māra fears that the object will transcend his domain and cause harm to the objective sphere;
therefore, he comes forth. To "transcend the domain" means to destroy the intention of the world.

Next, one should again eliminate [the thought of] departing, which destroys the intention for the benefit of others. Next, one should again guard against the thought of departing, which destroys the intention for remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).

This achieves both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). It is the great wisdom of observation. Fearing that these [thoughts] might arise, one pre-emptively destroys them. Regarding the phrase "destroying the roots of goodness":

because they accord with Bodhi, they are universally cautioned against. Regarding the phrase "one's own realm": this refers to guarding against the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception from afar, and suppressing the Desire Realm heavens from nearby. One clearly knows [this] as it accords [with the truth].

There is. Furthermore, it gives rise to the appearance of intimacy. "Shu" (戌) means to obstruct. The phrase "as stated in the Sūtra" below refers to the text from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter on the Deeds of Māra (*Māra-karman-varga*).

It is so called because sins arise due to Māra; as the Sūtra says (at length). Regarding the knowledge of the realm of Māra as stated below, the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that the two principles are non-dual, as in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
After the Buddha had transformed the demonesses, Māra said: "My own retinue cannot [be transformed] by themselves..."
Thereupon, the demonesses displayed an appearance of timidity and proclaimed the sublime principle, saying to Māra: "We do not now leave your realm.
Why is this? The suchness of the realm of Māra is the suchness of the realm of the Buddha; for there is no realm apart from this that is the realm of the Buddha."

In the subsequent detailed explanation, we first distinguish between similarities and differences. While [the former] lacks a counterpart in terms of karma and objects, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are distinguished in relation to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As with the ten armies mentioned previously, these possess all four inversions; therefore, in relation to the four [truths], the inversions are merely afflictions. If it were the ten armies [previously mentioned]:
These are established by Māra and are further encompassed by Māra.

If one distinguishes them according to the boundaries (dhātu), those situated outside the boundaries are the "Māras outside the boundaries. Although the Mahāyāna sūtras identify the four factors such as impermanence as being outside the boundaries, [they are so designated] in relation to the boundaries.
These are general remarks and do not fall within the scope of the present context. For now, I shall speak of the Māras based on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

Regarding the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*) in relation to the three [categories] beginning with the devaputras, there are seven for each of the internal and external [spheres]. Therefore, it is necessary to carefully examine the three starting with the devaputras.

As for what is meant by "different," it simply means that one must not pair the four [inversions] with the four [Māras], and so forth, up to the statement that the three Māras have already been transcended by those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). This...

This refers to the path of instruction. In terms of actual reality, they must be equal. Regarding the absence of a sixth [heaven] and so forth: since this is explained according to actual reality, all four [realms] are fully present.

How then could there be a separate "Heaven of the Sons of Gods" (Tianzi)? Therefore, it must be explained that this is merely the red-colored samādhi of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) among the twenty-five samādhis;
because the three truths are not yet fulfilled and one grade of delusion remains, it is called "not yet ultimate."

Next, regarding the citation of sutras for clarification: in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of that sutra, there are ten kinds of *māra*: first, the aggregates (*skandha*); second, afflictions (*kleśa*); third, karma; fourth, the mind;

fifth, death; sixth, the gods; seventh, roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); eighth, meditative absorption (*samādhi*); ninth, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); and tenth, the knowledge of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhidharma-jñāna-abhijñā*).
This treatise applies these ten names to both the internal and external realms, explaining them through these ten designations as applicable to both. If discussed separately:

Regarding these: six internal [factors] are common to one among the six; furthermore, three of the five internal realms are *māras*, and the afflictions within the second, third, and fourth realms are also included.

As for the remainder, they are common as previously stated. Therefore, those whose names correspond to the four categories within the realms are explained according to their specific definitions, while those with different names are explained generally.
In the section on the "Manifestation of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇotpāda*), first is the "Lord of Men. Next, in the "Exegesis," regarding the term *jiū* (啾[口*祭]), it refers to the chirping of insects.

Next, in the "Twelve Hours of Charm," regarding the "Twelve Animals of the Great Assembly": the *Wuxing* states there are twelve "semblances" (*sì*); they are called such because they resemble those [animals].
In the *Mahāsannipāta*, each mountain where they dwell is distinguished by its height; the names of their caves are the abodes of the animals, and the Venerable Deity serves as their attendant. One.
Each had two rākṣasī women and five hundred attendants, who each made offerings according to their respective directions.

Those beasts all claimed to practice "compassion conditioned by dharmas" (dharmālambana-maitrī). One beast would patrol Jambudvīpa day and night in rotation, while the others practiced loving-kindness (maitrī).
Regarding the phrase "those who vex others" in the text below: this refers to those of the secondary branches.

The section beginning with "if [the mind is] deviant and base" correctly clarifies the manifestation of the arousal [of afflictions]. The section beginning with "now, wishing to... uses the seasons to verify the animal signs. As for the statement that these nine belong to the Eastern Wood and so forth: among the nine, three are primary;

therefore, the three primaries are matched against the first, middle, and last months (*mèng*, *zhòng*, *jì*). Regarding the mention of "before and after," the first month (*mèng*) stands at the beginning.
Therefore, the primary animals are placed at the rear; because the second [rank] is in the center, the primary animals occupy the center;

because the third [rank] is at the end, the primary animals occupy the beginning. This is the case for all other directions as well. This is done so that the seats of the first, middle, and last ranks may be equal.

While the texts for the other five elements all contain only twelve items, only the *Liuzhu shi* (The Six Modes of Abiding) fully enumerates thirty-six. That text states: "There are already three types of cicada-slugs (*chánshān*)."
"Snake. I suspect the current text is erroneous. The remaining names follow the same pattern. Since we must prevent their arrival, it is necessary to briefly distinguish their characteristics.

"I" (吾): [The character for] "marten" (狢) has large feet; it should be written as [豸*角] (pronounced *hú*). The *Erya* states: "The female is called [豸*(止/(止*止))] (pronounced *nǎi bù*). People in Jiangdong today call it *kuāng-li*. The character *yú* (羭) is derived from [豸].
*Yū-yǔ* (猰貐) belongs to the class of *chū* (pronounced *rèn zhū*); they have tiger claws, eat people, and run swiftly. [This section] is further opened.
As for the one hundred and eight [names]: fearing that the time would be too long, each [category] was expanded by three, returning to the original number of beasts;
thus, by merely reciting thirty-six names, the one hundred and eight are naturally eliminated. Now, according to the laws of ghosts and spirits, they fear being known by name;
how much more so when their forms are recognized and they are called by those very names—they dare not commit evil.

Next, regarding the arising of demonic offenses (*māra-āpatti*): first, the intention to destroy and the destruction of the Dharma are explained. Of these, the present case is a proximate connection, while the other two are remote connections;

therefore, they are more difficult [to recognize] than the former. Regarding "two good and two evil": the Four Great Vows constitute one's own goodness, while all [other] practices constitute the goodness of others.
Seeing and thinking constitute past evils; ignorance constitutes future evils.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, cites scriptural evidence for this. Regarding the "flower-arrows" and so forth, the treatise asks: "What is called Māra? It answers: "He is the one who destroys the life of wisdom and ruins the Dharma of the Path.

Because he leads people to give rise to attachment, he is called a "flower"; because he damages the five faculties, he is called an "arrow"; and because he destroys the Buddha-dharma... [he is called Māra].

Because it is "skillful" (*kuśala*), it is called *māra*. Regarding the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) each lasting for a single moment: at the time one perceives an object, if a single moment of attachment arises, [the Māra] immediately gains an opportunity.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*, even while the Buddha was begging for alms, he was still troubled by Māra. Māra asked the Buddha, "Where are you going?
Knowing this was Māra, the Buddha said to him, "I am going to that place where the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) do not exist. Then [Māra] acted...

This is the recollection: the śramaṇa knows me to be Māra; therefore, in the present text, although the external patrons (dānapati) do not appear among the six, the mention here of "five" refers to the five ways of entering the mind and the five ways of destroying the mind.

Furthermore, the following section provides a detailed explanation of those who come from outside [the Buddhist fold]. First, they cause one to fall into evil; next, they cause one to fall into goodness.
Such people are originally worldly gentlemen capable of making such claims; originally being commoners, they fundamentally belong to Māra.

For such individuals, what could be discussed regarding "falling"? Next, they cause one to fall into the Two Vehicles; next, they cause one to fall into emptiness and so forth that lack skillful means—this refers to the "evil" of emptiness and the provisional. It is not...

Regarding the contemplation of nature and characteristics: to be deluded regarding the four natures and fail to understand their essential character (lakṣaṇa) while merely giving rise to an empty understanding is called "lack of skillful means.

To still harbor attachment and views is called "false lack of skillful means. Moreover, since this [contemplation] was originally not intended for the benefit of sentient beings, yet deviates from emptiness, it is all termed "partial."

"Ānanda, descend. This raises the profound to illustrate the shallow: even at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was still afflicted by sixty-four trillion demons; how much more so for ordinary people?
The intent clarifies that those of the Hīnayāna are not skilled at discerning māras, nor are they tamers of māras. How can they avoid [affliction] for themselves and others?

Each of the six sense-faculties has three aspects, each of which turns toward the mental faculty (manas), thus resulting in eighteen. Māras create afflictions of their own and further incite others to do so.

Section Thirty-six. "If one knows the lower" refers precisely to harmonizing according to principle. Because of delusion regarding the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one perceives a distinction between demons and Buddhas;

if one perceives the reality-limit, then demons and Buddhas are equal, as previously stated by the celestial maiden in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Because the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle sever their afflictions, it is said they "harmonize demons. As [the text continues]:

Because the essence of the *Kukuda* and others is like the *dharmadhātu*, there is nothing to be disciplined. When the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* was taught, it was said that their own bonds were not discipline.

Next, regarding the obstruction of distraction, it is distinguished by means of ten dharmas; in the present text, compared to the correct [teaching], all are said to be excessive. This is based on the context of the meditative states (*dhyāna-viṣaya*).
Furthermore, it does not reach that number.

Regarding the subsequent enumeration which mentions "three hundred heterodoxies," this is merely an approximation based on external factors; when combined with the internal sense of the three hundred and sixty [channels], the text states:
"Initially, it is due to the five faculties."

Regarding the phrase "stealing years" (*tōshō*) and so forth in the *Zhìyì* (Treatise on Tranquility): this refers to privately increasing one's monastic age (*fǎsuì*) in order to scheme for profit and evade labor service. "Shō" (years) means the age.

From the Han dynasty until the present, as for the term *kichi*, this is the name of a ghost. It originally arises from breaking the precepts; even upon hearing the precepts, one should still feel shame.
How much more so when protected by the deities of the precepts and when the ghosts of broken precepts depart!
Regarding the subduing of Māra, it says: "Do not accept anything whatsoever. This "contemplation of non-attainment" is precisely the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

It pervades the six sense faculties; there is nothing that emptiness does not subdue. The *Āgama* states: "Māra has five powers, namely the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The noble disciples of the Buddha..."

A single power is able to counteract [these faults]: namely, heedfulness (*apramāda*). The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "How can one ensure that Māra finds no opportunity? It is by practicing emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).

Next, it explains the three types of evil practitioners who cultivate contemplation (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "making others one's own": whenever one gives anything, one causes it to belong to others.
I. A major sutra states: "If one practices giving because they are subject to others, they will fall into the evil realms.

Now, while being subject to the Three Jewels is based on the objective aspect of the matter, falling into evil follows from the mind; thus, even if one is born in the good realms and so forth, since one has performed the deeds of Māra, one will be subject to Māra life after life.
As for the passage in the sutra beginning with "The scripture says," this is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Ānanda asked the Buddha: "Does Māra afflict all bodhisattvas?"
"Are there also those who are not troubled? The Buddha said: "If one does not believe the words of the profound *prajñā*, and others say, 'I do not even know its depths;
why do you study it? You have many other matters to attend to,' such a person will be troubled by Māra.
If these things do not occur, then Māra will not trouble them."
Next, regarding the phrase "one demon is all Buddhas" within the section on the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*):

since the demon is identical to principle (*li*), and principle subsumes all things, this refers to the merit of wondrous contemplation (*prajñā*) described below. Therefore, this is termed "subduing demons to manifest principle. As for the phrase "cultivation through conditions" (*yuánxiū*) and so forth:

those on the stages prior to the *dhāraṇī-bhūmi* (the stage of holding the world) have not yet attained quiescent illumination; they experience entering and emerging from contemplation, and thus are schemed against by demons. This refers to Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
He came; therefore, he comforted him well. He further admonished him, saying: "You should contemplate impermanence to seek the root of goodness. Māra used the adornments of women to corrupt his mind;
had it not been for Vimalakīrti, Māra would have nearly found an opportunity. Since Vimalakīrti occupies such a high station, how could he wait for his own mind to become clear?

Therefore, he told that he was not Śakra, but Māra, who had departed after developing the aspiration for enlightenment. Compassion allows both Māra and those who know the Buddha-realm to understand one another.
The joy of this [practice] lies in its compassion for uprooting the sufferings of the Buddha-realm as well as the demonic realm; thus, immeasurable loving-kindness and immeasurable compassion arise.

When the demons desire to depart, one settles the mind by temporarily entrusting it to the narrative of Śākyamuni; therefore, this is discussed in relation to Siddhārtha. Next, the following section establishes the characteristics of the practitioner’s method for settling the mind.
Following the subduing of Māra, [the four māras] are destroyed in succession: first collectively, then individually. Within the teachings, the first three *piṭakas* subdue the four [māras];

only upon sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) does one destroy the *kleśamāra*, which is called the Path of Bodhi. After entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is called the *dharmatākāya*; only then can one destroy the *skandhamāra*.

Because these two [destructions] are attained, birth and death are forever destroyed; thus they are said to be "destroyed together. Therefore, while there remains a permanent residual body, [the others are not yet destroyed].
Regarding "named as defeating the two demons of the aggregates and death, and attaining immovability, etc.": it is as described in the *Mahāsamaya-sūtra*.

First, he commands his various armies; next, he commands his crown prince; then, he dispatches his three consorts. When these are unable to destroy [the enemy], he subsequently leads his own army himself, only to retreat in dispersal and fall headlong.

The crown, the parasol, and the sword—each fell in a separate place. These all constitute the Great Collection (Mahāsaṃnipāta). Now, the text extends through the explanations of the latter three teachings.

In the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), it is identical to the stage of suppression (*vibhava*) in the Tripitaka Teaching. Upon reaching the sixth ground, it becomes identical to the abandonment (*prahāṇa*) in the Tripitaka Teaching.

The śrāvakas of both teachings do not destroy the devaputras; therefore, they are tormented by them. Although the Shared Teaching attains suppression, it is still not called "abandonment. This is fully [stated] within the teaching.

There is no name for "red" [passion] as it is distinct from the path of teaching; therefore, afflictions are severed sequentially. How could one sever universal delusions while merely suppressing particular delusions and yet not destroy Māra?

In the true path of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there is no longer any sequence of before and after; one must instead distinguish degrees of depth and shallowness by means of the six identities (*liuji*).
Regarding the simultaneous destruction of the eight and ten māras at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*): it is destroyed partially at the first stage; the rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the "openings and blockages" for each of the stages above, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are as stated in the text.

As for the "if the gate has not yet opened" section below, these six types of auxiliary paths (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) become obstacles to the Way (*mārga*) while they serve as means of deliverance against the māras. Now, by relying on principle (*li*), one rejects the phenomenal deliverances (*dharma-pāramitā*). For this reason...

Regarding the six matters for subduing the six types of Māras: the first four [perfections] clearly transcend birth and death; yet the meditative concentrations attained may involve communication with spirits, and the Prajñā studied may not be free from views and attachments.

As for what is called "correctly crossing over," it does not go beyond the Four Teachings, as is fully clarified in the section on the "Aids to the Path" (*zhùdào*) and the "Compendium of Dharmas" (*shèfǎ*).
Regarding what is called "subduing both," two [categories] are included within the Māras; therefore, one must borrow [from other methods]. If they are mixed...

Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*), they are treated as in the previous two objects. As for the "mixed karma" of borrowing mindfulness of the two Buddhas: because there is evil, one is mindful of form (*rūpa*);

because there is good, one is mindful of the Dharma-gate (*dharmamukha*). Regarding those with wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*): in the four teachings, they are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) outside the stages;

in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), they are at the five grades (*wupin*). "To cast out" (*chu*) means to retreat or to be degraded. This accords with the *Mahāsārathiparivarta*; what is not in the text is omitted for brevity.

Furthermore, below the section on "the universal application of a single intention," the text concludes by distinguishing between the universal and the particular through the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) as objects.

Because this contemplation applies universally to the nine subsequent [categories], it is said that the universal is but a single contemplation. Once one has first understood the universal in relation to the ten dharmas, their individual characteristics can be discerned;
therefore, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* is cited as an example for both the universal and the particular.

Next, in the section on critical analysis, the question is as stated in the text. The answer first addresses the question in a contrary manner, hence it says, "the conditions are distinct. Next, it cites a passage from the treatise, which answers the question in a conforming manner.
Although there is a conforming sense, it cannot be taken as absolute; therefore, this is not the same as the departure of winter and the arrival of spring.
For twelve years, the brahmin Mahādharmarata sought the Dharma but could not obtain it; there was no Buddha in the world, nor was there any Buddha-Dharma.
A certain brāhmaṇa said, "I possess one verse of the sublime Dharma. If you truly delight in the Dharma, I shall give it to you.
He replied, "I truly delight in it. The brāhmaṇa said, "If you truly delight in it, take skin for paper, bone for a pen, and..."
"The marrow shall serve as water; you should give it to him. He then wrote down the Buddha’s verse exactly as instructed. The verse said: "One should practice in accordance with the Dharma;
one should not practice what is contrary to the Dharma. Whether in this life or in future lives, those who practice the Dharma dwell in peace and security.
It is said that while his skin was being flayed, Māra vanished.
*Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll Eight;
*Zhi guan fu xing sou yao ji*, Scroll Nine.
Recorded by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Zhanran at Fulong.
First, the explanation of the meditative state (*dhyāna*). Regarding the phrase "long-term illness, etc. mentioned in the initial section on the purpose of the coming [of this treatise]:

according to the *Āgamas* of various schools, there are five causes for the retrogression from the fruits [of the path]: long-term illness, traveling afar, engaging in disputes, managing affairs, and excessive recitation. Although these texts are minor, the meaning regarding their obstructive nature is certainly universal.
As for the thirty-six impurities (*mala*), I have not yet examined them.

The meaning of the passage following the aforementioned various objects is as follows: "The pond" refers to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). Because the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) has been perfected, it is said that one has "entered the stream deeply.
At this stage, one is fully endowed with all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) pertaining to both phenomena and principle; what further need is there for contemplation?

Regarding "if demonic affairs [arise]," since the transgressions of Māra have no objective basis, one must rely on supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for cultivation. If these were not explained, views and attachments would inevitably arise; therefore, it is said that they "increase daily."
Next, as for the phrase "if one deems it inferior" and so forth: even if one were to tolerate such a judgment, if one preserves [the practice] but does not contemplate it, many faults will arise.

I fear that if one abandons it and fails to practice, one will instead fall into a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*). With a distracted mind as one's object, how could one reach the various *dhyānas*? Since contemplation leads to entry into the various stages (*anupūrva-vihāra*), it must not be abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "but the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*) and so forth," this is an invocation of the teachings to praise them. Although the nine dhyānas are not the [exclusive] object [of discussion here], they are cited generally for now;

moreover, since most of the nine dhyānas consist of *vastu-dhyāna* (dhyāna as a basis), which possesses a substantial body and transforms others, they differ from the Śrāvaka vehicle. Therefore, there is no teaching, whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, that does not praise them.

As for the statement regarding the "four dhyānas and eight concentrations" (*aṣṭa-samādhi*), the four are included within the eight. The reason they are paired again here is that, according to various sūtras, these are universally applicable when contrasted with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The designation of the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). If one directly gives rise to the nine dhyānas, they are subsumed within the domain of a Bodhisattva.

Next, the individual explanations follow. First, regarding the opening and closing [of the gates], there is first a listing and then an analysis. As for the five gates of separation and combination, these refer to the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastu-citta-sthiti*).

Because they are entered through them, they are called "gates. Regarding the fifteen gates: each of the five [categories] is further divided into three, thereby completing the practice of phenomena (*dharma*), principle (*li*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Thus, the subsequent text states: "If there are only five gates, that which is not included therein is termed 'narrow' and consists solely of phenomena.
Among the fifteen, principle is not the present object; therefore, to ensure that phenomena are complete, the concise is expanded into the detailed, setting aside principle and retaining phenomena."

Because the combined and expanded sections might not be understood by others, they must be explained through comparative analysis; therefore, the inquiry is first raised. In the response, there is first a general explanation followed by a specific one.
Within the specific explanation, the five [categories] are first opened up into fifteen. When a practice lacks a corresponding object, it is expanded according to that object.

If an expansion is based solely on principle, one maintains the original practice while retaining the objective reality. Thus, *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) each have three expanded forms, totaling nine when combined with the three original ones. As for *devatā* (divine beings)...

The "Pervasive" (tōng) is not one of the nine. As for the nine schools' practice of "reciting the Buddha's name," and the Abhidharma’s term "expedient means" (fangbian), these differences in the opening of the teachings have already been analyzed above.
Next, regarding the consolidation of the fifteen into ten: the first six do not merge; within the subsequent nine gates, they are merely consolidated into three. There is none [else].

From the three types of objects of compassion (*karuṇā*), one immediately establishes the preservation of the objective referent. Regarding the three types of compassionate mind, there is the preservation of the "object-condition of sentient beings" (*sattvālambana*).

First, if the "object-condition of dharmas" (*dharmālambana*) is opened, it belongs to the Two Vehicles; the "unconditioned object" (*anālambana*) belongs to the Bodhisattvas. Generally speaking, these pertain to both realms. The Two Vehicles possess only the object-condition of dharmas, whereas the Bodhisattvas encompass all three teachings.

Only by distinguishing them according to their respective teaching-stages can the various meanings be fully set forth. Next, regarding the preservation of the "condition of causes and conditions" (*hetupratyaya*), the three periods of time are entirely [contained therein].

Regarding the phenomena (*dharma*), they are attached to principle (*li*) within a single thought-moment across two lifetimes. If [the teachings] are expanded, they are likewise subsumed under the realm of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As for mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*), it consists solely of mindfulness directed toward the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*);

since the Dharma-Body (*dharmakāya*) and Reward-Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) belong to the realm of principle, they are not discussed here as they are easily understood. As for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), if they include the untainted powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*), these too are subsumed under the realm of the Two Vehicles.

If one were to merely summarize the intent of the opening and closing sections, although there are [factors] such as opening and closing, they are combined into five solely for the purpose of counteracting obstacles.

However, if one were to encompass both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*), fifteen must be maintained. Now, in order to distinguish the arising [of the faculties] from the latter two objects, there are only ten gates.

Next, regarding the determination of what is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and what is without-outflow (*anāsrava*): first, I shall briefly refute two theories. Since this present [position] does not entirely negate them, it is said to differ slightly from them.

Although they are alike in being with-outflow, because they lack the contemplation of the Truths (*satya*), they are compared to a melon; why then would they need to take the Truths as their object? Therefore, these three [theories] are merely abbreviated.

These then belong to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*). Regarding the forty-eight years: this refers to the realization of the outflow-tainted dhyānas. Since there are twelve gates for each of the four [categories], such as self-cultivation and so forth, there are forty-eight.
All of these are outflow-tainted. The twelve gates consist of the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

As stated below in the *Kāśyapa-vardhana-sūtra*, it is proven that through the practice of dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) path, one attains the fruit of arhatship by practicing for ninety days according to the secret essentials of the dhyāna-dharma as taught by the Buddha.

Next, the *Mahā-sūtra* is cited, which likewise attests to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Since the Sūtra designates these as the noble precepts, concentration, and wisdom (*ārya-śīla-samādhi-prajñā*), they are nevertheless not something known by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
How, then, can the two treatises judge them to be tainted? Regarding the phrase "Buddha and so forth," this refers to the noble practice of wisdom.

At the end of the passage, it is thus revealed to the two vehicles that Bodhisattvas, having heard this, practice accordingly. Therefore, one knows that the two vehicles practice only a limited portion. [Citation ends.]

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is the initial gateway to the supramundane and to nirvāṇa; it should not be associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). Regarding the statement that the nine perceptions open the gateways to all impurities:
because these various causes are impure, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) obtained thereby are called "impure gateways," and thus one turns away from them.

Because all [meditations] are based on impurity, the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) serve as the initial gateway. Since impurity is thus established, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) are also established;
therefore, they are not exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). The analogy of the two stones is as follows: the southern stone is cold by nature, while the northern stone is hot by nature.

Although the names of the two ointments are identical, their uses differ. Thus, although one practices dhyāna, there is a distinction between that which is with-outflows and that which is without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
If [the opponent argues that] the untainted (anāsrava) takes the lower [stages] as its object, this is a general objection.

The intention of the objector is to simultaneously challenge the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) by asserting that since they are all capable of taking the untainted as their object, they should all be untainted. Regarding the statement "in six stages," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "How does one attain the heavenly realm?"

Regarding the attainment of certainty (*niyāma*) and the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*): The answer is that "certainty" refers to the six stages—the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas.
In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the preliminary stage is not included; it is replaced by the "desire-concentration" (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). The rest is the same as in the *Vibhāṣā*.

As for the attainment of the untainted, one should say it pertains to nine stages: the aforementioned six plus the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Thus, the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) constitutes both the attainment of certainty and the attainment of the untainted of an arhat (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the statement "seven stages," some masters do not include the *anāgamya* (preliminary) and the intermediate (*antara*) concentrations; this is the intended meaning of the *Mahā-śāstra*. Others maintain that the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) and the *anāgamya* are included, depending on the person.

Next, regarding "the six stages below the earth": The respondent now discusses *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) alone, without opening up the discussion on the wisdom of the truths (*satya-jñāna*).

For this reason, the fundamental [stages] differ from the various *dhyānas*. Regarding "below," it refers to the process of rejecting or not rejecting [certain factors]. As for the "ten perceptions" (*daśa-saṃjñā*): these ten perceptions are divided into three categories; they are situated within the stages of seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Because they possess the function of severing delusions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), they are not included here. Regarding "beneath the mind of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-citta*): this judges the *dhyāna* of loving-kindness; loving-kindness reaches the divine.
Ultimately, nothing exists in isolation. Therefore, these various dhyānas are all categorized according to others.

Regarding the "subsequent intent" and so forth: the question is as stated in the text. The answer first addresses the *Dhyanamukha* (Gate of Dhyāna). Within that *Dhyanamukha*, under the section on skillful means (*upāya*), it says:
"Skillful means are of two kinds, namely, external and internal. The external refers to the twenty-five dharmas; the internal consists of five gates."

First, cessation; second, examining the roots and nature of good and evil; third, settling the mind; fourth, treating illness; fifth, demonic activities. Within the gate of cessation, there are again three parts:

first, binding the object of focus; second, restraining the mind; third, realizing the truth. Following the realization of the truth through cessation, the manifestation of the five wheels is clarified.

It is only after the practice of the five wheels of dhyāna that good and evil are verified; therefore, it is said that "in the gate of dhyāna, [the signs] manifest first," and so forth. This is merely according to the sequence of the text.

If one discusses the characteristics of their arising, there is a distinction between sharp and dull faculties. If one discusses them in relation to one another, they likewise possess both sharp and dull aspects.

Furthermore, if the present text were entirely not to observe the aggregates (skandhas), it would constitute dullness of wisdom. Below, in the section on "Antidotes," this is contrasted with the five gates.

Next, regarding "shallow and deep," this refers to the sequence of arising of the ten gates. The former is shallow and the latter is deep. Because the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) is particularly superior, it is placed at the beginning;

the subsequent [gate] is generally clear and subtle compared to the former, and thus the former explains the general while the latter explains the specific. These three [categories] refer to the latter two.

Because they rely upon the fundamental [stage], they are collectively called "fundamental. Furthermore, because they do not depend on the fundamental stage and possess a powerful force for subduing afflictions (*kleśa*), they are so designated.

It ranks third from the end. The nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) remedy external objects but have not yet remedied one's own mind; therefore, because they remedy both the internal and external, they follow the nine perceptions.

The nine perceptions are the *vimokṣas* (liberations). When the observation of these perceptions is still brief, it is called "general" (*sāmānya*) due to its brevity. When it encompasses both the primary and secondary environments (*niśraya-vipākaphala*), it is called "particular" (*viśeṣa*) due to its detail.

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, what is called "right view"? It is so called because it destroys the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and because it remedies the notions of a self and a person. Since these were previously explained separately, they are not discussed here.

Furthermore, regarding the two lifetimes that destroy the self—the ordinary being as the lower cause and the noble one as the higher fruit—among the subsequent pairs, the first eight types are excluded;
this is because the seven categories of the aggregate-object are subsumed within the preceding nine, and thus are not treated here. Within those nine pairs, further exclusions are made.
Regarding mental attention (*manasikāra*): in the previous [stages], attention was applied to the preceding aggregates while the other nine occurred spontaneously;

now, since it is solely spontaneous, it is not discussed. The second major section concerns the causes and conditions for the arising of dhyāna. The internal seed serves as the internal cause, and external application serves as the condition.

Within the initial internal seeds, there are two parts each: the Dharma exposition and the analogy. First, regarding the Dharma exposition, the *Mahāyāna Sūtra* is cited concerning the "flavor of dhyāna" in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). All sentient beings...

All have previously attained the fundamental dhyāna through two conditions. Descending from the perspective of immediate circumstances, this explains that at the time the fire calamity arises at the beginning of a kalpa, there are none who do not attain the second dhyāna.
Since the formation of this kalpa, nine cycles of decrease have already passed; for the time being, we consider the eighth.

Therefore, it is said that this accords with immediate circumstances. From the section on "from long ago" downwards: since time immemorial, prior to the eight periods of decrease, who has not cultivated and attained [this]?
There is none who does not possess the seed; thus, its manifestation is indeterminate. Next, the analogy for what is near is easily perceived.

Next, the differences are distinguished. First, regarding the "Dharma": as for the passage stating "In the past there was... and so forth, this refers to the first of the eight pairs concerning the sequential and non-sequential.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "cultivation and so forth," this refers to cultivation and non-cultivation. Cultivation is mental attention (*manasikāra*); non-cultivation is non-mental attention.
Although the gates of cultivation and non-cultivation are not the final ones, they briefly encompass the remaining seven.
