Thus, it is said that "up to the point where one wishes to distinguish between what was cultivated and what was not cultivated in the past," the gates of mental attention and non-attention are taken up. Now, first observing the aggregates (skandhas) is called "neither factual nor rational.
Cultivating and attaining the various dhyānas is called "factual attainment. Within those dhyāna-gates, the four types of cultivation—factual and rational—are fully enumerated.
The four types of arousal [of the aspiration for enlightenment] consist of sixteen phrases. To contrast them with the present [context], they should likewise be understood as such.

Next, regarding the analogy concerning the "four plums" and so forth: at the time of ripening, each is distinct, just as the arousal [of the aspiration] differs. Following this is the section on "past habitual tendencies."

Taken together, the term "seeds" refers to the eight pairs. Therefore, what is now produced is likewise eightfold and not identical. Furthermore, although the seeds of dhyāna exist within the ground, they can only be brought to fruition as the factors [of enlightenment] by means of the rain of śamatha and vipaśyanā and the sunlight of the noble ones.

This is clear from the text regarding the first "object" among the external additions: first the object, then the subject; within the object, first the phenomenon (dharma), which is visible in the text. Next, regarding the analogy: it is the nature of mind.
Although the seeds of dhyāna exist within the ground, they require the rain of śamatha and vipaśyanā and the sunlight of the noble ones to be able to form the branches.
Regarding the leaves, flowers, and fruits:
in the subsequent detailed explanation, the first part concerning the Dharma is understandable. In the analogy, "hong" means large; it is as stated in the text.

As for the citation from the *Jingdu jing* (Sutra on the Pure Deliverance), the sutra says: "For such people as these, even hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas could not deliver them, let alone a single Buddha."
Human beings act for their own deliverance alone. Jingdu Bodhisattva said: "Sentient beings must hear the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Now, I shall synthesize these texts;
it is simply a matter of resonance and response.
Next, the characteristics of the arousal [of the thought of enlightenment] are correctly explained. First, the degree of its extent is determined by means of four modes of practice.

Because the "constant" mode is the least, it is not mentioned; yet, because it is not entirely absent, it is simply said to be "few. Thus, the sutra cited previously states: "There are distinctions among dwellings—few, middling, and many.
Regarding whether these exist or not, the two treatises differ. Here, we rely on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: the ten wholesome paths of action belong to that desire realm.
Regarding the Dharma: as for "lightning," a sutra states that those who first enter the Dharma and attain deliverance upon hearing it are like lightning;
this refers to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Ānanda attained the fourth fruit by means of this [Dharma], and therefore his concentration also received the name "Vajra."
Descending from the *Vajra*, he resolves a doubt. The doubt asks: "Why is the concentration of desire (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) named 'Vajra'?

The explanation is as follows: Now, "lightning-flash" (*vidyut-prabhā*) signifies swiftness; it is given the name "lightning-flash" because of its swiftness. It receives the designation "Vajra" because of its total severance [of defilements].
This is called "Vajra" by way of being like a lightning-flash; it is not that every instance of lightning-flash receives the name "Vajra. This is the meaning.
The sun is luminous and bright.
The passage beginning with "There is nothing known" refutes falsehood. First it provides the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy. Within the analogy, it says "ashes covering fire":

the fire of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is like the fire, the essence of concentration is like the ashes, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is like treading upon them. When such conceptualization is perfected, one falls into suffering, as if being burned.

If one relies on the two treatises below, they each hold their own positions. Next, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is explained according to the Buddha’s intention that these do not differ in being exclusively pure.
Now, in explaining the Buddha’s intention, it is said that there are four parts in general because the four characteristics are distinct; since all possess these parts, they are called "four parts."
The portion for progress (*pragraha-bhāga*) constitutes the characteristics of the present text.

As for the portion for decline (*hāni-bhāga*), there is "decline due to conditions" (*pratyaya-sparśa-hāni*), which occurs when there is a cause or condition; there is also "spontaneous decline," which consists of twenty-five types such as exhaling and inhaling.

Regarding "exhaling and inhaling": exhaling means to cast out, and inhaling means to take in. The five conditions or five factors all involve taking up the rejection of desire and the discarding of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
It is called "going. Within the cultivation of the five matters, there is both going and taking; this is because one removes non-discipline and takes up discipline.
Regarding the three obstacles and four māras mentioned among the causes and conditions for the settling of the mind: generally speaking, the three and the four each encompass ten objects.
Therefore, the three obstacles subsume the four māras. Furthermore, when the celestial son (devaputra) is added, these constitute the four māras.

Next, regarding the "protective stage" (*anurakṣaṇā-bhāga*), the phrase "skillfully by means of [the factors] such as goodness" is explained in full detail as previously clarified in the *Dhyāna-gate*.

Regarding the "abiding stage" (*sthiti-bhāga*), this is because each stage possesses two kinds of abiding. As for "horizontal and vertical," it is as described in the section on the mutual arousal of the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*).
Next, the characteristics of the mutual interpenetration of the four divisions are explained. One may grasp this through reflection by cross-referencing what has already been explained.
Now, for the formal explanation: from the forty [factors], three are excluded and ten remain. These are explained starting from the proximate in order to clarify their pervasiveness;

within the remaining ten, they are further explained starting from the spontaneous, as this clarifies the ease of their manifestation. Within the first dhyāna, the eight tangibles are first distinguished, followed by the ten functional factors.
Virtue. The five branches of the third dhyāna and the four categories of numerical groups.

Within the first eight contacts, the former is external and the latter is internal. Regarding the phrase "all [beings] etc.," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess the 'taste of the first stage' dhyāna.
Since each of the two schools relies on its own particular source, the present critique states that both are biased toward their respective natures and fail to cultivate it exclusively.
The fundamental [treatise] should not distinguish their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). What is stated here is spoken with the intent of the Mahāyāna in order to refute attachments;

it says that essence and function are mutually inclusive. Lightness, warmth, coldness, and heaviness are the essence; movement, itching, roughness, and smoothness are the functions. If there is downward movement, touch is analyzed according to these four factors.

Having understood these three characteristics, one should appropriately guard against regression. Regarding the movement that touches the ten virtues below, the text on the realm of Māra is abbreviated; it is explained in detail here.
In the commentary on the "wholesome mind," it says, "to believe in all worthies and sages," etc.; as previously distinguished by nature, this also relies upon the Mahāyāna gate.
"Like the brain": the brain is the medicinal substance *shuppi* (matured hide); it is the marrow within the head. "Boiling soup and the like": whether cold or hot, their flavors are not equal.
A single touch possesses ten virtues; the flavor of bliss is eternally distinct. "Like opening [a door] and so forth": possessing desire is like opening a gate;
entering through deviance is like a thief advancing; ghosts then follow in after them. This is also called "ghost-dhyāna."

Regarding the mention of "wind and so forth" in the *Mahā-śāstra*, the treatise explains the three types of perception (*saṃjñā*). These three perceptions bring about both the formation and the destruction of dhyāna.
As for "northeast and so forth," wind and rain are added; reading it thus is more convenient: when the clouds are long [continuous], it rains; when the clouds disperse, it clears.
"Tranquil joy" (*tianyú*) is simply delight and pleasure.

Regarding the twenty-three mental factors (*caitasika*) in the *Abhidharma*: there are the ten universal wholesome factors (*mahākuśalabhūmika*), the ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), joy (*prīti*) and aversion (*daurmanasya*) which function according to circumstances, and the pair of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

When these five factors arise, it is not that other factors are absent; therefore, they are said to occur "simultaneously. However, among these five factors, their respective characteristics are predominant.
It is named after its predominant factor.
Some say that below this point, the determination of the factors (*aṅga*) differs. Regarding the "ninth mind of the desire realm," others say it refers to the ninth grade of the desire realm mind;
upon reaching the ninth mind, it then belongs to five factors. It is said that prior to the concentration of the desire realm, [the factors] are most deficient.

Regarding the phrase "arising simultaneously" (*sahotpanna*) and so forth, there are differences between the two treatises. This [explanation] follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā) for now; according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, they are sequential.
As explained below, the intent of this sequence is as follows: initially, there is a subtle sound that is obscured by a coarse one; once the coarse sound has passed, the subtle sound then manifests.

Regarding the phrase "next, the initial opening," etc.: they arise in succession to manifest the single mind (*ekacitta*). Awakening (*bodha*) is called the factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*); knowing what is noble is the factor of investigation (*dharmanidhyāna-anga*);
joy and bliss are the factors of joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha-aṅga*); and the characteristic of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the single mind itself.

Although the initial awakening possesses all four [factors], because it is obscured by its status as the "initial" stage, it does not yet receive the four names. The same applies to investigation and the others; this can be seen through reflection. Next, regarding the section on "differentiation," it is an analogy.
The remaining factors are established. "Discernment" refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); the others are the three remaining factors.

As in the passage "As when a person descends," this specifically clarifies one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). "When eating" is a metaphor for the preceding four factors; "having eaten" is a metaphor for one-pointedness of mind. This is also as explained below.

The "weight" is a metaphor for single-mindedness. Although desire may seem pleasant when confronted with it, the reverse leads to extreme exhaustion. Desire is like the four limbs; it is not equal to single-mindedness.
Therefore, one should enter into oneness; then all four [limbs] become sources of affliction.

If [the discussion] is below the fourth dhyāna, the doubts are resolved. First, the doubt is raised; next, under "Now, dividing," it is explained. If [the discussion] proceeds below, the meaning of the distinct factors (*aṅga*) is explained.
Next, the names of the factors are explained, pointing toward their cultivation and realization. Furthermore, based on the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one may briefly understand them as follows.

The treatise asks: "What is the meaning of 'factor' (*aṅga*)? The treatise answers: "The meaning of conformity, the meaning of fulfillment, the meaning of firmness, and so forth. It conforms to its respective stage and is fulfilled.
"Local" (pratyupasthita). What is the meaning of "five"? Answer: Awakening is called *vitarka* (applied thought); subtle mental discrimination is called *vicāra* (sustained thought);

rejoicing is called *prīti* (joy); serenity is called *sukha* (bliss); and tranquility is called *ekāgratā* (one-pointedness). These five factors are established in opposition to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "should correspond," the character "should" (*ying*) must be added.
Regarding the statement "if one wishes to descend," this clarifies the second dhyāna. First, one applies the preparatory means (*upāya*).

As for the statement "merely censuring vitarka and vicāra," it may also mean censuring all thirty-two factors beginning with them, while the others follow suit and depart. Furthermore, regarding that which is difficult to sever, one censures it; as soon as it arises, [the factors] are equalized.

Once the five factors have ceased, there remains only concentration (*samādhi*) without further factors. Therefore, it is said that "dhyāna-concentration follows the single mind and is then tranquil. Thus.

The clouds turn into stillness. Regarding the phrase "retreating from dhyāna": it refers to abandoning the initial [attainment], not to a loss [of what was previously gained]. Because the prior merit is absent, it is called "negligible" (mièxiè).

If one does not descend from dhyāna, the arising of dhyāna mingles with the four great elements; this is not the same as the eight tactile sensations, for the four great elements are each distinct. Therefore, it is said they "mingle."
Regarding the four factors (*catur-aṅga*): because it is free from the defilements of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is called "internal tranquility" (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*).

Because it arises together with joy (*prīti*), it is named "rejoicing" (*prāmodya*). Because one experiences pleasure (*sukha*) within that joy, it is named "bliss" (*sukha*). Because the mind rests in the experience of bliss, it is named "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*).

If one wishes to refute [the claim that there is] joy, it should be understood according to the explanation of the first dhyāna. Regarding the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*): the arising of bliss gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*) and joy; this is named "equanimity. It is protected so as to cause it to increase.
Mindfulness is called *smṛti*. Skillful detachment from attachment is called *prajñā*. Bliss pervading the entire body is called *sukha*.
This bliss is distinct from the bliss of the first and second dhyānas. When this bliss subsides, one enters a state of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).

Next is the fourth dhyāna. It also first establishes the preliminary preparations. Regarding the four factors (*aṅga*): the relinquishing of inferior and superior pleasures is called equanimity (*upekṣā*);

the clear illumination through equal wisdom is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); the absence of defilement from lower stages is called purity (*viśuddhi*); and the immovability of the essence of concentration is called one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).
The four formless bases (*ārūpya-āyatana*). The method for extinguishing form is as previously explained.

Next, the explanation of that which is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). First, regarding the intent of the introduction: according to the *Dhyanamukha*, there are three types of spiritual capacity (*indriya-gotra*).

For those with more wisdom and less concentration, the Six Sublime Gates (*ṣaḍ-ārya-mukha*) are taught; it is not necessarily required to ascend to the higher stages (*bhūmi*) in order to give rise to the outflow-free state. This is because one must traverse all [stages]...
Because all dhyāna methods are involved, when concentration (*samādhi*) is predominant and wisdom (*prajñā*) is slight, it is called "Special Excellence" (*viśeṣa-mukti*);

this is because the nature of wisdom is deficient, and one must ascend to the higher stages (*ūrdhva-bhūmi*) to be able to produce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. If concentration and wisdom are equal, it is called "Universal Clarity" (*sarvākārābhisaṃbodha*); being fully developed in both higher and lower stages, one is able to attain the outflow-free state in both.

As for the "Counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*), it is explained as the opposite of the former; here, we clarify that attainment occurs according to what is produced. Question: Regarding the present text...

Why is it that the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-anupūrva-vihāra*) are not explained? Answer: Counting (*gaṇanā*) and following (*anugama*) have already been explained within the fundamental [section]. The latter four involve entering into principle (*tattva*), which is not the intended meaning here.
Question: Why is the "special victory" (*viśeṣa-mukha*) explained? Answer: One cultivates the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) to recognize faults; now, one cultivates the special victory.

It is so named because it excels the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*). Regarding the phrase "as stated in the Vinaya," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says that at the Pārā River, and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says that in the Pārā Garden, because bhikṣus were practicing the nine perceptions, immeasurable bhikṣus took up knives to commit suicide or attempted to kill others.

Therefore, the Buddha changed their meditation and had them practice the *viśeṣa* (special) meditations. If this is so, why are they not placed earlier? The answer is: they are based on their specific antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
That is so; however, their depth and shallowness are not the same.

As for the "great yellow" (turmeric) and other such things: the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) views bodily desire as a feverish illness, while the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) are like purgatives.

Self-harm is like an overdose. One who has not yet known the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is called "weak. To be solely intent on loathing the body is like a crude medicine; for medicine is fundamentally intended for treatment.

Illness. Now, conversely, one is obscured; therefore, further cultivate the *viśeṣa* (special) meditations while still concurrently practicing the *aśubha* (impurity). As in the preceding section, supplement this; advance and give rise to the *anāsrava* (outflow-free), as in the "body-return" [section].

Regarding "those who eat sparingly" and so forth: this refers to those who subdue their desires. They cultivate the contemplation of the body as if eating pig's fat; they regard the body in the *smṛtyupasthāna* as a vessel for holding excrement.
Not immediately taking their own lives is like continuing to eat despite the food being unpalatable. When the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) are accomplished, it is like the fat becoming putrid.
Hiring someone to take one’s life is like no longer eating at all. The character "lian" (廉) should be written as "jian" (兼); it means "meager food."

Regarding the "Superiority of Arising" (*viśeṣa-utpāda*), the following section clearly elucidates the characteristics of its arising. The reason why the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are mentioned in each stage is that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are included within the factors of enlightenment.
There are five in the first and last stages, and three in each of the intermediate stages, which correspond respectively to the four foundations of mindfulness, such as the body and so forth.
The first five pertain to the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Regarding the initial mention of "entering and exiting," entering refers to reaching the navel, and exiting refers to reaching...
The nose: when illuminating it, one is not confused by its lightness or heaviness, coarseness or subtlety, and so forth;

knowing its length and shortness is like a master turner and his disciple who know the length of the string. The "fundamental" section below distinguishes the differences; these three analogies all illustrate the fundamental.

"Darkly verifying what exists now" refers to the present; "the observer of wisdom" clarifies the present. The section beginning with "the eight [earlier points]" further refutes the fundamental. As for the "five grains": [text continues].

Millet, broomcorn millet, wheat, rice, and hemp—from "receiving joy according to one's mind" to the [next] three [sections], these correspond to the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). From "the mind acts" to the [next] three, these correspond to the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding "the *Mahāsannipāta* and others," there is no internal purity; from "contemplating impermanence" downward, these are the five foundations of mindfulness (*pañca-smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding "other places and so forth," from the beginning until...
This also contemplates impermanence; therefore, it is called "other places. This dhyāna eliminates the externalist reckoning of permanence, thereby constituting a specific antidote.

The four formless states require the most careful discernment, yet the textual descriptions are extremely brief. It says that the scattering of emptiness is desire, and the admonition against desire is called detachment.
Furthermore, contemplating this detachment is called the contemplation of detachment from desire. Regarding the sphere of nothingness, it says: "whether much or little," and so forth.

In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), [the perception] is called "much"; in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is called "little. Because they are distinguished by much and little, it is said that both are "non-existent.

Since "little" is equivalent to cessation, it is said that one "contemplates cessation. These are contrasted horizontally with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Their principles differ from those of the fundamental [dhyānas].

Because the foundations of mindfulness are horizontal, they are called "horizontal contrasts"; because the fundamentals are vertical, they are called "vertical contrasts. Therefore, the analogy is given: "food without salt," and so forth.
Next, the general clarifications are explained. First, regarding the intent of the introduction: the "thirty-six objects" are the same as those in the *Viśeṣa* (Distinct Victories).
Various texts all state that there are twelve each for the internal, external, and intermediate [objects], whereas only the *Chanmen* (Gate of Dhyāna) divides them into internal and external only;
it has twenty-six internal objects and ten external ones, as detailed in the *Chanmen*. Regarding the *Avataṃsaka* and other [texts]: the *Chanmen* states, "There are people..."

This is attained through cultivation. Its name is unknown; the masters of the Northern Kingdoms established the name "Penetrating Clarity" (Tongming). Because one is able to attain the three knowledges (trividyā) and the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), it is called "Penetrating Clarity," speaking of the fruit within the context of the cause.

Next, the actual explanation of the arousal [of the mind] is presented. First, the five branches are explained by reference to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. The sūtra contains five phrases, which are combined into three. First, "as the mind can be seen" is explained.
Furthermore, from "consciousness of the conventional" (*vijñapti-saṃvṛti*) downward, "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*) is explained.

Regarding the "ninety-nine," etc., it is as stated in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate): "The large and small bones number three hundred and sixty; the marrow has ninety-nine layers. The details are found in the *Chan* [texts].

This is the section on the Gates. It proceeds from reflection (*cintā*). Regarding the terms "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) and "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*), these refer precisely to the ultimate and conventional as clarified above.

As for the mention of the "higher factors of enlightenment" (*uttarabodhipakṣa*) and so forth, these are distinguished in contrast to the fundamental [factors]. Because those [higher factors] lack the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), they are dismissed by the term "understanding" (*adhimokṣa*).
Regarding the statement that "the first dhyāna is like a bubble and so on up to the fourth, which is like a reflected image," this distinguishes the dharmas by means of metaphors;

they become progressively deeper and more subtle. Since there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor for the formless realms (ārūpya), one stops at the fourth dhyāna. Therefore, regarding the formless realms, only three matters are mentioned.

Regarding the "extinction of the three types of sensation and perception in emptiness," a practitioner of the Dharma (dharmacārin) reflects as follows: "In the formless realm, there still exist the perception of consciousness, the perception of contact, and the perception of space.

If one cultivates the state of non-perception (asaṃjñin), these three are eternally extinguished. Furthermore, one also extinguishes the mental factors of sensation and perception within the ten universal mental states (mahābhūmika).
Therefore, speaking generally, it is said that if the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Vibhāṣā*) says 'only the extinction of the two, sensation and perception,' [it refers to this]."

Regarding the phrase "observed conventionally" (*sāṃvṛta-darśana*) and so forth: this distinguishes between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). This specifically judges the passage concerning the conventional and ultimate within the context of the mind and so forth.
That which is accompanied by skin, flesh, and the like is termed the conventional; that which is somewhat deeper and subtler than the former is termed the ultimate.

Regarding these meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth: that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is termed "phenomena" (*vastu*), while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is termed "principle" (*nyāya*).

Since each of the stages already possesses contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), how much more so upon reaching the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*)? Therefore, the treatise-master’s ignorance in not employing them as the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) is refuted.

"Path" (*mārga*) refers to that which is concomitant with the path (*mārga-samprayukta*); "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to that which is concomitant with concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta*). The meaning of the *Abhidharma* is authoritative; it is cited here to refute the treatise-master’s impropriety. You possess only...

If the principle of the untainted (*anāsrava*) were fixed, then there would be no dhyāna of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). According to your treatise, there would likewise be no person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).
As for those who rely on non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), you are correctly refuting them by using precepts and wisdom to refute their meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If this were the case, since they would lack "guest" concentration, how would they differ from non-Buddhists? Regarding the "eight arts," the *Mahā-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there is a skilled physician who understands the eight kinds..."

The *Śāstra* itself explains this through eight successive arguments (*aṣṭabhiḥ punarvārāiḥ*). Many ancient masters have offered explanations; for our part, we take the four [alternatives] regarding permanence and the four regarding impermanence to constitute these eight.

Thus, all eight are absent. If one were to admit the existence of both morality (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it would be possible for the four [qualities] such as impermanence to coexist with impermanence and so forth;
yet even in that case, the eightfold set would not be established.
Next, following the section on impurity, the untainted dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) is explained. First, two types of persons are identified; next, the signs of their development are shown.

Regarding the mention of the "knowledge of vows" (*praṇidhijñāna*) and so forth within the dhyāna of breaking down phenomena (*bhedana-dharma*): since one has already progressed to the stage of the "burning perception" (*parīttābhā-saṃjñā*), there is nothing further to be cultivated through the meditative abandonments (*vairāgya*) and other such dhyānas.

Within the category of mundane dhyāna (*vastu-dhyāna*), this is the highest point of transcendence; therefore, it is called the "summit" (*mūrdhan*). Furthermore, because this dhyāna can transform longevity into merit, it is so named.

Regarding *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve): the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it is called "knowledge resulting from resolve" because one understands things exactly as they have been resolved. Although it is said that [the body] is incinerated and so forth, while the perception of the body may be absent, the body itself actually remains.

This person is inferior. To distinguish between those who destroy the Dharma as to whether they fall away or do not fall away, it is as stated in the *Abhidharma* and other texts. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

"If an Arhat falls away, should the [holders of] the second and third fruits also fall away? It answers: "By virtue of falling away from the fourth fruit, one is led to fall away from the second and third as well."
It is like a sand well: there are bricks above and below, but none in between. If the upper brick falls, it drags the lower one down;

the first fruit is the bottom [of this well], and for this reason, one does not fall back from it. If that is so, then one should also say that there is falling back from the second and third fruits. Answer: Although it is not explicitly stated, [it is understood].
In reality, there are three types of regression. If this is so, why does one not regress from the first fruit? The answer is: prior to that [fruit], there was no fruition;

in the case of regression, there is no place to abide, because there is no further possibility of becoming an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). However, even for one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), regression does not occur simultaneously;

since there is the sense of regression, it must be explained. In the *Āgama*, the regression from the third fruit is cited as an example for the fourth, and this too refers to one liberated by wisdom. Therefore...
Although there is regression, even if one regresses, in this life one will certainly attain [the fruit].
Regarding the phrase "one of non-declining nature" (*abhedya-dharman*), the following explains the person of non-declining nature. First, it clarifies the characteristics of the non-declining nature.

As for the mention of "contemplation, refinement," and so forth, these four are fully detailed in the *Dharmadhātu-krama*. The nine successive concentrations range from the first dhyāna up to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
They enter sequentially and without interval.

If, during cultivation, one is inferior, the arising [of the result] is distinguished by contrast with what is cultivated. Regarding those who have an abundance of craving and so forth, "internal" and "external" are defined in relation to one's own body and the bodies of others, respectively.

At the beginning, they gather and observe together; once the gathering is mature, the flesh is removed. Those who do not destroy the Dharma all reach the eighth stage. *Jeng* (pronounced with the initial *deng* as a rough approximation) means to dissolve and disperse.
Regarding those such as the Brahmins who grasp at pure dharmas, the text is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
In the explanation of the contemplation on the impurity of food: A Brahmin who has extensively cultivated pure practices may have occasion to travel to an impure land.
There, upon eating another’s cake, he considers it pure and clean; yet realizing it is utterly impure, he beats his breast and vomits dryly, thinking, "How shall I destroy this pure practice?
I have already understood its nature. This can be seen by applying the analogy to the contemplative visualization. (The character "嗚" is likely a scribal error for "鳴").
"Making a sound" (*mǐ*)—this is simply the character for "sounding" (*míng*).

Regarding the passage "one who conceives such an image," the following section distinguishes the specific excellences (*viśeṣa*). "Like a person greedy for food" means that craving the body is like being greedy for food;

the body is like a pig's snout. "Actual observation" (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) is like knowing with certainty; "maintaining the body" is like eating forceful food; and "seeing worms" is like a mental construction (*parikalpa*).

The aversion is as intense as that of one who has not eaten. This corresponds to the "Specific Victories" (*viśeṣa*) section below. The "six thieves" refer to the six desires. Generally, all nine [contemplations] treat all six [desires]; if treated individually:

the contemplation of death treats the two desires of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and speech; the contemplations of bloatedness, disintegration, and being devoured collectively treat the desire for physical form (*rūpa*);

the contemplations of blood-stained, festering, and livid corpses collectively treat the desire for color (*varṇa*); the contemplations of bones and burning collectively treat the desire for smoothness (*ślakṣṇa*). Thus, the single desire is dispersed.
Regarding the treatment of those with the marks of enmity and deceit: one who loves the truth is treated as an enemy, and one who is close is treated as a deceiver.

Thus, from the lower stages down, even up to the arousal [of the mind], because of the two conditions of the fundamental practice and the present observation (*abhisamaya*), both Great and Small Vehicles are equally obstructed by desire.

When the obstruction is removed, the practice is aroused according to their respective original vows. In the lower section of the *Śāstra*, the errors are refuted while simultaneously providing proof for the arousal of the Great Vehicle.
Thus we know that the various masters do not understand the purport of the treatise.

Next, the liberations (vimokṣa) will be explained; first, their sequence will be distinguished in contrast to the preceding section: first the mundane (sāsrava) fundamental [dhyānas], followed by the pure (anāsrava) fundamental [dhyānas].

Next, regarding the four types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) within the untainted (*anāsrava*), only the attainment of observation (*vipaśyanā*) is explicitly mentioned; the remaining three belong to the principle (*nyāya*).

Within the sequence of observation, after the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), one must clarify the liberations (*vimokṣa*). As for the terms "general" and "specific": the general applies in common with those who possess the non-disintegrating dharma (*abhedya-dharmin*).
This applies specifically to the Bodhisattva; it is the definitive noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).

Furthermore, regarding the passage "Furthermore, turning away from and abandoning" (*prātikūlya-vairāgya*), which distinguishes cause and effect and explains the terminology: it receives its name from the cause.

Because at the time of the cause one feels aversion and turns away, abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "turning away and abandoning" (*prātikūlya-vairāgya*). When the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms are exhausted, the name changes to "liberation" (*vimokṣa*). From the passage "From that which turns away... onwards, [the text] reiterates...
This describes the sequence of causes. Regarding the phrase "pure and clean five desires": the five desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are not called pure or sublime.

From the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), although there is still an attached mind, they are termed "pure and clean five desires" because one employs the practice of renunciation (*vairāgya*) as an antidote;

through wearying detachment and non-attachment, they are thus called "pure and clean five desires by way of renunciation. The phrase "first, those who possess them internally" is a brief enumeration of the beginning and the end; this is the explanation.
Within this, all is complete. Suddenly one sees one’s own body and so forth; these arise based on cultivation and likewise originate from the feet.
"Kha" refers to a deep mountain valley; the corpse is like that valley. "Sattva" and so forth refers to the Prince Sattva of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Those who cultivate the Mahāyāna obtain the aid of this visualization, which enables them to become weary of the body and achieve the Great Dharma.

From the lower section of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the citation of scriptural evidence: The "Chapter on Noble Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*) enumerates in full how the bones and joints mutually depend upon one another.
Relying on the metacarpal bones as a support for the tarsal bones, and so on up to the skull above; again, relying on the cranial bone down to the carpal bones as a support for the phalanges.
In the present text, one first visualizes the skin and flesh until the skeletal structure is fully formed; this is the method.
Regarding "increasing" and so forth, the sūtras and śāstras differ. Some speak of blue, yellow, red, and white.
As for "the light follows upward," etc., this refers to the stage before full accomplishment; once it gradually reaches accomplishment, it pervades the ten directions.
Regarding "like Mount Sumeru," just as all four sides of Mount Sumeru follow its single color, so too do the four colors; they pervade everywhere without mutual obstruction.

Regarding "thus, for a long time, etc.," this is again a restatement of what was previously mentioned. At the very beginning when first developing [the meditation], one simply observes the bones for a long duration;
light should then naturally arise. As for the "eight colors": one sees the earth as a pure ground, yellowish-white; water as clear water from a deep abyss;
fire as a smokeless, pure flame; wind as a cloudless, soaring breeze; blue like a mountain of refined gold; yellow like a grape flower; red...
It is like the morning dew of spring; white as conch shells or snow. Furthermore, through favorable and unfavorable conditions, it is made to be swiftly accomplished.

The character "tàn" (with the phonetic gloss "tāgǎn") should be written as [black * gǎn]. That which possesses skin and flesh is distinguished by means of the *viśeṣa-bhāvanā* (special cultivation). If one follows the Tripiṭaka, it is the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth).

Proceeding from the Mahāyāna, our present school investigates the intent of the Vaipulya teachings to reveal the provisional; thus, it concludes below by stating that these are "dharmas outside the realms.
Within the text, the three trainings are first cited to illustrate the eight types of form; one should know that these are none other than the inconceivable dharmas.

These are two separate treatises that have come here to distinguish [the subject] from others. Now, relying on the *Mahāśāstra*, both differ from the preceding three; as they are not universal paths, I shall not adopt them here.

Regarding "next, internally there is no form," etc.: this next section clarifies the second [stage]. First, it clarifies the contemplation of breaking down the internal skeleton; next, it clarifies the contemplation of the destruction of the substance (*tattva*).

Within this, there are two parts: first, the teaching (*dharma*); second, the analogy (*upamā*). Regarding the analogy of the "good horse" and so forth: it perishes immediately upon the desire for its perishing.

The reason why both the "breaking down" and the "contemplation of the substance" are employed is that, according to the methods outside the *dhātu*, these still encompass the *Pratyekabuddha* (Separate) and *Bodhisattva* (Perfect) vehicles; how much more so in the case of the emptiness of substance (*tattva-śūnyatā*)? Furthermore, one fears that [the practitioner] might become habituated [to mere cessation].
Because they have been introduced, they are listed together. Regarding those new dharmas that have not yet been introduced:

since there is no internal purity (*adhyātma-śubha*), they are distinguished and shown by means of "impurity" (*aśubha*). From "Suddenly seeing... onwards is the formal explanation of the intermediate stage; from "Now... onwards is the formal judgment.

By this single principle, all three preceding [positions] are simultaneously refuted. Why? Because it is extremely pure, it resides in the fourth dhyāna. All the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)...

It does not fail to be established as the fourth station because there is the realization of the body (*kāyasākṣin*). Thus, it resides in the third dhyāna; yet, the distinction between the third and fourth is made based on the initial and final [stages].

If one must determine the station according to the formal definition of meditative absorption, it must be assigned to the third. However, according to this interpretation, the previous three [stations] would all be subverted.

As for "pure because it takes the pure as its object," the fourth dhyāna is taken as the ultimate purity. Regarding "taking these forms and so forth as objects": when the third and fourth [dhyānas] arise, they are luminous.
Because the first two [stages] are practiced, the third and fourth are called the "conditions for the first two. Therefore, only the third and fourth receive the name "pure" (*śubha*).

For this reason, four alternative formulations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are further opened to explain them: the first three belong to the first two [stages], while the fourth belongs to the third. As for the first formulation:

it is actually impure (*aśubha*), yet a further conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) is superimposed upon it. The second, the "mutually alternating" formulation, corresponds to the first two; in these first two, there is purity.
Because it has not yet transcended the conditions for purity, it is not called "pure. Now, this third purity lacks the preceding impurity; therefore, it is called "purity of purity.

Regarding the phrase "transcending all" in the sphere of infinite space, it is explained in detail as in the sixth fascicle. However, that [passage] relies on the fundamental [dhyāna], whereas here we follow the pure dhyānas.
The mention of "ordinary persons" and so forth excludes the fundamental [dhyānas]; the mention of "noble ones" and so forth establishes the noble and excludes the ordinary. Yet, this...
The "liberation" (visamyoga) actually applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones.

Furthermore, following the passage on the arising and ceasing of consciousness, the state of "nothingness" (ākiṃcanya) is explained. Next, regarding the explanation of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana):

because it can avoid the three preceding states, it is called the "abandoning of consciousness and the absence of consciousness. This "absence of consciousness" is precisely the station of nothingness; therefore, it is named "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Consciousness...

Regarding "abiding like an abscess, etc.": as for the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), they are as previously explained in the context of the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*). As for what are called "subtle afflictions" (*sūkṣma-kleśa*):

there are ten subtle delusions, namely—sensation, perception, mental formations (*saṃskāra*), contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

This [text] refutes that there are such delusions therein. Regarding "now abandoning the subjective grasper (*ālambaka*) and so forth," this explains the name "cessation of sensation and perception. It establishes the essential nature (*svabhāva*) based on the name; for within the sphere of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-bhūmi*), there still exists a subjective grasper. Now...
When the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is extinguished, and that which extinguishes it is further extinguished, only then can it be called the extinction of both its own stage and other stages.

From the phrase "if one uses what is to be extinguished" (*yad yena nirudhyate*) downwards, [the text] refutes the old view; there, it merely extinguishes other stages. How does this differ from the fundamental [view]? Now, from the section "from below" (*ita ūrdhvam*), the correct explanation begins.

This explains the initial solution regarding the relinquishing of the object of cognition and so forth: that is, by extinguishing other stages, there is no longer anything that can extinguish them, and thus one's own [stage] is extinguished.

The *Dìlùn* (Treatise on the Stages) criticizes the masters, stating that regarding the latter four [liberations], the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Treasury) holds that the untainted (*anāsrava*) states rely solely upon the fundamental dhyānas.
Thus, it uses the first three liberations (*prahāṇa*) to challenge the proponents of the [opposing] view; this involves both concession and refutation.

Among the eight [liberations], setting aside for now the one involving the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), among the remaining seven, it is permissible for the latter four to take only emptiness as their object—this is the concession. However, the first three liberations involve impurity (*aśubha*).
Regarding the eight formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*): why discard them when they differ from the fundamental [dhyānas]? This is precisely what is being refuted.

If one were to surpass the lower levels, it would be judged as "cultivation" (*abhyāsa*). Since the first seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) encompass all eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the discussion of the arising of cultivation is based on these eight absorptions.

Because the single absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) cannot be discussed in terms of cultivation, this was not raised as an objection previously either. Regarding the nine successive [attainments]...

Regarding "the concentrations and so forth": the initial passage of the nine perceptions has already listed them, but there was no opportunity to specifically extract the four concentrations. Therefore, they are now explained again.
These do not exist in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), though they may exist in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) in the sense of awakening latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Next, regarding the "Great Impurity," as for its general and specific characteristics, these are also to be determined according to the preceding text. Next, for the formal explanation:

*kūṭa* means a small hill. Regarding the description of the broth as foul liquid and so forth, it is detailed in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, where the Buddha answers Kāśyapa by clarifying that all phenomena are entirely without reality; thus, he cites the bhikṣu’s contemplation of the perception of impurity.

Furthermore, the following passage clarifies the transformation of objects. Since this transformation occurs by virtue of the mind’s transformation, it cites two conditions as examples to illustrate the mind’s transformation.

Although the past and present differ, both are transformed by the mind; how much more so is the manifestation of the present [object] dependent on the past mind? As for those who grasp at stones and the like: [the text continues].
Just as in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra it is explained that whatever Śreṇika Vatsagotra grasped was entirely transformed into jewels, so too was it for Saṃgharakṣita.
Because he had gone with a merchant to gather jewels and had returned to the shore, he lost his company and encountered fifty-three places of hell;
for all the environmental retributions (niśraya-vipāka) he perceived were nothing other than hells.

If one clings to the lower [stages], there is the power to destroy the fetters because of the transformation of the object. To say that "this contemplation accords with transformation" and so forth means that when the visualization becomes a true vision, it is like a practitioner of supernatural powers transforming objects;

because it accords with that universal power of transformation, it is called "accordance. Furthermore, since objects possess the principle of transformability, only through supernatural power can they be transformed;

thus, one should know that impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is likewise. How much more so, since its fundamental nature is the principle of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). To grasp [it]...
This is their own differentiation. What you all practice is the bodhisattva path.
As for "whether great or small," the fundamental outflows (*āsrava*) have already been explained as before; impure karmic conditions do not immediately become untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one employs the abandonment of delusions according to any given stage (*bhūmi*), it is therefore said that "everything above and below is eliminated."

Regarding the "lower" [stage], it explains the liberations (*vimokṣa*) by means of the great impurity (*mahā-aśubha*), wherein both the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka* and *ālambana-vipāka*) are fundamentally destroyed from beginning to end.

Regarding the "further" [stage], it explains the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) by means of the liberations. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "They are called 'spheres of mastery' because they master the afflictions (*kleśa*)."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Part II, cites the treatise to distinguish the faculties (*indriya*). The *Chanmen* states: "Having completed the cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), one cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); this refers to those of inferior faculty.
Now, following those of middling faculty, one achieves the spheres of mastery at the third [liberation]. Those of superior faculty achieve the four spheres of mastery prior to that."

Up to this point, one is able to accomplish the latter four [meditations]. This is still based on the teachings. As for those of superior faculties, they follow the visualization of the skeleton from the "many" (*bahu*) onwards;
this correctly clarifies the characteristics of the arising [of the meditative state]. "Many" refers to the great [number of bones], while "few" refers to their destruction.

All possess both beauty and ugliness, up until the final stage where all are entirely impure. Within the "liberations" (*vimokṣa*), even that which is pure is termed "impure. One has not yet been able to progress through increasingly excellent stages.

Because it is ugly; furthermore, that upon which they rely is impure, and their dimensions differ. The "Victorious Places" (*abhibhvāyatana*) also have the distinction between the primary and the secondary.

Regarding the phrase "yielding one's position": for example, Taibo of Wu was the eldest son of King Tai; because he yielded his place to his younger brother, he withdrew to Eastern Wu. Regarding the phrase "returning the ox":
when Yao invited Xu You to serve as the head of the Nine Provinces, Xu You heard of this and washed out his ears. [This] was criticized by Qi Fu.
Since he did not even drink the ox’s water, let us now allow him to ultimately achieve the state of having few desires.
Regarding the "blue, yellow," and so forth mentioned in the *Mahā-śāstra*: from the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), there are only four colors; here, eight colors are listed.

This is to show that the listings in the sūtras and śāstras differ because they distinguish between the provisional and the real. These are based on samādhi; as for the mind taking form as its object, it must certainly be determined [as such].

Because it is obtained through the same faculty as the visual organ (*cakṣur-indriya*), the perception of visible forms (*rūpa*) is judged to be substantial (*dravya*). Because names such as "earth" (*pṛthivī*) and so forth are established [based on conceptual aggregation], they are termed provisional (*prajñapti*).
Thus, since both the provisional and the substantial are perceived in all instances, this is the reverse of the provisional and substantial categories as presented in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the statement that "in these four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), internal and external forms are all [equal]": one's own body is taken as "internal" and others as "external.

Since there are only eight types of form (*rūpa*), there is no distinction between beauty and ugliness; rather, the difference lies only in their quantity, which serves to distinguish the extent—broad or narrow—of the forms.
Next, to clarify "all-places" (sarvatraga): excluding the first four of the eight [liberations], one contemplates both the conventional and the real;

by further adding emptiness and consciousness, they receive the name "all" because they are all pervasive. As for "only the immovable" and so forth: "immovable" refers to the first factor within the fourth dhyāna.
And mindfulness and wisdom constitute the third limb. Next, to correctly explain "entering" (*praveśa*):
first is the "abiding" (*sthāna*), and next is the "entering. While their names differ, their substance is the same; they are brought together to clarify their distinction.
Because one enters after having pervaded [the object], it is called "entering. Since pervading does not mean not entering, these are synonymous terms.

This is the lower [section]. It refutes others who claim that the "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana) takes external objects as its condition; our intention here is not so, because it is emitted from the skeleton and because the mind itself possesses it.

Since even previously it was judged to be matter outside the [internal] realm, how could it be entirely something that comes from without? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, lower [section], explains these doubts.
Fearing that [the reader] might not understand the argument, I shall expand upon it by citing [scriptural authority]; hence it is said, "borrowing from the external.

If one understands clearly what follows, one may extend the analysis to distinguish [the stages]: after the clear-comprehension contemplation (*paricaya-vipaśyanā*), it is possible to take the eight colors as objects for the renunciations (*vairāgya*).

Therefore, they are not the same. Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, the Bodhisattva... onwards: even when a Bodhisattva merely gives rise to [the intention], they already possess all the perfections (*pāramitās*);

how much more so regarding the eight forms of giving? Thus it says, "they are accomplished according to the mind. This uses the universal and particular Bodhisattvas as an illustration. The text enumerates the six perfections; the first, *dāna* (giving), is evident.
Within *śīla* (precepts), three types of precepts are briefly set forth: "harming others" refers to killing; "enticing beings" refers to stealing; "deceitful fraud" refers to... [lying].
False. Even up to the section on wisdom, it says "neither arising nor ceasing. Know that this is not the *ālayavijñāna*. From "all below" onwards, it universally encompasses all dharmas;
the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are wisdom. Regarding the phrase "like a swift horse," etc., this is a metaphor for the mind of the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

At this time, the lower [level] takes the functional power of the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) as its sublime object; by frequently entering the five grades, one thereby enters and abides [in the stage], which is why it is called "near the pond.

Regarding those who are "equal" to this, this merely clarifies the limit of the distinction. Furthermore, regarding those who "may also be equal," they are like those previously mentioned who, having refuted the old [view], do not understand the intent of the treatise.

Next, the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) is explained. Regarding the initial statement, "attaining liberation": this refers to the manifestation [of the state] through cultivation;

according to the teachings, its perfection is termed "liberation. There are three types of objects: namely, enemies, friends, and neutral persons. In terms of location, these refer to the vast and immeasurable ten directions.

When all three types of persons are elevated [to a state of well-being], it is termed "perfection. The characteristics of cultivation are fully present in the various sūtras and śāstras. These are the characteristics of cultivation.
What does this mean? It refers to three categories each for enemies and relatives, with neutral persons added to make seven. These are correlated with three grades of happiness.

First, one begins by correlating the highest relative with the lowest grade of happiness, and thus gradually increases: the highest relative with middling happiness, the middling relative with low happiness, and so on, until the highest enemy attains the highest grade of happiness.

Furthermore, pervading the ten directions constitutes the characteristic of perfected loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise; however, equanimity proceeds from neutral persons.

This is taken as the initial contemplation. Next is the enemy, and next is the friend; the enemy is taken from the highest grade and the friend from the lowest grade, because these are both easier to begin with.
Regarding "hidden" and so forth: only in the fundamental dhyānas are both the internal and external hidden, or neither the internal nor external is hidden;
in all other cases, they are not hidden. This applies to everything from the causal conditions downward.
In the explanation of the factors (*aṅga*) of dhyāna, it says: "Or one may obtain the bliss of humans or the heavens. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "With what kind of bliss? The answer states:
Some say it is because it is superior among the blisses of the third dhyāna; others say it is because the four matters have already been obtained previously.
Regarding the statement "this is called 'equal'": among all the pure dhyānas, the factor of contact (*sparśa*) is identical in name, though the flavor of the bliss (*sukha-rasa*) differs.

Regarding the phrase "if one generates [the thought]," etc., this refers to the accomplishment of merit through cultivation. The *Brahmapurohita* gods are so called because they serve as ministers to the *Mahābrahmā*; the *Brahmakāyika* gods are so called because they constitute the retinue of the Great Brahmā.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "What is 'Brahma-merit' (*brahma-puṇya*)? It answers: Some say it is the merit of all sentient beings; others say it is the merit of a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).

Likewise, there are those who say it is the merit of kings from the Śakra-devānām-indra up to the Mahābrahmā. Others say it is the merit of all persons except for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are close to Buddhahood. At times, the Buddha...
Regarding the term "etcetera" (ādi): the list provided in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is exactly as it appears in the present text. One should know that the Hīnayāna also possesses both explanations.
From the section on the Bodhisattva downward, it clarifies that these exist everywhere within the Mahāyāna. In the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, a question is asked:
"Why do the other three immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) exist in the formless realm? The answer is: "Maitreya alone knows."

From "If one first attains the lower [stages]" onwards, it clarifies that from the second dhyāna upward, one may attain the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). However, by simply mentioning the "fundamental" [dhyānas], all such cases are subsumed.
One should also clarify the stages [of attainment] and distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles, and so forth.

If one relies on the *vītarāga* (special excellence) dhyānas at a lower level, and subsequently relies on the pure (*śuddha*) dhyānas, it is said within the context of generating the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) that these constitute "one side.
Since the characteristics of the concentrations differ, they may occur simultaneously or sequentially; hence, they are called "one side. Regarding the phrase "impurity and grasping, etc.":

because they destroy and oppose bliss, the concentration of loving-kindness is not accomplished. Although there is no lower [level], the answer is that while it accords with *nirvāṇa*, it is conjoined with conditions for phenomena (*dharmālambana*). This...
This addresses the objection raised by way of a general response. Because untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas resemble *nirvāṇa*, they take it as their object.

Regarding the question of how the two meanings—taking sentient beings as the object in the case of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so forth—are mutually contradictory and yet can arise together: the intended meaning of the answer is that the dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are difficult to conceive;

one should simply have faith in them from above. Even in the Mahāyāna, it is accepted that six [mental factors] arise together and mutually induce one another; why then should one harbor doubt regarding the concentration of loving-kindness?
It can also be explained as "adornment. Why stop at saying that [the marks] mutually inspire adornment? It is even more so for the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*).

This being the case, the other three [immeasurables] follow this same principle. Alternatively, they may mutually inspire one another. These four characters clarify how the impurities of both the Great and Small Vehicles inspire the mind of loving-kindness.

The current text is preserved in an abbreviated form. Regarding the statement that they "mutually induce one another": although the phrasing encompasses the preceding [sections], the present text specifically clarifies that the contemplation of impurity induces loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
As for the other three immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), they are to be explained by analogy with the mind of loving-kindness.
If the four immeasurables are classified as either with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), this is determined by analyzing the supported (*āśrita*) based on its basis (*āśraya*).

Regarding the phrase "causes and conditions" and so forth, this clarifies the basis of the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). Since the bases are manifold, the supported accordingly follows along. Next, regarding the analogies: they illustrate that because the bases are many, the supported are likewise many.
There are two intentions in these analogies: the first illustrates that the essence of the dharma is profound and vast; the second illustrates that the dharma is subtle and difficult to fathom.

Contemplation. Next, regarding the section on "Convergence": first, it directly converges with *maitrī* (loving-kindness); second, it concurrently converges with the other four [immeasurables]. Regarding the phrase "to the left of the mountains" and so forth: the area east of Mount Tai is called "the Left.
Its inhabitants were unaware of the flavors of the delicacies from the capital region. Zhou and Kong’s commentary states: "To set aside flavorful things is called *xiū* (delicacy);

'precious' (*zhēn*) refers to that which is supreme among flavors. Regarding the phrase "the well-frog" and so forth: *Haire* is the name of a sea deity. "Not" (*fēi*) is used here as a term of censure.
It is thus: to boast that one's well is broad while disparaging the ocean as narrow is a mistake.

For those who practice through causes and conditions, this is the essential object for establishing contemplation by the practitioner; it is the initial practice for turning away from the heterodox and heading toward the correct.

The essence is the Buddha-nature of the three causes; as it is the true seed capable of accomplishing the wondrous Mahāyāna vehicle, the characteristics of this vehicle are explained in detail herein.

Regarding the statement "the subjective perceiver, the objective perceived, and so forth" when clarifying the arousal [of the mind], there are two kinds of contemplation regarding the twelve links of dependent origination. If...

One knows the cause by inferring from the effect, as previously explained in the contemplation of craving, in full accordance with the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Text). If one knows the effect by inferring from the cause, it is as in the present passage.

Although it clarifies that [karma] is obtained through manifestation, it is only through reliance on cultivation that it is known. Within the concentrated mind, when the object—whether wholesome or unwholesome—and the subjective faculties are in union, this is termed "karma" (*karman*).
Because karma inevitably brings forth its fruit, it is called "containing" (*saṃgraha*).
Next, one investigates [the causes] from grasping (*upādāna*) back to ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, by extinguishing the present causes, one avoids the future results.

Regarding the "six blisters" (*ṣaḍ-phupphusa*): they are the head, body, hands, and feet. Alternatively, it is said that the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and twenty fingers constitute the twenty-four blisters.

If [these] are based on the root [causes] and so forth, then the root and so forth all become causal conditions; specifically, longing and admiration serve as the cause, while receiving the teachings serves as...

The causal condition (*pratyaya*) is the established essence; it is called the "produced phenomenon" (*janyadharma*). Thus, the causal condition itself is designated as the "accomplisher. This refers to the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Whichever meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is attained, one accordingly accomplishes the corresponding factor of existence. When speaking of "the various dhyānas," this refers for the time being to the fundamental [absorptions], specifically pointing to the fundamental states as they are discussed vertically across the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding those who attain such states as far as the characteristics of the first dhyāna, one should say "non-perception" (asaṃjñā).
However, for the sake of beginning from the outset, coarse and subtle abidings and so forth are not what the mind intends; therefore, they are not discussed here.

Regarding the twenty-five preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*) mentioned previously, their respective original intentions are as explained in detail in the fourth [section], within the exposition of the five factors (*pañcadharma*) in relation to the first dhyāna.
As for the term "aspiration" (*prārthanā*), it refers to "desire" (*chanda*) among the five factors; thus, all twenty-five factors pertain to the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "knowing these feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth," the designations are established differently according to the objects of observation (*ālambana*).
Regarding the phrase "the three worlds, up to the [highest] equality": all that is bound to the realms (*dhātu-saṃyukta*) belongs to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

This is not the same as the classification of realm-bondage found in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as previously analyzed. As for "causes and conditions giving rise to the fundamental," the initial arising of causes and conditions refers to investigating the increase and decrease throughout the three periods of time.

The four modes of birth differ, as fully detailed in the section on the "Object of Conditions" (*pratyaya-viṣaya*) in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning), as well as in the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
These are all distinctions perceived within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), extending even to the differences in the characteristics of the three periods of time, which establish twelve names.

By tracing back to the root and so forth, the twelve are established; furthermore, from these twelve, the roots and so forth are produced, up to the "Extraordinary Victorious" (*viśeṣa*) and others. Regarding this, it should be said:

The *viśeṣa* (special) and other [meditations] arise from causes and conditions; since these causes and conditions primarily rely upon the fundamental [dhyānas], they are said here to "arise from the fundamental cause" by way of their basis (*āśraya*).

This is the same as how the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arises from the fundamental [dhyānas] and is judged to belong to the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) category. Since the *viśeṣa* and *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery), as well as the *vidyā* (clear knowledges), likewise rely on the fundamental [dhyānas] just like the mind of loving-kindness, it is said that they follow this analogy.

Next, following this contemplation, the text clarifies that the names for "reception" (*vedanā*) differ. Regarding the phrase "the three periods of time, etc.," it distinguishes between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*).

Although it is said that mere reflection cannot destroy delusions, the subsequent analogy states that the five cessations (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*) are like a sealed chamber, while the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) are like a bright lamp. Thus, one knows that a sealed chamber lacks the power to dispel darkness.

As in the passage following Fu-na, it is proven that only that which can destroy delusions is called a contemplation of principle (*li-guan*); this is what one desires to hear regarding wisdom (*prajñā*).

The term "this" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). Regarding the phrase "understanding through realization": it is as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, where the Buddha asks:
"Do you perceive the world as permanent, impermanent, or even as finite or infinite? If one says it is permanent and so forth, this is called "viewing" and "clinging.

Furthermore, he asks: "If you were to light a fire, when that fire is extinguished, do you know it? He answers: "It is so," and so on, up to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); if craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is extinguished...
At that time, the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are extinguished. Therefore, the *Lingjie* (Understanding) states: "I have already understood.

From the passage on these causes and conditions below, it is determined that this belongs to the category of phenomena (*vastu*). Next, various different sources from the sūtras and śāstras are cited; all of these may serve as objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
Regarding the "Tenfold Ornament" (*ratnāvalī*): it clarifies the ten kinds of contemplative methods of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*).
These ten are fully enumerated within the sixth [contemplation], the Contemplation of Causes and Conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-vipaśyanā*), as cited in detail in the second fascicle.
Next, the explanation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Generally speaking, the ten dhyānas constitute a single method of contemplation, as detailed in the subsequent list.

If discussed specifically, each one would be distinguished from the others; however, they are not singled out here because they are few in number. As for the nine *dhyānas*, their arising depends on specific causes and conditions and does not occur in this manner.
They somewhat resemble the objects of the aggregates (*skandha*) because they manifest constantly; since they manifest both continuously and intermittently, they can be separately contemplated.

First, under the section on Nāgārjuna, it clarifies the *Vigrahavyāvartanī-śāstra*, which encompasses both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and takes dependent origination as its central tenet; therefore, it is cited here to prove its universal applicability.
Under the section on the Master of the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, errors are identified.

Regarding the phrase "Now, [the words] 'below' refute errors": Generally speaking, what is called a "thesis" (*zong*) specifically reveals its fundamental intent. Since the term "two truths" is general and insufficient for precise differentiation, one asks: "Which category?

This implies that because the treatise’s meaning is universal, it refutes the notion of having no distinct thesis; moreover, since it pervades all teachings, how could it be a thesis belonging solely to this treatise?

Next, in the formal explanation: A bhikṣu of the four dhyānas [falls into] the hell realm; a flying weasel is a name for the animal realm; and a *kumbhāṇḍa* is a name for the hungry ghost realm.

Regarding the reference to "such as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and others," this refers to the Brahmās of those kalpas and the present-day devas who do not come [to hear the Dharma];

Regarding the phrase "if one is exclusively focused on the impure, etc.": this clarifies that those who attain the untainted (anāsrava) state do so by relying on these [meditations]. The term "etc.
includes the *viśeṣa* (special/superior) dhyāna, because the *viśeṣa* dhyāna also incorporates the tainted (*sāsrava*). Therefore, it is not mentioned at the beginning.

Next, regarding the two layers of explanation from "If one observes... downwards: they are called *bodhisattvas* because they can destroy obscurations; they are called *śrāvakas* from the perspective of the Four Noble Truths.

As for the mention of the morality, concentration, and wisdom of the nine dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), bodhisattvas are likewise subsumed within these nine realms; moreover, all within the nine realms cultivate the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
Only in the Avīci Hell is there an absence of active manifestation; yet, based on a single practice, five names are established.

Whether considered collectively or individually, each ground possesses the five practices and the ten merits; furthermore, the correlation between the ten merits and the grounds remains perfectly distinct.

Next, regarding the explanation of "inconceivability," it says: "Infinite concentration and distraction. A single thought-moment of meditative mind already encompasses the ten realms, whether in a state of concentration or distraction.
Why is this so? The explanation below states: "To perceive the nature [of reality] is concentration; to perceive commonality is distraction.
Both concentration and distraction are understood as non-dual within a single thought-moment. The same applies to the dharma-nature and ignorance. Therefore, this is called the inconceivable realm.

"Although it transcends the lower [stages]" explains that the aforementioned distinction between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and distraction is not something known by those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), as the Lesser Vehicle is also subsumed within the realm of ordinary sentiment;

The principle is thus. Therefore, it is said that "from the beginning not" [is it so], lest there be confusion with the fruit; thus it is said that "from the beginning not" [is it] "so. Because they are not identical, it is not "so"; because they are not separate, it is not "not.

Regarding the phrase "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) mentioned in the *Anxin zhong* (The Section on Settling the Mind), this refers to the sixty-four [contemplations].

If one observes the names of the three types of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) within the section on "Observing Departure to Reveal the Essence," each of these now fully possesses the three truths (*tri-satya*).
