Thus, from the very beginning of *śamatha* and the initial contemplation, the three truths are fully present; the other two [contemplations] should be understood accordingly. Therefore, the concluding summary states: "They exist within a single moment of mind.

Regarding the phrase "to destroy the two extremes," etc.: the essence of the truths is fundamentally devoid of one, three, middle, or extreme. To destroy the two is called "one"; to destroy the extremes is called "middle. To destroy...

It is called "perfect" (yuan) as a designation for what is partial; it is called "quiescent extinction" (jimiè) because it shatters the view of arising and ceasing; and it is called "one mind" (yixin) because it shatters the notion of sequential progression.
In reality, the wondrous principle possesses no such distinctions.

Regarding the phrase "What is the meaning of 'below'? It refers to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) as remedies for obscurations. As previously stated, if even the "flavoring" dhyānas constitute obscurations when compared to the Truth, how much more so would they be obscurations when compared to the Middle Way principle?

Question: Since the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā) have already been abandoned, how can there still be obscurations? Answer: Although the dhyānas themselves are not obscurations, it is because of attachment to them that such a state occurs.

The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding *nirvāṇa* is likewise so. If even the cultivation of the "hugua" [meditation] as a cause can still lead to rebirth in hell, how much more so when one’s obscurations still allow for the presence of wholesome states—what is there to be surprised at?

Therefore, failing to relinquish the ten dhyānas is termed stinginess (*mātsarya*). If one has already relinquished the ten realms of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), why would one be stingy regarding the dhyāna of phenomena?

If attachment to the flavor of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*) still destroys the path-concomitant [wholesome roots], how much more so when it is fully present? The remaining four [stinginesses] should be understood by analogy.

As for the Brahmā Kṛṣṇadanta, even Brahmā himself still harbors anger; how much more so, then, could others avoid it? Hence, the word "still" (*shang*) is used in all such cases. Regarding those who "suffer to the point of exhaustion" and so forth:

this constitutes an obscuration to dhyāna. If one must still suffer to the point of exhaustion in order to repent and eliminate [faults], how much more so should one not abandon the afflictions, karma, and māras by letting them run wild?
As for those people in the world who claim they are without fault and need not repent: this is not so. Within each of the methods of governance, one measures affairs through affairs;

yet, by being unobscured regarding these affairs, one assists in the fulfillment of the principles of governance. Therefore, it is said that one "destroys [delusions] in accordance with the Way," and so forth.
Next, regarding the "Middle" [section], it is fully explained as being like the seventh [section] concerning the practitioner who integrates phenomena through principle and fact (*shili shefa*).

This is because the phenomena to be contemplated do not exceed the preceding seven. As for the "Successive Stages," this is primarily intended to prevent confusion; the final two dharmas serve to spur those at shallow levels toward the profound.

First, a general summary; next, the opening of the chapters. Regarding the phrase "not one": it does not exceed the one hundred and forty kinds of views.

Furthermore, in the section beginning with "Furthermore, to explain and know," the character for "view" (見) is explained again, wherein one interpretation arises for each of the one hundred and forty [views].

Now, in listening to those below, one must first distinguish between what is not true insight. Those who listen to students claim they have a basis for their practice as if they were truly alive, while they denigrate those who cultivate meditation as being without foundation, as if dead.
Conversely, those who practice dhyāna and abandon partial views claim their own realization is a sublime awakening, while they denigrate those who study as being like "those who wait by the stump.
To take such sentiments as objective reality is to fail to point out that they are merely delusions. As for the term "waiting by the stump," there was once a farmer in the state of Song.

There was a rabbit that touched a tree stump and died; subsequently, it constantly guarded it, hoping for another rabbit to appear. These two men were originally of a nature inclined toward faith in the Dharma, yet they did not understand its great principles.
They argued with one another over right and wrong, but now they have reached a judgment: although both have erred, they have not yet formed a fixed view.

If one sees the "explanation of departure," this briefly indicates the arising of seeing. The former constitutes an infinite questioning; if one explains the latter, it constitutes an infinite answering.

Therefore, the metaphor of shooting with a curved arrow is used for the question. It is like the story of Yang Yu: because he was a skilled archer, when a monkey saw him, it would cling to the tree and cry out.
Seeing the "explanation" is what is produced by *dhyāna*; seeing the "names" is what is produced by the written text. Thus, both are seen; they are not different in their study.
It questions those who practice seated meditation, thereby challenging those who possess insight and familiarity with names;

it can shatter those who practice meditation without insight, like causing a flyer to lose their way. It challenges those who study through inquiry without insight, like causing a runner to lose their way.

All one hundred and forty [cases] are likewise without exception. Regarding "chuo" (绰), Guo Pu states it means "broad and generous. This refers to those who lack insight into the distinctions [between phenomena].
Below this, the distinctions based on their causes are explained; below that, examples are cited. Faith is like hearing, while the Dharma is like meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This should be understood through hearing and reflection. There are those who possess subtle penetration; they engage in refutation and reconciliation as if they had realized the sublime principle. These two belong to the category of views and do not pertain to the realization of discernment.

Regarding "the South" and so forth: formerly, because the Qi territory was separated [from the center], Chen was designated as the South. Those who attain visionary realization (*darśana*) through the cause of true *dhyāna* are those who have mastered *dhāraṇī*.
Those who attain visionary realization through the cause of hearing [the teachings] are those who have mastered the profound.

As for the phrase "those who are confused regarding equality," this refers to the ignorant class who judge those with visionary realization to be attached to high status, or else, out of lack of faith, judge them to be ghosts or madmen; therefore, we now provide the correct [explanation].

The judgment is that both are not the two [types]. Now, regarding "ghosts" (*bhūta*), it refers to those of lower [status]; "releasing" (*visarga*) refers to the non-duality of the two types. Since "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) belongs to the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*), it is called "view-wisdom. Regarding "generally discussed" below, this correctly clarifies the intent of the coming [passage].
As for the statement that there are "many" regarding the two meanings: these refer to those in whom dhyāna has already arisen and those in whom it arises simultaneously. If view were to arise...
Since one who has already [lost] dhyāna no longer attains it, how much less can one who has not yet attained dhyāna be said to "see"?

Therefore, it is called "slight. The following serves as an illustration. This illustrates the sequence of dhyāna and seeing. Regarding the phrase "all dhyānas universally give rise to [insight]," this refers collectively to the desire, form, and formless realms.

As for the phrase "arising in six stages or nine stages," this follows the two meanings mentioned previously. Furthermore, the stage of *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) also possesses the sense of giving rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). It is not...

Furthermore, it is said that [those who attain] "few" do so by relying on dhyāna. The "six" refers to the four dhyānas, the intermediate state, and the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).

The "nine" refers to these six plus the three formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*). Regarding the phrase "able to rectify oneself": those who encounter the teachings and associate with virtuous friends are all able to rectify themselves.

While the fault of holding views is already rare among those who have attained dhyāna, it is even more difficult for one to rectify oneself when views arise from the power of dhyāna. As for the phrase "True Dharma," etc., it refers to realization.

It is difficult to find such a person and difficult to find such a teaching; this refers to the teaching of the True Dharma. The "speaker" is the person [who imparts it], and the "audience" is those who are capable of discerning and rectifying it.

Because they must correctly extinguish and investigate their own minds, such people are difficult to find. Regarding the phrase "dense forest" (*ghana-vana*) and so forth: *yāta* means to drag or pull.
Those with crooked wood of false views are within the dense forest of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). How could those attached to views be able to drag [themselves out]?
Next, regarding the three systems of tenets explained within this chapter: the various external schools' tenets do not exceed those of two gods and three sages.
As for the two gods, they are Maheśvara and Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is here translated as "Pervasive Victory" (Biànshèng) or "Pervasive Purity" (Biànjìng).

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that he is at the summit of the third dhyāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides an extensive explanation of Maheśvara, translating him as "Great Self" (Dazì).
He resides at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). He has three eyes and eight arms, and he holds the World-Honored One aloft as his presiding teacher.

As for the three sages: the first is Kapiḷa, which translates as "Yellow-Headed"; his head is like the color of gold. Fearing that his body would perish, he went to the Heaven of Maheśvara to inquire [about immortality].
The gods commanded him to go to Mount Piṇḍa to eat *āmalaka* fruits, which would prolong his life. Having eaten them, he transformed into a great stone within the forest.
Second is Uruṅga, also known as this ascetic Hui-liu; by day he hides in mountain valleys to compose scriptures, and by night he wanders about preaching the Dharma to convert others.
Third is Leshapa, which is translated here as "Asceticism"; he takes the calculation of numbers as his holy dharma.

Next, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* clarifies the four schools regarding action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). First, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The hands, body, and so forth are called 'action,' while the *puruṣa* (self) is the 'agent.

One calculates that the body and the spirit are one, and that form itself is the self. This refers to the relationship between the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which possesses the characteristic (*lakṣya*).

First is "oneness" (*ekatva*). This refers to the four [characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth. "Oneness" is also the divine self (*puruṣa*). There is the part (*bhāga*) and the whole (*bhāgin*).
"Part" refers to a minor portion of the body, such as the head; the "whole" refers to the body itself.

To reckon the body as one with its hands, feet, and so forth, and further to reckon it as one in terms of color, is merely to reckon the body and the self as one. If Ulluka reckons them as different, that is not [the case].

However, regarding the previous body, they conceive of it as distinct from the spirit (*ātman*). Furthermore, there are no phenomena that they do not conceive of [in this way]; for example, the analogy of clay and a jar.

The two conceptions of identity and difference can be understood by applying the same explanation. Moreover, the *Catuḥśāstravibhaṅga* (Treatise Refuting the Four Schools) refutes these four conceptions:
the Sāṃkhya conceives of identity; the Vaiśeṣika conceives of difference; the Nirgrantha conceives of both identity and difference; and the Jaina conceives of neither identity nor difference.
Regarding the "Six Teachers," their original progenitor was simply Kapila and others; from his lineage, six branches were formed. As for the phrase "three are the same and three are different":
when comparing the translations by Master Kumārajīva with the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, the names of the six teachers are identical, yet in terms of their doctrines, three are different.

The "three differences" refer to the numbers two, four, and five. The "two" refers to Makkhali Gosāla; Kumārajīva stated that he [Makkhali] held that the transgressions and blessings of sentient beings do not exist.
Regarding causes and conditions, a sutra states: "The bodies of all sentient beings consist of seven constituents: earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life-span.

The fourth refers to Ajita Keśakambala; Kumārajīva translated this as "taking asceticism as the Way. A sutra states: "To kill one..."

Kumārajīva says that one should generally give rise to views and answer according to whether something exists or does not exist.

The Sūtra states: "One who is without shame or remorse does not fall into hell. This is because it accords with the question [in one sense] and contradicts it [in another]; thus, contradiction and accord are not the same. It is said:
Regarding the three similarities: the first is similarity in their initial position. The first refers to Pūraṇa. Kumārajīva says that he reckons all phenomena to be like empty space.

this is because they are essentially identical in terms of cause and effect."

Next, regarding those outside the Buddha-dharma who are attached to it: they take the Buddhist scriptures as the basis for their own calculations. Both of these groups appear together within the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise).

Their two schools generally agree that "tortoise hair" and "hare's horns" are examples of the impermanent and the non-self; however, the *Vaipulya* school further adds that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty.
Thus, the Vātsīputrīyas' calculation of a self residing in the "fifth treasury" is said to transcend the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Question: For what reason?
The four phrases in the current text differ from those in the treatise. Answer: The four phrases listed in the current text are precisely the four phrases of the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
First the four phrases are presented, and subsequently the scriptural evidence is cited; therefore, one knows that while the wording differs, the meaning is the same.
The commentary on the *Vātsīputrīya* states: Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the *Vātsīputrīya-abhidharma*:

the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are not separate from the person, and the person is not separate from the five aggregates; yet it cannot be said that the five aggregates are the person, nor can it be said that the person is the five aggregates.

Because the person is subsumed within the fifth category, the "inexpressible treasury" (*avaktavya-kośa*), the first two propositions thus encompass the twenty propositions of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the latter two [sections] merely clarify that the "self" (ātman) exists outside of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) and is therefore inexpressible. Now, in the section below on the Vātsīputrīyas, the distinctions are analyzed.
There are four types of outsiders (tīrthika): first, those who are external yet within the four propositions; second, the Vātsīputrīyas, who are external to them;

third, those who are external and further external, branching out from the original four types to form twenty; and fourth, the Vātsīputrīyas, who are simply human beings. Thirdly, those who are external and further external postulate the self as being truly real.

Whether [the self] is eternal or annihilated, the Vātsīputrīya calculation remains, for now, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). While the four non-Buddhist outsiders calculate a "divine self" (*ātman*), the Vātsīputrīyas merely posit a "human self.
Therefore, it is said they differ from the Buddha's Dharma. The twenty views of individuality (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) held by the six masters are likewise refuted by the Vātsīputrīyas.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the three times and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—such as the unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*)—are also [refuted], the non-Buddhist outsiders likewise...
They calculate this to be permanent. Now, the Vātsīputrīyas certainly do not regard the "person" (pudgala) as the fourth category or the "ineffable collection" (avaktavya-kāya).
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīyas also employ the analysis of the causal conditions (pratyaya) to destroy delusions.

Next, regarding the Vaipulya (Extensive) school: those who propose ten metaphors—such as the illusion and so forth—belonged previously to the Vātsīputrīya sub-sect of the Hīnayāna, but now they affiliate with the Mahāyāna.

Having acquired names such as "illusion" and so on, yet having lost the true reality, they become non-Buddhists (tīrthika). One should know that the Vaipulya also possesses four characteristics that show it is not a gateway to the Mahāyāna:
first, ignorance of the true principle; second, ignorance of the characteristics of the delusions that arise; and third, ignorance of the conceptualizing faculty.

They are "born followers" (*jāti-hetu*). Because the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) do not destroy their delusions, they remain attached to the Buddha-dharma yet are still called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). For this reason, Nāgārjuna cites them to refute them.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that "one who does not obtain the skillful means (*upāya*) of Prajñā," the intent of the treatise is that those who study the Hīnayāna fall [into error].
Regarding existence and non-existence: those who study the Mahāyāna are scorched by the fire of false views; therefore, these two types of people are said to have "lost the means" (*upāya*).

The gate fundamentally leads to principle; if one loses the principle, it is no longer a gate. The same applies to the horns of a hare or illusory transformations. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states below, citing the great to illustrate the small:

if even adhering to the Mahāyāna's "neither of the two" constitutes folly, how much more so for the adherents of the Small Vehicle to cling to the fourth alternative—how could that not be a false view?
Regarding the phrase "Thus, the *Śataśāstra* and so forth": this refers to the refutation by the Master [Vasubandhu], who treats the Small Vehicle as "external.

If there is attachment, then both the Great and Small Vehicles are not [the truth]; if there is no attachment, then all four gates are [equally] correct. How could one suddenly refute them all equally as being external heterodoxies? First, the primary intent of the *Śataśāstra* is clarified:

it is a mistaken refutation of the Mahāyāna. "Yan" (炎) means "incidental" or "secondary. Establishing the refutation of the Small Vehicle while upholding the Great Vehicle is the primary refutation; that the Small Vehicle is considered "external" is [merely incidental].

In the *Páng* (Commentary), it is said that there was a master of treatises named Yan who formulated this refutation: "It may be acceptable to refute the two masters' reckoning of the mind as being identical to external objects;
however, if one were to directly refute the two masters as being non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), this would entail a fault. Therefore, the following defense states:

"One must not [refute them] like thunder and so forth. If one were to broadly refute the Mahāyāna while disparaging the Hīnayāna, this would merely be a matter of contrasting skill and clumsiness—a superficial depreciation—and how could such a thing constitute a definitive judgment?
It is the same as the non-Buddhists; therefore, it results in error.
However, in the latter part of the treatise, a scriptural passage is cited to provide a defense: in reality, the meaning of emptiness is not the same as that of the non-Buddhists.

As for the statement that it "appears to be nothingness," while the name "nothingness" may seem identical, how can this possibly manifest the true principle? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the same as the hundred schools," etc., it refers next to the critique of the Master [Vasubandhu] and the hundred...

Regarding the establishment and refutation of the tenets of the treatise and their similarities and differences: both schools regard the tenets of their own treatise as correct and that which is refuted as incorrect.

Since they both take the Mahāyāna as their common tenet, they are the same as the "hundred schools" in what is correct. Because the masters of the treatise refute the Hinayana and refute external [non-Buddhist] doctrines, it is said that they differ from the hundred schools.

Regarding "not grasping the meaning" and so forth: both schools should refute the externalist and the Hinayanist; yet now each preserves one side, which is called "alternating appearance and disappearance.

Furthermore, regarding "resembling" and so forth: this criticizes the Master for refuting both treatises simultaneously; how does this differ from the Lokāyata view that both existence and non-existence exist?

Knowing that they are not entirely identical, it is therefore said merely that they "resemble" one another. Furthermore, as for the term *kun-le*: speaking of them together, they do not differ from *kun-le*, because they share the same nature of both [being and non-being].

"At that time, [the opponent] was directly refuted. The Master [Vasubandhu], in order to defend the two treatises, nevertheless conceded, saying: 'This should be conceded; it may be that there is grasping, but it is not that there is no grasping.
As for the phrase 'what fault, etc.', this refers to Uruvilvā and others. If one were to say 'the Great [Vehicle] refutes the Small [Vehicle],' etc."
This addresses the anticipated objection. The objection states: "If he were not a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), why did Vimalakīrti rebuke Subhūti by saying, 'Those non-Buddhists are your teachers'?
Therefore, the present response clarifies: He rebuked him for being devoid of the Middle Way, thereby humbling him by equating him with non-Buddhists.
Next, the differences in how heterodox persons obtain the Dharma are explained. First, citing the *Guanzhong shu* (Commentary from Guanzhong), it says: "One master has three reckonings.
As for "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) as listed here, and "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*), these are as described among the three types of sages mentioned previously.

Regarding the phrase "transforming cities" and so forth within the section on supernormal powers: *luo* (鹵) refers to salty soil; *mó* (捫) refers to touching with the hand, as in the second fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary). *Veda* refers to the non-Buddhist...

Regarding human classics, they are fully explained at length in the *Mātaṅga-sūtra*. Fundamentally, there are only four: first, recitation; second, sacrifice; third, chanting; and fourth, the averting of calamities.
Later, disciples successively expanded these until they became one thousand two hundred and sixteen. As for "astrology and medicine" and so forth:
"astrology" refers to those such as Qi Bo in China and Jīvaka or Vāryaśvī in the West. "Military arts" [refers to the science of warfare].

As clarified in works such as the *Huangshigong* and the *Taigong Liubao*, there are three types of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The details are found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. It is commonly held that these attain both the phenomenal (*vastu*) and the principial (*tattva*).
"Phenomenal" refers to the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); "principial" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Condition" (*ālambana*) refers to the verbal teachings of the four gates within the current instruction. All such teachings take that which is expressed (*vācya*) as their object; this object is that which is to be attended to.

Regarding the passage from the *Abhidharma* stating "the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and so forth": the afflictions are that which obstruct; liberation (*vimukti*) is that which is obstructed.
Regarding "dhyāna-concentration obstructs liberation": dhyāna-concentration is itself liberation, and liberation is that which is obstructed. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise.
Because one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and all dharmas by breaking through hindrances, it is said thus. This is a provisional analysis according to the Tripiṭaka.

Next, regarding the section beginning with "If one clings to the lower," there are three types according to the Mahāyāna gate. Following the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness*, each of the four teachings has its own three types;

within each teaching, there are both phenomenal and principle-based teachings and methods. Question: Why was it previously stated that the thousand great arhats have all attained freedom from doubt? Answer: They have all attained it.
This simply attributes [the result] to the Buddha.
Next, the explanation of the arising of vision contains both a simile and its application. First, the simile illustrates two causes; the subsequent simile resolves two conditions.

When the obstruction of darkness is removed, the application does not correspond [to the cause], but corresponds only to the condition. "Jùn" (濬) means deep; "jùn" (駿) is an elegant term for a fine horse.

Next, regarding the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): since the primary gate therein already includes those of sharp faculties who perceive the Middle Way, here too it refers to the illusory transformations within the obstructions.
These arise from the latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-vasana) within the obstructions, giving rise to views and attachments. The Separate Teaching (Biejiao) is as stated in the text.

Next, within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), even those who have not yet reached the stage are said to possess the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti); how much more so for the vision of the Perfect Gate?
As for "true words" and so forth, these are originally true words; they become false because views arise from them. Nirvana is also like this: the dharmas of birth and death are entirely nirvana.

Because of the arising of attachment, one instead falls back into birth and death. It is the same with the nectar of immortality: the Buddha’s teaching arises like this nectar; to transcend views is like consuming it in excess;
and to lose the principle is like meeting an untimely death.
Regarding the statement that "the four views are the basis of all views," etc.: by adding the simple, the compound is formed; by adding the compound, the complete set is established.

To avoid the three, one reaches the absolute. Regarding "self and other are likewise equal," there are two aspects: first, "self-equality," which shares the same meaning as "equality with existence. Thus, these two texts are used interchangeably.

If explained according to their conceptualization, within a single view of existence, self-equality and the others are fully present; all employ the three provisional designations and the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
To refute this, "neither with nor without cause" is merely a dualistic calculation. Since neither [cause] nor [self] nor [other] exists, the first two of the four positions constitute the basis.
This applies equally to "existence" and so forth; the four positions regarding "the effect being within the cause" and so on are likewise the same.

Next, regarding the citation of Nāgārjuna: having finished refuting [the views of] both self and other, he merely states that there are two faults in [asserting] a common cause, and that a causeless [arising] is impossible.
This is precisely the meaning of the phrase "the root is uprooted and the branches break."

Now, below the sections on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, I shall provide an interpretation by analogy using the Buddha-dharma. Although the internal and external differ, the branches and the root share the same meaning; the refutation is likewise.

Below the section on the Tripiṭaka, I shall interpret the characteristics according to the teachings: first the Zàng and Tōng, then the Bié and Yuán. Within the first [the Zàng and Tōng], I shall first clarify the two teachings.
Next, we distinguish between the internal and external realms of oneself and others. Generally speaking, each teaching possesses four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The specific details are as in the third [section], where each of the four permutations is applied individually to a single teaching. Now, however, we distinguish the four teachings based on the common and the particular, merely contrasting the internal and external of oneself and others.
These three [distinctions] differ from one another, each following its own logical momentum.

Next, regarding the explanation of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], first is the formal explanation. Second, concerning the judgment of "ruler and minister": one who can govern the world is also "honored" (the ruler).

The Master of the Teaching is likewise so; each governs the myriad affairs of state. The "minister" assists the ruler in governing the people. Now, between these two there is a relative strength and weakness:
within the paths of skillful means of the two teachings—Tripitaka and Separate—the ruler has not yet achieved merit, and thus it is said that the ruler is weak. The merit is attributed to...

The subject, therefore, is said to be strong. Both the *Tongyuan* (Comprehensive and Perfect) and others state that this is due to the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena). Since the *dharmatā* is the sovereign, it is said that the ruler is strong;
because it does not rely exclusively on skillful means (*upāya*), it is said that the minister is weak. Herein, we provisionally distinguish between the two teachings of Separate and Perfect.

The previous reference pointed to the Separate Teaching, hence "the minister is strong"; the present reference points to the Perfect Teaching, hence "the minister is weak. The other two—Tripitaka and Shared—may be understood by analogy with these explanations.

"Know that. Regarding "due to hearing" (*yīnwén*) below, this briefly clarifies the degree [of realization]. Regarding "the practitioner" (*xíngzhě*) below, this correctly clarifies the arising of visions. Although it is said to be "due to hearing," it is not entirely a distracted mind;
nor do they arise due to [mere] dhyāna. Because one subsequently hears even a little, it is called "due to hearing. This is because [visions] do not exist within a distracted mind.
This clarifies the meaning of the manifestation.

Regarding the initial mention of "the other three" within the outer-of-the-outer section: if there were only three patriarchs, it should simply state "one"; however, because they enter into the Mahāyāna, it is possible to speak of "three.
In the section on the texts of the Buddha-dharma, only one is listed, which includes by extension the Vaipulya (fangguǎng) scriptures.

Next, the Buddha-dharma is explained. First the Small [Vehicle], then the Great [Vehicle]. Regarding the statement in the Great Vehicle, "Although one has generated [the view]," etc., this judges the essential nature of the view:
although it relies on the Great Gate, if after generating the view one is unable to penetrate through, then the basis relied upon is not a great expedient;
furthermore, since it does not constitute the Small [Vehicle], the view that arises results in birth and death. As for the two blessings in China: the first is the absence of rākṣasas.
Second, there are no non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). If there were those in this land possessing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and so forth, who would not turn to them?
For instance, during the Yao Qin period, a non-Buddhist came and was defeated by Master Daorong; he returned to India, whereupon he sent a treatise from this land to refute him.
Since the three types of non-Buddhists do not exist here, they have merely used the examples of Zhuangzi and Laozi to parallel the Vedas.
Next, regarding the enumeration: according to the *Mahāyānāvatāra*, there should be twenty-eight. As for "mastery of supernormal powers and wisdom":

"supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the various psychic faculties, while "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Regarding the mention of the Vedas and so forth: even Kāpyila saw fit to privately study the minor branches [of the Vedas].
Those who rely on faith cite scriptures as their authority, yet this is not yet acceptable.

Next, regarding the detailed explanation of the differences, it says in the section on "Omniscience": "As for those who rely on the power of debate, they consider themselves the greatest; therefore, they are called 'those of the power of debate.
Having accepted the challenge of the Brahmin Li Chang, he composed five hundred difficult questions and went to the Buddha's dwelling. Upon seeing the Deer-Headed One [Mṛgaśiras],..."
Transformed by the Buddha, they naturally enter the Way.
Regarding the phrase "the basis upon which supernatural powers arise" and so forth: among the various external [practitioners], these rely solely on the fundamental dhyānas;

within these, there are inherent distinctions of superiority and inferiority between the upper and lower stages. Compared to the disciples of the Buddha, those who are particularly superior possess a more excellent basis for their powers, up to and including the Buddhas.
The principles may be understood by analogy with what has been explained.
As for the mention in the Vedas of "governing the household" and so forth, it is also like this land: filial piety is used to govern the household, and loyalty is used to govern the state.
To assist the state and benefit the people;
hence it is called "rescue" (*ji*). Regarding "verifying them as equal": [The questioner] asks, upon what basis is omniscience and so forth attained? Regarding "examining them as equal":
one examines from which school their calculations originate and what they cite as proof. Furthermore, one investigates by using new and old [doctrines] to provoke delusions and thereby test them.

"Beans" refers to legumes. Thus, the clear and the turbid are naturally distinguished, just as beans and wheat are different. Since those who are both heterodox and orthodox are already equalized, they cannot even distinguish between heterodoxy and orthodoxy;
how then could they judge between the Great and the Small?
Zhou Hongzheng’s explanation of the "Three Profundities" (*sanxuan*) is as follows: "Profundity" (*xuan*) refers to that which is obscure and abstruse.

Because the world regards these three as the ultimate in obscurity, the *Yijing*—since it does not transcend the Way of Yin and Yang—is categorized as "existence. Laozi, since he maintains the female and preserves weakness, asserting that all things return from existence to non-existence, is categorized as "illusory non-existence.
As for Zhuangzi, his *Inner Chapters* speak of "nothingness" (*wu*) and "not being nothing" (*wubuwu*), and so forth; how could this not be [the case]?
Regarding existence and non-existence, it is explained at length according to the teachings.

Under the systems established by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, it is clarified that while the fruit is refuted, the cause is not. Allowing for such things as the protection of the body is an instance of not refuting the cause;

however, establishing [only] the lower [rebirths] explains the non-refutation of the cause without mentioning the "invoking of retribution," which constitutes the refutation of the fruit. Alternatively, it is said that "blessings flow on to subsequent generations."
This is precisely "having existence," which carries the meaning of the persistence of results.

To find the sublime within these various desires is to find the sublime in desirelessness; thus, all such desires are sublime. Since this sublimity is ungraspable, it is said that they are all non-existent.

"Sublime" refers to *nirvāṇa*, while "desires" refer to the fetters of the realms (*dhātu-bandhana*). Therefore, for one who realizes the Truth, both desire and the sublime are non-existent; however, this has not yet been fully manifested.
Regarding the term "equal" (*deng*): the teachings are still provisional (*upāya*). The people of the world often say that Confucius was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Rutong).

While it is said that the three teachings follow different paths but reach the same destination, this statement only exists once the Buddhist teachings have opened the way for such provisional means. Where in the Classics (*jing*), Histories (*shi*), Philosophical Treatises (*zi*), or Collections (*ji*) is this ever mentioned?
To say they are equal is as absurd as calling a cripple agile.

Regarding the passage where Zhuangzi denounces benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*): "Zhuang" refers to [Zhuangzi] calling Confucius a thief of benevolence and righteousness. Although one may guard against petty thieves, one does not anticipate a great thief.

This thief takes up benevolence to scheme for his state. The character *jie* (pronounced *qùliè*) means the appearance of lifting something high, as if carrying a tall drum while searching for a lost child—how could he possibly find it?
Thus, he denounces Confucius for taking up benevolence and righteousness. It is not... [the sentence continues].
One should know that this reveals the inherent fallacies [of their positions].
Next, regarding the three [positions] of the Westerners: those who "refute the cause but not the fruit" do not admit a past cause while maintaining the present fruit.
They posit a present cause as "not refuting the cause" and the disappearance of the future fruit as "refuting the fruit. The second [position] refutes both, yet does not refute one.

Regarding "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*): as previously stated, both cause and effect are refuted and declared non-existent; hence it is said they are "refuted together. However, one cannot refute the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Outsiders also reckon space (*ākāśa*) to be eternal; although the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) do not exist [in that sense], they still dare not refute them.

This is because the three unconditioned phenomena encompass all phenomena exhaustively; therefore, it is called "all phenomena. If one were to refute them further, one would no longer reckon space to be eternal.
There is no delusion to be destroyed, nor is there any condition for delusion to be absent; therefore, both are refuted. As for the question of how this differs from the Buddha-dharma:

it is because one fears being confused with the Buddha-dharma that [the text] also demonstrates the refutation of worldly cause and effect, does not permit the reckoning of emptiness as permanent, and does not designate the two types of cessation as ultimate truth.

Furthermore, it avoids confusion with the Mahāyāna by refuting the small-vehicle (Hīnayāna) notions of cause and effect as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta). Thus, the question is posed.
[Question: What distinguishes this from the third type of non-Buddhist (tīrthika)? [Answer:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 25, quotes a treatise to answer: "In the Buddha-dharma, one distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox, and the Great and the Small. Each has already refuted instances where they were previously mixed. [Objection:

Furthermore, [the text] below the section on "essence" (*svabhāva*) again challenges the non-Buddhists regarding their differing false causes (*mithyā-hetu*). [Response: It is answered again: "There are those who expose the errors of others..."

The objection states: "An outsider also refutes; to refute is to dismantle. Thus, the outsider’s objection would lack substance yet possess dismantlement. [The text] now clarifies this below as the response:

Although the term "refutation" (pó) is common to both, the heterodox and the orthodox are inherently distinct. This is because, for example, each chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is titled "Refutation" (Pò).

Within the Buddha-dharma, it is commonly said that "dismantling the substance" is also termed "refutation. Therefore, one should know that being "refuted" applies equally to neither the Mahāyāna nor the Hīnayāna.

"Those who practice true contemplation," etc., refers to those who cultivate the realization of emptiness; such persons do not even perform mundane, out-flowing virtues, let alone the evils of the three miserable realms.
"Those who do not know," etc., refers to those who see but do not understand emptiness, whom they treat with contempt as if they were mere dust.
"Those who possess shame and remorse," etc., refers to Kāḷodāyin, as explained in detail above.
Regarding those who carve fish fillets from the backs of wooden Buddha images and use Buddhist scriptures as waste paper: when they hear the thunder of heaven, they even urinate into the well.
Although the Buddhadharma spans across different lifetimes, its cause and effect remain real; how could it be that the retributions of the present and future are unimpeded?

Next is "Below the Human. Next, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are clarified. Since views regarding emptiness are prevalent, they merely constitute [wrong] views rather than the three types of supernormal powers.
Furthermore, "Extensively Seeking Below" clarifies the *Veda*. Holding onto views is like snarling; destroying others is like barking.

Next, the explanation of transforming others also consists of four points. In all cases, one's own practice is taken as the reality, while the transformation of others is taken as the provisional means.

Regarding the two types of shackles—gold and iron—the function of binding them both is identical. The iron shackle is like being bound externally, while the gold shackle is like being bound internally.
Although their value differs, the meaning of being fettered is the same. Regarding the two raw blocks of jade and mouse-stone: "pó" (璞) refers to jade; the people of Zheng regarded it as true jade.
Regarding the jade-like raw material (*pó*): Zhou used a dead mouse as his "jade. Although the name "jade" is the same for both, their purity and filthiness are as distinct as heaven and earth.

One who is free from attachment is like Zheng; one who gives rise to views is like Zhou. The various gates of the Buddha-dharma are like Zheng; giving rise to craving is like Zhou. As for the milk of the ox and the donkey, though their color is the same, their substance differs;

yet when both are subjected to churning and processing, one succeeds while the other fails. Internally and externally, there is the same presence [of the potential], such as non-killing, compassion, and so forth.
As for the name: when examined externally, it is found to be entirely illusory and false.

Regarding terms such as *kāla-vṛnta* and others, they appear in the "Four Reliances" chapter (*catuḥpratisaraṇa-parivarta*) of a Mahāyāna sūtra; I have borrowed them here for their application. Two fruits may resemble each other, yet the *kāla* fruit is poisonous.
Though their internal and external names are identical, the latter leads one toward heterodoxy and delusion.
Regarding the fundamental transformations (*mūla-nirmāṇa*): if one relies on the fundamental dhyānas, there are fourteen transformations.

There are two in the first dhyāna, three in the second, four in the third, and five in the fourth. This is because those above are able to produce those below; furthermore, the first dhyāna includes the desire realm, hence it has two.
The others all include the lower stages, and thus each increases by one. As for the eighteen transformations, they all belong to the supernormal power of the body (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).

There are eight because water and fire emerge alternately from the left and right, as well as from above and below. There are two because earth and water manifest as each other. There are two because the earth appears and disappears in space.
There are four because of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) in mid-air. There are two because of manifesting large and small forms in mid-air. Combined with the preceding, these total ten.
8. Regarding the Buddha manifesting the eighteen transformations for Kāśyapa:

although the number of shared activities differs from those [of other sūtras], as for the texts they recite and so forth—since these are the Vedas, which are not even included within the Tripiṭaka, how could they possibly be the dhāraṇī of the total dharma-realm of the Perfect Teaching?

Regarding the phrase "although they have severed," etc.: since it is reckoned that by severing the volitions of the lower stages, one reaches the end of the lifespan in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñisattva) and receives retribution according to the Path, the text cites the flowers and leaves of insentient things as a metaphor for the arising of [false] views.

However, regarding those below the Pratyekabuddhas, the teachings upon which they rely differ in being either heterodox or orthodox; yet despite these differences, they all cause one to awaken to the principle.

As for texts such as the *Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi*, they clarify that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as the years and months gradually pass, those who attain the Way become fewer while those who give rise to attachments become more numerous.
This is true even for the Buddha-dharma, let alone for external teachings.

Regarding the phrase "long-dwelling at the city gates" and so forth: although the four gates differ from one another in being either refined or coarse, there is none that cannot lead one to the presence of the king.

To briefly cite two examples of what is not [the way], the intention reaches all four gates; yet if one clings to a specific gate and habituates oneself to it, how can one accord with the ultimate principle?

When the time for cultivation has passed, the true Path is difficult to expect. A matchmaker is the master who brings about union; a procuress is one who goes about selling her own person. Thus it is proclaimed.

The words of a go-between are thus called "beating the drum. Because one cannot let go of things, it is called "self-importance. Because one’s physical demeanor stands out among the assembly, it is called the "pinnacle of pride.

Regarding the *Vaipulya-praśna-puṇya* (The Vaipulya Sutra on Asking about Merit), in that sutra the Buddha himself spoke of his past causes and conditions, saying: "At that time, I was poor and wished to attend a great [festival]."
He was to receive various offerings at an assembly. On the way, he encountered a bridge and asked others, "What wood is this bridge made of?

Who built it? and so forth. He posed seven thousand eight hundred such questions in succession. Once he had finished asking, those who answered rebuked him; only then did he reach the venue of the assembly.
By the time he arrived, the assembly had already dispersed, and he obtained nothing at all.
Regarding "the aged lack samādhi," the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "For example, once sugarcane has been pressed, its residue is no longer of use.
Once one has been pressed by old age, there is no longer the capacity for leaving the household life, reciting scriptures, practicing seated meditation, or attaining samādhi."

Regarding the phrase "the heavenly gate, straight flowers, etc.": "curved" and "straight" are paired with "flowers" and "coarse. These should be analyzed as two distinct entities for both the internal and external realms:
one is the straight flower, and the other is the curved coarse. The "heavenly gate" refers to the principal gate of the imperial palace; the "other gates" refer to the side gates.

In the *Jianzhen jianzhong* (Seeing Reality and Seeing the Center), each is analyzed as a single entity. Although they are not explicitly distinguished here, the underlying meaning must necessarily include them both.

Second. Observing from below, this is fully elucidated. As for the terms "clear" and "turbid," they simply refer to the various teachings and gateways being mutually contrasted in terms of attachment and non-attachment.
Regarding the five categories, these generally combine the two external [teachings] along with those attached to the Buddha-dharma into one.

Is it one? The four teachings constitute four [categories]. Regarding the extensive discussion of the immeasurable: based on dhyāna and based on hearing, there are respectively one hundred and forty [types].

Those who practice śamatha and vipaśyanā in common observe the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas). Although the common practice is one, their manifestation must necessarily rely on different bases.

Therefore, seeing is the nature of wisdom; its manifestation must necessarily rely on vipaśyanā. Dhyāna is the nature of concentration; its manifestation must necessarily rely on śamatha. "Like a person," etc., refers to the name "like."
Wisdom is difficult to forget; delusion is easy to lose. In past lives, there were brothers whose resolve was biased;
this is called "demon-dhyāna" (ghost-cultivation). Wherever they were reborn, demons would afflict them. The conditions for attaining sainthood are analogous to this.

Furthermore, the following clarifies the intention behind observing objects. It is for fear that those who do not recognize [the nature of defilements] might act upon them, or for fear that they might abruptly sever [the practice] and lose their skillful means (*upāya*).

As with a *gū* (a type of malevolent spirit), which can harm a person by entering the stomach through food: if one is possessed by a *gū* and simultaneously suffers from the "inch-long white worm" (*cunbai*), one should not treat the inch-long white worm;
rather, one should nourish it so that it devours the *gū*. The dull-facultied afflictions (*kleśa*) are like the *gū*, and the [objects of] perception are like the inch-long white worm.

The analogy can be understood through this synthesis. As for the "stem-bead," it refers to the seed of the *yìyǐ* (Coix lacryma-jobi). Although there is no visible affliction, one who is dull-witted does not hear the Dharma.
If one enters the lower [stage], it clarifies the intention of nurturing the view (*dṛṣṭi*). Since this is the essence of the Mahāyāna, why must it be abruptly severed?

It is simply that once the dullness is severed, the realization of its essence is not delayed. The view acts as an attendant; entering and exiting follows the person. Nurturing the view is like exiting; realizing the contemplation is like entering. Externally...
If this is still the case for those on the outside, how much more so for those who are correct?

Regarding the "Threefold Wisdom" and so forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the treatise, in its commentary on the title "Teacher of Gods and Humans," poses the question: "The Buddha is also born in other realms; why is he described as such only for gods and humans?

The answer is: "Because they are few, they are not mentioned. However, those in the three evil realms who attain the Way do so by virtue of wisdom gained from past lives (*pūrvadṛṣṭa-jñāna*); although they may have produced merit, [they are not counted here].
O Heavenly One, that those who do not awaken to the Way are truly due to a lack of wisdom.

As for the term "foxes and barbarians," it refers generally to the remote borderlands where rites and teachings do not reach; they do not even understand common worldly speech, so how could they know the sublime teaching?

Such is the state of the world in general, and this was also the case before the Buddha appeared. Regarding the phrase "dividing his form" and so forth, he therefore first caused those of great transformative power (*mahā-upāya*) to instruct them.

Having seen [this], they subsequently demonstrate the acceptance of its refutation, and both enter the right path. Next, the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) proves that they were initially the same but later became different.

If one is initially inferior, it is stated that they are "the same" based on the judgment of whether their views have been severed or not. Regarding the "three outsiders," this refutes the views that have arisen, not the basis upon which they rely.

As for those who had already severed [their views] in previous lives, either their views are exhausted while their discursive thoughts remain, or their discursive thoughts are eliminated while their views persist, or their discursive thoughts...

It is not yet exhausted. If it were entirely exhausted, this [view] would not arise. Thus, those who give rise to views are not the same as the various lower [stages]. Even among the "outermost of the outer" (bāhyabāhya), such is the case; how much more so for others?

Regarding those such as the *Vimalakīrti*, they suppress [the view] to be the same as other views in order to advance by relying on the fundamental [truth], whereas the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha) fall back because they do not know the Middle Way (*madhyamārtha*).
They temporarily dismiss [it] as a view; even the outermost of the outer still maintain [it], let alone the Two Vehicles. This is a matter of suppression and exaltation (*nigrahasthāna* / *utkarṣa*).
These words cannot be taken as absolute.

If one were to establish a formal thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, taking sectarian views (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*) to compare with various treatises, then combining internal and external schools, there would be one hundred and forty sects;
furthermore, even within the Buddha-dharma alone, there are one hundred and twelve sects. How could these possibly be compared to [the categories of] various treatises?

There is but a single gate. Although the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s examination of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*) is extensive and detailed, when it comes to the gates of the treatise, even the gates themselves are not sufficient to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox;
thus, one knows that our present school differs profoundly from that [Madhyamaka] tradition.

Now, regarding the Dharma of the Buddha, one may further clarify its underlying intent. The Buddha’s transformation of beings does not go beyond the two gates of *saṃgraha* (gathering) and *vidarśana* (subduing).

*Saṃgraha* refers to nurturing views and refining the mind; *vidarśana* refers to leaving not even a grain of mustard seed behind, as it involves analysis. Thus, he cites the intent of two sūtras to verify these two methods of subduing and gathering.
As for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and others, the details are as found in the sūtra: when King Bhadraśrī, in order to protect the Buddha-dharma, took up a sword against the bhikṣu Bodhi.

The arrows and so forth are like the four *siddhāntas*, which encompass all teachings: the worldly and the personal correspond to the intention of gathering [beings], while the remedial corresponds to the intention of subduing.
The two bodies—the medicinal and the jewel—encompass all bodies; the destruction of dharmas and the establishment of dharmas include all teachings.
Since the general principle is entirely thus, they are taken as examples.

Regarding the phrase "approximately for each view" and so forth: if one takes each of the one hundred and forty [views] and multiplies them by ten, they can all be condensed into a single object (*ālambana*) for the duration of the summer retreat.

Even if one were to collectively apply the ten modes of multiplication (*daśa-guṇa*), they would still not be exhausted. As for these "views of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth mentioned here, they appear to refute two treatises.

The general principle is that these are unwholesome; this meaning is the same as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. Specifically, they may also be termed "causes" (*hetu*) and so forth. The mind arises from causes—whether wholesome or unwholesome—and is capable of producing [results];

the meaning regarding the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) is the same. In the *Abhidharma*, it is said that by creating evil through the cause of emptiness (*ākāśa*), one enters the realms of the three miserable destinies (*tridurgati*); the meaning is the same as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Regarding those such as the icchantikas: even icchantikas still possess the goodness of compassion and affection; they are not like those with nihilistic views who revile their fathers and are arrogant toward their mothers.
They are already inferior to the most evil icchantikas, let alone when considering those who generally lack faith and so forth, or those characterized by stinginess and greed.

Because there was no pure livelihood (*ājīva*) as the cause, one consumes filth at the time of the fruit; because the precepts were broken during the causal stage, one is constantly hungry at the time of the fruit.
Next, regarding the realm of the *śrāvakas*, the initial general censure states "not knowing" and so forth. First, by citing "not knowing," it reveals what is known:
if one follows the flow of views, then the Four Truths are each threefold.
"Why is this so? and below, the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths are explained. First, because it is fully endowed with the five aggregates (*skandhas*), it is called "if" (*yadi*).

In the initial passage: "receiving" is form (*rūpa*); "accepting" is sensation (*vedanā*); "grasping at emptiness" is perception (*saṃjñā*); "arising of formations" is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and "discrimination" is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Next, "the view of emptiness" and below refer to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Among the five dull faculties (*mūḍhendriyas*), ignorance (*moha*) is omitted; one should say that the "view of emptiness" does not comprehend cause and effect. As for the phrase "not like chickens or dogs," etc.:
Because taking emptiness as the path is different from consuming excrement.
The text on the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) states: "One who accepts the second phrase accepts what is not to be accepted; they diligently break and discard it.

This refers to the inclusion within the marks and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Regarding the "single and multiple" and so forth, this serves as an example for refuting all views. Having finished speaking.
"Thus" means that because nothing new is created.

Regarding the phrase "The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says, etc.," this describes the questions and answers of the treatise to elucidate the *Śata-śāstra*. In the opening passage of the treatise, the question concerns the contemplation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
However, in the response, the *Abhidharma* is cited to extensively refute the sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭi-gata*). At first glance, these appear to be inconsistent.

It is appropriate. Therefore, the question is posed to bring forth the realization that there is no distinction; thus it says, "This very thing is it. The answer is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"To penetrate deeply into dependent origination is to sever all false views."

Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of moments (*kṣaṇa*), this precisely clarifies the arising of contemplation. As for the statement in the *Aṅga* [treatise] that "existence (*bhava*) contains the fruit," this is provisionally based on the Kāpila [system];

however, it must be universally applied to all [views] arising from the Buddha’s Dharma, as well as to those adhering to the sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśa-dvāra*). All such [speculations] belong to the branch of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "the nasal septum and so forth": if one merely stops the mind at the nasal septum without practicing rational contemplation (*yukti-vipaśyanā*), there is not even a minor degree of insight (*vipaśyanā*);
how much less could one contemplate emptiness and achieve the vision of the wondrous realm? If this is the case for merely stopping the mind, how much more so for those who rely on words?

Those who provide "dark testimony" are like ordinary tortoises, lacking the ability to resolve doubts; thus they are compared to those who give dark testimony. Although they cannot resolve their own doubts, their ability to resolve the doubts of others is still superior to that of a blind dog barking wildly.
Vai. However, these two individuals possess no sense of aspiration; how, then, could aspiration itself distinguish them?

Once "the inferior" is recognized, this refers back to the objects of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) as the causes for the vow; likewise, these very causes are taken as the objects of the vow.

Regarding the phrase "such as one person" and so forth: this specifically refers to making a vow based on the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Within this, the meaning of the Four Great Vows encompasses both the internal and external.

That is to say, sentient beings are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of each moment; each individual sentient being constitutes the "external. Using the internal to illustrate the external, it is said:

"If even one person is many, how much more so many people? The remaining three great vows may be understood by analogy with this. Sentient afflictions (*kleśa*) act as the cause, and sentient beings as...
Fruit. Because causes and fruits are manifold, the Dharma-gates are immeasurable; all of them open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way. Question:

Since cause and fruit are a single thought-moment, how can they be divided into the two distinct Great Vows? Answer: It is still based on the internal mind: by grasping at the five aggregates as empty, one constitutes a "sentient being.
By possessing the view of emptiness, one is endowed with the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which constitute afflictions. When this is so for one person, it is likewise for all.
The same applies to many people: though they are not distinct, they differentiate themselves, their characteristics remaining within their own respective categories.

If one clings to the lower [vehicles], the view of emptiness arises within the practice of the six perfections. As for what is called "demonic giving," it is seen as fundamentally belonging to the external;

such giving accords with birth and death, and its meaning is likewise demonic. Herein, the three baskets and the three vehicles are explained in general; only then does the explanation of the Shared Teaching begin.
The general and specific categories are not fixed and cannot be standardized.

Those who contemplate emptiness and perceive [the truth] belong to the realm of the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). "Ignorance" indicates the Pratyekabuddha; "arising of suffering" indicates the Śrāvaka.
The objects of the truths (*satya*) are merely opened; this is simply a matter of combining different [categories].

Regarding "the two vehicles know emptiness" and below: this distinguishes the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Regarding "although they deliver" and below: this is the formal explanation. As for "as before and as after":
"before" refers to the preceding and preceding objects, while "after" refers to the subsequent inconceivable object.

Furthermore, the following section distinguishes how the four teachings differ in their treatment of views (*dṛṣṭi*). Because the views to be treated are different, there is a difference between intentional application (*manasikāra*) and spontaneous operation (*anābhoga*).
Next, regarding "spontaneous operation," this refers for the time being to the abandonment of views (*darśana-heya*); one does not enter the three evil realms.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) below criticizes the mere use of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), noting that if views suddenly arise from within emptiness, how can emptiness itself treat them? One may understand this by analogy with water producing fire.
Now, knowing [the meaning of] "departure" (gati), one knows that it is merely one gate among the sixteen gates discussed in the *Cheng lun* (Treatise on Establishment).

Regarding the departure of the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings], this clarifies the sequence of destroying false views. If this is so, although there are four teachings, in terms of how the beginner (*ādikarmika*) treats delusions, the principles are only two distinct types:

first, in the three teachings, the beginner always eliminates false views first; second, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the beginner contemplates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to eliminate the stubborn [delusions].
"Laoqu" (Lao’s Departure) and "Jiechi" (The Rejection of Bonds). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states below [in the section] "Releasing Doubts":

"As if suffering from a cold ailment," which serves as the explanation. First, the principle is like physical strength; the view of emptiness is like a cold ailment; ginger and cinnamon are like impermanence.

Seeing True Suchness (tathatā) is further empowered. The five stones—namely white crystal, purple crystal, cream, milk, and fat—are suchness as emptiness; seeing emptiness nourishes form. The five stones refer to white crystal, purple crystal, cream, milk, and fat.
Observing dharmas is like the heavy enclosure (gahvara). Augmenting life is like provisional wisdom. Being able to fly is like entering the provisional.
The "double-layered" refers to *huángjīng* (yellow essence). The "Golden Elixir" is the method of perfection. From the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one is named a Buddha-Mahāsiddha.

Regarding the phrase "to treat [the afflictions of] views and so forth," this uses other delusions as examples; for now, it cites the afflictions of the realm within and those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The delusions of the realm beyond are not included within the former two categories.

"Regarding these four below," this cites the Buddha’s final testament (*parinirvāṇa-śāsana*). "To clarify that the Dharma possesses four [aspects]"—why is this so? "Regarding the four types of people below," this explains the intent of the testament.

Since those four types of people possess views and do not transcend the six realms of existence, their possession of views is cited as the fruit and designated by the name "instrument of suffering. Their fetters and karma resulting from such views are used as a metaphor for ghosts and spirits.

Below the section on the "Three Vehicles," the teachings are analyzed to explain the similarities and differences among these three vehicles. Within these four teachings, nine types of *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) are established in total:
three for the Three Vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching, and one for the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching, because they equally contemplate non-arising (*anutpāda*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), the stages prior to the Grounds constitute the three types of emptiness, wherein the provisional nature of the substance is analyzed and dismantled; however, from the eighth ground onward, these are termed "true reality.

For the person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*), there is only one kind from beginning to end. Therefore, the expression "three carts" has both a general and a specific sense. The specific sense refers to the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*);

the general sense subsumes all seven types [of teachings], excluding those who have already entered the Grounds and the Perfect Teaching, as these are what are to be reconciled. This is called [the general sense].

Because it is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Although the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) involves the path of instruction when entering the stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that the realization is identical [to the Perfect Teaching].

Therefore, in the subsequent text, the phrase "from Śākyamuni" explains the gateways of the teachings throughout a single lifetime according to the ritual of transformation; it simply means first providing the three carts and later providing the one Great Cart.

Regarding the phrase "briefly explained, etc.": if expanded, there are seven categories; if abbreviated, it is simply the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). When fully explained in terms of both the subject and object, these are the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, in relation to the factors of the path (*mārga*), they are called "intermediate."
Next, I shall further sequence the methods of conversion. Although there are seven different types ranging from gradual to sudden, each possesses its own underlying intent.

At the Deer Park, the Tripitaka was used as the primary method; in the Vaipulya period, it was used as a secondary method. Furthermore, the Tripitaka was sublated by the three [vehicles]. In the Prajñāpāramitā period, the Shared [Vehicle] was used as a secondary method, while the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles] were used as the primary methods.
In the Lotus Sūtra, these seven types are harmonized to return to the single reality.
Based on this view of emptiness, the inconceivable treatment encompasses all things; this treatment does not contradict the teachings.

By opening from one, all are revealed, just as within the conceivable, it likewise does not contradict the various teachings. Therefore, using the analogy of dust for the single view of emptiness: dust contains the great scripture.
Departing from Vimalakīrti, one realizes the mind of the view of emptiness. The ten realms and five aggregates are called sentient beings; sentient beings are [emptiness].
Liberation. Liberation does not transcend vision; therefore, the three dharmas are identical in nature.
[The passage] "All sentient beings" below explains the seeking of the Buddha’s liberation within the aforementioned liberation. It explains the aforementioned liberation of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, regarding "observing the lower": this is further explained as seeking within the mental activities (*citta-saṃskāra*). "Seeking" refers to employing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to observe that there is only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and no longer perceiving a mind.
"Able to unify form and the lower" concludes the formation of the wondrous realm; this refers to the two worlds of the five aggregates and sentient beings.

Only the world of the land (*bhūmi*) is missing, but it may be understood by analogy. Neither vertical nor horizontal, these conclude the formation of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), even unto the three metaphors.

"Regarding this object below": generating the aspiration for enlightenment is explained from the perspective of the ultimate object; it is said that ignorance itself is the *dharmatā*. "Regarding this contemplation below":

settling the mind consists of universal cessation (*samatha*) as empty stillness and universal contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) as space. "Regarding skillful means below": the sixty-four methods. "Regarding seeing the aggregates below": [the following].

Regarding "breaking through universally" (*pobian*): from the single and the multiple, down to the pervasive and the obstructed, these exclusively manifest distinct characteristics; hence it is said, "phrase by phrase. As for "if not entering below," regarding the primary and auxiliary:

formerly one practiced the six obscurations with a view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*); now, by cultivating the perfections of phenomena (*vastu-pāramitā*), the obscurations are removed and the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭi-skandha*) is eliminated.
Therefore, in each and every passage, both the view of emptiness and one specific obscuration are raised—such as the examples of the bridge, the earth, and the ocean.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like a bridge; when people and horses tread upon it, the earth and sea are cited as examples.

In the introduction, it says: "As soon as one arrives and perceives the realm, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma ceases. Regarding the latter three [chapters] and the preceding text, the comparison has been briefly concluded.

Since it says, "He shall escort the practitioner to that Sāṃkhyā," and because the latter three major chapters contain no mention of the "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they have been omitted.

Regardless. The "Chapter on the Gift of Dharma" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "To transform sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges so that they attain the six supernatural powers is not as good as writing out the *Prajñāpāramitā* for others to read and recite.
Furthermore, the merit of causing others to read and recite it is not as good as correctly recollecting (*samyak-smṛti*) the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Moreover, the merit of correct recollection is not as good as explaining it to others so that it is easily understood. What does "easily understood" mean?

This refers to the contemplation of non-duality, which neither enters nor exits. Even a direct exposition of its unique merits alone would be vast; how much more so when it expounds the *Lotus Sūtra*, the wondrous teaching that reveals the provisional to reveal the real?
Since the purpose of the teaching is to induce practice, this text constitutes the wondrous contemplation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Therefore, the "Chapter on Rejoicing" states:
"Suppose one were to bestow the four requisites upon all beings within six realms and four modes of birth across four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds."
He then causes them all to attain arhatship. This is not even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the merit of the first person who rejoiced (anumodana).
Causing others to hear the rejoicing brings great merit. Furthermore, why must the fiftieth person necessarily be at the beginning of the five stages? This applies to those at the stage of rejoicing;

how much more so for the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which states that it is superior even to one’s own correct recollection, let alone being able to explain it while simultaneously [practicing it].

One practices by acting according to what has been taught, thereby giving rise to great learning (*bahuśruta*). By preaching the Dharma one attains liberation; by listening to the Dharma one attains liberation.

These words are not deceptive. How much more so in the "Distribution of the Propagation" section of all the teachings, which exhorts bodhisattvas, those of the two vehicles, and ordinary beings alike to turn the wheel of teaching and preach it themselves.
I respectfully pray that future sages will diligently preach and diligently practice, thereby establishing the seeds for faith in the Dharma of the One Vehicle.

My son, although I wished to expand this work extensively, I was unable to do so in writing. Generally, those who prefer brevity find it difficult to achieve their aim while wandering about all day long following various circumstances.
Therefore, returning to the Buddha’s burial mound, I swept and cleaned the shrine hall; amidst the duties of ritual service, I took advantage of my leisure to edit and extract these essentials.
As years pass, my awareness grows dim and I gradually feel myself becoming negligent. Fortunately, there remains the "Broad Text" (Guǎngwén) by which I may still seek and examine;

I have searched through its essential principles to prepare for practice. Should even a single phrase moisten the spirit, it shall serve forever as a Dharma scroll. Thus, all regrets are withdrawn and the machinations of the myriad affairs are stilled.
*Zhiguan fuxing souyao ji*, Scroll Ten (End).

Copied on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Dazhong era of the Great Tang, at the West Hall of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai in Taizhou, in the quarters of Preceptor Yuanzhang. By Preceptor Wuwai of this same temple.
Aspiration: To transmit together the Buddha’s wisdom and the Great Teaching of the Master’s *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, benefiting both self and others.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Zhenji, who traveled to Enryaku-ji in Japan to seek instruction and serve as an attendant.
